reference.approach: Collect/sort/rewrite values, then recursive merge sort using existing nodes.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java algorithms were checked. Their node declaration contains C++ Node* and nullptr; this version uses a valid Java Node class. The split is written inside sortList.

145.baselineTime: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

146.problem: Sort a list containing only 0, 1 and 2 by rearranging its nodes.
146.assumptions: The list has no cycle and every data value is 0, 1 or 2. The tracker explicitly asks to change links, so the final solution keeps every node’s data unchanged.

example.explanation: Collect the two zero nodes, then the one node, then the two two nodes, preserving order within each group.

146.baseline: Count zeros, ones and twos, then overwrite values in that order. Striver teaches this first. It has O(1) extra space, but it does not meet the tracker’s requirement to sort by changing links.
146.approach:
Build three chains, one for each value. A dummy node gives each empty chain a place to start, and a tail reference lets us append without searching. Save the current node’s original next, detach it, and append it to its matching chain.

After the scan, join zeros to ones and ones to twos. If the ones chain is empty, zeros must connect directly to twos. The dummy heads are temporary; the result contains only the original nodes.
steps: Create zero, one and two dummy heads and tail references.
Save next, detach the current node, and append it to the correct chain.
Join zero → one → two, skipping an empty middle chain.
Return the first nonempty chain’s head.
146.space: O(1); three dummy nodes and a fixed number of references.
pitfalls: Count-and-rewrite changes data, so it is only a comparison approach for this tracker item.
Handle a missing ones chain when joining.
Old next links must not remain attached to the wrong group.
tests: int[] values={2,0,1,0,2};Node[] a=new Node[5];for(int i=0;i<5;i++){a[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=sort012(a[0]);for(int i:new int[]{1,3,2,0,4}){assert p==a[i]&&p.data==values[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;

Random r=new Random(146);for(int run=0;run<400;run++){int n=1+r.nextInt(40);Node[] a=new Node[n],b=new Node[n];List<Node> expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=new Node(r.nextInt(3));b[i]=new Node(a[i].data);if(i>0){a[i-1].next=a[i];b[i-1].next=b[i];}}for(int v=0;v<3;v++)for(Node x:a)if(x.data==v)expected.add(x);Node p=sort012(a[0]),q=sort012ByCounting(b[0]);for(Node x:expected){assert p==x&&q.data==x.data;p=p.next;q=q.next;}assert p==null&&q==null;}

reference.title: Sort a Linked List of 0s, 1s and 2s by Changing Links
reference.approach: Frequency rewriting, then stable relinking into three value chains.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The primary method follows the relinking approach required by the tracker; the counting method is explicitly a comparison.

146.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(1) space; it rewrites data.

147.problem: Find the first node shared by two singly linked lists, or return null if they share none.
147.assumptions: Both lists are finite and have no cycles. Intersection means the same Node object. Equal data in separate objects is not an intersection. Do not modify either list.

example.input: A: 4 → 2 → [7 → 9], B: 6 → [7 → 9]; bracketed nodes are shared
example.explanation: The two prefixes lead into the same tail objects. The first shared reference is the node holding 7.

147.baseline: For every node in A, scan B for the same reference. This directly checks the definition but can take n × m comparisons.
147.approach:
Let one pointer walk A and then B, while the other walks B and then A. When a pointer is null, redirect it to the other head. This makes them cover both prefix lengths, so the initial difference in list length disappears.

If there is a shared tail, they meet at its first node. If there is no shared tail, both eventually become null and the same loop stops. Only local pointer references change; the next fields stay untouched.
steps: Start first at headA and second at headB.
While they differ, advance each pointer, switching to the other head when it is null.
Return the reference where they meet, which may be null.
pitfalls: Compare first == second, not first.data == second.data.
Return null for separate lists even if every data value matches.
Do not connect the lists physically to implement switching. Reassign only the local pointer.
tests: Node shared=new Node(7);shared.next=new Node(9);Node a=new Node(4);a.next=new Node(2);a.next.next=shared;Node b=new Node(6);b.next=shared;assert intersection(a,b)==shared&&intersectionNested(a,b)==shared&&intersectionWithSet(a,b)==shared;assert b.next==shared&&a.next.next==shared;
Node a=new Node(5),b=new Node(5);assert intersection(a,b)==null;assert intersection(null,a)==null;assert intersection(null,null)==null;assert intersection(a,a)==a;

for(int left=0;left<12;left++)for(int right=0;right<12;right++)for(int tail=0;tail<6;tail++){Node shared=null;for(int i=0;i<tail;i++){Node x=new Node(4);x.next=shared;shared=x;}Node a=shared,b=shared;for(int i=0;i<left;i++){Node x=new Node(4);x.next=a;a=x;}for(int i=0;i<right;i++){Node x=new Node(4);x.next=b;b=x;}assert intersection(a,b)==shared;assert intersectionNested(a,b)==shared;assert intersectionWithSet(a,b)==shared;}

reference.title: Find the Intersection Point of Two Linked Lists
reference.approach: Nested reference comparisons, hashing, then pointer switching.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. Node equality remains reference identity.

147.baselineTime: O(n × m) time and O(1) space.

better.explanation: Store all node references from A in a set, then walk B. The first reference found in the set is the intersection. The Node class does not override equality, so equal data does not merge separate objects.
better.space: O(n) for references from A.

148.problem: Add one to a number whose digits are stored from most significant to least significant in a linked list.
148.assumptions: Each node stores a digit from 0 to 9. The list normally contains at least one digit; this implementation treats an empty list as zero and returns a single 1. The digits are updated in place.

example.explanation: The last 9 becomes 0 and carries 1. The next 9 does the same. Finally, 4 + 1 becomes 5 and the carry stops.

148.baseline: Recurse to the end and return a carry of 1 from the null base case. While the calls return, update each digit and pass any carry towards the head. This uses O(n) call-stack space.
148.approach:
Addition starts at the last digit, but a singly linked list only moves forward. Reverse the list so the last digit becomes first, then carry out ordinary addition. Store sum % 10 in the current node and carry = sum / 10.

Stop changing digits once carry becomes zero. If a carry remains after the last node, append a 1 to the reversed list. Reverse the whole list again to restore the required digit order. The number may gain a new head when every old digit was 9.
steps: Reverse the list and start carry at 1.
Add carry to each digit until it becomes zero or the list ends.
Append a node if a final carry remains.
Reverse again and return the resulting head.
148.space: O(1) working space; at most one new output node.
pitfalls: These digits are in forward order. The next question stores the units digit first.
Do not convert the entire number into int or long; a long list can represent a much larger number.
The recursive approach is for learning; long lists can exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
tests: Node a=new Node(4),b=new Node(9),d=new Node(9);a.next=b;b.next=d;Node h=addOne(a);assert h==a&&a.data==5&&b.data==0&&d.data==0&&a.next==b&&b.next==d&&d.next==null;

for(int value=0;value<1000;value++)for(int method=0;method<2;method++){String digits=Integer.toString(value);Node dummy=new Node(0),tail=dummy;for(char ch:digits.toCharArray()){tail.next=new Node(ch-'0');tail=tail.next;}Node h=method==0?addOne(dummy.next):addOneRecursive(dummy.next);StringBuilder result=new StringBuilder();for(Node p=h;p!=null;p=p.next)result.append(p.data);assert result.toString().equals(Integer.toString(value+1));}

for(int method=0;method<2;method++){Node head=null;for(int i=0;i<100;i++){Node x=new Node(9);x.next=head;head=x;}Node h=method==0?addOne(head):addOneRecursive(head);assert h.data==1;h=h.next;int count=0;while(h!=null){assert h.data==0;count++;h=h.next;}assert count==100;}

reference.title: Add One to a Number Represented by a Linked List
reference.approach: Recursive carry propagation, then reverse/add/reverse using constant working space.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. Empty input is handled explicitly instead of dereferencing an absent previous node.

148.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(n) recursive stack space.

149.problem: Add two numbers stored as linked lists with the units digit first. Return the sum in the same reverse digit order.
149.assumptions: Each input normally has at least one digit, each digit is 0 through 9, and neither number has unnecessary leading zeros. Build a new result without changing either input. Empty inputs are treated as zero.

example.explanation: The lists represent 48 and 37. Their sum is 85, stored with 5 first and 8 second.

149.baseline: Copy each input’s digits into an array, then add by matching array positions and carrying. It works, but copying is unnecessary because the list order already matches the order used in addition.
149.approach:
The heads already hold the units digits, so walk both lists together. Start each sum with the previous carry, then add any available digit from each list. A missing digit contributes zero.

Append sum % 10 to a new result and carry sum / 10 into the next turn. Continue while either input still has digits or carry is nonzero. That final condition handles 9 + 1: the first output digit is 0, and a second turn creates the 1.
steps: Create a dummy result node, a tail, and carry = 0.
While digits or carry remain, add the available digits to carry.
Append a new node holding sum % 10 and set carry = sum / 10.
Return dummy.next; the dummy is not a result digit.
149.space: O(1) working space, plus O(max(n, m)) nodes in the returned result.
pitfalls: Do not reverse these inputs; the units digit is already first.
Use OR in the loop condition. AND would stop when the shorter list ends.
Keep going for a final carry even when both input pointers are null.
Output nodes are new objects. Reusing an input node would let later result edits affect the input.
tests: Node a=new Node(8);a.next=new Node(4);Node b=new Node(7);b.next=new Node(3);Node h=addNumbers(a,b);assert h.data==5&&h.next.data==8&&h.next.next==null;assert a.data==8&&a.next.data==4&&b.data==7&&b.next.data==3;assert h!=a&&h!=b;
assert addNumbers(null,null).data==0&&addNumbersBuffered(null,null).data==0;Node a=new Node(9);Node b=new Node(1);Node h=addNumbers(a,b);assert h.data==0&&h.next.data==1&&h.next.next==null;

Random r=new Random(149);for(int run=0;run<300;run++){String left=new BigInteger(180,r).toString(),right=new BigInteger(160,r).toString();Node a=null,b=null;for(char ch:left.toCharArray()){Node x=new Node(ch-'0');x.next=a;a=x;}for(char ch:right.toCharArray()){Node x=new Node(ch-'0');x.next=b;b=x;}Set<Node> inputs=new HashSet<>();for(Node p=a;p!=null;p=p.next)inputs.add(p);for(Node p=b;p!=null;p=p.next)inputs.add(p);String expected=new BigInteger(left).add(new BigInteger(right)).toString();for(Node h:new Node[]{addNumbers(a,b),addNumbersBuffered(a,b)}){StringBuilder digits=new StringBuilder();for(Node p=h;p!=null;p=p.next){assert !inputs.contains(p);digits.append(p.data);}assert digits.reverse().toString().equals(expected);}StringBuilder x=new StringBuilder(),y=new StringBuilder();for(Node p=a;p!=null;p=p.next)x.append(p.data);for(Node p=b;p!=null;p=p.next)y.append(p.data);assert x.reverse().toString().equals(left)&&y.reverse().toString().equals(right);}

reference.title: Add Two Numbers in Linked Lists with Digits in Reverse Order
reference.approach: Copy digits then add, followed by direct simultaneous list traversal with carry.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. Empty inputs are treated as zero; the normal nonempty-input behavior follows the lesson.

149.baselineTime: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) extra digit storage, in addition to the result.

150.problem: Remove every node whose value equals key from a doubly linked list.
150.assumptions: The list has consistent next and prev links and no cycle. It may be empty. Keep all nonmatching nodes in their original order.

example.explanation: Remove matches at the head, in the middle and at the tail. The remaining two nodes must point to each other in both directions.

150.baseline: Building a new list containing only nonmatching values would work, but would allocate extra nodes. The existing prev and next references already identify both neighbours of every node to remove.
150.approach:
Walk through the list and save current.next before changing links. For a matching node, connect its previous node to its next node, then connect the next node back to the previous one. If there is no previous node, update head instead.

Then continue using the saved next reference. This visits consecutive matches too. The method below also clears the removed node’s own links so an outside reference to it no longer leads into the surviving list.
steps: Save next = current.next.
For a match, update the previous node’s next, or head if there is no previous node.
Update next.prev when next exists, and detach current.
Continue at the saved next and return the final head.
pitfalls: A matching head can occur several times in a row. Keep updating head until a survivor remains.
Changing next links alone leaves a broken backward chain.
Save the next node before detaching the current one.
tests: int[] values={5,2,5,7,5};Node[] a=new Node[5];for(int i=0;i<5;i++){a[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0){a[i-1].next=a[i];a[i].prev=a[i-1];}}Node h=deleteAll(a[0],5);assert h==a[1]&&h.prev==null&&h.next==a[3]&&a[3].prev==h&&a[3].next==null;

Random r=new Random(150);for(int run=0;run<400;run++){int n=1+r.nextInt(35),key=r.nextInt(5);Node[] a=new Node[n];List<Node> expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=new Node(r.nextInt(5));if(i>0){a[i-1].next=a[i];a[i].prev=a[i-1];}if(a[i].data!=key)expected.add(a[i]);}Node p=deleteAll(a[0],key),prev=null;for(Node x:expected){assert p==x&&p.prev==prev;prev=p;p=p.next;}assert p==null;for(int i=expected.size()-1;i>=0;i--){assert prev==expected.get(i);prev=prev.prev;}assert prev==null;for(Node x:a)if(x.data==key)assert x.prev==null&&x.next==null;}

reference.title: Delete All Occurrences of a Key in a Doubly Linked List
reference.approach: One pass reconnecting both neighbours around every matching node.
reference.adaptation: The public Java solution was checked. This version also clears each removed node’s own references after reconnecting its neighbours.

151.problem: Find all pairs of values that add to target in a sorted doubly linked list.
151.assumptions: The source promises positive, distinct values in increasing order. Use two different nodes. Return pairs in increasing order of the first value. An empty list returns an empty result.

example.explanation: 1 + 10 and 3 + 8 both give 11. No other pair does.

151.baseline: Keep previously visited values in a set. For each value, check whether target − value is already present. Collect matching pairs, then sort them by their first value.
151.approach:
Find the tail and put one pointer at each end. If their sum is too small, move the left pointer forward. The current left value cannot work with any smaller right value, so it is safe to discard it. If the sum is too large, move the right pointer backward for the symmetric reason.

On a match, save the pair and move both pointers inward. Distinct values mean neither value has another partner for the same target. Stop when the pointers meet or pass each other; using one node twice is not allowed.
steps: Set left = head and walk right to the tail.
Compare the two values using long arithmetic.
On equality, record the pair and move both. Otherwise move the side that makes the sum closer to target.
Stop at the same node or when right.next equals left.
151.space: O(1) working space plus O(p) returned pairs.
pitfalls: Sorted order is what makes moving one pointer safe. This method is not for an unsorted list.
The source assumes distinct values. Counting all index pairs with duplicates is a different task.
Promote before adding: (long) left.data + right.data avoids int overflow.
tests: int[] values={1,3,4,6,8,10};Node head=null,tail=null;for(int v:values){Node x=new Node(v);x.prev=tail;if(tail==null)head=x;else tail.next=x;tail=x;}assert pairsWithSum(head,11).equals(List.of(List.of(1,10),List.of(3,8)));assert pairsWithSumHash(head,11).equals(pairsWithSum(head,11));

Random r=new Random(151);for(int run=0;run<200;run++){TreeSet<Integer> values=new TreeSet<>();for(int i=0;i<20;i++)values.add(1+r.nextInt(50));Node head=null,tail=null;for(int v:values){Node x=new Node(v);x.prev=tail;if(tail==null)head=x;else tail.next=x;tail=x;}for(int target=1;target<=100;target++){List<List<Integer>> expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int x:values)for(int y:values)if(x<y&&x+y==target)expected.add(List.of(x,y));assert pairsWithSum(head,target).equals(expected);assert pairsWithSumHash(head,target).equals(expected);}}

reference.title: Find pairs with given sum in Doubly Linked List
reference.approach: Complement hashing with sorted output, then inward pointers from head and tail.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. Long arithmetic prevents sum/complement overflow, and the pair comparator avoids subtraction.

151.baselineTime: O(n + p log p) expected time and O(n) set space, plus the p result pairs.

152.problem: Remove repeated values from a sorted doubly linked list, keeping one node for each value.
152.assumptions: The list is sorted in increasing or equal order, with consistent next/prev links and no cycle. Keep the first node of each equal-value group. Empty input returns null.

example.explanation: Keep the first 2, remove its two repeats, then keep 5 and the first 7.

152.baseline: Collect one value from each equal-value group and build a fresh doubly linked list. This leaves the original list unchanged but allocates a new node for every distinct value.
152.approach:
Sorted order puts equal values next to each other. Compare current with current.next. If they match, skip the next node and fix the following node’s prev link. Keep current where it is, because another duplicate may now follow it.

Move current only when the next value differs. This preserves the first node in every group and removes each later duplicate once.
steps: Start current at head.
While current and current.next exist, compare their data.
On equality, bypass current.next in both directions and keep current fixed.
Otherwise advance current. Return the original head.
pitfalls: Do not advance current after deletion; a run of three equal values needs another comparison at the same node.
Update the backward reference of the next surviving node.
This removes duplicates from a sorted list. Nonadjacent repeated values in an unsorted list will not be removed.
tests: int[] values={2,2,2,5,7,7};Node[] a=new Node[6];for(int i=0;i<6;i++){a[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0){a[i-1].next=a[i];a[i].prev=a[i-1];}}Node h=removeDuplicates(a[0]);assert h==a[0]&&h.next==a[3]&&a[3].prev==h&&a[3].next==a[4]&&a[4].prev==a[3]&&a[4].next==null;

Random r=new Random(152);for(int run=0;run<300;run++){int n=1+r.nextInt(40);int[] values=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)values[i]=r.nextInt(12)-6;Arrays.sort(values);Node[] a=new Node[n];List<Node> expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0){a[i-1].next=a[i];a[i].prev=a[i-1];}if(i==0||values[i]!=values[i-1])expected.add(a[i]);}Node copy=uniqueCopy(a[0]);Node p=removeDuplicates(a[0]),prev=null,q=copy;for(Node x:expected){assert p==x&&p.prev==prev&&q.data==x.data;assert q!=x;if(q.next!=null)assert q.next.prev==q;prev=p;p=p.next;q=q.next;}assert p==null&&q==null;for(int i=expected.size()-1;i>=0;i--){assert prev==expected.get(i);prev=prev.prev;}assert prev==null;}

reference.title: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Doubly Linked List
reference.approach: Collect unique values and rebuild, then remove adjacent duplicate nodes in place.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. Removed nodes are additionally detached from the surviving chain.

152.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(n) space for the collected values and new nodes.

153.problem: Reverse each complete group of k linked-list nodes. Leave a final group smaller than k in its original order.
153.assumptions: k is positive. Change links, not node values. The tracker’s LeetCode problem and Striver’s recursive/optimal methods keep an incomplete group unchanged, although the article’s introduction and stack method describe reversing it.

example.explanation: Reverse the complete group [4, 1, 8]. Only two nodes remain, so [2, 9] stays as it was.

153.baseline: Collect a complete group in a stack and reconnect nodes in pop order. First confirm that k nodes exist; otherwise attach the remaining chain unchanged. That extra check makes the source’s stack idea match the tracker’s rule.
153.approach:
Find the kth node before changing any link. When it exists, save the start of the next group and cut the current group after its kth node. Reverse this detached group using the normal list-reversal loop.

The old kth node becomes the group’s head, and the old first node becomes its tail. Connect the previous group’s tail to this new head, then remember the old first node as the next connector. If fewer than k nodes remain, connect that untouched remainder and stop.
steps: Find the kth node from the current group head.
If there is no kth node, attach the remainder unchanged and stop.
Save kth.next, detach the complete group, and reverse it.
Connect the previous group, update the result head for the first group, and continue at the saved next group.
153.time: O(n); group checking and reversal each visit nodes a constant number of times.
pitfalls: Verify the incomplete-group rule in the actual problem; the current source page mixes two variants.
Save the next group before cutting kth.next.
The old group head becomes its tail after reversal.
Do not return the last reversed group’s head as the entire list’s head.
tests: Node[] a=new Node[5];int[] v={4,1,8,2,9};for(int i=0;i<5;i++){a[i]=new Node(v[i]);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=reverseKGroup(a[0],3);for(int i:new int[]{2,1,0,3,4}){assert p==a[i]&&p.data==v[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;

for(int n=1;n<=30;n++)for(int k=1;k<=n+2;k++)for(int method=0;method<3;method++){Node[] a=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=method==0?reverseKGroup(a[0],k):method==1?reverseKStack(a[0],k):reverseKRecursive(a[0],k);for(int start=0;start<n;start+=k){int end=Math.min(n,start+k);if(end-start==k){for(int i=end-1;i>=start;i--){assert p==a[i]&&p.data==i;p=p.next;}}else{for(int i=start;i<end;i++){assert p==a[i]&&p.data==i;p=p.next;}}}assert p==null;}

reference.title: Reverse a Linked List in Groups of K Nodes
reference.approach: Stack grouping, recursive full-group reversal, then iterative detach/reverse/reconnect.
reference.adaptation: All three Java algorithms were checked. The page is inconsistent about an incomplete group. The tracker and the source’s recursive/optimal methods preserve it; the stack variant here adds that same full-group check.

153.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(k) space for a complete group.

better.explanation: Check that a full group exists, reverse its first k nodes, and recursively process the rest. Connect the old group head, now its tail, to the returned remainder. Recursion saves the group connections but uses call-stack space.
better.space: O(n / k + 1) call-stack frames; k = 1 returns immediately.

154.problem: Rotate a singly linked list to the right by k places.
154.assumptions: k is nonnegative and the list has no cycle. A right rotation moves the tail to the front. Reuse the same nodes and preserve their values.

example.explanation: The last two nodes become the first two, in the same order.

154.baseline: Count the length and reduce k modulo that length. For each remaining rotation, find the last two nodes, detach the last node, and move it before head. Repeated tail searches can take quadratic time.
154.approach:
Rotating by the list length changes nothing, so only k % length matters. After that reduction, the new head has zero-based index length − k, and the node before it becomes the new tail.

Connect the old tail to the old head to make one temporary circle. Walk to the new tail, save its next as the new head, then set newTail.next to null. Breaking that circle is part of the algorithm, not optional cleanup.
steps: Find the length and the old tail.
Reduce k modulo length; return the original head if the result is zero.
Connect tail.next to head. Walk length − k − 1 steps from head to the new tail.
Save newTail.next, cut that link, and return the saved new head.
pitfalls: Right rotation is not left rotation: the last k nodes move to the front.
Handle an empty list before taking k % length.
Cut the temporary circle before returning.
The new tail index is length − k − 1, one before the new head.
tests: int[] v={3,6,1,8,4};Node[] a=new Node[5];for(int i=0;i<5;i++){a[i]=new Node(v[i]);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=rotateRight(a[0],2);for(int i:new int[]{3,4,0,1,2}){assert p==a[i]&&p.data==v[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;

for(int n=1;n<=30;n++)for(int k:new int[]{0,1,2,7,30,101,Integer.MAX_VALUE})for(int method=0;method<2;method++){Node[] a=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=method==0?rotateRight(a[0],k):rotateRightRepeated(a[0],k);int start=(n-k%n)%n;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){assert p==a[(start+i)%n]&&p.data==(start+i)%n;p=p.next;}assert p==null;}

reference.title: Rotate a Linked List to the Right by K Places
reference.approach: Repeated tail-to-head moves, then a temporary circle broken at the new tail.
reference.adaptation: Both Java algorithms were checked. The public snippets contain a shadowed constructor assignment and C++ pointer syntax; these examples use a valid Node constructor and Java dot access.

154.baselineTime: O(n + n × (k % n)) time, O(1) extra space.

155.problem: Merge several sorted bottom-linked chains into one sorted chain using bottom pointers.
155.assumptions: Top-level heads are connected by next. Each head begins a sorted bottom chain. Chains contain separate nodes and have no cycles. The final result reuses every node, follows bottom links, and clears next links.

example.explanation: Keep the smallest available front node from the chains. After taking 1, the next candidate from that chain becomes 6.

155.baseline: Collect all values, sort them, and build a new bottom-linked list. This ignores the order already present in each chain and uses O(T) extra space for T total nodes.
155.approach:
The smallest remaining value must be at the front of one of the sorted chains. Put those front nodes in a min-heap, which lets us remove the smallest candidate quickly.

After removing a node, add its bottom child to the heap. That child is now the first remaining node in the same chain. Append the removed node to the result through bottom, and clear its old next link.

There is at most one candidate per chain in the heap. With K chains and T total nodes, this takes O(T log K) time rather than sorting all T values together. This is the heap approach in the current Striver article.
steps: Add every top-level head to a min-heap ordered by data.
Remove the smallest node and add its bottom child, if any.
Detach its old links and append it to the result’s bottom chain.
Repeat until the heap is empty, then return the first result node.
155.time: O(T log(K + 1)), where T is the total node count and K is the number of chains.
155.space: O(K) working space for the heap; the result reuses input nodes.
pitfalls: Use bottom to walk the final result, not next.
Save or enqueue the old bottom child before clearing the link.
This tracker item is the next/bottom structure. A related merge-k-lists problem supplies an array of ordinary list heads instead.
Use a safe integer comparator; subtracting two values can overflow.
tests: Node a=new Node(2);a.bottom=new Node(7);Node b=new Node(1);b.bottom=new Node(6);b.bottom.bottom=new Node(9);Node d=new Node(4);d.bottom=new Node(8);a.next=b;b.next=d;Node p=flatten(a);for(int v:new int[]{1,2,4,6,7,8,9}){assert p.data==v&&p.next==null;p=p.bottom;}assert p==null;

Random r=new Random(155);for(int run=0;run<300;run++){int k=1+r.nextInt(8);Node root=null,lastHead=null;Set<Node> originals=new HashSet<>();List<Integer> values=new ArrayList<>();for(int chain=0;chain<k;chain++){int[] v=new int[1+r.nextInt(10)];for(int i=0;i<v.length;i++)v[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;Arrays.sort(v);Node head=null,tail=null;for(int x:v){Node node=new Node(x);originals.add(node);values.add(x);if(head==null)head=node;else tail.bottom=node;tail=node;}if(root==null)root=head;else lastHead.next=head;lastHead=head;}Collections.sort(values);Node copy=flattenCopy(root),p=flatten(root);Set<Node> remaining=new HashSet<>(originals);for(int v:values){assert p!=null&&remaining.remove(p)&&p.data==v&&p.next==null;assert copy!=null&&!originals.contains(copy)&&copy.data==v&&copy.next==null;p=p.bottom;copy=copy.bottom;}assert p==null&&copy==null&&remaining.isEmpty();}
Node a=new Node(Integer.MAX_VALUE),b=new Node(Integer.MIN_VALUE);a.next=b;Node h=flatten(a);assert h==b&&h.bottom==a&&a.bottom==null;

reference.title: Flatten a Linked List with Sorted Bottom Pointers
reference.approach: Collect/sort/rebuild, then min-heap merging with one active node per sorted chain.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. The primary implementation clears both old links after enqueuing the bottom child, then rebuilds only bottom links.

155.baselineTime: O(T log T) time and O(T) space for values and newly allocated nodes.

156.problem: Make an independent copy of a linked list whose nodes have next and random references.
156.assumptions: The next chain is finite and has no cycle. Each random reference is null or points to a node in that same chain, possibly itself. Every result node must be new, and the original list must be restored before return.

example.input: Nodes A(5) → B(5) → C(9); random: A→C, B→A, C→C
example.output: New nodes A′(5) → B′(5) → C′(9); random: A′→C′, B′→A′, C′→C′
example.explanation: Matching values do not make A and B the same node. Each original needs its own copy, and copied references must stay inside the copied list.

156.baseline: Create a map from each original node to a new node. In a second pass, set the copied next and random references by looking up the corresponding original targets.
156.approach:
Place each copy immediately after its original: A → A′ → B → B′. This temporarily makes original.next a direct way to find that original’s copy, so we do not need a map.

For an original node whose random target is R, the copied target is R.next. Assign those random links while every copy is still interleaved. Then separate the chains: restore each original next and connect each copy to the next copy. Save the copied head before separation.

This uses constant working space, excluding the required output nodes. It temporarily changes the original chain, so the map version is a better fit if other code must read the original while copying is in progress.
steps: Insert one copied node immediately after every original.
Set each copy’s random to original.random.next, or null if there is no target.
Save head.next as the copied head.
Restore original next links and connect copied next links, then return the saved copied head.
156.space: O(1) working space plus O(n) new output nodes.
pitfalls: Assigning copy.random = original.random points into the old list and is not a deep copy.
Set every random link before separating the interleaved lists.
Map keys must identify original nodes, not data values. Repeated data is allowed.
Save the copied head before restoring head.next.
tests: Random r=new Random(156);for(int run=0;run<300;run++){int n=1+r.nextInt(40);Node[] a=new Node[n];int[] target=new int[n],data=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){data[i]=r.nextInt(5);a[i]=new Node(data[i]);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}for(int i=0;i<n;i++){target[i]=r.nextInt(n+1)-1;a[i].random=target[i]<0?null:a[target[i]];}Set<Node> originals=new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(a));for(int method=0;method<2;method++){Node p=method==0?copyRandomList(a[0]):copyWithMap(a[0]);Node[] copies=new Node[n];Set<Node> unique=new HashSet<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++){assert p!=null&&!originals.contains(p)&&unique.add(p)&&p.data==data[i];copies[i]=p;p=p.next;}assert p==null;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){assert copies[i].random==(target[i]<0?null:copies[target[i]]);assert a[i].next==(i+1==n?null:a[i+1]);assert a[i].random==(target[i]<0?null:a[target[i]]);assert a[i].data==data[i];}copies[0].data++;assert a[0].data==data[0];}}

reference.title: Clone a Linked List with Random and Next Pointers
reference.approach: Original-to-copy mapping, then interleave, assign random links and separate.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The separating pass explicitly names the saved nextOriginal to make restoration easier to follow.

156.baselineTime: O(n) expected time and O(n) map space, in addition to the new output nodes.

157.problem: Read an integer from the beginning of a string, using recursion for the digit conversion. Return a 32-bit signed result.
157.assumptions: Ignore leading spaces only, then accept at most one sign. Read consecutive ASCII digits and stop at the first other character. If no digits were read, return 0. Clamp overflow to Integer.MIN_VALUE or Integer.MAX_VALUE. The source limits the string to 200 characters.

example.explanation: Skip the spaces and sign. The digits build 0, 0, 7, then 72. Stop at j and apply the minus sign.

157.baseline: A loop can read the same characters in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The tracker specifically asks for a recursive implementation, so each digit here is handled by one call.
157.approach:
Think of value as the number formed by the digits already read. Reading digit 4 after value 23 gives 23 × 10 + 4 = 234. Pass that new value and the next position to the next call. Stop when the string ends or the next character is not a digit.

Check the limit before multiplying. The negative limit has magnitude 2147483648, one more than the positive limit. Store this magnitude in a long. If the next digit would cross the limit, we can return the clamped answer immediately: later digits cannot bring the number back into range.
steps: Skip leading spaces and read an optional sign.
Choose the magnitude limit for that sign.
For each digit, check whether value × 10 + digit would exceed the limit.
Recurse with the updated magnitude. Stop at the first non-digit.
Apply the sign and return the int result.
157.time: O(n), where n is the number of characters examined.
157.space: O(n) recursive call space; the source bounds n by 200.
pitfalls: Do not skip letters to find a later number: "word 12" gives 0.
A second sign ends the digit scan: "+-12" gives 0.
Checking after int multiplication is too late because it may already have overflowed.
tests: assert myAtoi("  -0072java")==-72;assert myAtoi("4193 with words")==4193;assert myAtoi("3.14")==3;
Random r=new Random(157);for(int i=0;i<2000;i++){int x=r.nextInt();assert myAtoi("   "+x+"end")==x;}

reference.title: String to Integer (atoi)
reference.approach: The public problem statement and constraints were checked.
reference.adaptation: The current sheet exposes a practice problem without a public Java editorial. This is an original, tested Java implementation for that exact task.

158.problem: Calculate x raised to the integer power n, including negative powers.
158.assumptions: x is a double and n is any Java int. Zero is allowed only with a positive exponent. Floating-point results are approximate. The helper also returns 1 for exponent 0.

example.explanation: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal: 3^-3 = 1/(3 × 3 × 3).

158.baseline: Multiply x by itself |n| times, then invert for a negative exponent. That takes O(|n|) multiplications and is too slow when the exponent is near two billion.
158.approach:
We do not need one multiplication per unit of the exponent. For an even power, x^10 = (x^5)^2. For an odd power, x^11 = x × (x^5)^2. Repeatedly halving the exponent leaves only about 32 steps for an int.

The loop keeps a result and a base. When the remaining exponent is odd, use one copy of base in result. Then square base and halve the exponent. For a negative exponent, replace x with 1/x first. Convert n to long before negating it, because -Integer.MIN_VALUE does not fit in an int.
steps: Copy n into a long. For a negative exponent, invert x and negate the long.
Start result at 1.
If the exponent is odd, multiply result by the current base.
Square the base and halve the exponent. Repeat until it is 0.
pitfalls: Do not call Math.abs(n) while n is still an int; MIN_VALUE stays negative.
In the recursive version, compute the half power once. Calling the same recursion twice loses the logarithmic running time.
Use a tolerance when testing doubles, rather than exact decimal equality.

reference.title: Pow(x,n)
reference.approach: The public problem statement and constraints were checked.
reference.adaptation: The current sheet exposes a practice problem without a public Java editorial. This is an original, tested Java implementation for that exact task.

better.explanation: The same halving idea can be written recursively. Ask for the half power once, square it, and multiply by x once more when the exponent is odd. This version fits the recursion chapter; the loop above saves the call stack.
better.space: O(log(|n| + 1)) recursive call space.

159.problem: Count digit strings whose even positions contain even digits and whose odd positions contain prime digits. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.
159.assumptions: Positions start at 0. Even digits are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8; prime digits are 2, 3, 5, 7. Leading zeroes are allowed. The source permits lengths up to 10^15. The code also defines the empty string count as 1.

example.explanation: The three positions have 5, 4, and 5 choices, so there are 5 × 4 × 5 = 100 strings.

159.baseline: Try every allowed digit at each position and recurse to the next position. This visits exponentially many branches, about 5^ceil(n/2) × 4^floor(n/2) leaves, and uses O(n) call space. It is only useful for tiny examples.
159.approach:
Choosing a digit does not change the choices at any other position. So multiply the number of choices: one factor of 5 for every even index and one factor of 4 for every odd index. There are (n + 1)/2 even indices and n/2 odd indices.

The answer is 5^even × 4^odd. Use repeated squaring to calculate each power in logarithmic time. Take the remainder after every multiplication; otherwise even long will overflow long before we reach a large n. Two remainders below 1,000,000,007 can safely be multiplied in a Java long.
steps: Count even and odd positions.
Compute each modular power by squaring the base and halving the exponent.
Multiply the two results and take the remainder once more.
pitfalls: An even index is about its position, not whether the whole number is even.
Zero is a valid first digit here.
Use long for n and for multiplication before taking the remainder.

reference.title: Count Good Numbers Using Modular Exponentiation
reference.approach: Count independent digit choices and use iterative modular exponentiation.
reference.adaptation: The public Java implementation was checked. This follows the same two-power calculation with shorter comments. The recursive baseline uses O(n) call space, despite the article labelling it O(1).

160.problem: Sort a stack recursively so its greatest element is on top.
160.assumptions: Use only push, pop, peek, isEmpty and recursive calls in the algorithm. Values may repeat or be negative. In the examples below, stack order is written from top to bottom.

example.explanation: Popping the sorted stack should produce values in descending order.

160.baseline: Copying into an array and sorting would take O(n log n), but it breaks this exercise’s stack-operation and recursion rules.
160.approach:
Remove the top value and ask recursion to sort the smaller stack. Now only that removed value is out of place. To insert it, compare it with the top: if it is at least as large, push it immediately. Otherwise temporarily pop the larger top value, insert into the smaller stack, and put that larger value back.

The empty stack is already sorted. Building back from this case means every insertion starts with an already sorted stack. No loop or second collection is needed; the recursive calls hold the temporarily removed values.
steps: Pop one value unless the stack is empty.
Recursively sort what remains.
Insert the saved value by temporarily removing any larger top values.
Restore those removed values as the insertion calls return.
160.time: O(n²) in the worst case: an insertion may pass through every value already sorted.
pitfalls: Largest must be on top. Reversing the comparison sorts in the opposite direction.
Do not describe this as O(1) space just because there is no extra collection: recursive calls take space.
tests: Random r=new Random(160);for(int n=0;n<=100;n++){List<Integer>a=new ArrayList<>();for(int j=0;j<n;j++)a.add(r.nextInt(21)-10);Deque<Integer>s=new ArrayDeque<>(a);sortStack(s);a.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());assert new ArrayList<>(s).equals(a);}

161.problem: Reverse a stack using recursion and only standard stack operations.
161.assumptions: No loops, arrays or additional collections may be used by the algorithm. The supplied Deque is used strictly as a stack. The source limits its size to 100. Empty stacks are also supported.

example.explanation: The old top becomes the bottom, and the old bottom becomes the top.

161.baseline: An extra stack or list would make reversal straightforward, but the exercise rules exclude those extra data structures.
161.approach:
Pop the top and reverse the remaining stack. The popped value was first before reversal, so it must be last afterward: insert it at the bottom.

To reach the bottom using only stack operations, pop until the stack is empty, push the new bottom value, then restore every saved top value. These restoration calls keep the already reversed part in the right order.
steps: Pop and save the top value.
Reverse the smaller stack recursively.
Insert the saved value at the bottom using another recursive helper.
161.time: O(n²), because bottom insertion scans stacks of sizes 0 through n − 1.
pitfalls: Pushing the saved value straight onto the top would rebuild the original order.
The call stack is allowed auxiliary space; an extra explicit stack is not.
tests: Random r=new Random(161);for(int n=0;n<=100;n++){List<Integer>a=new ArrayList<>();for(int j=0;j<n;j++)a.add(r.nextInt(11)-5);Deque<Integer>s=new ArrayDeque<>(a);reverseStack(s);Collections.reverse(a);assert new ArrayList<>(s).equals(a);reverseStack(s);Collections.reverse(a);assert new ArrayList<>(s).equals(a);}

162.problem: Generate every length-n binary string that has no adjacent 1s, in increasing dictionary order.
162.assumptions: The tracker’s short title says all binary strings, but its linked problem excludes consecutive 1s. The source allows 1 ≤ n ≤ 20. For n = 0, this helper returns the one empty string.

example.explanation: For example, 1010 is allowed; 0110 is not because its middle two digits are both 1.

162.baseline: Generate all 2^n binary strings and reject any containing 11. This works, but builds many prefixes we already know cannot lead to a valid answer.
162.approach:
Fill one position at a time. Zero is always safe. One is safe only at the first position or after a zero. Those two rules prevent an invalid pair as soon as it would be created.

Try zero before one. All answers beginning with the current prefix plus zero then appear before answers beginning with that prefix plus one, which gives the required ordering. Once the array is full, copy it into a String and save it.
steps: Allocate a character array of length n.
Write 0 and recurse to the next position.
Also write 1 and recurse if the previous character is not 1.
At position n, add a copy of the completed string.
162.time: O(n × A), where A is the number of valid strings. A follows the Fibonacci recurrence, rather than being 2^n.
162.space: O(n) working space and O(n × A) for the returned strings.
pitfalls: The source excludes consecutive 1s, not consecutive 0s.
Saving the same mutable character buffer would not preserve separate answers; new String(current) copies its contents.

163.problem: Generate all correctly matched strings containing n pairs of parentheses.
163.assumptions: A closing bracket must match an earlier opening bracket. The source allows 1 ≤ n ≤ 8; the helper also returns the empty string for n = 0.

example.explanation: Both strings have two opens and two closes. )( is invalid even though its counts match, because it closes before anything has opened.

163.baseline: Generate every length-2n string of opening and closing brackets, then check balance. That examines 2^(2n) strings, most of which are invalid.
163.approach:
Keep track of how many opening and closing brackets are already in the prefix. Add an opening bracket while fewer than n have been used. Add a closing bracket only while fewer closes than opens have been used. This makes every prefix valid, so we never need to repair a bad prefix later.

When both counts reach n, the string is complete. Try each allowed next bracket and undo it afterward so the other choice starts from the same prefix.
steps: Start with an empty prefix and counts of zero.
Append ( if open < n. Recurse, then remove it.
Append ) if close < open. Recurse, then remove it.
Save a string when its length is 2n.
163.time: O(n × Cn), where Cn is the nth Catalan number, the number of answers. Copying each answer takes O(n).
163.space: O(n) working space and O(n × Cn) output space.
pitfalls: Equal final counts are not enough: every prefix must also have at least as many opens as closes.
Undo each appended bracket after returning from its branch.
tests: int[]counts={1,1,2,5,14,42,132,429,1430};for(int n=0;n<=8;n++){List<String>a=generateParenthesis(n);assert a.size()==counts[n];assert new HashSet<>(a).size()==a.size();for(String s:a){assert s.length()==2*n;int balance=0;for(char ch:s.toCharArray()){balance+=ch=='('?1:-1;assert balance>=0;}assert balance==0;}}

164.problem: Return every subset of an array of distinct integers, including the empty subset.
164.assumptions: Input values are distinct. Keep the relative input order inside each returned subset. The order of the subsets themselves does not matter. The source bounds n by 10.

example.explanation: Each value is either included or left out. Two choices for each of two positions give four subsets.

164.baseline: A bit mask from 0 to 2^n − 1 can describe each subset: bit i says whether to include nums[i]. That is another valid O(n × 2^n) method. This chapter practices the same decisions with recursion.
164.approach:
At each index, make two calls: one without this value and one with it. Every subset has exactly one sequence of these choices, so all subsets appear once.

The current list is reused while exploring. After the take branch, remove its last value before returning. At the end of the array, save a new list containing the current values. Saving the current list itself would let later edits change answers we already recorded.
steps: At each index, first recurse without choosing the value.
Add the value, recurse to the next index, then remove it.
At the end, save a copy of the current subset.
164.space: O(n) working space; O(n × 2^n) for the returned lists.
pitfalls: Include the empty subset.
This version assumes distinct input values; duplicate values need the later Subsets II rule.
Use remove(current.size() − 1). Removing an Integer by value can remove the wrong occurrence.
tests: for(int n=0;n<=10;n++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=i-5;Set<List<Integer>>expected=new HashSet<>();for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){List<Integer>s=new ArrayList<>();for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0)s.add(a[j]);expected.add(s);}List<List<Integer>>actual=subsets(a);assert actual.size()==(1<<n);assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);}

165.problem: Learn take/skip subsequence recursion, then solve the different problem attached to this tracker row: count distinct non-empty subsequences of a string.
165.assumptions: The row title is a theory lesson, but its existing link is LeetCode 940, Distinct Subsequences II. The recursive example generates subsequences by position; the final method counts unique resulting strings. The linked problem uses lowercase English letters and length at most 2000.

example.output: 5 distinct non-empty strings: a, b, aa, ab, aab
example.explanation: Choosing the first a or the second a gives the same string "a". Distinct counting must count it only once.

165.baseline: For the theory lesson, take or skip each character and save the resulting string at a leaf. To list all answers, explore both branches; to count index choices, add both branch counts; to ask whether any choice works, use OR and stop at the first success. Generating strings into a set solves the linked distinct problem for small inputs, but costs O(n × 2^n) time and storage.
165.approach:
For the linked problem, group the distinct strings by their last character. Let ending[c] be how many currently end in c, and total be the number of non-empty strings so far.

When a new c arrives, every existing string can have c appended, and c alone is also valid. So the new count ending in c is total + 1. Replace the old ending[c], rather than adding to it: those old strings are already included among these new possibilities. Other last-character groups do not change. Subtract the old group, add the new group, and keep the result modulo 1,000,000,007.
steps: For the theory example, make a skip call and a take call at every character.
For distinct counting, start total and all 26 ending counts at zero.
At each character, set newEnding = total + 1.
Replace that character’s previous ending count and update total.
Take a non-negative remainder after subtraction.
165.time: O(n) for distinct counting. The separate theory generator takes O(n × 2^n).
165.space: O(1): 26 counts for distinct counting. The theory generator stores exponential output.
pitfalls: Do not confuse different index selections with different resulting strings.
The linked task excludes the empty string.
Do not update total before calculating the new group from the old total.
tests: Random r=new Random(165);for(int n=0;n<=12;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<12;trial++){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)b.append((char)('a'+r.nextInt(3)));String s=b.toString();Set<String>expected=new HashSet<>(subsequencesByPosition(s));expected.remove("");assert distinctSubseqII(s)==expected.size();}
165.baselineTime: O(n × 2^n) time and stored output; O(n) recursive working space. This demonstrates the theory title, not an efficient submission for the linked problem.

166.problem: Count the non-empty subsequences whose values add to k.
166.assumptions: The source uses at most 20 positive values and a positive target. Different index selections count separately, even when their values are equal. This implementation also handles zeroes, negatives and target 0, while still excluding the empty choice.

example.explanation: Choose the first 2 with 3, or 3 with the last 2. These are two different index selections.

166.baseline: Enumerate all non-empty bit masks and sum the selected values. This takes O(n × 2^n). Recursion can carry the partial sum instead of recomputing it from scratch.
166.approach:
At each value there are two choices: include it in the sum or leave it out. The number of answers below this call is the number from the take branch plus the number from the skip branch.

At the end, return 1 only if the sum matches and at least one value was chosen. That final non-empty check matters for target zero. We do not stop early when the sum reaches k: later zeroes or negative values can create more valid selections in the supported extension.
steps: Carry the index, current sum and whether anything has been chosen.
At the end, return 1 for a matching non-empty selection, otherwise 0.
Add the counts from taking and skipping the current value.
pitfalls: Equal values at different indices are separate choices in this task.
Do not prune when sum > k if allowing negative values.
This recursive method is intended for the source’s small n; the subset-sum DP chapter handles larger inputs.
tests: assert countSubsequences(new int[]{2,3,2},5)==2;assert countSubsequences(new int[]{1,2},9)==0;assert countSubsequences(new int[]{},0)==0;

Random r=new Random(166);for(int n=0;n<=12;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<15;trial++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(7)-3;int k=r.nextInt(15)-7;long expected=0;for(int mask=1;mask<(1<<n);mask++){long sum=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0)sum+=a[i];if(sum==k)expected++;}assert countSubsequences(a,k)==expected;}

167.problem: Decide whether any non-empty subsequence adds to k.
167.assumptions: The source has positive numbers, a positive target, and n ≤ 20. This implementation also supports zeroes and negatives, and defines target 0 to require a non-empty selection.

example.explanation: Taking 3 and 2 makes 5. We can stop as soon as we find that selection.

167.baseline: Count every valid selection and then ask whether the count is positive. That works, but it keeps searching even after an answer has been found.
167.approach:
The choices are the same as in the counting problem: take this value or skip it. The difference is how results are combined. Counting uses addition; existence uses OR. Java’s || skips the second call when the first has already returned true.

Only the end of the array decides whether a complete selection matches. The chosen flag excludes the empty selection when k is zero. No partial-sum pruning is used, so negative values are safe too.
steps: Carry index, sum and a chosen flag.
At the end, check sum == k and chosen.
Return the take result OR the skip result.
167.time: O(2^n) in the worst case; finding a solution can stop the search early.
pitfalls: Use ||, not |, to stop after a successful branch.
Returning false after just the take branch fails would miss answers from the skip branch.
tests: assert hasSubsequence(new int[]{3,8,2},5);assert !hasSubsequence(new int[]{3,8,2},6);assert !hasSubsequence(new int[]{},0);assert hasSubsequence(new int[]{0},0);assert hasSubsequence(new int[]{-2,2},0);

Random r=new Random(167);for(int n=0;n<=12;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<15;trial++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(9)-4;int k=r.nextInt(19)-9;boolean expected=false;for(int mask=1;mask<(1<<n);mask++){long sum=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0)sum+=a[i];if(sum==k)expected=true;}assert hasSubsequence(a,k)==expected;}

168.problem: Find every combination of candidate values that adds to target. A candidate may be used repeatedly.
168.assumptions: Candidates are distinct positive integers. Order within a combination does not create a new answer. The source uses candidates ≥ 2 and target ≤ 40. The input array is not changed.

example.explanation: The value 3 can be reused. [7, 3] is the same combination as [3, 7], so it is not returned again.

168.baseline: Try every candidate at every position and remove duplicate permutations afterward. That repeats the same combination in different orders and wastes work.
168.approach:
Keep an index for the candidate we are deciding about. Taking it reduces the remaining sum but keeps the same index, because reuse is allowed. Skipping it moves to the next candidate. Once skipped, we never return to it, so each combination is built in candidate-index order.

A remaining sum of zero means the current selection is complete. Positive candidates ensure that taking a value always moves us closer to zero and cannot recurse forever. If a candidate is larger than the remaining sum, only the skip branch is possible.
steps: Start at candidate 0 with the whole target remaining.
Take the current candidate when it fits, recurse at the same index, then undo the choice.
Skip it by recursing at index + 1.
Save a copy when remaining is 0. Stop when all candidates are exhausted.
168.time: Exponential in the search depth. A conservative bound is O(2^(n + d) + A × d), where d = floor(target/minCandidate) and A is the number of answers.
168.space: O(n + d) working space; O(A × d) output space.
pitfalls: Taking must stay at the same index; moving forward would allow each candidate only once.
Zero and negative candidates are outside this problem’s constraints and would break the stopping argument.
The output follows input-index order; its numbers need not be sorted unless the input is sorted.
tests: for(int t=1;t<=30;t++){Set<List<Integer>>expected=new HashSet<>();for(int a=0;a*2<=t;a++)for(int b=0;a*2+b*3<=t;b++)for(int d=0;a*2+b*3+d*5<=t;d++)if(a*2+b*3+d*5==t){List<Integer>x=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<a;i++)x.add(2);for(int i=0;i<b;i++)x.add(3);for(int i=0;i<d;i++)x.add(5);expected.add(x);}List<List<Integer>>actual=combinationSum(new int[]{2,3,5},t);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);}

169.problem: Find unique combinations adding to target when each candidate position may be used only once.
169.assumptions: Candidates are positive and may contain duplicates. Different permutations are the same answer. Sort a copy so the caller’s array is preserved. The source asks for sorted combinations.

example.explanation: Both 1s may be used because they come from different positions. A single position cannot be reused.

169.baseline: Generate every index subset, keep those with the right sum, and use a set to remove duplicate value lists. This spends time building duplicates that sorting lets us avoid.
169.approach:
Sort the values and choose the next element from the remaining suffix. After choosing position i, continue at i + 1, so that position cannot be used again.

At a particular recursion level, skip a value if it is equal to the previous value at that same level. Those two choices would start identical combinations. Do not skip the first value of a deeper call: choosing a second 1 after a first 1 is how we correctly build [1, 1, 2]. Since the values are sorted and positive, stop the loop when a value exceeds the remaining sum.
steps: Sort a copy of the input.
Loop from start through the remaining candidates.
Skip equal neighbours only when i > start.
Choose a value, recurse from i + 1, then remove it.
Save a copy when the remaining sum becomes zero.
169.time: O(n log n + n × 2^n) as a conservative worst-case bound, including output copies. Pruning often avoids much of that search.
169.space: O(n) working space, plus the returned combinations.
pitfalls: The duplicate test is i > start, not i > 0.
Recurse with i + 1; staying at i incorrectly reuses a candidate.
A set must not be used to remove repeated input values: [1, 1] can be a valid combination.
tests: Random r=new Random(169);for(int n=0;n<=11;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<15;trial++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(6);int[]before=a.clone();int target=1+r.nextInt(15);Set<List<Integer>>expected=new HashSet<>();for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){List<Integer>x=new ArrayList<>();int sum=0;for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0){x.add(a[j]);sum+=a[j];}if(sum==target){Collections.sort(x);expected.add(x);}}List<List<Integer>>actual=combinationSum2(a,target);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);assert Arrays.equals(a,before);}

170.problem: Return the sum of every index subset, including the empty subset’s sum of zero.
170.assumptions: This is Subset Sum I / Subsets I. The TUF practice link asks for sums, even though the current sheet also has a LeetCode link that asks for the subsets themselves. Follow the tracker’s TUF task here. Equal sums from different selections must be kept. Source n ≤ 15.

example.explanation: There are two ways to choose one 3, so the sum 3 appears twice.

170.baseline: Build every subset as a list and then add its elements. Carrying only the running sum avoids making all those intermediate lists.
170.approach:
Each value is either included in the sum or left out. Make both recursive calls and advance the index. Once every position has been considered, save the sum. There are exactly 2^n leaves, including the branch that skips every value.

The task allows any output order, so sorting is unnecessary. If you want sorted sums for display, sort the returned list afterward; that adds O(n × 2^n) time.
steps: Start at index 0 with sum 0.
Recurse with the current value added.
Recurse without adding it.
At the end of the array, append the sum, even if an equal sum is already present.
170.space: O(n) recursive working space and O(2^n) output space.
pitfalls: Use a list, not a set: duplicate sums are required.
The source maximum sum is 15 × 10,000, which fits in int. Larger constraints may need long.
Do not confuse this with returning the actual subset elements.
tests: Random r=new Random(170);for(int n=0;n<=15;n++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(21)-10;List<Integer>expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){int sum=0;for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0)sum+=a[j];expected.add(sum);}List<Integer>actual=subsetSums(a);Collections.sort(actual);Collections.sort(expected);assert actual.equals(expected);}

171.problem: Return every distinct subset when the input may contain repeated values.
171.assumptions: Subsets are compared by their values, not by the indices that supplied them. Include the empty subset. Values may be negative. The source bounds n by 10. The input array is preserved.

example.explanation: There is one subset [2], but [2, 2] is also valid because two copies are available.

171.baseline: Generate all index subsets, sort each, and insert them into a set. This is correct but generates duplicate value lists before discarding them.
171.approach:
Sort a copy so equal values sit next to each other. At the start of every call, save the current subset: it is already a valid answer. Then try each remaining value as the next element.

Skip repeated choices only at the same recursion level. If we already tried starting this extension with a 2, starting it with the next 2 would repeat the same answers. But inside the call that has already chosen one 2, the next 2 is allowed, giving [2, 2].
steps: Sort a copy of the input.
Save a copy of the current subset on entry to each call.
Loop through remaining positions, skipping equal neighbours when i > start.
Choose position i, recurse from i + 1, then undo it.
171.time: O(n log n + n × 2^n) in the worst case. Repeated values reduce the number of answers.
171.space: O(n) working space; up to O(n × 2^n) output space.
pitfalls: Skipping all duplicate input values would lose subsets containing two or more copies.
Save a copy of current each time.
tests: Random r=new Random(171);for(int n=0;n<=10;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<15;trial++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(5)-2;int[]before=a.clone();Set<List<Integer>>expected=new HashSet<>();for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){List<Integer>x=new ArrayList<>();for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0)x.add(a[j]);Collections.sort(x);expected.add(x);}List<List<Integer>>actual=subsetsWithDup(a);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);assert Arrays.equals(a,before);}

172.problem: Choose exactly k different numbers from 1 through 9 whose sum is n.
172.assumptions: Each number may be used once. Return combinations, so changing their order does not create another answer. The source uses 2 ≤ k ≤ 9 and 1 ≤ n ≤ 60.

example.explanation: Every pair has two different values and adds to 9.

172.baseline: There are only 512 subsets of 1 through 9. Testing each subset’s size and sum is a valid simple solution. Backtracking makes the exact-size and remaining-sum conditions explicit.
172.approach:
Build each combination in increasing order. After choosing value v, the next choice starts at v + 1, so no number repeats and no permutation is generated twice. Keep track of how many values are still needed and how much sum remains.

When no more values are needed, save the selection only if the remaining sum is zero. If fewer values are available than the number still needed, stop that branch. Positive values also let us stop once the next value exceeds the remaining sum.
steps: Start with value 1, k slots and remaining sum n.
Try each possible next value in increasing order.
Recurse with one fewer slot, a smaller remaining sum and next value v + 1.
Save only when both slots and remaining sum reach zero.
172.time: O(9 × 2^9) is a simple upper bound, including result copies. The universe is fixed at nine numbers.
172.space: O(k) working space, plus O(k) for each returned combination.
pitfalls: Reaching the target with too few numbers is not an answer.
The number 0 is not a candidate.
Move to value + 1 to prevent reuse.
tests: for(int k=1;k<=9;k++)for(int target=1;target<=60;target++){Set<List<Integer>>expected=new HashSet<>();for(int mask=0;mask<512;mask++){if(Integer.bitCount(mask)!=k)continue;int sum=0;List<Integer>x=new ArrayList<>();for(int j=0;j<9;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0){sum+=j+1;x.add(j+1);}if(sum==target)expected.add(x);}List<List<Integer>>actual=combinationSum3(k,target);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);}

173.problem: Return every letter string represented by a phone keypad digit string.
173.assumptions: Digits are from 2 to 9. The source allows up to four digits. The tracker’s LeetCode version also allows an empty input; return an empty list for that case. Standard mapping: 2 abc, 3 def, 4 ghi, 5 jkl, 6 mno, 7 pqrs, 8 tuv, 9 wxyz.

example.output: [at, au, av, bt, bu, bv, ct, cu, cv]
example.explanation: Choose one letter from abc, then one from tuv.

173.baseline: Start with one empty prefix and repeatedly extend every prefix by every letter for the next digit. That iterative approach is valid too; recursion holds just one unfinished prefix at a time.
173.approach:
Each position has its own small list of allowed letters. Pick a letter for the first position, then let recursion fill the remaining positions. When the buffer is full, save it as a string.

There is no take-or-skip choice here: every digit must contribute exactly one letter. The buffer can be reused because a new String is created for each complete answer.
steps: Return an empty list for an empty input.
Find the letters mapped to the current digit.
Write each letter into the current position and recurse.
Save the completed buffer at the end.
173.time: O(n × A), where A is the product of the letter counts. At most O(n × 4^n).
173.space: O(n) working space and O(n × A) output space.
pitfalls: Digits 7 and 9 have four letters, not three.
An empty digit string returns no combinations for the linked task.
Digits 0 and 1 are outside the stated input constraints.

174.problem: Split a string into contiguous pieces so every piece is a palindrome. Return every valid split.
174.assumptions: Use every character exactly once and keep the original order. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. The source has lowercase strings of length at most 16. The helper defines the empty string as one empty partition.

example.explanation: Each row joins back to noon, and every piece in that row is a palindrome.

174.baseline: Choose whether to cut at each gap, then check every piece of every completed partition. There are 2^(n−1) cut patterns. Backtracking rejects a non-palindrome piece before exploring the rest of that partition.
174.approach:
At the current start position, try every possible end position for the next piece. Compare the piece’s ends while moving inward. If they all match, add that piece and recurse on the suffix after it. If they do not, try a longer piece instead.

When start reaches the string length, every character has been used, so save the partition. Undo the last piece after each recursive call. A longer piece can be a palindrome even when a shorter one is not, so a failed check does not end the loop.
steps: Try each substring starting at the current position.
Check whether it is a palindrome with two pointers.
For a palindrome, choose it, recurse after its end, then remove it.
Save a copy of the partition when the entire string is consumed.
174.time: O(n² × 2^n) is a conservative bound for trying cuts, checking substrings and copying answers. The number of returned partitions can itself be exponential.
174.space: O(n) working depth and selected-character storage; up to O(n × 2^n) output space.
pitfalls: Pieces must be contiguous substrings, not subsequences.
Use continue after a failed palindrome check, not break.
Every partition must cover the full string.
tests: Random r=new Random(174);for(int n=1;n<=10;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<15;trial++){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)b.append((char)('a'+r.nextInt(3)));String s=b.toString();Set<List<String>>expected=new HashSet<>();for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<(n-1));mask++){List<String>pieces=new ArrayList<>();int start=0;boolean valid=true;for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if(j==n-1||(mask&(1<<j))!=0){String part=s.substring(start,j+1);if(!part.equals(new StringBuilder(part).reverse().toString()))valid=false;pieces.add(part);start=j+1;}if(valid)expected.add(pieces);}List<List<String>>actual=partition(s);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);}

175.problem: Decide whether a word can be traced through horizontally or vertically adjacent board cells without reusing a cell.
175.assumptions: The board is rectangular and contains English letters. Matching is case-sensitive. The source allows dimensions up to 6 × 6 and word length up to 15. The helper also handles an empty board and defines an empty word as found.

example.explanation: Start at C, move right to A, then down to T. "CAC" is false because it would reuse the C cell.

175.baseline: Generate paths and compare their letters only at the end. Checking the next letter immediately avoids exploring paths that already disagree with the word.
175.approach:
Try every cell as a starting point. A recursive call asks whether the rest of the word can start at this cell. Reject an out-of-bounds cell or a wrong letter. When a letter matches, temporarily mark the cell as unavailable and try its four neighbours.

Restore the original character before returning, even when a neighbour found the word. The mark belongs only to the current path. Keeping it permanently would wrongly block later searches and change the caller’s board.
steps: Try starting at each board cell.
Reject bounds errors and character mismatches.
After matching the last character, return true.
Otherwise mark the cell, try four directions, restore it, and return whether any direction worked.
175.time: O(R × C × 4 × 3^(L−1)) is an upper bound for non-empty words: the first move has four choices, and later moves cannot immediately revisit the previous cell.
175.space: O(L) recursive call space; the board is restored before returning.
pitfalls: Diagonal moves are not allowed.
Repeated letters are fine; reusing the same cell is not.
Do not return straight from the neighbour calls before restoring the cell.
The # marker is safe because the stated board and word alphabet contains only letters.
tests: Random r=new Random(175);for(int trial=0;trial<200;trial++){char[][]b=new char[2][3];for(char[]row:b)for(int j=0;j<3;j++)row[j]=(char)('A'+r.nextInt(3));StringBuilder w=new StringBuilder();int length=1+r.nextInt(6);for(int i=0;i<length;i++)w.append((char)('A'+r.nextInt(3)));Set<String>paths=new HashSet<>();Deque<int[]>queue=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int i=0;i<6;i++)if(b[i/3][i%3]==w.charAt(0))queue.add(new int[]{i,1<<i,1});boolean expected=false;while(!queue.isEmpty()){int[]state=queue.remove();int pos=state[0],mask=state[1],used=state[2];if(used==length){expected=true;break;}for(int next=0;next<6;next++)if(Math.abs(pos/3-next/3)+Math.abs(pos%3-next%3)==1&&(mask&(1<<next))==0&&b[next/3][next%3]==w.charAt(used))queue.add(new int[]{next,mask|(1<<next),used+1});}char[][]before=Arrays.stream(b).map(char[]::clone).toArray(char[][]::new);assert exist(b,w.toString())==expected;assert Arrays.deepEquals(b,before);}

176.problem: Return every n × n board containing n queens with no two attacking each other.
176.assumptions: Q marks a queen and . marks an empty cell. Queens attack along rows, columns and both diagonals. Source n is between 1 and 9. Follow the tracker’s LeetCode return convention: no solution means [], not a list containing an empty board.

example.explanation: Its queen columns by row are 2, 0, 3, 1. No pair shares a row, column or diagonal.

176.baseline: While placing queens, scan earlier columns to check the row and both diagonals. That backtracking solution works. Boolean arrays make each safety check constant time.
176.approach:
Place exactly one queen in each column. A new queen is safe if its row and both diagonals are unused. Squares on one diagonal share row + column; squares on the other share column − row. Add n − 1 to the second expression to make its index non-negative.

Mark all three lines, place the queen and solve the next column. On return, remove the queen and clear the marks so another row can be tried. Once all columns are filled, copy the board into strings.
steps: Create an empty board and three boolean arrays for occupied lines.
For each row in the current column, check row and diagonal occupancy.
Place a safe queen and recurse into the next column.
Undo the board change and all three occupancy marks.
Save a board when column reaches n.
176.time: O(n × n! + A × n²) as a conservative bound, including row trials and copying A solution boards. Diagonal pruning reduces the search.
176.space: O(n²) for the working board, O(n) for marks and calls, plus O(A × n²) output.
pitfalls: There are 2n − 1 diagonals in each direction.
Clear every occupancy mark after a branch, not just the board cell.
For n = 2 or 3, return no boards. The public TUF n = 2 example displays [[]], but the linked LeetCode task expects [].
tests: int[]counts={0,1,0,0,2,10,4,40,92};for(int n=1;n<=8;n++){List<List<String>>boards=solveNQueens(n);assert boards.size()==counts[n];assert new HashSet<>(boards).size()==boards.size();for(List<String>b:boards){assert b.size()==n;List<int[]>queens=new ArrayList<>();for(int row=0;row<n;row++){assert b.get(row).length()==n;for(int col=0;col<n;col++)if(b.get(row).charAt(col)=='Q')queens.add(new int[]{row,col});}assert queens.size()==n;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<n;j++){int[]a=queens.get(i),d=queens.get(j);assert a[0]!=d[0]&&a[1]!=d[1]&&Math.abs(a[0]-d[0])!=Math.abs(a[1]-d[1]);}}}

177.problem: Return all paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a square maze without revisiting a cell within one path.
177.assumptions: 1 means open and 0 means blocked. Moves are down, left, right or up. Source n is 2 through 5. This helper also handles a 1 × 1 maze: one open cell has one empty path. The input maze is restored.

example.explanation: Go down then right, or right then down. A path cannot loop back through its starting cell.

177.baseline: Trying moves without marking the current path can loop forever. A single permanent visited set is also wrong: a cell used in one path may be needed in a different path.
177.approach:
Mark a cell only while it belongs to the path currently being explored. Try each legal next move, then undo it. When that branch is finished, unmark the cell so another route can use it.

The maze itself can hold the temporary mark: change the current 1 to 0 and restore it before returning. Save the direction string as soon as the destination is reached. Trying D, L, R, U in that order produces paths in dictionary order.
steps: Return no paths if the start or destination is blocked.
At each cell, mark it unavailable for the current route.
Try D, L, R, U into open neighbours, appending and then removing each direction.
At the destination, save the path string.
Restore the current cell before returning.
177.time: Exponential in the number of open cells. O(4^(n²) × n²) is a conservative upper bound including saved paths.
177.space: O(n²) working depth and path length, plus the stored result strings.
pitfalls: Visited belongs to one path, not the whole search.
Check the destination is open before treating it as reached.
Return an empty list when there is no route; the empty string is a route only for an open 1 × 1 maze.
tests: int[][]a={{1,1},{1,1}};assert mazePaths(a).equals(List.of("DR","RD"));assert Arrays.deepEquals(a,new int[][]{{1,1},{1,1}});assert mazePaths(new int[][]{{0,1},{1,1}}).isEmpty();assert mazePaths(new int[][]{{1}}).equals(List.of(""));

for(int cells=0;cells<512;cells++){int[][]a=new int[3][3];for(int i=0;i<9;i++)a[i/3][i%3]=(cells>>i)&1;int[][]before=Arrays.stream(a).map(int[]::clone).toArray(int[][]::new);Set<String>expected=new HashSet<>();Deque<int[]>states=new ArrayDeque<>();Deque<String>paths=new ArrayDeque<>();if((cells&1)!=0){states.add(new int[]{0,1});paths.add("");}while(!states.isEmpty()){int[]st=states.remove();String path=paths.remove();int pos=st[0],mask=st[1];if(pos==8){expected.add(path);continue;}for(int next=0;next<9;next++)if(Math.abs(pos/3-next/3)+Math.abs(pos%3-next%3)==1&&(cells&(1<<next))!=0&&(mask&(1<<next))==0){char move=next/3>pos/3?'D':next/3<pos/3?'U':next>pos?'R':'L';states.add(new int[]{next,mask|(1<<next)});paths.add(path+move);}}List<String>actual=mazePaths(a);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);List<String>sorted=new ArrayList<>(actual);Collections.sort(sorted);assert actual.equals(sorted);assert Arrays.deepEquals(a,before);}
