178.problem: Decide whether a string can be split completely into words from a dictionary.
178.assumptions: A dictionary word can be reused. Words must cover the string in order, with no gaps. Source limits: string length 300 and word length 20. Dictionary entries are non-empty. The helper also treats an empty string as successfully consumed.

example.explanation: Use red, then blue, then red again. Reusing a word is allowed.

178.baseline: Try every dictionary-matching prefix, then recursively split the remaining suffix. Without remembering results, different earlier choices may repeatedly solve the same suffix.
178.approach:
A call at start asks one question: can the suffix beginning here be split? Try each next piece up to the longest dictionary-word length. If the piece is in the dictionary and the remaining suffix works, return true.

Remember true or false for each start index. Earlier choices do not affect which words can cover this suffix, so the saved result is safe to reuse. Reaching the end means every character was covered. Returning false must wait until all possible next pieces have failed.
steps: Put the dictionary in a set and find its longest word length.
At each start index, reuse a saved answer if available.
Try every possible next dictionary word within the length limit.
Return true if its remaining suffix works; otherwise save false after all choices fail.
178.time: O(W + n × L²) expected time with hashing, where W is total dictionary characters and L is the longest word. Java substring creation and hashing cost O(L).
178.space: O(W + n) for dictionary storage, memo entries and recursive calls, plus temporary substring storage.
pitfalls: Finding a dictionary word at the beginning is not enough; the whole suffix must also split.
Do not remove a dictionary word after using it.
Memoize by start index, not by the previously chosen word.
A primitive boolean array alone cannot distinguish not-yet-computed from computed-false.
tests: Random r=new Random(178);for(int trial=0;trial<500;trial++){int n=r.nextInt(15);StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)b.append((char)('a'+r.nextInt(2)));String s=b.toString();List<String>d=new ArrayList<>();for(int length=1;length<=3;length++)for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<length);mask++)if(r.nextBoolean()){StringBuilder w=new StringBuilder();for(int j=0;j<length;j++)w.append((mask&(1<<j))==0?'a':'b');d.add(w.toString());}boolean[]reachable=new boolean[n+1];reachable[0]=true;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(reachable[i])for(String w:d)if(s.startsWith(w,i))reachable[i+w.length()]=true;assert wordBreak(s,d)==reachable[n];}

179.problem: Decide whether an undirected graph can be coloured using at most m colours so adjacent vertices have different colours.
179.assumptions: Vertices are numbered 0 through n − 1. A colour may be shared by non-adjacent vertices. The graph may be disconnected. Source n ≤ 20. The helper accepts an edge list and rejects a self-loop because a vertex cannot differ from itself.

example.explanation: A triangle needs three colours: the third vertex touches both of the first two.

179.baseline: Assign a colour to every vertex in all m^n ways, then check every edge. Backtracking can reject an assignment as soon as it conflicts with an already coloured neighbour.
179.approach:
Colour vertices one at a time. For the current vertex, try each colour. Scan its neighbours to see whether that colour is already used next to it. If it is safe, assign it and try to colour the next vertex.

If the remaining graph cannot be completed, erase this assignment and try another colour. Once all vertices have colours, return true. Working through all vertex numbers also handles disconnected components; no special traversal is needed.
steps: Build a symmetric adjacency matrix from the undirected edges.
Try each colour for the current vertex.
Reject colours used by an already coloured neighbour.
Recurse after a safe assignment; reset it if that branch fails.
Return true after every vertex has been assigned.
179.time: Exponential. O(n × m^(n+1)) is a conservative upper bound accounting for colour trials and neighbour scans.
179.space: O(n²) for the adjacency matrix; O(n) for colours and recursive calls.
pitfalls: The requirement applies to adjacent vertices, not every pair of vertices.
Add each edge in both directions.
Zero means uncoloured; actual colours run from 1 through m.
Disconnected vertices still need to be processed.
tests: for(int n=1;n<=4;n++){List<int[]>pairs=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<n;j++)pairs.add(new int[]{i,j});for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<pairs.size());mask++){List<int[]>edges=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<pairs.size();i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0)edges.add(pairs.get(i));int[][]e=edges.toArray(int[][]::new);for(int m=1;m<=n;m++){int possibilities=1;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)possibilities*=m;boolean expected=false;for(int assignment=0;assignment<possibilities;assignment++){int x=assignment;int[]colors=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){colors[i]=x%m;x/=m;}boolean valid=true;for(int[]edge:e)if(colors[edge[0]]==colors[edge[1]])valid=false;if(valid){expected=true;break;}}assert graphColoring(n,e,m)==expected;}}}

180.problem: Fill the empty cells of a 9 × 9 Sudoku board so every row, column and 3 × 3 box contains digits 1 through 9 exactly once.
180.assumptions: An empty cell contains . . The source guarantees valid initial clues and exactly one solution. The method edits the supplied board in place. It is a solver under those assumptions, not a general validator for arbitrary completed boards.

example.input: A solved board’s first row is 534678912, but its first cell is replaced by .
example.explanation: The row already contains every other digit. The column and box must also allow 5 before it is placed.

180.baseline: Try all digits in all empty cells and validate the completed board. That makes up to 9^E assignments for E blanks. Checking row, column and box before each placement rejects invalid branches much earlier.
180.approach:
Find the first empty cell. Try digits 1 through 9, keeping only those absent from its row, column and box. Place one candidate and ask recursion to fill the rest. If that attempt fails, restore the dot and try the next candidate.

The box begins at row/3 × 3 and column/3 × 3. Adding i/3 and i%3 for i from 0 through 8 visits its nine cells. When no empty cell remains, the search has succeeded and the placed digits are kept.
steps: Scan for the next dot.
Try each digit that is safe in the row, column and box.
Place it and recurse. Keep it if the recursive call succeeds.
Otherwise restore the dot and try another digit.
If no dot remains, return success.
180.time: O(9^E) as a loose worst-case bound for E empty cells; board scans are bounded by the fixed 81-cell board.
180.space: O(E) recursive call space. The board is edited in place.
pitfalls: After all digits fail for one blank, return false immediately; moving to another blank would skip a required cell.
Undo only guesses, never the original clues.
Do not restore a successful placement when returning true.
The unique valid solution is an input guarantee; this method does not count solutions.
tests: String[]solved={"534678912","672195348","198342567","859761423","426853791","713924856","961537284","287419635","345286179"};Random r=new Random(180);for(int trial=0;trial<30;trial++){char[][]b=Arrays.stream(solved).map(String::toCharArray).toArray(char[][]::new);for(int removed=0;removed<35;removed++)b[r.nextInt(9)][r.nextInt(9)]='.';char[][]clues=Arrays.stream(b).map(char[]::clone).toArray(char[][]::new);solveSudoku(b);for(int i=0;i<9;i++){Set<Character>row=new HashSet<>(),col=new HashSet<>(),box=new HashSet<>();for(int j=0;j<9;j++){assert b[i][j]>='1'&&b[i][j]<='9';if(clues[i][j]!='.')assert b[i][j]==clues[i][j];row.add(b[i][j]);col.add(b[j][i]);box.add(b[(i/3)*3+j/3][(i%3)*3+j%3]);}assert row.size()==9&&col.size()==9&&box.size()==9;}}

181.problem: Insert +, − or × between digits to create every expression that evaluates to target. Adjacent digits may also stay together as one number.
181.assumptions: Keep all digits in their original order. Operands cannot have leading zeroes, except the single digit 0. Multiplication has higher precedence than addition and subtraction. Source length is at most 10; use long for calculations even though target is an int.

example.explanation: 10 is a valid operand, but 05 is not. Keeping digits together is one of the choices.

181.baseline: At each gap, choose an operator or no operator, then parse each finished expression. That works, but repeated parsing is unnecessary if recursion carries the running value.
181.approach:
Try every possible next operand by extending its end position. For the first operand, start the expression without an operator. Later operands can be added, subtracted or multiplied.

To handle multiplication, remember the last signed term as well as the total. Suppose the expression is 2 + 3 and we append *4. The total should become 2 + 12, so replace the old term: total − 3 + 3 × 4. After subtraction the saved term is negative; this same rule then handles 2 − 3 × 4 correctly. Every recursive call restores the StringBuilder length before the next branch.
steps: Extend the next operand one digit at a time. Stop extending after a leading zero.
For the first operand, set both total and last term to that value.
For + or −, adjust total and set the signed last term.
For ×, replace the previous last term with its product.
At the end of the digits, save the expression only if total equals target.
181.time: O(n × 4^(n−1)) as a conservative bound for n ≥ 1: each gap can join digits or hold one of three operators, with expression construction costs.
181.space: O(n) working space, plus the returned expression strings.
pitfalls: Saving last as positive after subtraction breaks multiplication precedence.
Single zero operands are allowed; 00 and 05 are not.
Do not use int for intermediate operands such as 9999999999.
There is no division operator and no unary operator before the first operand.
tests: Random r=new Random(181);for(int trial=0;trial<150;trial++){int n=1+r.nextInt(7);StringBuilder digits=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)digits.append(r.nextInt(5));String num=digits.toString();int target=r.nextInt(41)-20;Set<String>expected=new HashSet<>();int choices=1<<(2*(n-1));for(int mask=0;mask<choices;mask++){StringBuilder expression=new StringBuilder();expression.append(num.charAt(0));for(int gap=0;gap<n-1;gap++){int op=(mask>>(2*gap))&3;if(op>0)expression.append(" +-*".charAt(op));expression.append(num.charAt(gap+1));}String e=expression.toString();long sum=0,term=0;char operation='+';int index=0;boolean valid=true;while(index<e.length()){int begin=index;long operand=0;while(index<e.length()&&Character.isDigit(e.charAt(index))){operand=operand*10+e.charAt(index)-'0';index++;}if(index-begin>1&&e.charAt(begin)=='0'){valid=false;break;}if(operation=='*')term*=operand;else{sum+=term;term=operation=='+'?operand:-operand;}if(index<e.length())operation=e.charAt(index++);}if(valid&&sum+term==target)expected.add(e);}List<String>actual=addOperators(num,target);assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert new HashSet<>(actual).equals(expected);}

182.problem: Understand how to read and change individual bits of a Java int.
182.assumptions: A Java int has 32 bits. Count positions from the right, starting at 0. The highest bit also determines the sign. Helper bit positions must be between 0 and 31.

example.explanation: Bit 0 starts as 0. Setting it makes it 1; clearing an already-zero bit changes nothing.

182.baseline: You can convert a value to a binary string to inspect it, but changing flags by editing that string needs conversions and extra storage. A mask selects the relevant position directly.
182.approach:
Think of an integer as 32 switches. The mask 1 << i has just switch i turned on. AND keeps a bit only when both sides contain 1. OR turns it on when either side contains 1. XOR turns it on when the two sides differ, so XOR with the mask toggles exactly that switch.

To clear a bit, invert the mask with ~, leaving a zero only at that position, then AND it with the number. NOT flips all 32 bits, including the leading ones we usually omit when writing binary. In Java, >> preserves the sign while >>> fills from the left with zeroes. Neither operation changes the original variable unless its result is assigned.
steps: Build a mask with 1 << i.
Check with (n & mask) != 0.
Set with n | mask, clear with n & ~mask, and toggle with n ^ mask.
Keep numeric meaning separate from the raw bit pattern, especially for bit 31.
182.time: O(1) for each operation on a 32-bit int.
pitfalls: ^ means XOR in Java, not exponentiation.
Java does not allow integers as boolean conditions; write a comparison such as != 0.
An int shift uses only the lowest five bits of its distance, so 1 << 32 behaves like 1 << 0. The helper rejects such indices.
For negative values, >> is not generally the same as division toward zero: -3 >> 1 is -2, but -3 / 2 is -1.
tests: Random r=new Random(182);for(int t=0;t<1000;t++){int n=r.nextInt();for(int i=0;i<32;i++){assert checkBit(setBit(n,i),i);assert !checkBit(clearBit(n,i),i);assert toggleBit(toggleBit(n,i),i)==n;assert (setBit(n,i)^n)==(checkBit(n,i)?0:1<<i);}}

183.problem: Check whether bit i of n is 1.
183.assumptions: Bit positions are zero-based from the right. Source i is from 0 through 31 and n is positive. The helper also works on all signed int bit patterns.

example.explanation: Bit 4 contributes 16, so it is set. Bit 3 is not set.

183.baseline: Repeatedly shift the number right i times and inspect the final low bit. A single mask selects the same position directly.
183.approach:
Create 1 << i. This mask is zero everywhere except the position we want to inspect. AND with n clears every other position. If anything remains, the selected bit was set.

Compare the result with zero, not with one. For bit 4, a successful mask gives 16. For bit 31, the masked int is negative, but it is still non-zero.
steps: Build the mask for bit i.
AND it with n.
Return whether the result is non-zero.
pitfalls: Use != 0, not == 1 or > 0.
The rightmost position is 0, not 1.
tests: Random r=new Random(183);for(int t=0;t<2000;t++){int n=r.nextInt();for(int i=0;i<32;i++)assert isSet(n,i)==(((n>>>i)&1)==1);}

184.problem: Return whether an integer is odd.
184.assumptions: The source uses non-negative integers. The bit check also works for negative Java ints.

example.explanation: All places except the rightmost contribute multiples of 2. The rightmost 1 makes the number odd.

184.baseline: n % 2 != 0 is a clear, correct arithmetic solution. This bit lesson uses the least significant bit to express the same property.
184.approach: Every binary place above bit 0 has an even place value: 2, 4, 8 and so on. Only bit 0 can add an odd contribution. AND with 1 removes all the other bits, leaving 1 for an odd number and 0 for an even number.
steps: Read the lowest bit using n & 1.
Return true if that bit is 1.
pitfalls: Zero is even.
For negative inputs, n % 2 == 1 is not a reliable odd check; use != 0 or the bit test.

185.problem: Decide whether n is a positive power of two.
185.assumptions: Input can be any Java int. One counts because 2^0 = 1. Zero and negative values do not count.

example.explanation: Exactly one bit is set. By contrast, 40 is 101000 and has two set bits.

185.baseline: For positive n, repeatedly divide by 2 while it is even, then check whether 1 remains. The bit method does the same classification without a loop.
185.approach:
A positive power of two has one set bit. Subtracting one turns that bit off and every lower bit on. The original and the result therefore have no set bit in common.

More generally, n & (n − 1) clears the lowest set bit. It becomes zero exactly when there was only one. Require n > 0 as well: zero would otherwise pass, and the negative int with only its sign bit set is not a positive power of two.
steps: Reject n ≤ 0.
Clear the lowest set bit with n & (n − 1).
Return whether nothing remains.
pitfalls: The n > 0 check is required.
The largest positive int power of two is 1 << 30, not 1 << 31.
tests: Set<Integer>powers=new HashSet<>();for(int i=0;i<31;i++)powers.add(1<<i);for(int n=-10;n<=10000;n++)assert isPowerOfTwo(n)==powers.contains(n);for(int value:powers)assert isPowerOfTwo(value);Random r=new Random(185);for(int i=0;i<10000;i++){int n=r.nextInt();assert isPowerOfTwo(n)==powers.contains(n);}

186.problem: Count the 1 bits in one integer’s binary representation.
186.assumptions: This source asks about one number, not the total set bits from 1 through n. It uses 0 ≤ n ≤ 10^9. The helper also counts all 32 bits of a negative Java int.

example.explanation: Clear the rightmost 1 repeatedly: 11010 → 11000 → 10000 → 00000.

186.baseline: Inspect the lowest bit, add it to a count, and unsigned-shift right until nothing remains. That examines every bit position up to the highest set bit.
186.approach:
Subtracting one flips the rightmost 1 to 0 and turns all lower zeroes into ones. AND with the original number clears those lower changes, so n & (n − 1) removes just that rightmost 1.

Repeat until n is zero and count the removals. Each iteration accounts for exactly one set bit. This also terminates for negative ints because their representation still has only 32 bits.
steps: Start count at 0.
While n is non-zero, replace it with n & (n − 1).
Increment the count after each removal.
186.time: O(k), where k is the number of set bits; at most 32 iterations for a Java int.
pitfalls: Use n != 0 rather than n > 0 if supporting negative bit patterns.
Zero has no set bits.
This is not the separate problem that sums set-bit counts for all numbers up to n.
tests: Random r=new Random(186);for(int i=0;i<10000;i++){int n=r.nextInt();assert countSetBits(n)==Integer.bitCount(n);}

187.problem: Set the lowest zero bit of n. Also distinguish this lesson from the different Maximizing XOR problem attached to the tracker row.
187.assumptions: The tracker title says Set/Unset the rightmost unset bit, but its HackerRank link asks for the maximum XOR of two values in [l, r]. The current Striver practice task asks only to set the lowest zero bit. Both are shown separately. For the bit task, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^9; higher leading zeroes count.

example.explanation: Adding 1 gives 1100. OR with the original 1011 restores its lower 1s and sets the first zero.

187.baseline: Scan from bit 0 until a zero is found, then set that position. The expression n | (n + 1) does this directly. Clearing a lowest set bit is a different operation: n & (n − 1).
187.approach:
Adding one carries through all trailing 1s and stops at the first 0. OR with the original value restores the trailing 1s that the carry cleared, leaving exactly the first zero newly set. For 7 (111), the next leading zero is set, producing 15 (1111).

The linked HackerRank task is separate. Find the highest bit where l and r differ using l XOR r. Above that position every number in the interval shares the same prefix. The interval crosses the boundary at that position, so it contains the two values immediately on either side: their lower bits are complements. The maximum XOR therefore has 1s from that position down to bit 0.
steps: For the Striver task, return n | (n + 1).
To clear the lowest set bit instead, use n & (n − 1).
For the linked range-XOR task, examine l XOR r.
Build an all-ones result with the same bit length as that difference.
187.time: O(1) for setting or clearing a bit. Range XOR takes O(log(left XOR right + 1)), at most 31 iterations for non-negative ints.
pitfalls: Setting an unset bit and clearing a set bit are different operations.
When the visible digits are all 1s, the next leading zero still exists under this interpretation.
Do not submit the one-number bit helper to the two-bound HackerRank task.
tests: assert setRightmostZero(11)==15;assert setRightmostZero(7)==15;assert setRightmostZero(0)==1;assert clearRightmostOne(12)==8;assert maximizingXor(10,15)==7;assert maximizingXor(11,100)==127;
for(int l=0;l<=80;l++)for(int r=l;r<=80;r++){int expected=0;for(int a=l;a<=r;a++)for(int b=a;b<=r;b++)expected=Math.max(expected,a^b);assert maximizingXor(l,r)==expected;}

188.problem: Swap two integer values without a third temporary numeric variable.
188.assumptions: The source asks for arithmetic or XOR swapping. Java passes primitive arguments by value, so a helper returns the swapped pair. It cannot change the caller’s two int variables by merely reassigning its parameters.

example.explanation: After the XOR sequence, a holds the old b and b holds the old a.

188.baseline: A temporary variable is usually clearest: temp = a; a = b; b = temp. This exercise specifically asks to avoid that variable, so the code demonstrates XOR.
188.approach:
XOR cancels equal values: x XOR x is zero, and x XOR zero is x. First store a XOR b in a. XOR that combined value with the old b to recover the old a into b. Finally XOR the combined value with the new b to recover the old b into a.

Return the pair so the caller can use the results. The returned array is output storage; the swapping sequence itself uses only the two numeric variables. Do not use this sequence on the same array cell twice: the first XOR would erase it.
steps: Replace a with a XOR b.
Replace b with the new a XOR the old b.
Replace a with the new a XOR the new b.
Return the two results.
pitfalls: Reassigning Java int parameters does not swap the caller’s variables.
XOR swapping aliased locations can destroy the value; this helper uses two independent local variables.
Use a temporary variable in ordinary application code when it makes the intent easier to read.
tests: Random r=new Random(188);for(int i=0;i<10000;i++){int a=r.nextInt(),b=r.nextInt();assert Arrays.equals(swapNumbers(a,b),new int[]{b,a});}

189.problem: Divide two signed integers without multiplication, division or remainder operators, truncating the result toward zero.
189.assumptions: Divisor is non-zero. Inputs are 32-bit signed integers. Clamp the one overflowing result, Integer.MIN_VALUE divided by −1, to Integer.MAX_VALUE. Long is used internally for safe magnitudes and shifts.

example.explanation: Eight copies of 5 fit into 43. Apply the negative sign and discard the remainder, giving -8 rather than -9.

189.baseline: Repeatedly subtract one divisor magnitude and count the subtractions. This takes O(|quotient|), which is too slow for a very large dividend and a small divisor.
189.approach:
Subtract larger batches instead. A divisor shifted left by k is a batch of 2^k divisors. Check shifts from 31 down to 0; if a batch fits in the remaining dividend, subtract it and add 2^k to the quotient. This builds the quotient one binary bit at a time.

Convert each input to long before taking its absolute value. The magnitude of Integer.MIN_VALUE is 2147483648, which does not fit in an int. Apply the sign only after calculating the positive quotient, then clamp the positive overflow case.
steps: Remember whether the input signs differ.
Convert both magnitudes to long.
For shifts 31 down to 0, subtract any shifted divisor that fits and set that quotient contribution.
Apply the sign and clamp overflow before converting back to int.
189.time: O(32), which is O(1) for fixed-width int inputs. In a variable-width model, one pass over the quotient’s bit positions.
pitfalls: Math.abs(dividend) before widening fails for Integer.MIN_VALUE.
Use 1L << shift, not 1 << shift, for the quotient contribution at bit 31.
Negative division truncates toward zero.
A zero divisor is outside the problem; the helper rejects it explicitly.

reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. This follows the same long-magnitude and shifted-chunk algorithm, with a zero-divisor guard and a static helper.

190.problem: Find the minimum number of individual bit flips needed to change start into goal.
190.assumptions: The source uses non-negative integers. The helper also works on the full 32-bit representation of signed ints. A flip changes exactly one chosen bit.

example.explanation: Bits 3 and 1 differ. Flip each once; the other positions already match.

190.baseline: Compare the two numbers one bit at a time across all 32 positions and count mismatches. XOR collects those mismatches in a single integer.
190.approach:
XOR gives 1 exactly where the input bits differ. Every such position must be changed at least once, and changing each once is sufficient. The answer is therefore the number of 1s in start XOR goal.

Clear the lowest set bit repeatedly with value & (value − 1), counting each removal. Equal inputs produce zero immediately.
steps: Compute the difference mask with start XOR goal.
Count its set bits by clearing one on each iteration.
Return that count.
190.time: O(k) for k differing bits, at most 32 iterations.
pitfalls: Compare aligned bit positions, including leading zeroes.
OR does not identify differences; equal 1 bits must not be counted.

191.problem: Find the value that appears once when every other value appears twice.
191.assumptions: This is the linked Single Number problem. The tracker’s broader odd-occurrence title is also covered: XOR works when exactly one value has odd frequency and every other value has even frequency. It does not identify multiple odd-frequency values separately.

example.explanation: Both 8s cancel and both 6s cancel. Only -3 remains.

191.baseline: Count occurrences in a hash map and return the value with frequency 1. This takes expected O(n) time and O(n) extra space under the linked problem’s guarantee.
191.approach:
XOR has two cancellation rules: a XOR a = 0, and a XOR 0 = a. It also allows values to be regrouped, so matching values do not need to be adjacent. XOR every value into a result starting at zero. Every pair cancels; the unpaired value remains.

For the broader title, an even number of equal values cancels completely, while an odd number leaves one copy. The same reasoning works as long as exactly one value has odd frequency.
steps: Start result at 0.
XOR each array value into it.
Return the remaining value.
pitfalls: The frequency guarantee is necessary; otherwise the XOR result need not be an array element.
Negative values work too because XOR acts on the stored bit patterns.
tests: assert singleNumber(new int[]{8,-3,8,6,6})==-3;assert singleNumber(new int[]{0})==0;assert singleNumber(new int[]{Integer.MIN_VALUE,7,7})==Integer.MIN_VALUE;assert singleNumber(new int[]{2,2,2,4,4})==2;

Random r=new Random(191);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){Set<Integer>used=new HashSet<>();int unique=r.nextInt();used.add(unique);List<Integer>a=new ArrayList<>();a.add(unique);for(int j=0;j<30;j++){int x;do{x=r.nextInt();}while(!used.add(x));a.add(x);a.add(x);}Collections.shuffle(a,r);assert singleNumber(a.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray())==unique;assert singleByCount(a.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray())==unique;}

192.problem: Generate the power set using a bit mask for each subset.
192.assumptions: Input values are distinct and n ≤ 10 in the linked task. Include the empty subset. Result order is unrestricted. This is the bit-manipulation version of the earlier recursion lesson.

example.explanation: Bit 0 chooses the first array element and bit 2 chooses the third. Mask 0 chooses nothing.

192.baseline: The earlier take/skip recursion creates the same 2^n choices. Here each sequence of choices is stored as the bits of an integer.
192.approach:
A subset makes one yes-or-no decision for each array position. An n-bit mask records all those decisions. Enumerate masks from 0 through 2^n − 1. For each mask, inspect every position and add nums[i] when bit i is set.

The first mask creates the empty subset and the last mask creates the full subset. Each mask has a different set of selected positions, so distinct input values give distinct subsets.
steps: Compute the number of masks as 1 << n.
For every mask, create a fresh subset list.
Inspect each bit and include its corresponding value when set.
Add that subset to the answer.
192.space: Up to O(n × 2^n) for the returned subsets; O(n) for the subset currently being built.
pitfalls: Mask bits refer to indices, not to the numeric values stored there.
This int mask implementation relies on the small n constraint. It is not suitable for arrays of length 31 or more.
Repeated input values would produce duplicate value subsets and require a different rule.
tests: for(int n=0;n<=10;n++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=i;List<List<Integer>>actual=subsetsByMask(a);assert actual.size()==1<<n;assert new HashSet<>(actual).size()==actual.size();for(int i=0;i<n;i++){int occurrences=0;for(List<Integer>s:actual)if(s.contains(i))occurrences++;assert occurrences==(1<<(n-1));}}

reference.approach: The public problem statement was checked.
reference.adaptation: The current sheet has no public Java editorial for this entry. This Java uses the standard bit-mask method for the checked task.

193.problem: Find the XOR of every integer in the inclusive interval [left, right].
193.assumptions: Bounds are non-negative. Use long as in the current public Java article. An empty interval with left > right returns 0. This is the XOR of the whole range, not the maximum XOR of two chosen values.

example.explanation: 5 XOR 6 XOR 7 XOR 8 XOR 9 = 5.

193.baseline: Loop from left through right and XOR each value. That takes O(right − left + 1). At Long.MAX_VALUE, a naive value++ loop can wrap, so any such baseline needs an explicit final-value stop.
193.approach:
Let prefix(n) be the XOR from 0 through n. XOR prefix(right) with prefix(left − 1): all values before left appear twice and cancel.

The prefix follows a four-case pattern. If n modulo 4 is 0, 1, 2 or 3, the result is n, 1, n + 1 or 0 respectively. One way to see the repetition is to group four consecutive numbers beginning at a multiple of four; their XOR is zero. Only the final incomplete group contributes. For left = 0, define prefix(−1) as zero.
steps: Handle an empty interval.
Use the four-case rule to calculate each prefix XOR.
XOR the two prefixes to cancel values before left.
pitfalls: Use XOR to cancel the prefix, not arithmetic subtraction.
The right endpoint is included.
Handle left = 0 without treating a negative prefix as a real range.

reference.title: XOR of Numbers in a Range L to R
reference.approach: Cancel two prefix XORs; calculate each prefix with its four-case cycle.
reference.adaptation: The public Java loop and constant-time methods were checked. The final method follows the same long-based formula. Tests additionally cover Long.MAX_VALUE without using an overflowing baseline loop.

194.problem: Find the two values that appear once when every other value appears twice, and return them in ascending order.
194.assumptions: The tracker’s TUF practice link requires ascending order, although the current public article permits either order. The broader title also works for exactly two odd-frequency values with all others even. The input is unchanged.

example.explanation: The pairs cancel. A bit on which -2 and 9 differ separates them into different groups.

194.baseline: Count values in a hash map and collect the two frequencies equal to 1. This uses expected O(n) time and O(n) storage.
194.approach:
XOR the whole array. Every pair cancels, leaving a XOR b for the two missing partners. Since a and b differ, this XOR has at least one set bit. Isolate its lowest set bit with combined & -combined.

Split values according to that bit and XOR each group separately. Equal values always enter the same group and cancel. The two unique values have different values at the chosen bit, so one remains in each group. Finally put the smaller value first to satisfy the tracker’s practice link.
steps: XOR all values to obtain the XOR of the two answers.
Isolate one set bit as a mask.
XOR values into two groups according to that mask.
Return the two group results in ascending order.
pitfalls: Use (value & mask) != 0, not > 0: the selected bit may be the sign bit.
Java’s fixed-width arithmetic makes combined & -combined work even when combined is Integer.MIN_VALUE.
Returning combined alone gives a XOR b, not either individual answer.
The final ascending order is required by the tracker’s practice problem.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(twoSingleNumbers(new int[]{4,9,4,-2,7,7}),new int[]{-2,9});assert Arrays.equals(twoSingleNumbers(new int[]{Integer.MIN_VALUE,0}),new int[]{Integer.MIN_VALUE,0});

Random r=new Random(194);for(int t=0;t<1000;t++){int a=r.nextInt(),b;do{b=r.nextInt();}while(a==b);Set<Integer>used=new HashSet<>(List.of(a,b));List<Integer>values=new ArrayList<>(List.of(a,b));for(int j=0;j<15;j++){int x;do{x=r.nextInt();}while(!used.add(x));values.add(x);values.add(x);}Collections.shuffle(values,r);assert Arrays.equals(twoSingleNumbers(values.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray()),new int[]{Math.min(a,b),Math.max(a,b)});}

reference.title: Single Number III
reference.approach: XOR cancellation, lowest differing bit, then XOR each group.
reference.adaptation: The public Java code was checked. The tracker’s linked practice statement additionally requires ascending output, so this implementation orders the two results. Sign-bit cases are tested.

195.problem: List a number’s prime factors in ascending order, keeping repetitions, and apply that helper to the tracker’s query array.
195.assumptions: The title is about one number, but its TUF practice link accepts many numbers. A factor such as 2 appears three times for 8. Source queries are between 2 and 200,000. The single-number helper also returns an empty list for 1.

example.explanation: Multiplying each row’s factors reconstructs its original number.

195.baseline: Try every integer from 2 through the number and keep dividing while it is a factor. Testing only through the square root of the remaining number avoids unnecessary larger trials.
195.approach:
Try divisors in increasing order. Whenever one divides the remaining number, save it and divide it out repeatedly. By the time a composite divisor is reached, its smaller prime factors have already been removed, so it cannot add a new composite factor.

Stop when divisor is larger than remaining/divisor. If anything greater than 1 remains, it must be prime: a composite remainder would have had a factor at or below its square root. This trial-division lesson is useful for one number or a small batch. For the linked task’s large batch of up to 100,000 queries, use the smallest-prime-factor sieve in the later guide.
steps: Start divisor at 2.
While divisor divides the remaining number, record it and divide it out.
Advance divisor while it is at most the square root of the remainder.
Append the remaining prime if it is greater than 1.
Run the helper for each query.
195.time: O(√x) per number x in the worst case; O(q × √M) for q queries bounded by M. Use the later sieve method for the large-query limit.
195.space: O(log x) output factors per number, with O(1) other working space.
pitfalls: Keep dividing by the same prime to retain its repeated factors.
Do not return only distinct prime divisors for this linked task.
Use divisor <= number/divisor to avoid an overflowing divisor × divisor comparison.
Trial division is the teaching method here; preprocessing is preferable for many queries.
tests: for(int n=2;n<=5000;n++){List<Integer>f=primeFactors(n);long product=1;int previous=0;for(int x:f){assert x>=previous;previous=x;product*=x;assert BigInteger.valueOf(x).isProbablePrime(50);}assert product==n;}

reference.title: Prime factorisation of a Number
reference.approach: Return sorted prime factors, including repeated factors, for each input query.
reference.adaptation: The public practice statement was checked. It takes an array of queries, despite this tracker lesson’s singular title. No public Java editorial is linked; the code below implements the stated task.

196.problem: Return every positive divisor of n in ascending order.
196.assumptions: The tracker’s practice link asks for a list. The current linked Striver article instead counts divisors; we use its divisor-pair reasoning and collect the actual values. The source requires n ≥ 1.

example.explanation: The pairs are (1,18), (2,9), and (3,6). Searching the smaller side finds every pair.

196.baseline: Test every value from 1 through n and collect those that divide evenly. This takes O(n) and already gives sorted output.
196.approach:
Whenever d divides n, n/d is also a divisor. At least one member of each pair is no greater than √n, so only search that far. Add both members, except when they are equal at a perfect square.

The values arrive in pairs rather than sorted order. Sort the collected list before returning it, as the tracker’s practice problem requires. Using d <= n/d avoids multiplying d by itself near the int limit.
steps: Try d from 1 while d <= n/d.
If d divides n, add d and its partner n/d.
Add the partner only if it differs from d.
Sort the list and return it.
196.time: O(√n + k log k), where k is the number of divisors; the second term sorts the result.
196.space: O(k) for the returned list and sorting storage.
pitfalls: Count a square root only once.
One has the single divisor 1.
The count-only article cannot be submitted unchanged to a task requiring a sorted list.

reference.title: Count Divisors
reference.approach: Search divisor pairs up to the square root and avoid repeating the square root.
reference.adaptation: The public Java article counts divisors, while the tracker’s practice link requires their sorted list. This explicitly adapts the same pair search to collect and sort values, with an overflow-safe loop bound.

197.problem: Count the prime numbers strictly smaller than n using the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
197.assumptions: The tracker links to LeetCode Count Primes: n itself is excluded. The similarly named current TUF practice page counts through n inclusively, so its endpoint rule is different. Source n is from 0 through 5,000,000. Zero and one are not prime.

example.explanation: The primes below 11 are 2, 3, 5 and 7. Do not count 11 itself.

197.baseline: Check each number below n for divisors up to its square root. That takes O(n√n). A sieve shares the work by marking multiples of each prime.
197.approach:
Start with every number unmarked. When p is still unmarked, it is prime, and all its multiples from p² onward are composite. Smaller multiples already have a smaller prime factor and were handled earlier.

Only p with p² < n need marking work. Every composite below n has a prime factor no larger than its square root. Finally count unmarked values from 2 through n − 1. Allocate exactly n slots so the exclusive upper limit is clear.
steps: Return 0 when n ≤ 2.
Create a boolean composite array of length n.
For each unmarked p with p² < n, mark p², p² + p, and so on.
Count unmarked indices beginning at 2 and ending before n.
pitfalls: Strictly below n is different from at most n. Prime endpoints expose the difference.
Do not count array slots 0 or 1.
Start marking at p², not p, or the prime marks itself composite.
tests: assert countPrimes(0)==0;assert countPrimes(1)==0;assert countPrimes(2)==0;assert countPrimes(3)==1;assert countPrimes(11)==4;assert countPrimes(12)==5;

198.problem: Precompute the smallest prime factor of every number up to the largest query, then factor each query quickly.
198.assumptions: The tracker links to the same batch-factorization task as the earlier trial-division lesson. Return sorted factors with multiplicity for each query. Up to 100,000 queries can each be at most 200,000. The helper also returns no factors for 1.

example.explanation: For 45, repeatedly use its smallest prime factor: 45 → 15 → 5 → 1.

198.baseline: Trial-divide each query separately, taking O(q√M) in the worst case. Many queries repeat the same factor checks. A shared table avoids repeating that work.
198.approach:
Let smallest[x] store the smallest prime that divides x. Initially set smallest[x] = x. A number still holding itself when its turn arrives is prime. Visit its multiples starting at its square and fill only entries that have not already received a smaller prime.

To factor a query, append smallest[value] and divide by it until value becomes 1. Each division removes at least a factor of two, so there are only logarithmically many steps. The smallest factor rule naturally emits factors in ascending order.
steps: Find the largest query and initialize the smallest-factor table.
For each prime p, fill previously untouched multiples from p² onward.
For each query, repeatedly record smallest[value] and divide by it.
Keep a separate factor list for every query.
198.time: O(M log log M + q log M), where M is the largest query and q is the number of queries.
198.space: O(M) for preprocessing, plus the returned factors.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite a smaller factor found by an earlier prime.
A prime number must point to itself in the table.
Repeated queries need separate output lists, even when their contents are equal.
This table is intended for the stated maximum of 200,000, not arbitrary enormous integers.
tests: int[]queries={200000,199999,131072};List<List<Integer>>result=factorWithSieve(queries);for(int i=0;i<queries.length;i++){long product=1;int last=0;for(int x:result.get(i)){assert x>=last;last=x;assert BigInteger.valueOf(x).isProbablePrime(50);product*=x;}assert product==queries[i];}

reference.approach: Return sorted prime factors, including repeated factors, for each input query.
reference.adaptation: The public practice statement was checked. It takes an array of queries, despite this tracker lesson’s singular title. No public Java editorial is linked; the code below implements the stated task.

199.problem: Calculate x^n by reading the exponent’s binary digits.
199.assumptions: This tracker entry repeats Pow(x,n) in the maths/bit section. Use the same signed-int exponent contract as the earlier recursion guide. Negative powers mean reciprocals; zero is excluded when the exponent is non-positive.

example.explanation: Use the power blocks 3^1 and 3^4 because bits 0 and 2 are set. Their product is 3^5.

199.baseline: Multiply x by itself once per exponent unit. This takes O(|n|) and cannot handle a two-billion-step exponent efficiently.
199.approach:
Each set bit in the exponent selects a power block. Start with base x. After each step, square it so the next block represents x², then x⁴, then x⁸, and so on. If the current low bit of the exponent is 1, multiply that block into the result.

Shift the non-negative exponent right after each step. For a negative exponent, first use the reciprocal base and negate the exponent after widening it to long. This avoids overflowing when n is Integer.MIN_VALUE.
steps: Widen n to long and convert a negative exponent into a reciprocal base with a positive exponent.
Start the result at 1.
Multiply in the current base when the exponent’s low bit is set.
Square the base and shift the exponent right.
pitfalls: The exponent must be made non-negative before using this right-shift loop.
Convert to long before negating the minimum int.
Floating-point multiplication introduces rounding; test approximate results with a tolerance.
tests: assert myPow(3,5)==243;assert myPow(2,-3)==0.125;assert myPow(-1,Integer.MIN_VALUE)==1;assert myPow(2,Integer.MIN_VALUE)==0;assert myPow(4,0)==1;

reference.title: Pow(x,n)
reference.approach: Binary exponentiation with a long exponent and reciprocal handling for negative powers.
reference.adaptation: The public practice contract and linked LeetCode task were checked. No public Java editorial is linked. This repeats the earlier power problem with the exponent’s bit representation made explicit.

200.problem: Implement a last-in, first-out stack using an array.
200.assumptions: The practice API is push, pop, top and isEmpty. At most 100 calls are made, so the no-argument constructor uses capacity 100. An optional capacity constructor makes full-stack behaviour testable. This version throws on overflow or empty pop/top; the article prints messages instead.

example.explanation: The most recently pushed value, 9, is read and removed first. Reading top alone does not remove it.

200.baseline: Keeping the top at array index 0 would require shifting existing values on insertion or removal. Keep the top at the end of the occupied part instead.
200.approach:
Use topIndex to remember the last occupied slot. It starts at −1, meaning the stack is empty. A push moves it forward and writes the value. A pop reads the value and moves it backward. Old numbers can remain in unused slots; only indices through topIndex belong to the stack.

The size is topIndex + 1. Check the array boundary before pushing and the empty state before reading. A failed operation must leave the stack exactly as it was.
steps: Create the fixed array and set topIndex to −1.
On push, reject a full stack, then increment the index and store the value.
On pop, reject an empty stack, return its top value and decrement the index.
On top, read the same value without changing the index.
200.time: O(1) per operation; construction allocates and zero-initializes O(capacity) storage.
pitfalls: Increment before writing on push; read before decrementing on pop.
top() must not change the size.
Java judge scaffolding may require removing static when pasting the nested class as a top-level class.
The default capacity follows the stated call limit, not an unlimited-stack guarantee.
tests: ArrayStack s=new ArrayStack();s.push(4);s.push(9);assert s.top()==9&&s.size()==2;assert s.pop()==9;assert s.top()==4;assert s.pop()==4;assert s.isEmpty();

ArrayStack s=new ArrayStack(1);s.push(7);boolean full=false;try{s.push(8);}catch(IllegalStateException e){full=true;}assert full&&s.size()==1&&s.top()==7;s.pop();boolean empty=false;try{s.pop();}catch(NoSuchElementException e){empty=true;}assert empty&&s.isEmpty();try{s.top();assert false;}catch(NoSuchElementException expected){}

Random r=new Random(200);ArrayStack actual=new ArrayStack(50);Deque<Integer>expected=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int i=0;i<10000;i++){if(expected.isEmpty()||(expected.size()<50&&r.nextBoolean())){int value=r.nextInt();actual.push(value);expected.push(value);}else assert actual.pop()==expected.pop();assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert actual.isEmpty()==expected.isEmpty();if(!expected.isEmpty())assert actual.top()==expected.peek();}

reference.title: Implement a Stack Using an Array
reference.approach: Fixed array with a top index starting at −1.
reference.adaptation: The public Java and practice API were checked. The article logs operation results; this class returns values as the judge expects. top() replaces the article’s peek name. Overflow and underflow use exceptions, and the default capacity covers the 100-call practice limit.

201.problem: Implement a first-in, first-out queue using a circular array.
201.assumptions: The practice API is push, pop, peek and isEmpty. Its no-argument constructor and at-most-100-call limit are supported with capacity 100. This follows the public article’s boundary behaviour: a full push is ignored, and empty pop/peek return −1. Practice values are positive, so −1 is unambiguous.

example.input: capacity = 3; push(4), push(8), pop(), push(2), push(6)
example.explanation: Removing 4 frees index 0. The later push wraps around to reuse that slot without moving 8 or 2.

201.baseline: Keep the front at index 0 and shift every remaining value left after each pop. Push and peek are O(1), but pop is O(n).
201.approach:
Keep front at the oldest value and rear at the next insertion slot. After using an index, advance it modulo the capacity so it wraps to zero at the end. Store count separately: front and rear can be equal when the queue is empty or full.

Only count active values belong to the queue. A popped value may remain physically in the array, but it is outside the active range and will be overwritten later. Checking full or empty before index arithmetic also makes capacity zero safe.
steps: Initialize front, rear and count to zero.
On push, return if full; otherwise write at rear, advance rear and increase count.
On pop, return −1 if empty; otherwise read front, advance it and decrease count.
peek reads front without moving it; isEmpty checks count.
201.time: O(1) per operation; array construction takes O(capacity).
pitfalls: front == rear alone cannot distinguish full from empty in this design.
Advance indices with modulo to reuse freed slots.
A failed full push must not overwrite the oldest value.
The −1 sentinel follows this article; a general-purpose queue allowing all int values should expose emptiness separately or throw.
tests: ArrayQueue q=new ArrayQueue(3);q.push(4);q.push(8);assert q.pop()==4;q.push(2);q.push(6);q.push(99);assert q.size()==3;assert q.pop()==8;assert q.pop()==2;assert q.pop()==6;assert q.pop()==-1&&q.peek()==-1&&q.isEmpty();

ArrayQueue q=new ArrayQueue(0);q.push(1);assert q.isEmpty()&&q.pop()==-1;ArrayQueue single=new ArrayQueue(1);for(int i=1;i<=100;i++){single.push(i);assert single.peek()==i;assert single.pop()==i;assert single.isEmpty();}

Random r=new Random(201);for(int cap=1;cap<=20;cap++){ArrayQueue actual=new ArrayQueue(cap);Deque<Integer>expected=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int t=0;t<2000;t++){if(r.nextBoolean()){int x=1+r.nextInt(100);actual.push(x);if(expected.size()<cap)expected.add(x);}else{int x=expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.remove();assert actual.pop()==x;}assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert actual.peek()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.peek());assert actual.isEmpty()==expected.isEmpty();}}

reference.title: Implement a Queue Using an Array
reference.approach: Shifting-array baseline and circular-array implementation with front, rear and size.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods and the practice API were checked. This follows the circular method and its full/empty behaviour. The class and isEmpty method use the practice names, with a default capacity covering its 100-call limit.

202.problem: Implement a stack using only standard queue operations, with one queue.
202.assumptions: The tracker links to LeetCode MyStack with push, pop, top and empty. Its follow-up asks for one queue; the TUF practice version asks for one queue directly. Only enqueue at the back, remove/read at the front, size and emptiness are used. Pop/top calls are valid in the linked task.

example.explanation: After each push, move older values behind the new value. The queue front then represents the stack top.

202.baseline: With two queues, put the new value into an empty helper queue, move the old queue behind it, then swap queue roles. One queue can do the same rearrangement by rotating its older values.
202.approach:
Before insertion, remember how many values are in the queue. Append the new value at the back, then move exactly that many old values from front to back. The new value arrives at the front while the previous stack order stays behind it.

Now pop and top can use the queue front directly. Push pays for the rotation; removal does not need another rearrangement.
steps: Record the old queue size.
Enqueue the new value.
Repeat oldSize times: dequeue the front and enqueue it at the back.
Use the front for pop and top; test queue emptiness for empty.
202.time: O(n) for push, O(1) for pop, top and empty.
pitfalls: Rotate only the old values, not the new total size, or the new value returns to the back.
Do not use removeLast or push on the underlying deque; those would bypass the queue-only rule.
This code uses the linked LeetCode names; TUF calls the class QueueStack and its emptiness method isEmpty.
tests: MyStack s=new MyStack();s.push(3);s.push(8);s.push(5);assert s.pop()==5;assert s.top()==8;assert s.pop()==8;assert s.pop()==3;assert s.empty();

Random r=new Random(202);MyStack actual=new MyStack();Deque<Integer>expected=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int t=0;t<5000;t++){if(expected.isEmpty()||(expected.size()<100&&r.nextBoolean())){int x=r.nextInt();actual.push(x);expected.push(x);}else assert actual.pop()==expected.pop();assert actual.empty()==expected.isEmpty();if(!expected.isEmpty())assert actual.top()==expected.peek();}

reference.title: Implement Stack using Queue
reference.approach: One queue, rotated after each push so the newest value reaches the front.
reference.adaptation: The public practice task and linked LeetCode contract were checked. No public Java editorial is linked. The class uses LeetCode’s MyStack/empty names and only FIFO queue operations.

203.problem: Implement a queue with two stacks, making operations constant time on average across a sequence.
203.assumptions: Use only stack push, pop, peek and emptiness checks. The tracker’s LeetCode class is MyQueue. Valid pop/peek calls are guaranteed there; this version also returns −1 when empty, following the public article.

example.input: push(4), push(7), peek(), push(9), pop(), pop(), pop()
example.explanation: The new 9 must wait behind both older values, even after peek has moved them to the output stack.

203.baseline: Before every push, move old values aside, put the new value below them, and move them back. This makes push O(n) while pop and peek stay O(1).
203.approach:
Use incoming for new values and outgoing for values ready to leave. Popping everything from incoming into outgoing reverses the order, putting the oldest value on top.

Do that transfer only when outgoing is empty. If it already contains values, they are older than anything waiting in incoming and must leave first. Each value is pushed into incoming once, transferred once, and removed once. A particular pop or peek may do a large transfer, but the total work across many operations is linear in the number of inserted values.
steps: Push new values into incoming.
Before pop or peek, transfer incoming to outgoing only if outgoing is empty.
Read or remove the top of outgoing.
The queue is empty only when both stacks are empty.
203.time: Push and empty are O(1). Pop/peek are O(n) in the worst case but amortized O(1): each value transfers at most once.
pitfalls: Never transfer onto a non-empty outgoing stack; that would place newer values before older ones.
peek may transfer values but must not remove the front.
Amortized O(1) does not mean every individual call is O(1).
tests: MyQueue q=new MyQueue();q.push(4);q.push(7);assert q.peek()==4;q.push(9);assert q.peek()==4;assert q.pop()==4;assert q.pop()==7;assert q.pop()==9;assert q.empty();assert q.pop()==-1&&q.peek()==-1;

Random r=new Random(203);MyQueue actual=new MyQueue();Deque<Integer>expected=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int t=0;t<10000;t++){int op=r.nextInt(3);if(op==0){int x=r.nextInt();actual.push(x);expected.add(x);}else if(op==1)assert actual.pop()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.remove());else assert actual.peek()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.peek());assert actual.empty()==expected.isEmpty();}

reference.title: Implement a Queue Using Stacks
reference.approach: Two stacks with transfer only when the output stack is empty.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. This uses ArrayDeque through stack-only operations instead of legacy Stack, and uses the linked LeetCode MyQueue class name.

204.problem: Implement a stack with a singly linked list, using the head as the stack top.
204.assumptions: The practice class is LinkedListStack with push, pop, top and isEmpty. A size method is also included to show the article’s counter. Empty pop/top return −1 as in the public article. The practice stores positive values.

example.explanation: Pushing 6 adds a new head before 2. Popping removes that head and exposes 2 again.

204.baseline: Putting the top at a singly linked list’s tail would make removal expensive: finding its predecessor requires a traversal. The head supports both insertion and removal directly.
204.approach:
Keep a reference to the first node. To push, create a node whose next points to the old head, then make it the new head. To pop, save the head’s value and move head to head.next. No search is needed.

Maintain a count alongside the head so size is also constant time. Removing the last node naturally sets head to null. A later push works exactly like the first one.
steps: Start with a null head and count 0.
Push by linking a new node before the head.
Pop by moving the head forward, after saving its value.
Read the head for top; update count only on successful insertions/removals.
pitfalls: Link the new node to the old head before replacing the head.
Do not decrement count on an unsuccessful pop.
Java collects unreachable nodes; no manual delete statement is needed.
There is no fixed array capacity, but available memory still limits the number of nodes.
tests: LinkedListStack s=new LinkedListStack();assert s.pop()==-1&&s.top()==-1;s.push(2);s.push(6);assert s.pop()==6;assert s.top()==2;assert s.size()==1;assert s.pop()==2&&s.isEmpty();s.push(8);assert s.pop()==8;

Random r=new Random(204);LinkedListStack actual=new LinkedListStack();Deque<Integer>expected=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int t=0;t<10000;t++){if(r.nextBoolean()){int x=1+r.nextInt(100);actual.push(x);expected.push(x);}else assert actual.pop()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.pop());assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert actual.top()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.peek());assert actual.isEmpty()==expected.isEmpty();}

205.problem: Implement a first-in, first-out queue with a singly linked list.
205.assumptions: The practice class is LinkedListQueue with push, pop, peek and isEmpty. Use a head for removal and a tail for insertion. This helper returns −1 for empty pop/peek; practice values are positive. A size method is included.

example.input: push(2), push(6), pop(), push(9), pop(), pop()
example.explanation: Values leave in arrival order. The tail lets 9 be attached without walking through the list.

205.baseline: With only a head reference, adding at the end requires an O(n) traversal. Keep the tail as well so appending is constant time.
205.approach:
Head points to the oldest node and tail to the newest. A push appends a new node after tail, then moves tail to it. If the queue was empty, that node must become both head and tail.

A pop moves head to its next node. When that removes the final node, set tail to null too. Otherwise a stale tail would refer to a node that is no longer in the queue and complicate the next insertion.
steps: Start with both head and tail null.
On push, append after tail, or set head when inserting into an empty queue.
Set tail to the new node.
On pop, move head forward; clear tail if head becomes null.
Read head for peek and maintain count on successful changes.
pitfalls: Appending at the head would make this a stack.
After removing the last node, clear both ends of the queue.
peek must preserve head and count.
tests: LinkedListQueue q=new LinkedListQueue();q.push(2);q.push(6);assert q.pop()==2;q.push(9);assert q.pop()==6;assert q.pop()==9;assert q.isEmpty()&&q.size()==0;for(int i=1;i<=100;i++){q.push(i);assert q.peek()==i;assert q.pop()==i;assert q.isEmpty();}assert q.pop()==-1;

Random r=new Random(205);LinkedListQueue actual=new LinkedListQueue();Deque<Integer>expected=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int t=0;t<10000;t++){if(r.nextBoolean()){int x=1+r.nextInt(100);actual.push(x);expected.add(x);}else assert actual.pop()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.remove());assert actual.size()==expected.size();assert actual.peek()==(expected.isEmpty()?-1:expected.peek());assert actual.isEmpty()==expected.isEmpty();}

206.problem: Check whether round, square and curly brackets are correctly paired and nested.
206.assumptions: The linked task contains only ()[]{}. Every opening bracket needs the same type of closing bracket, in reverse nesting order. The helper also accepts the empty string as balanced and rejects other characters.

example.explanation: Close the innermost { first, then (, then [. The string [(]) has equal counts but the wrong closing order.

206.baseline: Repeatedly remove adjacent (), [] and {} pairs until none remain. An empty result means balanced, but repeated string scans and copies can take O(n²).
206.approach:
The latest unmatched opening bracket must close first. Push opening brackets onto a stack. For a closing bracket, require a matching opening bracket at the top and remove it. An empty stack at that moment means there was nothing to close.

After reading the whole string, the stack must be empty. Otherwise some opening brackets never received a closing partner. Counting each bracket type cannot check the nesting order, which is why a stack is needed.
steps: Push each opening bracket.
For a closing bracket, reject an empty stack or a different opening type on top.
Pop a correctly matched opening bracket.
At the end, accept only if no openings remain.
206.space: O(n) in the worst case when many openings are waiting.
pitfalls: Matching counts do not guarantee matching nesting.
A closing bracket at the start is invalid.
Do not forget to check for leftover opening brackets at the end.
tests: String alphabet="()[]{}";for(int length=0;length<=6;length++){int possibilities=1;for(int i=0;i<length;i++)possibilities*=6;for(int encoded=0;encoded<possibilities;encoded++){int value=encoded;StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<length;i++){b.append(alphabet.charAt(value%6));value/=6;}String s=b.toString(),reduced=s;while(true){String next=reduced.replace("()","").replace("[]","").replace("{}","");if(next.equals(reduced))break;reduced=next;}assert isValid(s)==reduced.isEmpty();}}

reference.title: Check Balanced Parentheses Using a Stack
reference.approach: Push unmatched openings and match each closing bracket against the stack top.
reference.adaptation: The public Java was checked. This follows the same stack method using ArrayDeque instead of legacy Stack and the linked LeetCode isValid method name. It additionally rejects characters outside the stated bracket alphabet.

207.problem: Implement a stack whose push, pop, top and getMin operations all take constant time.
207.assumptions: Pop, top and getMin are called only on a non-empty stack. The tracker links to LeetCode, which permits the full signed-int value range. The encoded method therefore stores long values internally. It returns int values to callers.

example.input: push(5), push(2), push(2), pop(), getMin(), pop(), getMin()
example.explanation: Removing one copy of the minimum must leave the other copy active. Removing the last 2 restores the previous minimum, 5.

207.baseline: Save a pair at each level: the pushed value and the minimum through that level. Then the top pair always knows the current minimum. This is a straightforward O(1)-per-operation solution with O(n) storage; the PairMinStack code is included.
207.approach:
The final version stores one number per level and keeps the current minimum separately. A value at least as large as the minimum is stored normally. When a smaller x arrives, store 2×x − oldMinimum instead, then make x the new minimum. This stored marker is smaller than x, so it can later be recognized by being below the current minimum.

When a marker reaches the top, the actual top value is the current minimum. Popping it restores oldMinimum = 2×currentMinimum − marker. Equal minima are stored normally, so duplicate minima work without special counting. Use long for this arithmetic: a marker can lie outside the int range even though every real pushed value fits.
steps: For the first value, store it and set the minimum.
For a new smaller value, store its encoded marker and update the minimum. Otherwise store it normally.
For top, return the current minimum when the stored top is below it.
For pop, restore the previous minimum if the removed value is a marker.
Return the maintained minimum for getMin.
207.space: O(n) for the stack and O(1) additional minimum state. Encoding does not make the total storage O(1).
pitfalls: Use long for the marker arithmetic to cover the linked full-int range.
A normal value equal to the minimum is not a marker; use a strict < comparison.
On an empty-to-non-empty push, replace the old minimum state.
The pair method is often easier to explain; both methods have the same O(n) total space complexity.
tests: Random r=new Random(207);MinStack encoded=new MinStack();PairMinStack paired=new PairMinStack();List<Integer>expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int t=0;t<10000;t++){if(expected.isEmpty()||(expected.size()<200&&r.nextBoolean())){int value=t%7==0?Integer.MIN_VALUE:t%11==0?Integer.MAX_VALUE:r.nextInt();encoded.push(value);paired.push(value);expected.add(value);}else{encoded.pop();paired.pop();expected.remove(expected.size()-1);}if(!expected.isEmpty()){int min=Collections.min(expected),top=expected.get(expected.size()-1);assert encoded.getMin()==min&&paired.getMin()==min;assert encoded.top()==top&&paired.top()==top;}}

208.problem: Convert an infix expression, where operators sit between operands, into postfix, where each operator follows its operands.
208.assumptions: Input is valid, has no spaces, and uses single lowercase letters or single digits. Operators are +, −, *, / and ^. Here ^ means exponentiation in the expression language, not Java XOR. Exponentiation groups right-to-left; the other operators group left-to-right.

example.explanation: Write b and c before their multiplication operator, then put the addition after its two inputs a and bc*.

208.baseline: An expression tree can represent precedence explicitly, then a postorder traversal produces postfix. An operator stack can produce the same output without storing the full tree.
208.approach:
Operands can go straight into the output. Operators wait on a stack until their right operand has been read. Before pushing a new operator, output any waiting operator with higher precedence. Also output equal-precedence operators when the new operator is left-associative.

Do not pop an equal ^ when another ^ arrives: a^b^c means a^(b^c), so the later exponentiation must appear first in postfix. An opening parenthesis marks a boundary. A closing parenthesis flushes operators back to that boundary, and both parentheses disappear from the output.
steps: Append operands immediately.
Push opening parentheses. On a closing parenthesis, pop until its opening parenthesis.
For an operator, pop higher-precedence operators and equal-precedence left-associative ones.
Push the new operator.
After the scan, append all remaining operators.
208.time: O(n): every operator is pushed and popped at most once.
208.space: O(n) for the stack and output.
pitfalls: Equal-precedence handling differs for ^.
Discard parentheses rather than copying them into postfix.
This parser follows the stated single-character, binary-operator grammar; it does not parse unary minus or multi-digit numbers.

209.problem: Convert prefix into fully parenthesized infix without changing operand order.
209.assumptions: The expression is valid and has single-character lowercase-letter or digit operands and binary operators +, −, *, /, ^. Every operator is placed before its two operands in prefix.

example.explanation: The outer operator is subtraction: its left operand is a and its right operand is the multiplication of b and c.

209.baseline: Parse a tree recursively from left to right, then print an opening parenthesis, left child, operator, right child and closing parenthesis for each internal node. A right-to-left stack scan performs the same assembly.
209.approach:
Scan from right to left so both operands are ready when their operator is encountered. Push an operand as a one-character string. For an operator, the first popped expression is the left operand and the second is the right operand. Combine them as (left operator right) and push the result.

Parenthesize every combination, even when normal precedence would make some parentheses optional. This preserves the exact expression structure and matches the task’s required format.
steps: Scan the prefix string from its final character toward the first.
Push operands.
For an operator, pop left first, then right.
Push the parenthesized combination.
Return the one expression left on the stack.
209.time: O(n²) in the worst case because Java string concatenation copies growing subexpressions. Stack operations alone are O(n).
209.space: O(n) live expression and stack storage; total temporary allocation can be O(n²).
pitfalls: In a right-to-left prefix scan, the first pop is the left operand.
Subtraction and division reveal accidental operand reversal.
Do not claim linear time for this string-building version. A tree plus one final traversal can achieve O(n).
tests: Random r=new Random(209);for(int trial=0;trial<200;trial++){List<String>in=new ArrayList<>(),pre=new ArrayList<>(),post=new ArrayList<>();for(char ch='a';ch<='h';ch++){in.add(""+ch);pre.add(""+ch);post.add(""+ch);}while(in.size()>1){int i=r.nextInt(in.size()-1);char op="+-*/".charAt(r.nextInt(4));String joined="("+in.get(i)+op+in.get(i+1)+")";String prefix=op+pre.get(i)+pre.get(i+1),postfix=post.get(i)+post.get(i+1)+op;in.set(i,joined);pre.set(i,prefix);post.set(i,postfix);in.remove(i+1);pre.remove(i+1);post.remove(i+1);}assert prefixToInfix(pre.get(0)).equals(in.get(0));}

210.problem: Convert a prefix expression into postfix notation.
210.assumptions: The input is valid and uses single-character operands and binary +, −, *, /, ^ operators. No spaces or separators are needed.

example.explanation: The expression is (a+b)/c. The addition follows a and b, then division follows that result and c.

210.baseline: Build an expression tree from prefix and print it in postorder. The stack version stores already-converted subexpressions instead of tree nodes.
210.approach:
Read prefix from right to left. An operand is already a valid postfix expression, so push it. At an operator, pop the left expression first and the right expression second. Postfix places both operands before the operator, so combine left + right + operator.

Each combined string represents one whole subexpression. When the scan finishes, the stack has one string for the full input.
steps: Scan right to left.
Push single operands.
For each operator, pop left then right.
Push left followed by right followed by the operator.
210.time: O(n²) worst-case time from copying concatenated strings.
210.space: O(n) live storage; up to O(n²) total temporary allocation.
pitfalls: The first popped expression is left, not right, for this scan direction.
Do not add parentheses to postfix output.
Adjacent digits are separate one-character operands under this grammar.
tests: Random r=new Random(210);for(int trial=0;trial<200;trial++){List<String>in=new ArrayList<>(),pre=new ArrayList<>(),post=new ArrayList<>();for(char ch='a';ch<='h';ch++){in.add(""+ch);pre.add(""+ch);post.add(""+ch);}while(in.size()>1){int i=r.nextInt(in.size()-1);char op="+-*/".charAt(r.nextInt(4));String joined="("+in.get(i)+op+in.get(i+1)+")";String prefix=op+pre.get(i)+pre.get(i+1),postfix=post.get(i)+post.get(i+1)+op;in.set(i,joined);pre.set(i,prefix);post.set(i,postfix);in.remove(i+1);pre.remove(i+1);post.remove(i+1);}assert prefixToPostfix(pre.get(0)).equals(post.get(0));}

211.problem: Convert a postfix expression into prefix notation.
211.assumptions: The linked problem guarantees valid single-letter lowercase operands and binary +, −, *, / operators. The helper also supports single-digit operands and ^ without changing the method.

example.explanation: The expression is (a−b)/c. In prefix the outer division comes first, followed by its two operands.

211.baseline: Construct the expression tree while scanning postfix, then traverse it in preorder. The stack version builds the prefix string directly at each operator.
211.approach:
Read postfix from left to right. Both operands appear before their operator, so they are already on the stack. The most recently pushed expression is the right operand; pop it first, then pop the left operand.

Prefix puts the operator first, followed by the left and right expressions. Push that combination so it can become an operand of a later operator.
steps: Scan from left to right and push operands.
At an operator, pop right first and left second.
Push operator + left + right.
Return the final stack entry.
211.time: O(n²) worst-case time because repeated string concatenation copies existing text.
211.space: O(n) live storage; O(n²) temporary allocation in the worst case.
pitfalls: Postfix scanning pops right before left, the reverse of the right-to-left prefix scan.
Changing operand order breaks subtraction and division.
The task assumes valid input; the method does not validate malformed operator/operand counts.
tests: Random r=new Random(211);for(int trial=0;trial<200;trial++){List<String>in=new ArrayList<>(),pre=new ArrayList<>(),post=new ArrayList<>();for(char ch='a';ch<='h';ch++){in.add(""+ch);pre.add(""+ch);post.add(""+ch);}while(in.size()>1){int i=r.nextInt(in.size()-1);char op="+-*/".charAt(r.nextInt(4));String joined="("+in.get(i)+op+in.get(i+1)+")";String prefix=op+pre.get(i)+pre.get(i+1),postfix=post.get(i)+post.get(i+1)+op;in.set(i,joined);pre.set(i,prefix);post.set(i,postfix);in.remove(i+1);pre.remove(i+1);post.remove(i+1);}assert postfixToPrefix(post.get(0)).equals(pre.get(0));}

212.problem: Convert postfix notation into fully parenthesized infix.
212.assumptions: The tracker’s HackerRank page has contradictory input/output prose, but its title and sample convert ab*c+ into ((a*b)+c). This guide follows that sample and the matching current TUF task: valid, unspaced, single-character operands and binary operators. It is not a space-separated multi-digit parser.

example.explanation: The division is completed first. Its result becomes the left side of the subtraction.

212.baseline: Build a tree from postfix and print it in infix order with parentheses around each operator node. A string stack performs those combinations directly.
212.approach:
An operand becomes a one-character expression on the stack. On an operator, pop the right expression first, then the left. Combine them inside parentheses with the operator between them.

The parentheses preserve exactly which results feed the next operator, so no precedence rule needs to be guessed. The final stack entry is the whole expression.
steps: Read left to right.
Push operands as strings.
On an operator, pop right and then left.
Push (left operator right).
Return the completed expression.
212.time: O(n²) worst-case time due to copying growing strings.
212.space: O(n) live stack/output storage, with potentially O(n²) temporary allocation.
pitfalls: The first popped expression is the right operand.
Keep the parentheses around every combined subexpression.
The old contest page’s format prose conflicts with its sample; use the sample-compatible single-character contract stated here.
tests: Random r=new Random(212);for(int trial=0;trial<200;trial++){List<String>in=new ArrayList<>(),pre=new ArrayList<>(),post=new ArrayList<>();for(char ch='a';ch<='h';ch++){in.add(""+ch);pre.add(""+ch);post.add(""+ch);}while(in.size()>1){int i=r.nextInt(in.size()-1);char op="+-*/".charAt(r.nextInt(4));String joined="("+in.get(i)+op+in.get(i+1)+")";String prefix=op+pre.get(i)+pre.get(i+1),postfix=post.get(i)+post.get(i+1)+op;in.set(i,joined);pre.set(i,prefix);post.set(i,postfix);in.remove(i+1);pre.remove(i+1);post.remove(i+1);}assert postfixToInfix(post.get(0)).equals(in.get(0));}

213.problem: Convert an infix expression to prefix while preserving precedence and associativity.
213.assumptions: The tracker title asks for prefix but its saved link opens infix-to-postfix. The current TUF infix-to-prefix task uses lowercase operands and +, −, *, /. The implementation also supports the single digits and right-associative ^ used by the saved postfix link, and exposes both conversion methods separately.

example.explanation: Subtraction groups left-to-right: (a−b)−c. The result must not be -a-bc, which means a−(b−c).

213.baseline: Build an expression tree according to infix precedence, then print its preorder traversal. The reverse-and-convert method reuses an operator stack without creating tree nodes.
213.approach:
Reverse the infix string and swap opening and closing parentheses. Convert this reversed expression to postfix, then reverse that output to get prefix.

Reversing also reverses the tie rule for equal-precedence operators. In this reversed pass, do not pop an equal +, −, * or /, but do pop an equal ^. Without this change, a−b−c would group in the wrong direction. The helper’s reversePass flag makes that rule explicit; the ordinary postfix wrapper uses the usual rule.
steps: Reverse the input and swap ( with ).
Run the operator-stack conversion with reversed associativity handling.
Reverse the result to obtain prefix.
Use the separate infixToPostfix wrapper if practising the tracker’s saved postfix link.
213.time: O(n): a fixed number of linear passes and at most one push/pop per operator.
pitfalls: Reversing characters without swapping parentheses breaks grouping.
The equal-precedence pop rule must reverse along with the input.
^ is an expression-language exponent operator here, not Java’s XOR calculation.
The tracker’s saved link asks for postfix; use the correctly named helper for that judge.
tests: Random r=new Random(213);for(int trial=0;trial<100;trial++){List<String>in=new ArrayList<>(),pre=new ArrayList<>(),post=new ArrayList<>();for(char ch='a';ch<='h';ch++){in.add(""+ch);pre.add(""+ch);post.add(""+ch);}while(in.size()>1){int i=r.nextInt(in.size()-1);char op="+-*/^".charAt(r.nextInt(5));String joined="("+in.get(i)+op+in.get(i+1)+")";String prefix=op+pre.get(i)+pre.get(i+1),postfix=post.get(i)+post.get(i+1)+op;in.set(i,joined);pre.set(i,prefix);post.set(i,postfix);in.remove(i+1);pre.remove(i+1);post.remove(i+1);}assert infixToPrefix(in.get(0)).equals(pre.get(0));assert infixToPostfix(in.get(0)).equals(post.get(0));}

214.problem: For each query value in nums1, return its first strictly greater value to the right in nums2.
214.assumptions: The tracker links to LeetCode Next Greater Element I, which has two arrays. All values in nums2 are distinct and every nums1 value occurs there. The current Striver article solves the underlying one-array next-greater task; this guide adds the required query mapping.

example.explanation: For 6, skip 4 and find 7. For 2, the first greater value is 6, even though 7 is larger.

214.baseline: For each query, locate it in nums2 and scan right until a larger value appears. This takes O(m × n) for m queries and n reference values.
214.approach:
Scan nums2 from right to left, keeping useful greater-value candidates on a stack. Remove candidates no larger than the current value. They cannot answer the current query, and for any earlier position the current value is at least as large and closer, so those removed candidates are no longer needed.

The surviving top is the first greater candidate. Store it in a map keyed by the current value, then push that value. Distinct nums2 values make the map unambiguous. Finally answer nums1 in its own order using the map.
steps: Scan nums2 right to left.
Pop stack values ≤ the current value.
Map the current value to the top, or −1 if the stack is empty.
Push the current value.
Look up each nums1 value in order.
214.time: Expected O(n + m), including hash-map lookups. Each reference value is pushed and popped at most once.
214.space: O(n) working space plus O(m) output.
pitfalls: Next greater means first greater, not maximum on the right.
A value-keyed map depends on nums2 having distinct values.
Answer in nums1 order, not nums2 order.
