For each source position, examine target positions from right to left.
On matching characters, copy start[j − 1], or use the current index for j = 0.
When the full target has a start, compare the candidate window.
Return the shortest saved range, keeping the first on ties.
241.time: O(n × m), where n is the source length and m is the target length.
241.space: O(m) working space, plus the returned string.
pitfalls: The target’s order matters; a frequency map cannot verify a subsequence.
Update target states backward so one source position cannot match multiple target characters.
Store the latest start for a matched prefix to shorten future candidates.
Use < rather than ≤ when replacing the best answer, preserving the leftmost tie.
A stored match may end before the current position; extending its window remains valid but cannot improve an already shorter answer.
tests: Random r=new Random(241);for(int trial=0;trial<5000;trial++){StringBuilder source=new StringBuilder(),target=new StringBuilder();for(int i=r.nextInt(14);i>0;i--)source.append((char)('a'+r.nextInt(3)));for(int i=r.nextInt(6);i>0;i--)target.append((char)('a'+r.nextInt(3)));String s=source.toString(),t=target.toString();String expected="";if(!t.isEmpty())for(int left=0;left<s.length();left++)for(int end=left+1;end<=s.length();end++){int j=0;for(int x=left;x<end&&j<t.length();x++)if(s.charAt(x)==t.charAt(j))j++;if(j==t.length()&&(expected.isEmpty()||end-left<expected.length()))expected=s.substring(left,end);}assert minWindowSubsequence(s,t).equals(expected);assert subsequenceByStarts(s,t).equals(expected);}

reference.title: Minimum Window Subsequence
reference.approach: Track the latest start for each matched target prefix, retaining character order.
reference.adaptation: The current public statement, leftmost-tie rule and size limits were checked. It exposes a starter method rather than a public Java editorial. This is an authored O(n × m) dynamic-programming solution with backward updates, tested against direct window enumeration; it is not presented as copied Striver Java.

241.baselineTime: O(n²) time and O(1) working space, excluding the returned string.

242.problem: Understand how a binary heap implements a priority queue, and use Java’s PriorityQueue to repeatedly take the smallest or largest value.
242.assumptions: This is a foundation lesson, not a single online-judge problem. A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array. A priority queue selects by priority rather than insertion order. Equal priorities have no guaranteed original order.

example.explanation: A min-heap exposes the smallest remaining value. Reversing its comparison makes the largest remaining value come out first.

242.baseline: An unsorted list can append quickly but must scan to find the next minimum. A sorted list exposes the minimum quickly but may shift many elements for insertion. A heap keeps only enough order to make both insertion and root removal efficient.
242.approach:
A min-heap requires each parent to be no greater than its children. A max-heap reverses that comparison. There is no ordering rule between siblings, so the backing array is not a sorted list.

For an index i, children are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent is at (i − 1) / 2 for i > 0. Insertion appends a value and moves it up while it outranks its parent. Removal replaces the root with the last value and moves it down through the better-priority child. The complete-tree shape keeps these paths logarithmic.

Java’s PriorityQueue<Integer> is min-first by default. Use Comparator.reverseOrder() for max-first. Repeated poll calls produce priority order; iterating over the queue does not promise that order.
steps: Choose the priority order: natural for minimum first, reversed for maximum first.
Insert with offer. Read the root without removing it with peek.
Remove the root with poll when you want the next item.
Check isEmpty before unboxing a possibly null result.
242.time: peek is O(1); offer and poll take O(log n) heap work. Each complete insert-and-drain demonstration is O(n log n). A backing-array resize can occasionally add linear work.
242.space: O(n) for the queue and returned order.
pitfalls: A heap is not a binary search tree and its array is not fully sorted.
Do not use queue iteration when you need sorted output.
Use a comparator such as reverseOrder(), not b − a, which may overflow.
peek and poll return null on an empty PriorityQueue; unboxing that into int throws.
Bottom-up heap construction takes O(n); inserting values individually is a different O(n log n) procedure.
tests: assert maxFirst(new int[]{Integer.MIN_VALUE,0,Integer.MAX_VALUE}).equals(List.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE,0,Integer.MIN_VALUE));Random r=new Random(242);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){int[]a=new int[r.nextInt(60)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt();int[]sorted=a.clone();Arrays.sort(sorted);List<Integer>min=minFirst(a),max=maxFirst(a);for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){assert min.get(i)==sorted[i];assert max.get(i)==sorted[a.length-1-i];}}

reference.title: Introduction to Heap
reference.approach: Complete-tree array layout, parent-child order, sift up/down and priority-queue operations.
reference.adaptation: The current theory article was read; it deliberately contains no Java code. These authored Java demonstrations use the same min/max-priority concepts. PriorityQueue ordering, empty results and iteration behaviour were also checked against Oracle’s Java API documentation.

243.problem: Implement both a min-heap and a max-heap with insertion, root lookup/removal, size, empty check, reset and an indexed key change.
243.assumptions: The pinned item combines min and max heaps, while its link opens the min-heap task. Both current TUF practice contracts were checked. changeKey refers to the current heap-array index, not insertion order. Extraction returns void in those contracts. Empty lookup/removal throws here because the public statement does not specify a sentinel; negative values are valid. For equal children, the max-heap contract requires choosing the left child.

example.explanation: The heap becomes [2,6,9], then [6,9]. Changing its current root to 12 requires moving down, producing [9,12].

243.baseline: Keeping values sorted after every update makes finding an extreme easy, but insertions and indexed changes can shift O(n) elements. A heap repairs only one path after each change.
243.approach:
Use an ArrayList as the complete tree. A comparison helper says which of two values should be nearer the root: smaller for a min-heap, larger for a max-heap. Everything else is shared.

Insert at the end, then sift upward. To remove the root, move the last value into its place, remove the last slot, then sift downward through the better child. When children tie, keep the left child. For changeKey, first replace the requested array position. If the new value outranks its parent, sift up; otherwise sift down. Only relationships along that path can have broken.
steps: Store values in an array-backed list and define the priority comparison.
Sift upward after appending a new value.
Replace the root with the last value and sift downward after removal.
For changeKey, choose up or down by comparing with the parent.
Expose min/max method names through small wrapper classes.
243.time: Root lookup, size and empty check are O(1). Insert is amortized O(log n); extraction and key changes take O(log n). Reset is O(n) because ArrayList.clear releases its stored references.
243.space: O(n) storage, with O(1) extra working space for iterative repairs.
pitfalls: Do not sift only down after every key change: a new extreme may need to rise.
Choose the better child before swapping down. Equal children choose left in this implementation.
A key’s array position can change after any heap operation.
After removing the only value, do not write a replacement root into an empty list.
Negating values to simulate a max-heap fails for Integer.MIN_VALUE; direct comparisons avoid that issue.
tests: MaxHeap max=new MaxHeap();for(int v:new int[]{10,9,9,8,7,6,5})max.insert(v);max.extractMax();assert ((BinaryHeap)max).values.equals(List.of(9,8,9,5,7,6));MinHeap min=new MinHeap();for(int v:new int[]{0,1,1,2,3,4,5})min.insert(v);min.extractMin();assert ((BinaryHeap)min).values.equals(List.of(1,2,1,5,3,4));

Random r=new Random(243);for(boolean min:new boolean[]{true,false}){BinaryHeap heap=new BinaryHeap(min);List<Integer>model=new ArrayList<>();for(int op=0;op<10000;op++){int action=r.nextInt(4);if(model.isEmpty()||action==0){int value=r.nextInt();heap.insert(value);model.add(value);}else if(action==1){int expected=min?Collections.min(model):Collections.max(model);assert heap.root()==expected;heap.removeRoot();model.remove(Integer.valueOf(expected));}else if(action==2){int index=r.nextInt(heap.heapSize()),old=heap.values.get(index),value=r.nextInt();heap.changeKey(index,value);model.remove(Integer.valueOf(old));model.add(value);}else{heap.initializeHeap();model.clear();}assert heap.heapSize()==model.size();for(int child=1;child<heap.values.size();child++){int parent=(child-1)/2;assert !heap.before(heap.values.get(child),heap.values.get(parent));}if(!model.isEmpty())assert heap.root()==(min?Collections.min(model):Collections.max(model));}}

reference.title: Implement Min Heap
reference.approach: Array storage with sift-up insertion, sift-down extraction and directional repair after changeKey.
reference.adaptation: Both public min-heap and max-heap operation contracts were checked, together with the current heap theory lesson. Those practice pages expose starter methods, not Java editorials. This authored shared implementation includes both wrappers and preserves the max-heap statement’s left-child tie rule.

244.problem: Check whether an array, read in level order as a complete binary tree, satisfies the min-heap rule.
244.assumptions: The array is already packed, so the complete-tree shape is given. Each parent must be ≤ each existing child. Equal values are allowed. The empty array is accepted here as an extra convenience.

example.explanation: 2 ≤ 6 and 3; 6 ≤ 8 and 7; 3 ≤ 4. The array is not sorted, but every parent-child relation is valid.

244.baseline: You could compare every node with all descendants, but checking direct children is sufficient: the order carries through every path. Sorting first would destroy the arrangement you were asked to validate.
244.approach:
Visit only parent indices 0 through n / 2 − 1. Every later index is a leaf and has no children to violate the rule. Check the left child and then the right child if it exists. Return false on the first parent larger than a child.

Why are direct checks enough? If each parent is no larger than its children, following a path downward can never decrease the value. The root is therefore no larger than any descendant, and the same argument applies to every subtree.
steps: Visit each non-leaf index.
Compare nums[parent] with its left child at 2 × parent + 1.
If a right child exists at 2 × parent + 2, compare it too.
Return true if no relation fails.
pitfalls: A min-heap need not be fully sorted.
Check all parents, not only the root.
Use > to detect failure so equal parent and child values remain valid.
The last parent may have only a left child.
tests: assert isHeap(new int[]{2,6,3,8,7,4});assert !isHeap(new int[]{1,4,2,3});assert isHeap(new int[]{1,1,1});assert isHeap(new int[]{});assert isHeap(new int[]{5});assert !isHeap(new int[]{3,2});

Random r=new Random(244);for(int n=0;n<100;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<100;trial++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(20)-10;boolean expected=true;for(int child=1;child<n;child++)if(a[(child-1)/2]>a[child])expected=false;assert isHeap(a)==expected;}

reference.title: Check if an array represents a min heap
reference.approach: Inspect every parent-child relation without changing the array.
reference.adaptation: The public practice definition and current heap theory’s parent-scan algorithm were checked. Neither exposes a Java solution for this task; this is an authored implementation of that algorithm.

245.problem: Rearrange a min-heap array into a valid max-heap, keeping exactly the same values.
245.assumptions: The input is a min-heap, but the bottom-up method works for any array. Several max-heap layouts can be correct. This Java method changes the supplied array in place and returns the same array.

example.explanation: Every parent is at least as large as its children, and all original values are still present.

245.baseline: Sort the values in descending order. That arrangement is a valid max-heap, but sorting costs O(n log n) and does more ordering work than needed.
245.approach:
The complete-tree shape is already present. Rebuild only the ordering, starting at the last parent and moving toward the root. Each repair assumes its child subtrees are already max-heaps, which is why the direction matters.

At a parent, choose the larger child. If that child is larger than the parent, swap and continue downward. Otherwise this subtree is already valid. Processing all parents this way takes O(n), not O(n log n): about half the nodes are leaves, about a quarter can move only one level, and progressively fewer can travel far.
steps: Start at index n / 2 − 1, the last non-leaf.
Sift that value down, always choosing the larger child.
Repeat for each earlier parent through index 0.
Return the same array after all repairs.
245.space: O(1) extra working space; the input array is reused.
pitfalls: Start at the last parent, not the root, because sift-down needs valid child subtrees.
Reversing a min-heap array does not generally create a max-heap.
Do not compare only with the left child; the right child may be larger.
Verify heap order and the preserved multiset, not one exact arrangement.
tests: int[]a={1,4,2,8,5,3};assert minToMaxHeap(a)==a;assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{8,5,3,4,1,2});assert minToMaxHeap(new int[]{}).length==0;

Random r=new Random(245);for(int n=0;n<200;n++)for(int trial=0;trial<20;trial++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(30)-15;int[]expected=a.clone();Arrays.sort(expected);minToMaxHeap(a);for(int child=1;child<n;child++)assert a[(child-1)/2]>=a[child];int[]after=a.clone();Arrays.sort(after);assert Arrays.equals(after,expected);}

reference.title: Convert Min Heap to Max Heap
reference.approach: Apply max-heap sift-down to every parent in bottom-up order.
reference.adaptation: The public practice contract and current Introduction to Heap conversion algorithm were checked. The practice page exposes a starter method rather than Java; this authored implementation follows that bottom-up algorithm and states its in-place behaviour.

246.problem: Return the kth largest array occurrence. Duplicates occupy separate positions in the ranking.
246.assumptions: 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length(). This tracker item explicitly asks for a priority-queue approach. The code leaves the input unchanged. The current Striver lesson also discusses Quickselect, which solves a different performance tradeoff and can modify the input.

example.explanation: Descending order is [8,8,6,3,1]. Both copies of 8 count, so position 3 contains 6.

246.baseline: Copy and sort the array in ascending order. Return index n − k. This is a useful O(n log n) baseline, but orders every element when we only need the kth largest.
246.approach:
Keep the k largest values seen so far in a min-heap. Its root is the smallest of those retained values, so it is the first candidate to discard when a new value arrives.

Insert every occurrence. If the heap grows to k + 1, remove its minimum. This leaves exactly the best k candidates from the scanned prefix. After the full scan, the root is the smallest of the overall top k, which is the kth largest.
steps: Create a min-first PriorityQueue.
Offer each array value, including duplicates.
Whenever its size exceeds k, poll its minimum.
Return peek after all values have been processed.
246.time: O(n log(k + 1)); the +1 also makes the bound meaningful for k = 1.
246.space: O(k) for retained candidates, temporarily k + 1 during insertion.
pitfalls: Use a min-heap to retain the largest k; its minimum is the weakest retained candidate.
Do not deduplicate values before ranking them.
k is 1-based, while the sorted-array baseline uses index n − k.
The input is not changed by the heap method.
tests: assert findKthLargest(new int[]{8,3,8,1,6},3)==6;assert findKthLargest(new int[]{5,5,4},2)==5;assert findKthLargest(new int[]{-7},1)==-7;

Random r=new Random(246);for(int n=1;n<=60;n++)for(int t=0;t<20;t++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;int[]original=a.clone();for(int k=1;k<=n;k++)assert findKthLargest(a,k)==largestBySorting(a,k);assert Arrays.equals(a,original);}

reference.title: K-th Largest Element in an Array
reference.approach: Sort a copy as a baseline; keep the largest k occurrences in a size-k min-heap.
reference.adaptation: The public sorting and priority-queue Java methods were checked. The tracker explicitly requests the heap approach, so that method is used here. An invalid-rank guard is added; the source’s valid-input algorithm is otherwise retained.

246.baselineTime: O(n log n) time and O(n) copied storage.

247.problem: Return the kth smallest array occurrence using a priority queue. Count repeated values as separate ranked occurrences.
247.assumptions: The pinned title says kth smallest, but its problem link opens kth largest. This guide follows the title and the correct current Kth Smallest problem linked below. 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length().

example.explanation: Ascending order is [1,3,6,8,8], so position 3 contains 6.

247.baseline: Copy and sort the array, then return sorted[k − 1]. This establishes the answer directly, but takes O(n log n) time and does not meet the practice prompt’s request to avoid sorting.
247.approach:
To retain the smallest k values, use a max-heap. The root is the largest value we are still keeping, so it is the one to remove when there are too many candidates.

Offer each value. If the heap has k + 1 entries, remove the largest. After the scan, the heap contains the k smallest occurrences, and its root is the largest of those: the kth smallest. This reverses the comparison used for the neighbouring kth-largest lesson.
steps: Create a max-first PriorityQueue using Comparator.reverseOrder().
Offer each occurrence.
When the heap size exceeds k, remove the maximum.
Return the remaining maximum after the scan.
pitfalls: Use a max-heap for the smallest k candidates.
The saved kth-largest URL describes a different ranking direction.
Duplicates count; this is not kth distinct smallest.
Use reverseOrder() rather than a subtraction comparator that may overflow.
tests: assert kthSmallest(new int[]{8,3,8,1,6},3)==6;assert kthSmallest(new int[]{2,2,3},2)==2;assert kthSmallest(new int[]{3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6},4)==3;

Random r=new Random(247);for(int n=1;n<=60;n++)for(int t=0;t<20;t++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;int[]original=a.clone();for(int k=1;k<=n;k++)assert kthSmallest(a,k)==smallestBySorting(a,k);assert Arrays.equals(a,original);}

reference.title: Kth Smallest Element in an Array
reference.approach: Retain the smallest k occurrences in a max-heap.
reference.adaptation: The correct public kth-smallest statement was checked; the pinned tracker URL points to kth largest. This page exposes a starter method rather than a Java editorial. The authored solution reverses the heap comparison from the source-checked neighbouring kth-largest Java method.

247.baselineTime: O(n log n) time and O(n) copied storage.

248.problem: Sort a k-sorted array: every occurrence is at most k positions away from its position in sorted order.
248.assumptions: The pinned title is Sort K sorted array, but its link opens Merge K Sorted Lists, which is the next tracker topic. This guide covers the nearly-sorted single-array meaning of the title. k is non-negative, and the displacement guarantee is a precondition. No matching current public TUF Java editorial was found for this pinned item.

example.explanation: Each group of three values is displaced by at most two positions. A heap of at most three candidates is enough to choose the next value.

248.baseline: Use a full O(n log n) sort. It works even without the displacement guarantee, but does not use the extra information supplied by k.
248.approach:
The smallest value must appear among the first k + 1 entries: otherwise it would have to move more than k positions to reach index 0. Keep those candidates in a min-heap and remove the minimum into the next output slot.

After choosing one value, bring the next unseen input value into the heap and choose again. The displacement guarantee ensures that the correct next value is always among the candidates already seen. The code below offers each value and polls when the heap size exceeds k, which gives exactly this k + 1-candidate choice. Finally drain what remains.
steps: Create a min-heap and a write index at zero.
Offer each input value. When heap size > k, write its minimum to the next output position.
After reading every input, drain the heap into the remaining positions.
Return the rearranged input array.
248.time: O(n log(min(n, k + 1) + 1)); usually written O(n log(k + 1)) for k ≥ 1. k = 0 takes O(n).
248.space: O(min(n, k + 1)) heap storage; the input is updated in place.
pitfalls: The displacement guarantee is essential; a small heap cannot generally sort an arbitrary array.
The next output needs k + 1 candidates, not k.
k = 0 means the array is already sorted.
Do not treat the mismatched Merge K Sorted Lists link as this array problem.
The write index never passes the read index, so unread input is not overwritten.
tests: int[]a={3,1,2,6,4,5};assert sortKSorted(a,2)==a;assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,2,3,4,5,6});assert Arrays.equals(sortKSorted(new int[]{-2,0,3},0),new int[]{-2,0,3});

Random r=new Random(248);for(int n=0;n<80;n++)for(int k=0;k<=n+2;k++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(50)-25;Arrays.sort(a);int[]expected=a.clone();for(int start=0;start<n;start+=k+1){int end=Math.min(n,start+k+1);for(int i=end-1;i>start;i--){int j=start+r.nextInt(i-start+1);int tmp=a[i];a[i]=a[j];a[j]=tmp;}}assert Arrays.equals(sortKSorted(a,k),expected);}
assert Arrays.equals(sortKSorted(new int[]{4,1,3,2},Integer.MAX_VALUE),new int[]{1,2,3,4});assert sortKSorted(new int[]{},0).length==0;

249.problem: Merge all nodes from k sorted singly linked lists into one sorted list and return its head.
249.assumptions: Each input list is sorted in non-decreasing order. Lists may be empty, and the array itself may be empty. The lists are acyclic and do not share node objects. The heap and sequential methods reuse nodes, so their next links change.

example.explanation: At each step, choose the smallest current head. After choosing 0, its next value 3 becomes that list’s candidate.

249.baseline: Collect all values, sort them, then build a new list. This takes O(N log N) time and O(N) storage for N total nodes. It ignores the sorted order already present in each list.
249.approach:
The next output node must be one of the current heads: every later node in a list is at least as large as that head. A min-heap finds the smallest current head without scanning all k lists.

Put each non-null head in the heap. Poll the smallest node, attach it to the output, and offer its original next node as that list’s replacement candidate. Keep at most one candidate per active list. A dummy node avoids a special case for the first attachment. Set the final tail’s next to null so the result ends cleanly.
steps: Offer every non-empty list head into a heap ordered by node value.
Poll the smallest node and remember its next node.
Attach the chosen node after the result tail.
Offer the remembered next node, if present.
Terminate the final tail and return dummy.next.
249.time: O(k + N log(k + 1)) for k head slots and N total nodes.
249.space: O(k) working heap storage; output reuses the existing nodes.
pitfalls: Offer only non-null nodes; PriorityQueue does not accept null.
Keep duplicates because every input node belongs in the output.
Use a safe value comparator, not subtraction that may overflow.
These relinking methods change the input lists; make copies if the originals must remain separate.
The algorithm assumes disjoint acyclic lists, not multiple heads into the same chain.
tests: ListNode a=new ListNode(1),b=new ListNode(1),c=new ListNode(2);a.next=c;ListNode out=mergeKLists(new ListNode[]{a,null,b});assert out.val==1&&out.next.val==1&&out.next.next==c&&c.next==null;assert mergeKLists(new ListNode[0])==null;assert mergeKLists(new ListNode[]{null,null})==null;

Random r=new Random(249);for(int trial=0;trial<500;trial++){int k=r.nextInt(10);ListNode[][]inputs=new ListNode[3][k];List<Integer>expected=new ArrayList<>();Set<ListNode>originals=Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>());for(int list=0;list<k;list++){int[]values=new int[r.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<values.length;i++)values[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;Arrays.sort(values);for(int value:values)expected.add(value);for(int variant=0;variant<3;variant++){ListNode dummy=new ListNode(0),tail=dummy;for(int value:values){tail.next=new ListNode(value);tail=tail.next;if(variant==0)originals.add(tail);}inputs[variant][list]=dummy.next;}}Collections.sort(expected);ListNode[]outputs={mergeKLists(inputs[0]),mergeSequentially(inputs[1]),mergeBySorting(inputs[2])};for(int variant=0;variant<3;variant++){ListNode cur=outputs[variant];for(int value:expected){assert cur!=null&&cur.val==value;if(variant==0)assert originals.remove(cur);cur=cur.next;}assert cur==null;}assert originals.isEmpty();}
ListNode low=new ListNode(Integer.MIN_VALUE),high=new ListNode(Integer.MAX_VALUE);ListNode out=mergeKLists(new ListNode[]{high,low});assert out==low&&out.next==high&&high.next==null;

reference.title: Merge K Sorted Linked Lists
reference.approach: Collect and sort values, merge sequentially, then keep one active node per list in a min-heap.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. The optimal method preserves safe integer comparison, node reuse and final null termination. It saves the next candidate before relinking to make that dependency explicit.

249.baselineTime: O(k + N log(N + 1)) time and O(N) storage for values and new nodes.

better.explanation: Merge the accumulated result with one list at a time using the usual two-list merge. This saves the copied values array, but early nodes may be scanned again for many later lists. It improves storage, not necessarily running time.
better.space: O(1) working space at a time; existing result nodes are reused.

250.problem: Replace each value by its 1-based position among the array’s sorted distinct values. Preserve the original order of positions.
250.assumptions: Equal values receive the same rank. Ranks have no gaps: [10,10,30] becomes [1,1,2]. This differs from kth-element problems, where duplicate occurrences occupy separate positions. The input may contain negative values.

example.explanation: The distinct sorted values are −5, 10, 25 and 40. Both copies of 40 receive rank 4.

250.baseline: For each value, collect all distinct smaller values in a set. Its rank is that set’s size plus one. Repeating the scan for every position takes O(n²).
250.approach:
Sort a copy so the input positions remain unchanged. Walk through the sorted values and assign a new rank only when a value has not been seen before. A map stores value → rank.

Then walk through the original array and look up each rank. Sorting is useful for assigning ranks, but the output must follow the original positions. A min-heap could visit values in the same ascending order; it has the same O(n log n) bound and is not needed for this task.
steps: Clone and sort the values.
Assign the next rank only to a new distinct value.
Look up each original value’s rank in order.
Return the new rank array.
250.time: O(n log n) time for sorting, followed by average O(n) map work.
250.space: O(n) for the copy, rank map and result.
pitfalls: Do not give duplicate occurrences different ranks.
Do not return ranks in sorted order; map them back to the original positions.
The next rank advances only for a new distinct value.
Start ranks at 1, not 0.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(replaceWithRank(new int[]{40,10,40,-5,25}),new int[]{4,2,4,1,3});assert Arrays.equals(replaceWithRank(new int[]{10,10,30}),new int[]{1,1,2});assert replaceWithRank(new int[]{}).length==0;

Random r=new Random(250);for(int trial=0;trial<2000;trial++){int[]a=new int[r.nextInt(50)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(30)-15;int[]original=a.clone(),actual=replaceWithRank(a);for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){Set<Integer>smaller=new HashSet<>();for(int v:a)if(v<a[i])smaller.add(v);assert actual[i]==smaller.size()+1;}assert Arrays.equals(a,original);}

reference.title: Replace Elements by Their Rank
reference.approach: Sort distinct values to assign dense ranks, then restore the original position order.
reference.adaptation: The current public practice definition, duplicate-rank rule and original-order requirement were checked. It exposes a starter method rather than a Java editorial; this is an authored sorting-and-map implementation.

251.problem: Find the minimum number of time slots needed to execute all tasks when equal task labels must have at least n intervening slots. Idle slots count toward the answer.
251.assumptions: Tasks are uppercase English letters and may be reordered. n is non-negative. Each task takes one slot. This returns only the minimum length, not an actual schedule. The linked task’s limits keep the result within int; an empty task list returns 0 here.

example.explanation: One shortest schedule is A, B, idle, A, B, idle, A. Every pair of A tasks has two slots between them.

251.baseline: Simulate time. At each slot, scan the 26 labels and choose the available label with the most copies left. If none is ready, spend an idle slot. A label used at time t becomes available at t + n + 1.
251.approach:
Let f be the largest task frequency, and let tied be the number of labels with that frequency. The first f − 1 appearances of a busiest label each need a block of n + 1 slots before the next appearance. Its last appearance needs no cooldown afterward.

If several labels tie for busiest, each needs a place in the final group. This gives a required length of (f − 1) × (n + 1) + tied. Other tasks fill the gaps. If there are more tasks than this frame has room for, the tasks themselves determine the length and no extra idle slots are needed. Therefore take the larger of the frame length and tasks.length.

For A×3 and B×2 with n = 2, f = 3 and tied = 1. The frame is 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 slots. For A×3 and B×3, tied becomes 2, so the answer is 8.
steps: Count each of the 26 task labels.
Find the maximum frequency f and how many labels reach it.
Compute (f − 1) × (n + 1) + tied.
Return the larger of that length and the task count.
251.time: O(M + 26), where M is the number of tasks.
pitfalls: There are n intervening slots, so repeated task start times differ by at least n + 1.
Count every label tied at the maximum frequency.
Take max with tasks.length; enough other labels can fill every potential idle slot.
Do not add idle slots after the final task.
This frequency solution assumes tasks can be reordered and all have equal duration and the same cooldown.
tests: class Search{Map<String,Integer>memo=new HashMap<>();int solve(int[]left,int[]wait,int cooldown){int total=0;for(int v:left)total+=v;if(total==0)return 0;String key=Arrays.toString(left)+Arrays.toString(wait);if(memo.containsKey(key))return memo.get(key);int best=1000000;for(int chosen=-1;chosen<left.length;chosen++){if(chosen>=0&&(left[chosen]==0||wait[chosen]>0))continue;if(chosen<0){boolean active=false;for(int v:wait)if(v>0)active=true;if(!active)continue;}int[]nextLeft=left.clone(),nextWait=wait.clone();for(int i=0;i<nextWait.length;i++)nextWait[i]=Math.max(0,nextWait[i]-1);if(chosen>=0){nextLeft[chosen]--;nextWait[chosen]=cooldown;}best=Math.min(best,1+solve(nextLeft,nextWait,cooldown));}memo.put(key,best);return best;}}for(int a=0;a<=3;a++)for(int b=0;b<=3;b++)for(int c=0;c<=3;c++)for(int cooldown=0;cooldown<=3;cooldown++){char[]tasks=("A".repeat(a)+"B".repeat(b)+"C".repeat(c)).toCharArray();int expected=new Search().solve(new int[]{a,b,c},new int[3],cooldown);assert leastInterval(tasks,cooldown)==expected;assert scheduleByHeap(tasks,cooldown)==expected;assert scheduleByScanning(tasks,cooldown)==expected;}

reference.title: Task Scheduler: Minimum Intervals with Cooldown
reference.approach: Ready-label simulation, max-heap cycles, then the maximum-frequency frame formula.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. This keeps the source’s tied-maximum formula and final-cycle handling. An empty-input guard is added to the formula because the source assumes at least one task.

251.baselineTime: O(26 × A + M) time for A elapsed slots and M tasks; O(1) space.

better.explanation: Use a max-heap of remaining frequencies. Process up to n + 1 different entries in a cycle, keeping unfinished counts aside until the cycle ends. If work remains, add the full cycle length; for the last cycle add only the slots actually used. This computes the interval count without scanning every idle slot.
better.time: O(M log(D + 1)), with D ≤ 26 distinct labels.
better.space: O(D + 26), effectively constant for this alphabet.

252.problem: Decide whether every card can be placed into groups of exactly groupSize consecutive integer values.
252.assumptions: Use every card once. Equal values may belong to different groups but cannot replace different consecutive values within one group. groupSize must be positive. The linked task uses non-negative values; this implementation also handles the full int range safely.

example.explanation: Use [2,3,4] and [3,4,5]. The two copies of 3 and 4 belong to different groups.

252.baseline: Try possible groups and recursively partition the remaining cards. This can become exponential because there are many ways to choose groups. We can avoid those choices by always considering the smallest unused card.
252.approach:
The smallest unused value must begin a group. It cannot appear later in a group because that would require an even smaller unused value before it. This forces the next group to contain start, start + 1, and so on through groupSize − 1.

Use a TreeMap to keep counts in sorted order. Take its first key as start and consume one copy of each required consecutive value. If any value is missing, no rearrangement can succeed. Remove zero-count keys and repeat with the new smallest unused value. This uses an ordered map because we need both the smallest value and counts for specific values.
steps: Reject a non-positive group size or a card count not divisible by it.
Count values in a TreeMap.
Start each group at the smallest remaining key.
Consume one copy of every required consecutive value, failing on a missing value.
Return true once all counts are consumed.
252.time: O(n log(D + 1)), where D is the number of distinct values. Each successful inner step consumes one card.
pitfalls: Divisibility is necessary but not sufficient; required intermediate values may be missing.
Do not skip a missing value to use a later card.
Duplicates need frequency counts, not a set.
Do not allow integer overflow to turn a value after Integer.MAX_VALUE into Integer.MIN_VALUE.
tests: assert isNStraightHand(new int[]{2,3,4,3,4,5},3);assert isNStraightHand(new int[]{1,2,3,6,2,3,4,7,8},3);assert !isNStraightHand(new int[]{1,2,4,5,6,7},3);assert isNStraightHand(new int[]{9,9,9},1);

class Search{Map<Integer,Boolean>memo=new HashMap<>();boolean solve(int[]a,int size,int used){if(used==(1<<a.length)-1)return true;if(memo.containsKey(used))return memo.get(used);int first=0;while((used&(1<<first))!=0)first++;for(int subset=1;subset<(1<<a.length);subset++){if((subset&used)!=0||(subset&(1<<first))==0||Integer.bitCount(subset)!=size)continue;int[]group=new int[size];int j=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)if((subset&(1<<i))!=0)group[j++]=a[i];Arrays.sort(group);boolean consecutive=true;for(int i=1;i<size;i++)if((long)group[i]-group[i-1]!=1)consecutive=false;if(consecutive&&solve(a,size,used|subset)){memo.put(used,true);return true;}}memo.put(used,false);return false;}}Random r=new Random(252);for(int trial=0;trial<700;trial++){int[]a=new int[r.nextInt(10)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(7)-3;for(int size=1;size<=4;size++){boolean expected=a.length%size==0&&new Search().solve(a,size,0);assert isNStraightHand(a,size)==expected;}}

reference.title: Hand of Straights
reference.approach: Start a forced consecutive group at the smallest unused card and consume value counts.
reference.adaptation: The public specification and constraints were checked. It exposes a starter method rather than a Java editorial. This authored TreeMap implementation keeps the greedy choice explicit and checks full-int overflow as an extension.

253.problem: Implement the practice problem’s simplified Twitter class: post tweets, follow or unfollow users, and return up to 10 newest visible tweet IDs.
253.assumptions: Each tweet ID is unique, but IDs do not encode time. A user sees their own posts plus posts by currently followed users, including posts written before the follow. This is an in-memory algorithm exercise. Self-follow is ignored, and repeated follow/unfollow calls are harmless extensions.

example.explanation: Tweet 5 was posted later, so it comes first even though its ID is smaller. After unfollow(1,2), user 1 sees [90].

253.baseline: Collect all posts from the user and their followees, sort by posting time, and take the first ten. A simple reference can instead keep a global posting log and scan it backward, selecting visible posts until ten are found.
253.approach:
Each user’s own posts are already ordered by time. Store them as a chain with the newest post at the head. A global increasing counter gives every post a distinct ordering time.

Finding the newest visible posts is a merge of sorted lists. Put the newest post from each relevant user into a max-heap ordered by time. Poll the newest post, add its ID to the result, and offer that post’s older neighbour. Stop after ten results or when the heap empties. Follow relationships are stored separately, so changing a follow affects visibility without deleting any posts.
steps: Map each user to their newest tweet, linked to older tweets.
Map each follower to a set of followees.
For a feed, offer the current user’s newest tweet and each followee’s newest tweet.
Repeatedly take the newest candidate and offer its older neighbour, up to ten times.
Keep the user’s own posts visible independently of the follow set.
253.time: Posting/follow/unfollow take average O(1). For F followees, this feed implementation takes O(F + (F + 11) log(F + 2)), including individual heap insertions and at most ten removals.
253.space: O(P + R + U) retained storage for posts, follow relations and users. A feed uses O(F + 1) working heap space and at most ten result IDs.
pitfalls: Sort by posting time, not tweet ID.
Include the user’s own posts exactly once.
Unfollowing changes visibility; it must not delete the followee’s posts.
Do not consume or modify stored post chains when reading a feed.
Use a set so repeated follow calls cannot duplicate feed entries.
tests: Twitter t=new Twitter();Map<Integer,Set<Integer>>follows=new HashMap<>();List<int[]>log=new ArrayList<>();Random r=new Random(253);int id=100000;for(int step=0;step<5000;step++){int user=r.nextInt(8),other=r.nextInt(8),op=r.nextInt(4);if(op==0){t.postTweet(user,id);log.add(new int[]{user,id--});}else if(op==1){t.follow(user,other);if(user!=other)follows.computeIfAbsent(user,x->new HashSet<>()).add(other);}else if(op==2){t.unfollow(user,other);if(follows.containsKey(user))follows.get(user).remove(other);}else{List<Integer>expected=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=log.size()-1;i>=0&&expected.size()<10;i--){int[]post=log.get(i);if(post[0]==user||follows.getOrDefault(user,Collections.emptySet()).contains(post[0]))expected.add(post[1]);}assert t.getNewsFeed(user).equals(expected);}}

reference.title: Design Twitter
reference.approach: Merge newest-first post chains with a heap, using follow sets to choose visible sources.
reference.adaptation: The current public class contract, ten-post limit and posting-time order were checked. It exposes a starter class rather than a public Java editorial. This is an authored heap-merge design tested against a global-log reference.

254.problem: Connect all ropes into one. Joining lengths a and b costs a + b and creates a new rope of that combined length. Return the smallest possible total cost.
254.assumptions: The tracker calls them ropes; the linked current TUF task calls them sticks. They have the same cost rule and positive lengths. A single rope needs no join, so its cost is 0. This implementation returns long and also accepts an empty array.

example.explanation: Join 3+5 for 8, then 7+8 for 15, then 9+15 for 24. The total is 8+15+24 = 47.

254.baseline: Try every possible pair to join, recurse on the shortened list, and keep the cheapest total. This explores many merge orders and is only practical for tiny cases.
254.approach:
Join the two shortest available ropes first. A rope that is merged early may be included in later joins, so its length can be charged several times. Keeping those repeatedly charged pieces small lowers the total.

One way to justify the choice is to look at a complete merge tree. The deepest two sibling leaves are charged the same number of times. Moving the two smallest original lengths into those positions cannot increase the total, because smaller lengths are then charged more often. Therefore some optimal solution joins those two first. Treat their combined rope as one item and repeat.

A min-heap supplies the two shortest current lengths. Add their sum to the answer and put the combined length back, because it may be joined again.
steps: Offer all lengths into a min-heap.
While at least two ropes remain, poll two minima.
Add their sum to total cost and offer the sum back.
Return the accumulated cost.
254.time: O(n log(n + 1)) time, with n − 1 joins for a non-empty input.
pitfalls: Add every intermediate join cost, not only the final rope length.
Put the combined rope back in the heap before choosing the next pair.
One rope costs zero because there is no joining operation.
Use long for both merged lengths and the accumulated cost when extending beyond the practice bounds.
tests: assert connectSticks(new int[]{3,5,7,9})==47;assert connectSticks(new int[]{2,4,3})==14;assert connectSticks(new int[]{8})==0;assert connectSticks(new int[]{})==0;

class Search{Map<String,Long>memo=new HashMap<>();long solve(List<Long>a){if(a.size()<2)return 0;Collections.sort(a);String key=a.toString();if(memo.containsKey(key))return memo.get(key);long best=Long.MAX_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<a.size();i++)for(int j=i+1;j<a.size();j++){long sum=a.get(i)+a.get(j);List<Long>b=new ArrayList<>();for(int x=0;x<a.size();x++)if(x!=i&&x!=j)b.add(a.get(x));b.add(sum);best=Math.min(best,sum+solve(b));}memo.put(key,best);return best;}}Random r=new Random(254);for(int trial=0;trial<120;trial++){int[]a=new int[r.nextInt(7)];List<Long>values=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){a[i]=1+r.nextInt(8);values.add((long)a[i]);}assert connectSticks(a)==new Search().solve(values);}

reference.title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
reference.approach: Repeatedly merge the two smallest lengths with a min-heap.
reference.adaptation: The public stick-joining cost rule and min-heap prompts were checked. The tracker’s ropes terminology is equivalent. No public Java editorial is exposed; this authored solution returns long to cover larger lengths than the current int-returning practice stub.

255.problem: After each new number arrives, return the kth largest number seen so far. Keep duplicate values as separate entries.
255.assumptions: k is positive. The constructor may receive fewer than k values, but each judged add call has at least k total values available. An add before that point throws in this version because a kth largest value does not yet exist.

example.explanation: After 5, the three largest values are 8,6,5. After 9, they are 9,8,6.

255.baseline: Store every value. On each add, sort a copy in descending order and read index k − 1. This is simple, but it sorts old values again and again.
255.approach:
Keep only the largest k values in a min-heap. The root is the smallest of those k values, so it is exactly the kth largest overall.

Offer each incoming value. If the heap grows to k + 1, remove its smallest value. That removed value already has k values at least as large as it, so keeping it cannot improve a future kth-largest answer. Duplicates still occupy separate heap entries.
steps: Save k and create a min-heap.
Feed the initial values into the heap, trimming it to k entries.
For each add, offer the value and remove the minimum if the size exceeds k.
Return the minimum once k values are present.
255.time: Constructor: O(n log(k + 1)). Each add: O(log(k + 1)).
255.space: O(k), independent of the total stream length.
pitfalls: Use a min-heap of the retained large values, not a max-heap of them.
Do not remove duplicate values.
The initial array may be shorter than k; a return value is required only once enough values have arrived.
tests: KthLargest h=new KthLargest(3,new int[]{6,2,8,4});assert h.add(5)==5;assert h.add(9)==6;assert h.add(6)==6;

Random r=new Random(255);for(int k=1;k<=20;k++){int[]start=new int[k-1];List<Integer>all=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<start.length;i++){start[i]=r.nextInt();all.add(start[i]);}KthLargest h=new KthLargest(k,start);KthLargestSorted b=new KthLargestSorted(k,start);for(int i=0;i<300;i++){int v=r.nextInt();all.add(v);List<Integer>copy=new ArrayList<>(all);copy.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());int want=copy.get(k-1);assert h.add(v)==want;assert b.add(v)==want;assert h.largest.size()<=k;}}

reference.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
reference.approach: Sort all values, then improve to a min-heap containing only the largest k.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. The heap logic is preserved; the class is named KthLargest for the linked judge. Explicit guards reject non-positive k and queries before k values exist.

255.baselineTime: O(m log m) per add when m values have arrived; O(m) retained and copied storage.

256.problem: Choose one value from each of two arrays and return the C largest pair sums, in descending order.
256.assumptions: The pinned InterviewBit task has two arrays of equal length N, values up to 100000, and 1 ≤ C ≤ N. Different index pairs count separately, even when their sums are equal. This implementation also accepts C = 0 and C up to N². Sums fit int under the task bounds.

example.explanation: The largest pairs are 4+6, 4+5, 3+6, and one pair totalling 8. Both ways to make 9 must be counted.

256.baseline: Generate all N² pair sums, sort them in descending order, and take the first C. This needs O(N²) storage and O(N² log N) time.
256.approach:
Sort copies of both arrays in ascending order. Imagine a grid where cell (i,j) holds A[i] + B[j]. Moving left or up cannot increase the sum. The bottom-right cell is therefore the largest.

Keep the next candidate cells in a max-heap. Remove the largest candidate, save its sum, and offer its upper and left neighbours. A cell can be reached from two parents, so remember visited index pairs. Do not remember only sums: two different cells with the same sum are both valid answers.

Why does the heap contain the next answer? Any cell not yet reached has a path from the bottom-right corner through cells with at least its sum. Until that path reaches the cell, an earlier cell on the path is on the heap. A hidden cell therefore cannot beat every candidate.
steps: Sort copies of A and B.
Offer the bottom-right index pair and mark it visited.
Poll the largest sum and add it to the answer.
Offer each in-bounds upper/left neighbour once.
Repeat C times.
256.space: O(N + C) including sorted copies, heap, visited pairs and output.
pitfalls: Count index pairs, not distinct sums.
Use long for i * N + j; N² can exceed the int range.
The original arrays are preserved because this code sorts copies.
The current TUF practice page permits more output pairs than the pinned InterviewBit version; the original tracker link is unchanged.
tests: Random r=new Random(256);for(int n=1;n<=9;n++)for(int t=0;t<70;t++){int[]a=new int[n],b=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=r.nextInt(11)-5;b[i]=r.nextInt(11)-5;}int[]ac=a.clone(),bc=b.clone();List<Integer>all=new ArrayList<>();for(int x:a)for(int y:b)all.add(x+y);all.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());for(int k=0;k<=n*n;k++){int[]got=maximumSumCombinations(a,b,k);assert got.length==k;for(int i=0;i<k;i++)assert got[i]==all.get(i);}assert Arrays.equals(a,ac)&&Arrays.equals(b,bc);}

reference.title: Maximum Sum Combination
reference.approach: Use a max-heap to explore the largest pair sums without building the full grid.
reference.adaptation: The current public practice statement and the pinned InterviewBit statement were checked. TUF exposes a starter rather than a public Java editorial here. This authored implementation preserves duplicate index-pair sums and is checked against all-pairs sorting.

257.problem: Support adding numbers to a stream and finding the median of all numbers seen so far.
257.assumptions: findMedian is called only after at least one number has been added. For an even count, return the average of the two middle values. Values may use the full int range.

example.input: add 8, add 2, find median, add 5, find median
example.explanation: Sorted values are first [2,8], whose middle average is 5, then [2,5,8], whose middle value is 5.

257.baseline: Keep an unsorted list. For every median query, sort a copy and read its middle value or middle pair. Adds take O(1) amortized; queries take O(n log n).
257.approach:
Split the values into a lower half and an upper half. A max-heap gives the largest value in the lower half; a min-heap gives the smallest value in the upper half. These are exactly the values needed at the middle.

Keep the lower heap the same size as the upper heap, or one entry larger. To add a value, put it in the lower heap, then move the largest lower value to the upper heap. If the upper heap becomes larger, move its smallest value back. These moves restore both the size rule and the rule that every lower value is at most every upper value.

With an odd count, the lower root is the median. With an even count, average both roots. Divide each root by 2.0 before adding, so two large ints cannot overflow during addition.
steps: Create a max-heap lower and a min-heap upper.
Add the new value to lower and move lower’s maximum to upper.
If upper is larger, move its minimum back to lower.
Read one root for an odd count, or average the roots for an even count.
257.time: O(log n) per insertion and O(1) per median query.
257.space: O(n) for the two heaps together.
pitfalls: PriorityQueue iteration is not sorted; only peek/poll gives its extreme.
Rebalance sizes after every insertion.
Avoid (a + b) / 2.0 with int operands, because a + b can overflow first.
Do not negate int values to simulate a max-heap; Integer.MIN_VALUE cannot be negated safely.
tests: Random r=new Random(257);MedianFinder h=new MedianFinder();MedianSorted s=new MedianSorted();MedianResort b=new MedianResort();List<Integer>values=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<1500;i++){int v=i%7==0?Integer.MAX_VALUE:i%11==0?Integer.MIN_VALUE:r.nextInt();values.add(v);h.addNum(v);s.addNum(v);b.addNum(v);List<Integer>ordered=new ArrayList<>(values);Collections.sort(ordered);int n=ordered.size();double want=n%2==1?ordered.get(n/2):ordered.get(n/2-1)/2.0+ordered.get(n/2)/2.0;assert h.findMedian()==want;assert s.findMedian()==want;assert b.findMedian()==want;assert h.lower.size()==h.upper.size()||h.lower.size()==h.upper.size()+1;if(!h.upper.isEmpty())assert h.lower.peek()<=h.upper.peek();}

reference.title: Find Median from Data Stream
reference.approach: Progress from sorting per query to sorted insertion, then two balanced heaps.
reference.adaptation: The public Java implementations were checked. The two-heap transfer order is preserved; the judge-facing class is MedianFinder and an empty-query guard is explicit.

better.explanation: Keep the list sorted all the time. Binary search finds where the new value belongs, but ArrayList still shifts later entries to make room. That makes insertion O(n), while a median query only reads the middle positions.
better.space: O(n).

258.problem: Return the k distinct numbers that occur most often in an array. The output can be in any order.
258.assumptions: 1 ≤ k ≤ the number of distinct values. The linked problem guarantees a unique answer set. Ties within that selected set do not matter; output order is unrestricted.

example.explanation: 4 appears three times and 7 twice, more often than 2. [7,4] is equally valid.

258.baseline: Count each value, sort the distinct values by decreasing count, and take k. With U distinct values this takes O(n + U log U) time and O(U) space.
258.approach:
A frequency can only be between 1 and n. Use that small range as an array of buckets: bucket[f] contains all values occurring f times. A value goes into one bucket, no matter how large or negative the value itself is.

Walk the buckets from n down to 1 and collect values until k have been taken. Larger frequencies are visited first, so no unvisited value can be more frequent than a value already selected. Counting, filling buckets, and reading them all take linear time.
steps: Count occurrences in a map.
Create n + 1 buckets, indexed by frequency.
Place each distinct value in its frequency bucket.
Visit buckets from highest frequency to lowest, stopping after k values.
258.time: O(n) expected time with hash-map operations.
258.space: O(n + U), which is O(n); buckets are indexed by frequency, not by value.
pitfalls: The answer contains distinct values, not repeated occurrences.
Do not use value as a bucket index. Negative or huge values are valid map keys.
A size-k min-heap is an alternative when allocating n buckets is undesirable.
Output order is unrestricted. Compare answer sets in tests.
tests: Random r=new Random(258);for(int u=1;u<=20;u++)for(int t=0;t<20;t++){List<Integer>values=new ArrayList<>();Set<Integer>keys=new HashSet<>();while(keys.size()<u)keys.add(r.nextInt());int[]key=keys.stream().mapToInt(x->x).toArray();for(int i=0;i<u;i++)for(int j=0;j<=i;j++)values.add(key[i]);Collections.shuffle(values,r);int[]input=values.stream().mapToInt(x->x).toArray();for(int k=1;k<=u;k++){Set<Integer>want=new HashSet<>();for(int i=u-k;i<u;i++)want.add(key[i]);for(int[]result:new int[][]{topKFrequent(input,k),topKSorted(input,k),topKHeap(input,k)}){Set<Integer>got=new HashSet<>();for(int x:result)got.add(x);assert result.length==k&&got.equals(want);}}}

reference.title: Top K Frequent Elements
reference.approach: Count values, then use sorting, a bounded min-heap, or frequency buckets.
reference.adaptation: The public Java sorting and bucket implementations and the heap method were checked. The same three algorithms are shown here; comparisons use Integer.compare.

better.explanation: Count values, then retain only k (frequency, value) pairs in a min-heap. When there are k + 1 candidates, remove the least frequent. The remaining pairs are the required set; polling them need not produce descending frequency order.
better.space: O(U + k).

259.problem: Give at most one cookie to each child. A child is satisfied when the cookie size is at least that child’s requirement. Maximize the number of satisfied children.
259.assumptions: Each cookie can be used once. Cookie sizes and requirements are positive. This version sorts copies, preserving both inputs.

example.explanation: Give 3 to the child needing 2, and 5 to the child needing 4. The cookie of size 1 cannot help any child.

259.baseline: Sort both arrays. For each child, scan the cookie array from the beginning for the smallest unused cookie that fits. A used array prevents assigning a cookie twice. Repeated scans can take O(nm) time.
259.approach:
Start with the easiest child to satisfy and the smallest remaining cookie. If the cookie is too small, skip it: all other remaining children need at least as much. Otherwise, give it to this child and move to the next child.

Using the smallest cookie that fits leaves all larger cookies available. This cannot reduce the number of later matches. If another assignment used this cookie for a harder child and a larger cookie for the easier child, swapping those cookies would still satisfy both.
steps: Sort requirements and cookie sizes.
Keep a pointer to the first unsatisfied child.
Scan cookies from smallest to largest.
Advance the child pointer only when the cookie fits.
Return the number of children passed.
259.time: O(n log n + m log m) for n children and m cookies.
259.space: O(n + m) for the preserved-input copies. The matching scan itself uses O(1).
pitfalls: Do not combine several small cookies for one child; each child gets at most one.
A cookie that is too small is skipped without skipping the child.
Sorting is part of the cost, even though the final scan is linear.
tests: assert findContentChildren(new int[]{2,4,6},new int[]{1,3,5})==2;assert findContentChildren(new int[]{},new int[]{1})==0;assert findContentChildren(new int[]{1},new int[]{})==0;

class Oracle{int solve(int[]g,int[]s,int i,int used){if(i==g.length)return 0;int best=solve(g,s,i+1,used);for(int j=0;j<s.length;j++)if((used&(1<<j))==0&&s[j]>=g[i])best=Math.max(best,1+solve(g,s,i+1,used|(1<<j)));return best;}}Random r=new Random(259);Oracle o=new Oracle();for(int t=0;t<400;t++){int[]a=new int[r.nextInt(7)],b=new int[r.nextInt(7)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(6);for(int i=0;i<b.length;i++)b[i]=1+r.nextInt(6);int[]ac=a.clone(),bc=b.clone();int want=o.solve(a,b,0,0);assert findContentChildren(a,b)==want;assert cookiesByScanning(a,b)==want;assert Arrays.equals(a,ac)&&Arrays.equals(b,bc);}

reference.title: Assign Cookies: Greedy Algorithm and Solution
reference.approach: Sort both arrays and match each child with the smallest remaining cookie that fits.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The repeated-scan and two-pointer choices are preserved; these snippets clone arrays before sorting.

260.problem: Fill a bag up to its weight capacity to get the greatest possible value. You may take a fraction of any item, but no more than the whole item.
260.assumptions: Each item has a positive weight and value. The current TUF task allows up to 100000 items, weights and values up to 10000, and capacity up to 1000000000. Return a double; format it to six decimal places only when displaying it.

example.explanation: The first item gives 6 value per unit of weight; the others give 4. Take the whole first item, then 3 units of either remaining item: 18 + 12 = 30.

260.baseline: Repeatedly scan unused items to find the highest value per unit of weight. Take as much of that item as fits, then repeat. This follows the same choice but finding each next item can take O(n²) time.
260.approach:
Compare items by value per unit of weight, not value alone. A unit of space spent on a higher ratio earns at least as much as the same space spent on a lower ratio. If a proposed solution used some lower-ratio weight while higher-ratio weight was still available, exchanging those portions could only improve its value.

Sort by decreasing ratio. Take whole items while they fit. When the next item is too heavy, take exactly the fraction that fills the remaining space and stop. This exchange works because fractions are allowed; it does not prove the same choice for 0/1 knapsack.
steps: Keep each value paired with its weight.
Sort items by descending value-to-weight ratio.
Take a whole item if its weight fits.
Otherwise add remainingWeight × value / weight and stop.
260.space: O(n) for paired items and object-array sorting; input arrays are preserved.
pitfalls: Use floating-point division when taking a fraction.
Do not sort weights and values independently.
Choosing the largest value alone can waste capacity.
The ratio rule depends on divisibility. It is not a correct general solution to 0/1 knapsack.
Avoid rounding each contribution; round only the final displayed result.
tests: assert Math.abs(fractionalKnapsack(new int[]{18,20,28},new int[]{3,5,7},6)-30)<1e-9;assert Math.abs(fractionalKnapsack(new int[]{60,100,120},new int[]{10,20,30},50)-240)<1e-9;assert Math.abs(fractionalKnapsack(new int[]{10},new int[]{3},1)-10.0/3)<1e-9;

class Oracle{double solve(int[]v,int[]w,int cap,int used){double best=0;for(int i=0;i<v.length;i++)if((used&(1<<i))==0){int take=Math.min(cap,w[i]);double value=(double)take*v[i]/w[i];if(take==w[i])value+=solve(v,w,cap-take,used|(1<<i));best=Math.max(best,value);}return best;}}Random r=new Random(260);Oracle o=new Oracle();for(int t=0;t<300;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(7);int[]v=new int[n],w=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){v[i]=1+r.nextInt(30);w[i]=1+r.nextInt(10);}int cap=r.nextInt(30);assert Math.abs(fractionalKnapsack(v,w,cap)-o.solve(v,w,cap,0))<1e-7;}
assert fractionalKnapsack(new int[]{5,8},new int[]{2,4},100)==13;assert fractionalKnapsack(new int[]{5},new int[]{2},0)==0;

reference.title: Fractional Knapsack
reference.approach: Take items in descending value-to-weight ratio, including a fraction of the final item.
reference.adaptation: The current public practice statement was checked. The older linked tutorial URL now returns Page Not Found, and no public Java editorial was available here. This authored ratio-based implementation is checked against exhaustive item orders.

261.problem: Understand when taking the largest coin first is safe, and solve the actual linked task: find the fewest coins for an amount using arbitrary positive denominations.
261.assumptions: The tracker title refers to a greedy lesson, but its current problem link accepts arbitrary denominations. Greedy needs a coin system for which its optimality has been established. coinChange below is the general solution; standardCurrencyCoins demonstrates the greedy lesson only for the fixed denominations shown. Unlimited copies are available. Amount 0 needs 0 coins.

example.explanation: Use 3 + 3. Taking the largest first would choose 4 + 1 + 1 and return 3, which is wrong for this input.

261.baseline: Try each possible first coin, recursively solve the remaining amount, and take the smallest successful result plus one. This explores the same remaining amounts repeatedly and takes exponential time.
261.approach:
For the fixed standard denominations in the lesson, scan from largest to smallest. Division tells you how many copies fit; remainder tells you what is still unpaid. That is the greedy method shown in the first function. Its restriction matters.

For the linked arbitrary-coin problem, save the answer for every amount instead. Let dp[x] mean the fewest coins needed for x. Start with dp[0] = 0. For each x, try every coin c ≤ x: if x − c is reachable, one more coin gives a candidate dp[x − c] + 1. Take the smallest candidate. Every valid payment has a last coin, so these candidates cover all possibilities.

The public lesson’s first recursive snippet uses a large sentinel for impossible amounts. This version converts that to −1 at the public method boundary, matching the linked problem.
steps: Use the greedy helper only with its fixed denomination list.
For arbitrary coins, initialize dp[0] to 0 and other amounts to an unreachable sentinel.
Fill amounts from 1 upward, trying each usable last coin.
Return dp[amount], or −1 if it remains unreachable.
261.time: General solution: O(n × amount). The fixed nine-denomination greedy helper takes O(1).
261.space: General solution: O(amount). Fixed greedy helper: O(1).
pitfalls: Greedy can return a non-minimum count, or even say impossible when a different combination works.
All denominations must be positive; a zero coin would break recursive progress.
Do not return Integer.MAX_VALUE to represent failure in the public result.
This item and the later DP coin-change item share a problem link, but the greedy limitation is the teaching point here.
tests: assert coinChange(new int[]{1,3,4},6)==2;assert coinChange(new int[]{3,4},6)==2;assert coinChange(new int[]{2,5},3)==-1;assert coinChange(new int[]{7},0)==0;assert standardCurrencyCoins(43)==4;

reference.title: Minimum Number of Coins
reference.approach: Largest-first division for suitable denominations, with a separate correct DP solution for the tracker’s arbitrary-coin link.
reference.adaptation: The public recursive and greedy Java were checked. The article explicitly warns that greedy fails for arbitrary denominations. Its first recursive snippet leaves impossible amounts as Integer.MAX_VALUE; the wrapper here returns −1. The general DP method is an authored addition required by the current problem link.

262.problem: Sell each lemonade for 5 and give exact change to customers arriving in order with bills of 5, 10, or 20. Decide whether every customer can be served.
262.assumptions: You start with no money. You cannot reorder customers or borrow bills from later customers. Each customer buys one lemonade.

example.explanation: For the 20, give 10 + 5. This saves one 5 bill, which provides change for the final 10.

262.baseline: At each 20 bill, try both possible ways to give 15 in change and recursively check the rest of the queue. This explores unnecessary choices; keeping smaller bills gives a safe rule.
262.approach:
Track how many 5 and 10 bills you have. A 10 requires one 5 as change. A 20 requires either 10 + 5 or three 5s. Prefer 10 + 5 whenever it is available.

Three 5s can do everything that a 10 and a 5 can do, and they can also serve separate customers paying 10. Saving those smaller bills therefore leaves at least as much flexibility. There is no need to track 20 bills because no required change exceeds 15.
steps: For a 5 bill, keep it.
For a 10 bill, require one 5, then keep the 10.
For a 20 bill, use 10 + 5 if possible; otherwise use three 5s.
Fail immediately if exact change is unavailable.
pitfalls: Process customers in their original order.
Having enough total money does not mean you have the right denominations.
For a 20, save the extra 5 bills when 10 + 5 is possible.
tests: assert lemonadeChange(new int[]{5,5,10,5,20,10});assert !lemonadeChange(new int[]{5,5,10,10,20});assert !lemonadeChange(new int[]{10});assert !lemonadeChange(new int[]{20});

class Oracle{boolean solve(int[]a,int i,int f,int t){if(i==a.length)return true;if(a[i]==5)return solve(a,i+1,f+1,t);if(a[i]==10)return f>0&&solve(a,i+1,f-1,t+1);return (f>0&&t>0&&solve(a,i+1,f-1,t-1))||(f>=3&&solve(a,i+1,f-3,t));}}Oracle o=new Oracle();for(int n=0;n<=9;n++){int total=(int)Math.pow(3,n);for(int mask=0;mask<total;mask++){int x=mask;int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=new int[]{5,10,20}[x%3];x/=3;}assert lemonadeChange(a)==o.solve(a,0,0,0);}}

reference.title: Lemonade Change: Greedy Algorithm and Solution
reference.approach: Count 5 and 10 bills and prefer 10 + 5 when giving change for 20.
reference.adaptation: The public Java method was checked. The same branch order is retained; exhaustive short queues are compared with a search that tries both change choices.

263.problem: Decide whether a string of (, ), and * can become balanced parentheses. Each * may become (, ), or nothing.
263.assumptions: Order matters: a closing parenthesis must have an opening parenthesis before it. This is the wildcard problem, not the earlier stack problem containing several bracket types. An empty string is accepted.

example.explanation: Treat * as (. The result is (()), which is balanced.

263.baseline: Try all three replacements for each star, rejecting any prefix with more closes than opens. With s stars there can be 3^s choices.
263.approach:
After each character, many counts of unmatched opening parentheses may be possible. Keep only the smallest and largest possible counts, low and high. The possible counts between them form a continuous range.

An opening parenthesis increases both bounds. A closing parenthesis decreases both. A star can decrease the count, keep it unchanged, or increase it, so low decreases and high increases. If high becomes negative, even the most generous interpretation has too many closes: return false. Clamp low to zero because a negative count is not a valid prefix.

At the end, zero must be a possible count. Since the lower bound never goes below zero, this is exactly low == 0.
steps: Start low = high = 0.
Update both bounds for the next character.
Return false if high < 0.
Replace negative low with zero.
After the full string, return whether low is zero.
pitfalls: Equal total numbers of opens and closes are not enough; every prefix must remain possible.
A star may be empty, so do not force every star to become a bracket.
Check high before clamping low. Clamping both would hide an impossible prefix.
Return low == 0, not high == 0. Some valid interpretations may still leave unmatched opens.
tests: class Oracle{boolean solve(String s,int i,int open){if(open<0)return false;if(i==s.length())return open==0;char c=s.charAt(i);if(c=='(')return solve(s,i+1,open+1);if(c==')')return solve(s,i+1,open-1);return solve(s,i+1,open)||solve(s,i+1,open-1)||solve(s,i+1,open+1);}}Oracle o=new Oracle();for(int n=0;n<=9;n++){int total=(int)Math.pow(3,n);for(int mask=0;mask<total;mask++){int x=mask;StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<n;i++){s.append("()*".charAt(x%3));x/=3;}assert checkValidString(s.toString())==o.solve(s.toString(),0,0);}}

reference.title: Valid Parenthesis Checker
reference.approach: Track the range of possible unmatched opening counts.
reference.adaptation: The current public statement and its low/high hint were checked. The page exposes a starter rather than a public Java editorial. This authored implementation is checked against all star replacements on short strings.

264.problem: Select the largest number of meetings that one room can hold. A selected meeting must start strictly after the previous selected meeting ends.
264.assumptions: Each meeting has start < end. Start and end at the same time are incompatible in this task. The method returns a count, not meeting IDs, and preserves the input arrays.

example.explanation: Choose (1,3), (4,6), and (7,8). Choosing the longer (2,5) would leave less room.

264.baseline: Try taking or skipping every meeting. Before taking one, check that it is compatible with every already selected meeting. There are 2^n subsets, and each compatibility check may scan n meetings.
264.approach:
Among meetings that can fit next, choose the one ending earliest. It leaves the room available at least as early as any other choice.

To see why this is safe, take an optimal schedule and replace its first meeting with the earliest-finishing one. Every later meeting still fits, because the replacement ends no later. Apply the same argument to the remaining meetings. Sorting by end time lets us make this choice in one scan.
steps: Pair each start with its own end.
Sort the pairs by ending time.
Select the first meeting, then select a meeting only when start > lastEnd.
Update lastEnd each time a meeting is selected.
pitfalls: Use >, not >=, for this task’s compatibility rule.
Sorting start and end arrays independently would create different meetings.
Earliest start or shortest duration alone does not guarantee the most meetings.
tests: assert maxMeetings(new int[]{1,2,4,7},new int[]{3,5,6,8})==3;assert maxMeetings(new int[]{1,2},new int[]{2,3})==1;assert maxMeetings(new int[]{},new int[]{})==0;

Random r=new Random(264);for(int t=0;t<800;t++){int n=r.nextInt(10);int[]s=new int[n],e=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){s[i]=r.nextInt(15)-5;e[i]=s[i]+1+r.nextInt(6);}int best=0;for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){boolean ok=true;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0)for(int j=0;j<i;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0&&!(e[i]<s[j]||e[j]<s[i]))ok=false;if(ok)best=Math.max(best,Integer.bitCount(mask));}assert maxMeetings(s,e)==best;assert meetingsSearch(s,e,0,new ArrayList<>())==best;}

reference.title: N Meetings in One Room: Maximum Meetings Using Greedy
reference.approach: Try compatible subsets, then sort by finishing time and select compatible meetings.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked, including their strict endpoint comparison. A long initial sentinel also supports negative start times without accidentally skipping the first meeting.

265.problem: Starting at index 0, decide whether you can reach the last index. nums[i] is the maximum forward jump length from index i.
265.assumptions: The array is non-empty and values are non-negative. A jump may be shorter than nums[i]. A one-element array is already at the destination.

example.explanation: Jump from 0 to 1, then from 1 to 4. Jumping the full distance from 0 would land on 2 and get stuck.

265.baseline: Try every reachable next index, remembering whether each index can eventually reach the end. Memoization avoids recomputing an index, but up to n next indices may be tried per state.
265.approach:
Track the farthest reachable position while scanning from left to right. Every position up to that boundary can be reached, because each jump permits all shorter lengths too. A reachable position i can extend the boundary to i + nums[i].

Before using a position, check that it is inside the boundary. If i is already beyond it, no earlier reachable position can cross this gap. If the boundary reaches the last index, stop successfully. This considers every reachable take-off point; it does not commit to always landing as far away as possible.
steps: Start farthest at 0.
Reject an index greater than farthest before using its jump length.
Extend farthest with i + nums[i].
Return true as soon as the last index is covered.
pitfalls: Never extend the boundary from an unreachable index.
A zero is only a problem when no earlier jump can pass it.
Maximum jump length is an upper limit, not a required jump size.
tests: assert canJump(new int[]{2,3,0,0,1});assert !canJump(new int[]{3,2,1,0,4});assert canJump(new int[]{0});assert !canJump(new int[]{0,1});

for(int n=1;n<=8;n++){int total=1<<(2*n);for(int mask=0;mask<total;mask++){int x=mask;int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=x&3;x>>=2;}boolean[]seen=new boolean[n];seen[0]=true;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(seen[i])for(int j=i+1;j<n&&j<=i+a[i];j++)seen[j]=true;assert canJump(a)==seen[n-1];assert canJumpMemo(a)==seen[n-1];}}

reference.title: Jump Game I: Can You Reach the Last Index?
reference.approach: Memoize reachable suffixes, then track the farthest reachable prefix.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The algorithms are preserved; reach arithmetic uses long so large int jump lengths do not wrap.

265.baselineTime: O(n²) time and O(n) memo/recursion space. Large recursive inputs can exhaust the Java stack.

266.problem: Return the fewest forward jumps needed to reach the final index, where nums[i] gives the maximum jump length from i.
266.assumptions: The linked problem guarantees that the last index is reachable. This version additionally returns −1 for unreachable input. The array is non-empty with non-negative values. One element needs zero jumps.

example.explanation: One jump can reach index 1 or 2. From index 1, the second jump can reach index 4.

266.baseline: For each index, try every legal next index and take one plus the smallest remaining jump count. Memoize each index so its answer is computed once; the total can still be O(n²).
266.approach:
Think in layers of reachable positions. With zero jumps, only index 0 is reachable. Scan all positions covered by the current jump count and find the farthest place one more jump could reach. Only after finishing that entire layer do you increase the jump count.

currentEnd marks the current layer’s boundary. farthest collects the next boundary while scanning. When i reaches currentEnd, every candidate take-off point in that layer has been considered. Moving to the next layer uses one more jump, just as breadth-first search moves one edge farther. Stop before scanning the final index, because arriving there requires no additional jump.
steps: Set jumps, currentEnd and farthest to zero.
Scan only indices before the final index.
Update farthest using the current position.
At currentEnd, fail if the boundary cannot advance; otherwise count a jump and advance the boundary.
Stop once the new boundary covers the destination.
pitfalls: Count a jump when the current layer ends, not at every scanned index.
Do not jump again from the last index.
The original problem promises reachability; the −1 branch is an explicit extension.
A large value at an unreachable index cannot rescue an earlier gap.
tests: assert jump(new int[]{2,3,0,0,1})==2;assert jump(new int[]{0})==0;assert jump(new int[]{0,1})==-1;assert jump(new int[]{1,1,1,1})==3;

for(int n=1;n<=8;n++){int total=1<<(2*n);for(int mask=0;mask<total;mask++){int x=mask;int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=x&3;x>>=2;}int[]d=new int[n];Arrays.fill(d,1000);d[0]=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<n&&j<=i+a[i];j++)d[j]=Math.min(d[j],d[i]+1);int want=d[n-1]==1000?-1:d[n-1];assert jump(a)==want;assert jumpMemo(a)==want;}}

reference.title: Jump Game II: Minimum Jumps to Reach the End
reference.approach: Compare memoized next-index choices with a greedy scan of jump layers.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The currentEnd/farthest scan is preserved; unreachable input returns −1 and reach arithmetic is widened and capped safely.

266.baselineTime: O(n²) time and O(n) memo/recursion space.

267.problem: Find the minimum number of railway platforms needed so that no train waits. Each train occupies a platform from its arrival through its departure time.
267.assumptions: Times are same-day HHMM integers with each arrival no later than its own departure. An arrival exactly equal to another departure needs a separate platform. We compare times, so HHMM values need no conversion to minutes. Overnight intervals are outside this contract.

example.explanation: At 9:30 the first two trains overlap. At 10:00 the first and third also overlap because equal arrival/departure times still need two platforms.

267.baseline: At each arrival time, scan all trains and count those already arrived and not yet departed. The largest count is the answer, because occupancy increases only at arrivals.
267.approach:
We only need the count of trains present, not their identities. Sort a copy of arrivals and a copy of departures independently. Compare the next arrival with the next departure.

If arrival ≤ departure, count the arrival first. Otherwise, process the departure and free one platform. Track the highest count reached. At that busiest moment, fewer platforms are impossible; that many are also enough because any newly free platform can be reused.
steps: Sort separate copies of arrivals and departures.
Start two pointers and an occupancy count at zero.
Process arrivals before departures when times are equal.
Increase on arrival and decrease on departure.
Return the greatest occupancy seen.
267.space: O(n) for copies that preserve the input. The sweep uses O(1) working variables.
pitfalls: Use <= for arrivals here. Changing it to < changes the problem’s equal-time rule.
For platform capacity, train identity is irrelevant, so independent sorting is valid. This is different from selecting meeting pairs.
