Do not subtract HHMM values as though they were durations in minutes.
tests: assert minimumPlatforms(new int[]{900,930,1000},new int[]{1000,945,1030})==2;assert minimumPlatforms(new int[]{900,900,900},new int[]{900,900,900})==3;assert minimumPlatforms(new int[]{},new int[]{})==0;

Random r=new Random(267);for(int t=0;t<3000;t++){int n=r.nextInt(40);int[]a=new int[n],d=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i]=900+r.nextInt(40);d[i]=a[i]+r.nextInt(15);}int[]ac=a.clone(),dc=d.clone();assert minimumPlatforms(a,d)==platformsByCounting(a,d);assert Arrays.equals(a,ac)&&Arrays.equals(d,dc);}

reference.title: Minimum Platforms Required for a Railway Station
reference.approach: Count simultaneous trains, then sweep independently sorted arrivals and departures.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods and the arrival-before-departure tie rule were checked. This version sorts copies to preserve the tracker example inputs.

268.problem: Schedule unit-time jobs to maximize total profit. Each job must finish by its deadline. Return the number of selected jobs and their total profit.
268.assumptions: Every job takes one time unit, deadlines are positive integers, and profits are positive. A slot numbered d finishes at time d and is allowed for deadline d. This version uses long for accumulated profit and returns long[]{count, profit}.

example.explanation: Put job 2 in slot 1, job 1 in slot 2, and job 4 in slot 3. Their profits total 40 + 60 + 20.

268.baseline: Try subsets of jobs. A chosen subset is schedulable if, after sorting its deadlines, the ith job can finish in slot i + 1. Compare profits of all feasible subsets; this is exponential.
268.approach:
Consider larger profits first, since every job consumes the same one unit of time. For each job, search backward from its deadline and place it in the latest free slot. A job with a late deadline should not occupy an early slot that another job may need.

The backward placement keeps earlier slots free whenever possible. If there is no slot by this job’s deadline, all those slots are already occupied by jobs considered earlier, each with at least as much profit. Adding this job would require giving up one of those jobs and cannot improve the total.

There are only n jobs, so no useful schedule needs more than n slots. Cap deadlines at n when allocating and searching the timeline; very large deadlines then do not waste memory.
steps: Sort a copy of the jobs by decreasing profit.
Create free slots 1 through min(maxDeadline, n).
For each job, search backward for the latest free slot no later than its deadline.
If found, occupy it and add the job’s count and profit.
268.time: O(n log n + nD), where D = min(n, maximum deadline). This is Striver’s backward-slot scan, not a near-linear slot data structure.
268.space: O(n + D) for the sorted copy and occupancy array.
pitfalls: A deadline is a latest finish time, not a mandatory slot.
Place a chosen job as late as possible.
The greedy rule assumes every job has the same duration.
Use a wide type for total profit; individual profits fitting int does not guarantee their sum fits int.
tests: Job[]a={new Job(1,2,60),new Job(2,1,40),new Job(3,2,30),new Job(4,3,20)};assert Arrays.equals(jobScheduling(a),new long[]{3,120});assert a[0].id==1;assert Arrays.equals(jobScheduling(new Job[]{}),new long[]{0,0});

Random r=new Random(268);for(int t=0;t<1000;t++){int n=r.nextInt(10);Job[]a=new Job[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=new Job(i,1+r.nextInt(12),1+r.nextInt(100));long bestProfit=0;int bestCount=0;for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){List<Integer>d=new ArrayList<>();long profit=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0){d.add(a[i].deadline);profit+=a[i].profit;}Collections.sort(d);boolean ok=true;for(int i=0;i<d.size();i++)if(d.get(i)<i+1)ok=false;if(ok&&(profit>bestProfit||(profit==bestProfit&&d.size()>bestCount))){bestProfit=profit;bestCount=d.size();}}assert Arrays.equals(jobScheduling(a),new long[]{bestCount,bestProfit});}

reference.title: Job Sequencing Problem: Maximize Profit Before Deadlines
reference.approach: Consider jobs by decreasing profit and place each in its latest free slot.
reference.adaptation: The public Java backward-slot algorithm was checked. This version caps the timeline at n, preserves job order by sorting a copy, and widens total profit to long. These adaptations are reflected in the complexity and return type.

269.problem: Give every child at least one candy. A child with a higher rating than an adjacent child must get more candies than that neighbour. Return the smallest possible total.
269.assumptions: Only immediate neighbours matter. Equal ratings impose no equality requirement on candy counts. The linked problem has at most 20000 children; this version returns long and also handles larger totals.

example.explanation: A minimum distribution is [1,3,2,1,1]. The peak needs 3 because two lower-rated children descend to its right. The final equal pair may each receive 1.

269.baseline: Start everyone at one candy. Repeatedly scan neighbour pairs and increase any count that violates a higher-rating rule. Eventually all rules hold, but long slopes may require many passes.
269.approach:
First satisfy the left neighbour: scan left to right, giving one extra candy whenever the rating rises. Then satisfy the right neighbour with a right-to-left pass.

During the second pass, keep the larger of the count already assigned and the count required by the right neighbour. Replacing rather than taking the maximum could undo the left-side rule. Each child must meet both lower bounds, and their maximum is enough; any larger value would be unnecessary.
steps: Initialize every candy count to 1.
On a left-to-right pass, increase the count when the rating rises.
On a right-to-left pass, take max(current, right + 1) when the rating is higher than the right rating.
Sum all counts using long.
pitfalls: Equal ratings do not force equal candy counts.
Use max on the reverse pass so the first pass is not undone.
A local rating peak may need enough candies for the longer of its two slopes.
tests: assert candy(new int[]{2,4,3,2,2})==8;assert candy(new int[]{1,0,2})==5;assert candy(new int[]{1,2,2})==4;assert candy(new int[]{})==0;

class Oracle{int solve(int[]r,int i,int[]c,int sum,int best){if(i==r.length)return Math.min(best,sum);for(int v=1;v<=r.length;v++){if(sum+v>=best)continue;if(i>0&&((r[i]>r[i-1]&&v<=c[i-1])||(r[i]<r[i-1]&&v>=c[i-1])))continue;c[i]=v;best=solve(r,i+1,c,sum+v,best);}return best;}}Oracle o=new Oracle();for(int n=1;n<=5;n++){int total=(int)Math.pow(3,n);for(int mask=0;mask<total;mask++){int x=mask;int[]r=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){r[i]=x%3;x/=3;}assert candy(r)==o.solve(r,0,new int[n],0,Integer.MAX_VALUE);}}

reference.title: Candy Distribution: Minimum Candies for Given Ratings
reference.approach: Use forward and reverse passes, keeping the larger neighbour requirement.
reference.adaptation: The current public Java uses a candy array and two passes; this guide follows that version. The total is widened to long. Exhaustive small assignments check minimality, including equal ratings.

270.problem: Schedule all processes using shortest job first and return the floor of their average waiting time.
270.assumptions: All processes are available at time 0. Each runs to completion once selected. Burst times are positive. Waiting time excludes a process’s own execution time. The linked task can have 100000 processes with burst times up to 100000, so both accumulated time and waiting sum use long.

example.explanation: Run 2, then 4, then 6. Their waiting times are 0,2,6. The average is 8/3, and its floor is 2.

270.baseline: Try every process order, calculate its total waiting time, and take the smallest. There are n! orders, so this is useful only for tiny test cases.
270.approach:
Sort burst times from shortest to longest. To understand why, compare two adjacent jobs of lengths a and b after the same elapsed time. Running a first makes the pair’s combined waiting time smaller than running b first exactly when a ≤ b. Swapping an out-of-order pair does not affect jobs after the pair, because the total duration stays a + b. Repeating such swaps leads to sorted order.

Before running each process, add the elapsed time to the waiting sum. Then add its burst time to elapsed. Divide the final sum by n using integer division, which gives the requested floor because all values are non-negative.
steps: Sort a copy of the burst times.
Start elapsed and totalWaiting at zero.
For each process, add elapsed to totalWaiting before advancing elapsed.
Return totalWaiting / numberOfProcesses.
pitfalls: Add waiting time before adding the current process’s duration.
Do not round to the nearest integer; the task asks for the floor.
If processes have different arrival times, sorting all durations upfront is no longer this problem’s solution.
Use long: valid input can exceed int even for the final average.
tests: assert averageWaitingTime(new int[]{6,2,4})==2;assert averageWaitingTime(new int[]{4,1,3,7,2})==4;assert averageWaitingTime(new int[]{8})==0;

class Oracle{long best(int[]a,int used,long elapsed,long waiting){if(used==(1<<a.length)-1)return waiting;long result=Long.MAX_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)if((used&(1<<i))==0)result=Math.min(result,best(a,used|(1<<i),elapsed+a[i],waiting+elapsed));return result;}}Random r=new Random(270);Oracle o=new Oracle();for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(7);int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(12);int[]copy=a.clone();assert averageWaitingTime(a)==o.best(a,0,0,0)/n;assert Arrays.equals(a,copy);}

reference.title: Shortest Job First
reference.approach: Sort burst times and accumulate the waiting time before each process runs.
reference.adaptation: The public statement, floor requirement, bounds and all-processes-available model were checked. It exposes a starter rather than a public Java editorial. This authored Java is checked against all process orders on small inputs.

271.problem: Count page faults under least-recently-used page replacement. On a miss, load the page; if memory is full, evict the resident page whose last use was longest ago.
271.assumptions: The tracker title says page replacement, but its link opens the LRU cache-design task, also covered earlier in the sheet. This page teaches the title’s page-fault simulation. Memory begins empty. A hit refreshes recency. With capacity 0, every request is a fault.

example.explanation: Load 1 and 2. The second request for 1 is a hit and makes 2 least recent. Loading 3 evicts 2; requesting 2 again faults and evicts 1.

271.baseline: Keep resident pages in a list from least to most recently used. For each request, find and remove the old entry if present, or count a fault and remove the first entry when full. Append the requested page. Searching and shifting can cost O(capacity) per request.
271.approach:
Use a LinkedHashSet, which combines fast membership checks with insertion order. Keep its first entry as the least recently used page and its last entry as the most recently used.

For a hit, remove the page and add it again so it moves to the end. For a miss, count one fault; if full, remove the first entry through an iterator, then add the new page. Reading a resident page must update its position—otherwise the policy becomes first-in-first-out rather than LRU.
steps: Return the request count immediately when capacity is zero.
Try to remove the requested page; success means a hit.
On a miss, count a fault and evict the oldest entry if full.
Add the page at the end on both hits and misses.
271.time: O(n) expected time with hash-set operations.
pitfalls: A hit changes recency even though it adds no fault.
Faults count failed lookups, including loads into an empty slot.
An ordinary HashSet does not preserve the eviction order.
This is an authored page-replacement adaptation, not a claim that TUF’s linked cache starter contains this exact method.
tests: assert pageFaultsLRU(new int[]{1,2,1,3,2},2)==4;assert pageFaultsLRU(new int[]{1,1,1},1)==1;assert pageFaultsLRU(new int[]{1,1,1},0)==3;assert pageFaultsLRU(new int[]{},4)==0;

Random r=new Random(271);for(int t=0;t<2000;t++){int[]a=new int[r.nextInt(70)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(12)-6;int capacity=r.nextInt(10),faults=0;Set<Integer>resident=new HashSet<>();for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){if(resident.contains(a[i]))continue;faults++;if(capacity==0)continue;if(resident.size()==capacity){int victim=0,oldest=Integer.MAX_VALUE;for(int value:resident){int last=i-1;while(last>=0&&a[last]!=value)last--;if(last<oldest){oldest=last;victim=value;}}resident.remove(victim);}resident.add(a[i]);}assert pageFaultsLRU(a,capacity)==faults;assert pageFaultsList(a,capacity)==faults;}

reference.title: LRU Cache
reference.approach: Apply the same least-recently-used ordering to page-fault counting.
reference.adaptation: The pinned URL is the cache-design problem, whose public contract was checked for the earlier LRU guide. It is not a page-replacement editorial. This page explicitly follows the tracker title and provides an authored simulation with an independent last-access oracle.

272.problem: Insert one closed interval into an already sorted list of non-overlapping closed intervals. Merge every overlap and return the result in order.
272.assumptions: Each interval is [start,end] with start ≤ end. The original intervals are sorted and mutually disjoint. Touching endpoints overlap. This version preserves the input arrays and returns new interval arrays.

example.explanation: The new interval touches the first and last intervals and overlaps the middle one, joining them into one range.

272.baseline: Append the new interval, sort all intervals by start, and run the usual merge scan. That works even without the sorted-input promise, but costs O(n log n).
272.approach:
The existing order already tells us where the new interval belongs. Copy intervals that end strictly before it starts. Then merge all intervals whose starts are at most the current merged end. Finally, copy the remaining intervals.

The merged end may grow as overlaps are absorbed, so use its updated value in the next comparison. Once an interval begins after that end, every later interval begins after it too; no further overlap is possible.
steps: Copy intervals with end < newStart.
While start ≤ mergedEnd, widen the new range with min(start) and max(end).
Append the completed merged range.
Copy the remaining intervals.
272.space: O(n) for the returned intervals; O(1) additional scan state.
pitfalls: Touching endpoints merge in this problem.
Use the updated merged end when checking the next interval.
This linear algorithm depends on sorted, non-overlapping input.
Copy each interval if the returned result must not share mutable arrays with the input.
tests: assert Arrays.deepEquals(insertInterval(new int[][]{{1,2},{5,7},{10,12}},new int[]{2,10}),new int[][]{{1,12}});assert Arrays.deepEquals(insertInterval(new int[][]{},new int[]{4,4}),new int[][]{{4,4}});assert Arrays.deepEquals(insertInterval(new int[][]{{1,9}},new int[]{3,4}),new int[][]{{1,9}});

Random r=new Random(272);for(int t=0;t<4000;t++){int n=r.nextInt(20);int[][]a=new int[n][2];int cursor=-30;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){a[i][0]=cursor+r.nextInt(3);a[i][1]=a[i][0]+r.nextInt(5);cursor=a[i][1]+1+r.nextInt(4);}int start=r.nextInt(100)-40;int[]added={start,start+r.nextInt(30)};String before=Arrays.deepToString(a),old=Arrays.toString(added);int[][]got=insertInterval(a,added),want=insertBySorting(a,added);assert Arrays.deepEquals(got,want);assert before.equals(Arrays.deepToString(a))&&old.equals(Arrays.toString(added));for(int[]row:got){assert row!=added;for(int[]input:a)assert row!=input;}for(int i=1;i<got.length;i++)assert got[i-1][1]<got[i][0];}

reference.title: Insert a New Interval
reference.approach: Append-and-sort as a baseline, then use the existing order for a three-part scan.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. Their comparisons are preserved; local bounds and cloned output rows avoid the source snippets’ input mutation and shared-row aliasing.

273.problem: Merge overlapping closed intervals into disjoint ranges that cover exactly the same points. Return them sorted by start.
273.assumptions: Input intervals may be unsorted, duplicated or nested. Each has start ≤ end. Touching intervals overlap because endpoints are included. This method preserves the original arrays and creates new output rows. This is the same problem as “Merge Overlapping Subintervals” in the earlier Arrays section.

example.explanation: The first pair in sorted order overlaps between 3 and 4. The last pair shares endpoint 11, so it also merges.

273.baseline: Striver’s look-ahead version sorts by start, expands a new range by scanning later overlapping intervals, and skips intervals already covered by the last completed range. Although it has nested loops, that skip rule means each merged group is scanned ahead once. For this exact code, total work after sorting is O(n), not O(n²).
273.approach:
Sort by start time. Maintain the result ranges in order. The next interval can only overlap the last result range: all earlier result ranges already end before the last one starts.

If the new start is greater than the last end, start another range. Otherwise, extend the last end to the larger of the two ends. Taking the maximum is essential for nested intervals; an interval inside the current range must not shrink it.

This one-pass form is easier to follow than the look-ahead version. Both shown methods take O(n log n) overall with their skip rules and sorting.
steps: Sort a copy of the interval references by start.
Append a cloned row when the result is empty or the next interval starts after the last end.
Otherwise extend the last end with max(lastEnd, nextEnd).
Return the merged rows.
273.time: O(n log n), including sorting; the merge scan is O(n).
273.space: O(n) for the sorted reference copy, sorting workspace and output.
pitfalls: Use max when extending an end; nested intervals must not shrink a range.
Touching intervals merge here. The later removal problem uses a different rule.
Two nested loops do not automatically imply quadratic time; count how often elements are actually scanned.
Integer.compare avoids overflow in endpoint comparisons.
tests: assert Arrays.deepEquals(mergeIntervals(new int[][]{{8,11},{1,4},{3,6},{11,13}}),new int[][]{{1,6},{8,13}});assert Arrays.deepEquals(mergeIntervals(new int[][]{{1,10},{2,3},{1,10}}),new int[][]{{1,10}});assert mergeIntervals(new int[][]{}).length==0;

Random r=new Random(273);for(int t=0;t<4000;t++){int[][]a=new int[r.nextInt(25)][2];for(int[]row:a){row[0]=r.nextInt(25)-12;row[1]=row[0]+r.nextInt(10);}String before=Arrays.deepToString(a);int[][]got=mergeIntervals(a);assert Arrays.deepEquals(got,mergeLookAhead(a));assert before.equals(Arrays.deepToString(a));for(int i=1;i<got.length;i++)assert got[i-1][1]<got[i][0];for(int twice=-30;twice<=50;twice++){boolean old=false,now=false;for(int[]row:a)if(2*row[0]<=twice&&twice<=2*row[1])old=true;for(int[]row:got)if(2*row[0]<=twice&&twice<=2*row[1])now=true;assert old==now;}for(int[]row:got)for(int[]old:a)assert row!=old;}

reference.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
reference.approach: Sort by start, then combine each overlap with the last merged range.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. Inputs are preserved by copying. The article labels its look-ahead Java quadratic, but its covered-interval skip rule makes the post-sort work linear; the guide explains that correction instead of repeating the bound.

273.baselineTime: O(n log n) overall. Each interval belongs to one look-ahead group and is then skipped by the outer loop; each group also checks at most one non-overlapping successor. O(n) space.

274.problem: Remove as few intervals as possible so that the remaining intervals do not overlap. Return the number removed.
274.assumptions: Each interval has start < end. In this problem, intervals sharing only an endpoint are compatible: [1,2] and [2,3] can both remain. This differs from the meeting-selection and interval-merging rules earlier in the sheet. The original row order is preserved.

example.explanation: Remove [1,5]. The other three intervals touch at endpoints but do not overlap under this problem’s rule.

274.baseline: Try every subset, keep those with no overlaps, and find the largest number that can remain. Subtract that count from n. This takes exponential time.
274.approach:
Minimizing removals is the same as keeping as many intervals as possible. Sort by ending time and keep the earliest-finishing interval that fits next. An earlier finish leaves at least as much room for the rest.

If an optimal choice began with a later-finishing interval, replacing it with this one would not block any later interval. Repeating that exchange gives an optimal sequence. While scanning, remove intervals starting before the last kept end; keep those starting at or after it.
steps: Sort a copy by ending time.
Keep the first interval if one exists.
Remove each interval whose start is less than the last kept end.
Otherwise keep it and update the last end.
274.space: O(n) for the copied references and Java object-array sorting workspace. The selection scan uses O(1).
pitfalls: Touching endpoints are compatible here, so start == lastEnd is kept.
Remove overlapping intervals without extending lastEnd; keep the earlier-finishing choice.
Do not use the merge-intervals algorithm. Merging changes ranges, whereas this task only permits deletion.
tests: assert eraseOverlapIntervals(new int[][]{{1,5},{1,2},{2,3},{3,4}})==1;assert eraseOverlapIntervals(new int[][]{{1,2},{2,3}})==0;assert eraseOverlapIntervals(new int[][]{{1,2},{1,2},{1,2}})==2;assert eraseOverlapIntervals(new int[][]{})==0;

Random r=new Random(274);for(int t=0;t<1500;t++){int n=r.nextInt(10);int[][]a=new int[n][2];for(int[]row:a){row[0]=r.nextInt(20)-10;row[1]=row[0]+1+r.nextInt(7);}int kept=0;for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){boolean ok=true;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0)for(int j=0;j<i;j++)if((mask&(1<<j))!=0&&a[i][0]<a[j][1]&&a[j][0]<a[i][1])ok=false;if(ok)kept=Math.max(kept,Integer.bitCount(mask));}String before=Arrays.deepToString(a);assert eraseOverlapIntervals(a)==n-kept;assert before.equals(Arrays.deepToString(a));}

reference.title: Non-overlapping Intervals: Minimum Removals
reference.approach: Keep compatible intervals in earliest-finish order and count the rest as removals.
reference.adaptation: The public Java method and touching-endpoint rule were checked. This version sorts a reference copy. Its space bound includes Java object-array sorting, rather than repeating the article’s constant-space summary.

275.problem: Understand a binary tree’s nodes, child links, leaves, depth and height. Use a small Java tree to count nodes and leaves and measure its height.
275.assumptions: A valid tree has no cycles, and each non-root node has exactly one parent. A binary tree has at most two children per node; it does not require left values to be smaller. This page measures height in edges: a leaf has height 0 and an empty tree has height −1. The later maximum-depth problem counts nodes instead.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; node 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: 8 is the root. 6 and 9 have no children, so they are leaves. The longest path 8 → 4 → 6 contains two edges.

275.baseline: Draw the tree and count by hand. For a program, following the child references is safer than assuming values or array positions identify the structure. A missing child is null, not a node holding zero.
275.approach:
Each node stores a value and two child references. The root is your entry point. A leaf has neither child; an internal node has at least one. A subtree is a node together with everything below it.

To count nodes, count the left subtree, count the right subtree, and add one for the current node. To measure edge height, take the larger child height and add one. Returning −1 for null makes a leaf’s height 0.

Keep the tree types separate: full means every node has zero or two children; complete means the last level fills from the left; perfect means every internal node has two children and all leaves are at one depth. Height-balanced means the two subtree heights differ by at most one at every node. None of these definitions makes a general binary tree a binary search tree.
steps: Represent missing children with null.
Stop recursion at null.
Combine the two subtree counts or heights.
State whether height counts edges or nodes before using a formula.
275.time: Each helper visits every node: O(n). Calling all three is still O(n).
275.space: O(h + 1) recursion space for edge height h, plus the existing tree. A long chain can exhaust Java’s call stack.
pitfalls: A single-node tree is also a leaf.
Depth measures the path from the root; height measures the longest downward path.
A non-empty tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges.
Inorder is sorted only when the tree also satisfies a BST ordering rule.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert countNodes(r)==4;assert countLeaves(r)==2;assert edgeHeight(r)==2;

276.problem: Understand the linked and array representations of a binary tree. Translate the pinned C++ representation lesson into Java, and build a complete tree from an array.
276.assumptions: The tracker keeps the original “Binary Tree Representation in C++” title. This Java-focused guide explains the same structure: C++ child pointers correspond to Java object references, and nullptr corresponds to null. The array builder here is specifically for a complete tree with no missing positions; it is not a parser for compact level-order arrays containing null.

example.output: 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has children 2 and 6
example.explanation: With zero-based indexing, the children of index 1 are at indices 3 and 4.

276.baseline: Connect every node manually when the tree is tiny. For a complete tree represented by an array, repeating those assignments by hand is unnecessary because child positions follow a formula.
276.approach:
In a linked tree, each node refers directly to its children. In a zero-based complete-tree array, the left child of position i is 2i + 1 and the right child is 2i + 2. A non-root node’s parent is (i − 1) / 2.

Create a Java node for each array value, then connect children using those indices when they are in bounds. This separates creating objects from wiring them together. It also avoids recursion. Sparse trees are usually easier to store with references: an array indexed by complete-tree positions can waste many empty slots.
steps: Allocate one TreeNode per value.
For each position, calculate its left and right child indices.
Connect existing child positions; leave others null.
Return node 0, or null for an empty array.
276.space: O(n) new tree nodes and O(n) temporary reference-array space.
pitfalls: The array formula describes tree positions, not BST value ordering.
Do not use 2i + 1 on a compact level-order serialization after null parents have been omitted.
Java has no C++ delete operation; unreachable objects are managed by garbage collection.
Two equal values still need two different node objects when they occupy different positions.
tests: assert fromCompleteArray(new int[]{})==null;TreeNode r=fromCompleteArray(new int[]{7,7,7});assert r!=r.left&&r.left!=r.right;

for(int n=1;n<150;n++){int[]a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=i;TreeNode r=fromCompleteArray(a);Queue<TreeNode>q=new ArrayDeque<>();q.add(r);int i=0;while(!q.isEmpty()){TreeNode x=q.remove();assert x.val==i++;if(x.left!=null)q.add(x.left);if(x.right!=null)q.add(x.right);}assert i==n;}

277.problem: Create a binary tree in Java with a node class, then connect and inspect its left and right children.
277.assumptions: Each new TreeNode is a separate object. left and right start as null. The root variable is a reference to the first node. A valid tree has no cycles or shared child nodes.

example.explanation: The code creates four objects. Assigning root.left.right connects node 6 beneath node 4; it does not change node 9.

277.baseline: Parallel arrays of values and child indices can represent a tree, but direct object references are simpler for irregular shapes and are the interface used by most linked-tree interview questions.
277.approach:
The constructor gives a node its value. Creating a node does not automatically attach it anywhere. Assignment makes the connection: root.left = new TreeNode(4) creates a node and stores its reference in root’s left field.

A second variable pointing to root refers to the same object. Changing a field through either reference changes that object. Reassigning the second variable to null only changes that variable; it does not delete the tree or change root.

The sample uses val to match the linked LeetCode conventions. Some TUF stubs call the field data; adapt the field name to the supplied class rather than defining a second node type inside a judge solution.
steps: Define value, left and right fields.
Create the root with new TreeNode(value).
Attach child objects through left and right.
Check for null before following another child link.
277.time: The fixed example takes O(1). Creating a general n-node tree takes O(n); accessing a known child reference takes O(1).
277.space: The fixed example allocates four nodes. A general linked binary tree uses O(n) storage.
pitfalls: null is a missing reference, not a node value. Zero is a valid value.
Do not compare values to decide whether two references identify the same node.
Do not attach the same child object under two parents if the algorithm expects a tree.
A node class must match the judge’s provided field names and constructor.

279.problem: Return the preorder traversal of a binary tree: Root → Left → Right.
279.assumptions: The input is a valid tree, may be empty, and may contain repeated values. The linked traversal task has a small node bound. For very deep trees, use the explicit-stack version later in this section to avoid Java call-stack overflow.

example.input: root 8 has left child 4 and right child 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: Follow Root → Left → Right at every node, not just at the root.

279.baseline: An explicit stack can remember unfinished nodes instead of the language call stack. Both approaches must visit every node, so both take O(n) time; recursion is the direct way to learn the order here.
279.approach:
Record a node before entering either subtree. Then finish the entire left subtree before starting the right subtree. The word “pre” refers to when the root is recorded: before its children.

The recursive helper follows exactly that order. null means there is no node to visit, so that call returns without adding anything. Keep one result list and append to it; making and joining new lists at every node can add unnecessary copying.
steps: Return immediately for null.
Append the current value.
Traverse the left subtree.
Traverse the right subtree.
279.time: O(n), because each node is visited once.
279.space: O(h) call-stack space for tree height h, plus O(n) output. A chain has h = n when height counts nodes.
pitfalls: Return an empty list for a null root.
Keep repeated values; traversal visits nodes, not distinct numbers.
Do not carry a result list over from a previous call.
Changing the position of output.add changes the traversal order.
tests: TreeNode root=new TreeNode(8);root.left=new TreeNode(4);root.right=new TreeNode(9);root.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert preorderTraversal(root).equals(List.of(8,4,6,9));assert preorderTraversal(null).isEmpty();

Random r=new Random(279);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(75);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);Map<TreeNode,String>path=new IdentityHashMap<>();path.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(r.nextInt(open.size()));TreeNode child=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||r.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;path.put(child,path.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<TreeNode>ordered=new ArrayList<>(path.keySet());ordered.sort(Comparator.comparing(x->path.get(x)+""));List<Integer>want=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode x:ordered)want.add(x.val);assert preorderTraversal(root).equals(want);assert preorderTraversal(root).equals(want);}

280.problem: Return the inorder traversal of a binary tree: Left → Root → Right.
280.assumptions: The input is a valid tree, may be empty, and may contain repeated values. The linked traversal task has a small node bound. For very deep trees, use the explicit-stack version later in this section to avoid Java call-stack overflow.

example.input: root 8 has left child 4 and right child 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: Follow Left → Root → Right at every node, not just at the root.

280.baseline: An explicit stack can remember unfinished nodes instead of the language call stack. Both approaches must visit every node, so both take O(n) time; recursion is the direct way to learn the order here.
280.approach:
Finish the left subtree, record the current node, then finish the right subtree. The root is recorded “in between” its two subtrees.

A recursive call finishes all of its own work before its caller continues. That is why the line adding the root runs only after every left-subtree value has been appended. Inorder gives sorted values for a binary search tree; an ordinary binary tree has no such guarantee.

Traverse the left subtree.
Append the current value.
Traverse the right subtree.
280.time: O(n), because each node is visited once.
280.space: O(h) call-stack space for tree height h, plus O(n) output. A chain has h = n when height counts nodes.

Keep repeated values; traversal visits nodes, not distinct numbers.
Do not carry a result list over from a previous call.
Changing the position of output.add changes the traversal order.

281.problem: Return the postorder traversal of a binary tree: Left → Right → Root.
281.assumptions: The input is a valid tree, may be empty, and may contain repeated values. The linked traversal task has a small node bound. For very deep trees, use the explicit-stack version later in this section to avoid Java call-stack overflow.

example.input: root 8 has left child 4 and right child 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: Follow Left → Right → Root at every node, not just at the root.

281.baseline: An explicit stack can remember unfinished nodes instead of the language call stack. Both approaches must visit every node, so both take O(n) time; recursion is the direct way to learn the order here.
281.approach:
Finish both child subtrees before recording their parent. “Post” means the root is recorded after its children. This order is useful when a parent’s result depends on completed child results, such as subtree height.

The left call finishes first, then the right call, and only then is the current value appended. A leaf reaches two null calls and is then added. No sorting or comparison of node values is involved.
steps: Return immediately for null.
Traverse the left subtree.
Traverse the right subtree.
Append the current value.
281.time: O(n), because each node is visited once.
281.space: O(h) call-stack space for tree height h, plus O(n) output. A chain has h = n when height counts nodes.
pitfalls: Return an empty list for a null root.
Keep repeated values; traversal visits nodes, not distinct numbers.
Do not carry a result list over from a previous call.
Changing the position of output.add changes the traversal order.

282.problem: Return the tree’s values grouped by level, from the root downward and left to right within each level.
282.assumptions: The pinned title mentions spiral form, but its LeetCode link asks for ordinary level order. This page solves that linked task. Zigzag/spiral order alternates direction and has its own later tracker entry. A null root returns an empty list.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: All nodes one edge from the root belong to the second list, even though one branch continues deeper.

282.baseline: A depth-first traversal can place each value into a list indexed by depth. It takes O(n) time too, but a queue directly represents the level-by-level order and avoids recursion.
282.approach:
Put the root in a queue. Remove nodes from the front and add their existing children at the back, left child first. The queue keeps earlier discoveries ahead of their children.

Before processing a level, save the queue’s current size. Process exactly that many nodes into one list. Children added during those removals belong to the next level; using the changing queue size as the loop limit would mix the levels.
steps: Return an empty result if root is null.
Offer the root to a queue.
Save levelSize before processing a level.
Poll exactly levelSize nodes, recording values and offering existing children.
Append that level and repeat.
282.space: O(w) queue space for maximum level width w, plus O(n) output. The queue can contain parts of two adjacent levels, still O(w).
pitfalls: Do not put null into ArrayDeque.
Freeze the level size before adding children.
Use a queue, not a stack.
Ordinary level order does not reverse every second level.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert levelOrder(r).equals(List.of(List.of(8),List.of(4,9),List.of(6)));assert levelOrder(null).isEmpty();

Random random=new Random(282);for(int t=0;t<400;t++){int n=1+random.nextInt(100);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(0);Map<TreeNode,String>path=new IdentityHashMap<>();path.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(i);boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;path.put(child,path.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<TreeNode>nodes=new ArrayList<>(path.keySet());nodes.sort(Comparator.<TreeNode>comparingInt(x->path.get(x).length()).thenComparing(x->path.get(x)));List<List<Integer>>want=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode x:nodes){int depth=path.get(x).length();if(depth==want.size())want.add(new ArrayList<>());want.get(depth).add(x.val);}assert levelOrder(root).equals(want);}

TreeNode root=new TreeNode(0),p=root;for(int i=1;i<50000;i++){p.right=new TreeNode(i);p=p.right;}List<List<Integer>>a=levelOrder(root);assert a.size()==50000;for(int i=0;i<a.size();i++)assert a.get(i).equals(List.of(i));

283.problem: Return preorder traversal without recursion: visit each node before its left and right subtrees.
283.assumptions: The tree may be empty and may contain equal values. The explicit stack stores node references. It never changes the tree.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: After visiting 8, push 9 first and 4 second. Because the stack is last-in-first-out, 4 is processed next.

283.baseline: Recursive preorder records the root, calls the left subtree, then calls the right subtree. This is also O(n), but Java’s call stack can overflow on a long chain.
283.approach:
Use a stack to hold nodes waiting to be visited. Pop the next node and append its value. Then schedule its children.

Preorder needs the left child next, so push the right child first and the left child second. The left child then sits on top. Its descendants will be processed before the waiting right subtree, reproducing the recursive order.
steps: Push the root if it exists.
Pop and record one node.
Push its right child, then its left child, when present.
Repeat until the stack is empty.
283.space: O(h) pending-stack space in a binary tree, plus O(n) output; h is at most n.
pitfalls: Push right before left to visit left first.
Skip null children because ArrayDeque rejects null.
Do not use a set of values; equal-valued nodes are separate visits.

TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.left=new TreeNode(i);p=p.left;}List<Integer>a=preorderTraversal(r);assert a.size()==100000;for(int i=0;i<a.size();i++)assert a.get(i)==i;

reference.title: Preorder Traversal
reference.approach: Use a stack, pushing right before left to preserve Root → Left → Right.
reference.adaptation: The current public traversal contract and foundation definitions were checked. A public Java editorial was not available; this authored stack implementation is checked against node-path order and a deep chain.

284.problem: Return inorder traversal without recursion: finish the left subtree, visit the node, then finish the right subtree.
284.assumptions: The input is a valid binary tree, not necessarily a binary search tree. A null root gives an empty list. The method does not change any child links.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: Visit 4 after reaching its missing left child, then visit its right child 6 before returning to 8.

284.baseline: Recursive inorder uses the language stack to pause a node while its left subtree is processed. The explicit stack below stores that same unfinished work without recursive calls.
284.approach:
Keep walking left, pushing every node you pass. When no left child remains, the top node is ready to be visited. Pop it, append its value, then move into its right subtree.

The stack remembers ancestors whose left subtrees are being processed. A node is popped only after its entire left subtree is finished. Moving right then repeats the same process there, which gives Left → Root → Right.
steps: Start current at root and create an empty stack.
Push current and move left until current is null.
Pop and visit the top node.
Move current to that node’s right child.
Continue while current exists or the stack is non-empty.
284.time: O(n): each node is pushed and popped once.
284.space: O(h) stack space, plus O(n) output.
pitfalls: The loop condition needs OR, because ancestors may remain after current becomes null.
Visit a node after popping, not when first pushing it.
Do not sort the result; inorder is a structural order and need not be numerically sorted.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert inorderTraversal(r).equals(List.of(4,6,8,9));assert inorderTraversal(null).isEmpty();

Random r=new Random(279);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(75);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);Map<TreeNode,String>path=new IdentityHashMap<>();path.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(r.nextInt(open.size()));TreeNode child=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||r.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;path.put(child,path.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<TreeNode>ordered=new ArrayList<>(path.keySet());ordered.sort(Comparator.comparing(x->path.get(x)+"M"));List<Integer>want=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode x:ordered)want.add(x.val);assert inorderTraversal(root).equals(want);assert inorderTraversal(root).equals(want);}

TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.left=new TreeNode(i);p=p.left;}List<Integer>a=inorderTraversal(r);assert a.size()==100000;for(int i=0;i<a.size();i++)assert a.get(i)==99999-i;

reference.title: Inorder Traversal
reference.approach: Store unfinished ancestors while descending left, then visit and move right.
reference.adaptation: The public traversal contract and current foundation definitions were checked. This is authored iterative Java because no public Java editorial was available. Tests independently order nodes by their paths and include a 100000-node chain.

285.problem: Return postorder traversal using two stacks: all left-subtree nodes, then right-subtree nodes, then their parent.
285.assumptions: The tree may be empty or contain repeated values. The stacks store node references, not a set of values. The original child links remain unchanged.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: The first stack produces Root → Right → Left order: 8,9,4,6. Popping the second stack reverses that to Left → Right → Root.

285.baseline: Recursive postorder directly visits left, right, then root. For an iterative version, an explicit stack must remember whether children have already been processed. Two stacks offer a simpler alternative: produce the reverse order first.
285.approach:
Use the first stack for a modified preorder walk. Pop a node into the second stack, then push its left child followed by its right child onto the first stack. The right child is popped next, so the generated order is Root → Right → Left.

Now pop every node from the second stack. Reversing the generated sequence puts the entire left subtree before the right subtree and the parent last. The second stack may hold all nodes, so this method uses O(n) extra space even when the tree is short.
steps: Push the root onto the first stack if present.
Pop a node from the first stack and push it onto the second.
Push left then right children onto the first stack.
After the first stack empties, pop the second into the answer.
285.space: O(n) for the two stacks, plus O(n) output.
pitfalls: Push left before right in this algorithm; this intentionally differs from ordinary iterative preorder.
Reverse Root → Right → Left, not Root → Left → Right.
Two stacks are simple but do not reduce the auxiliary bound to O(h).
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert postorderTraversal(r).equals(List.of(6,4,9,8));assert postorderTraversal(null).isEmpty();

Random r=new Random(279);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(75);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);Map<TreeNode,String>path=new IdentityHashMap<>();path.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(r.nextInt(open.size()));TreeNode child=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||r.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;path.put(child,path.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<TreeNode>ordered=new ArrayList<>(path.keySet());ordered.sort(Comparator.comparing(x->path.get(x)+"Z"));List<Integer>want=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode x:ordered)want.add(x.val);assert postorderTraversal(root).equals(want);assert postorderTraversal(root).equals(want);}

TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.right=new TreeNode(i);p=p.right;}List<Integer>a=postorderTraversal(r);assert a.size()==100000;for(int i=0;i<a.size();i++)assert a.get(i)==99999-i;

reference.title: Postorder Traversal
reference.approach: Reverse a Root → Right → Left walk using two stacks.
reference.adaptation: The public contract and current foundation traversal order were checked. The practice solution tab requires sign-in; this is an authored two-stack implementation for the pinned lesson, tested against node-path ordering and a deep tree.

286.problem: Return postorder traversal with one explicit stack, recording each parent only after both of its subtrees are finished.
286.assumptions: The tree may contain repeated values. Completion checks must compare node references, not values. No child links are changed. A null root returns an empty list.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: After finishing 6, node 4 can be recorded. Node 8 must still wait until its right child 9 has been processed.

286.baseline: The two-stack method first builds a reversed traversal and stores up to n nodes in its second stack. One stack can instead remember the unfinished ancestor path and the last node whose subtree was completed.
286.approach:
Walk left while pushing nodes. When current becomes null, inspect the top node without removing it. If it has a right subtree that has not yet been completed, enter that subtree. Otherwise, both children are finished: pop and record the node.

lastVisited identifies the most recently completed subtree root. When lastVisited is the top node’s right child, that entire right subtree has finished, so it is safe to record the parent. Reference identity is essential: two different nodes may hold the same value.
steps: Push nodes while moving left.
When current is null, peek at the pending parent.
Enter its right subtree if it exists and was not just completed.
Otherwise pop, record the node and set lastVisited to it.
286.time: O(n): each node is pushed and popped once, with a constant number of inspections.
286.space: O(h) stack space for height h, plus O(n) output.
pitfalls: Use lastVisited != node.right, not a comparison of their values.
Peek while deciding whether the right subtree is pending; popping early loses the parent.
Do not clear lastVisited after completing a subtree.
The condition is current != null OR stack not empty.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert postorderTraversal(r).equals(List.of(6,4,9,8));assert postorderTraversal(null).isEmpty();

Random r=new Random(279);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(75);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);Map<TreeNode,String>path=new IdentityHashMap<>();path.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(r.nextInt(open.size()));TreeNode child=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(11)-5);boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||r.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;path.put(child,path.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<TreeNode>ordered=new ArrayList<>(path.keySet());ordered.sort(Comparator.comparing(x->path.get(x)+"Z"));List<Integer>want=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode x:ordered)want.add(x.val);assert postorderTraversal(root).equals(want);assert postorderTraversal(root).equals(want);}
TreeNode r=new TreeNode(5);r.left=new TreeNode(2);r.right=new TreeNode(2);r.right.left=new TreeNode(7);assert postorderTraversal(r).equals(List.of(2,7,2,5));

TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.right=new TreeNode(i);p=p.right;}List<Integer>a=postorderTraversal(r);assert a.size()==100000;for(int i=0;i<a.size();i++)assert a.get(i)==99999-i;

reference.title: Postorder Traversal
reference.approach: Use one ancestor stack and the last completed subtree to delay each parent until both children finish.
reference.adaptation: The public postorder contract was checked, but its solution tab requires sign-in. This authored one-stack implementation follows Left → Right → Root and is tested with equal-valued sibling nodes and a 100000-node chain.

278.problem: Learn how preorder, inorder and postorder differ, and return all three lists from a single walk through a binary tree.
278.assumptions: The linked TUF task returns lists in the order [inorder, preorder, postorder]. That output order differs from the order in its title. Each list contains every node once, including repeated values. The tree may be empty.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: The structure stays the same. Only the moment when a node’s value is recorded changes.

278.baseline: Run three separate DFS traversals, recording the root before, between or after the child calls. Three O(n) passes are still O(n), but a single traversal can collect all three outputs together.
278.approach:
Imagine three moments during a visit to a node: before its left subtree, after the left subtree, and after the right subtree. Record the node at the first moment for preorder, at the second for inorder, and at the third for postorder.

A frame stores a node and which moment comes next. At stage 1, record preorder, schedule stage 2, then enter the left child. At stage 2, record inorder, schedule stage 3, then enter the right child. At stage 3, record postorder and finish the node. Scheduling the continuation before the child puts the child on top of the stack, so the subtree finishes first.

The explicit stack handles deep trees without relying on Java recursion. “One traversal” does not mean one operation per node: each node has three constant-size stages, still O(n) work.
steps: At stage 1, append to preorder and schedule the left subtree.
At stage 2, append to inorder and schedule the right subtree.
At stage 3, append to postorder.
Return the lists in the linked task’s required order: inorder, preorder, postorder.
278.time: O(n), with three stage events per node.
278.space: O(h) pending frames, plus O(n) space for each of the three output lists; total output is 3n values.
pitfalls: DFS ordering describes when a parent is recorded relative to its subtrees.
Do not return lists in title order; the public task expects inorder first.
A stage is per node, not a single global counter.
A value may appear repeatedly because different nodes can have equal values.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert treeTraversal(r).equals(List.of(List.of(4,6,8,9),List.of(8,4,6,9),List.of(6,4,9,8)));assert treeTraversal(null).equals(List.of(List.of(),List.of(),List.of()));

Random r=new Random(287);for(int t=0;t<500;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(9));Map<TreeNode,String>path=new IdentityHashMap<>();path.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(r.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(r.nextInt(9));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||r.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;path.put(child,path.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<List<Integer>>want=new ArrayList<>();for(String suffix:new String[]{"M","","Z"}){List<TreeNode>ordered=new ArrayList<>(path.keySet());ordered.sort(Comparator.comparing(x->path.get(x)+suffix));List<Integer>values=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode x:ordered)values.add(x.val);want.add(values);}assert treeTraversal(root).equals(want);assert treeTraversal(root).equals(want);}

TreeNode root=new TreeNode(0),p=root;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.left=new TreeNode(i);p=p.left;}List<List<Integer>>a=treeTraversal(root);for(List<Integer>v:a)assert v.size()==100000;for(int i=0;i<100000;i++){assert a.get(0).get(i)==99999-i;assert a.get(1).get(i)==i;assert a.get(2).get(i)==99999-i;}

reference.approach: Collect values at three stages of the same depth-first walk.

287.problem: Produce inorder, preorder and postorder in one iterative traversal, using a stack of nodes with stages 1, 2 and 3.
287.assumptions: The linked TUF task returns lists in the order [inorder, preorder, postorder]. That output order differs from the order in its title. Each list contains every node once, including repeated values. The tree may be empty.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: The structure stays the same. Only the moment when a node’s value is recorded changes.

287.baseline: Run three separate DFS traversals, recording the root before, between or after the child calls. Three O(n) passes are still O(n), but a single traversal can collect all three outputs together.
287.approach:
The separate recursive traversals differ only in the position of the “record this node” action. A stack frame lets us pause and resume one traversal at all three positions.

Stage 1 means neither subtree has been processed: record preorder, save stage 2, then enter the left child. Stage 2 means the left subtree is finished: record inorder, save stage 3, then enter the right child. Stage 3 means both subtrees are finished: record postorder and remove the frame permanently.

The child frame is pushed after its parent’s continuation, so it runs first. Every node moves through the three stages exactly once. Return [inorder, preorder, postorder] to match the current practice task.
steps: At stage 1, append to preorder and schedule the left subtree.
At stage 2, append to inorder and schedule the right subtree.
At stage 3, append to postorder.
Return the lists in the linked task’s required order: inorder, preorder, postorder.
287.time: O(n), with three stage events per node.
287.space: O(h) pending frames, plus O(n) space for each of the three output lists; total output is 3n values.
pitfalls: DFS ordering describes when a parent is recorded relative to its subtrees.
Do not return lists in title order; the public task expects inorder first.
A stage is per node, not a single global counter.
A value may appear repeatedly because different nodes can have equal values.

reference.approach: Collect values at three stages of the same depth-first walk.
reference.adaptation: The public statement, examples, 100000-node bound and output list order were checked, together with the current foundation definitions. No public Java editorial was available. This authored frame-stack implementation avoids recursion depth limits.

288.problem: Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on its longest root-to-leaf path.
288.assumptions: This problem counts nodes, so an empty tree has depth 0 and a single node has depth 1. That differs from the edge-based height used on the introduction page. Values do not affect depth.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has right child 6
example.explanation: The longest path is 8 → 4 → 6 and contains three nodes.

288.baseline: Recursively return 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth), with 0 for null. This is already O(n), but a deep chain may exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
288.approach:
Count the number of levels with breadth-first search. Start with the root in a queue. For each level, remove exactly the nodes already in the queue and add their children for the next level. Increase depth once per completed level.

The last non-empty level contains a deepest node. The number of levels, including the root’s level, is therefore the maximum number of nodes on a root-to-leaf path. This has the same linear time as recursion and avoids call-stack depth limits.
steps: For null, return 0.
Put the root in a queue.
Save the current level size and process exactly that many nodes.
Increase depth once per level and return it when the queue empties.
288.space: O(w) queue space for maximum level width w. Recursive depth uses O(h) call-stack space instead.
pitfalls: Return 1 for a leaf, not 0.
Depth uses the larger child path, not the sum of both paths.
A node missing just one child is not a leaf.
Freeze queue size before adding the next level’s children.
tests: assert maxDepth(null)==0;assert maxDepth(new TreeNode(9))==1;TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert maxDepth(r)==3;

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}int want=0;for(String path:paths.values())want=Math.max(want,path.length()+1);assert maxDepth(root)==want;assert recursiveDepth(root)==want;}
TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.left=new TreeNode(0);p=p.left;}assert maxDepth(r)==100000;

reference.title: Maximum Depth in BT
reference.approach: Count nodes on the deepest path, using recursive heights or queue levels.
reference.adaptation: The public statement explicitly counts nodes, and its BFS and recursive-height hints were checked with the foundation lesson. No public Java editorial was available; these are authored implementations of those two approaches.

288.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space. Prefer the iterative version for a very deep tree.

289.problem: Decide whether every node has left and right subtree heights differing by at most one.
289.assumptions: An empty tree is balanced. The condition applies at every node, not just the root. Heights here count nodes: null has height 0. Tree shape matters; node values do not.

example.input: root has a left chain of three nodes and a right chain of three nodes
example.explanation: The root’s two heights are equal, but each chain contains a node whose child heights differ by two. A balanced root alone is not enough.

289.baseline: For each node, separately calculate both subtree heights and then check the two subtrees. Repeated height scans cost at most O(nh) time; early failure can reduce the work, so a skewed tree rejected at its root does not actually require all those repeated scans.
289.approach:
Calculate heights only after the children are finished. At that point, compare the two child heights. If their difference exceeds one, the whole tree is unbalanced. Otherwise, save 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight) for the parent to use.

The recursive improvement returns −1 as an early failure signal. The iterative version below uses the same postorder dependency but stores heights in a map. A frame with ready = false schedules its children; the same node returns with ready = true after those children have heights. This avoids Java call-stack limits, at the cost of O(n) stored heights.
steps: Push the root in an unfinished frame.
On first seeing a node, schedule its finished frame and then its children.
On the finished frame, read child heights, using zero for missing children.
Reject a difference greater than one; otherwise store this node’s height.
289.space: O(n) stored heights plus O(h) stack frames. The recursive improvement uses O(h) space but can hit call-stack limits.
pitfalls: Check every node, including nodes deep inside an otherwise balanced-looking tree.
The recursive −1 sentinel must propagate before calculating a parent’s height.
Compare child heights, not child node counts.
Map nodes by identity, not by their possibly repeated values.
tests: assert isBalanced(null);assert isBalanced(new TreeNode(1));TreeNode r=new TreeNode(1);r.left=new TreeNode(2);r.left.left=new TreeNode(3);r.left.left.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(2);r.right.right=new TreeNode(3);r.right.right.right=new TreeNode(4);assert !isBalanced(r);assert !isBalancedRecursive(r);assert !balanceByRepeatedHeights(r);

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}boolean want=true;for(String path:paths.values()){int left=0,right=0;for(String other:paths.values()){if(other.startsWith(path+"L"))left=Math.max(left,other.length()-path.length());if(other.startsWith(path+"R"))right=Math.max(right,other.length()-path.length());}if(Math.abs(left-right)>1)want=false;}assert isBalanced(root)==want;assert isBalancedRecursive(root)==want;assert balanceByRepeatedHeights(root)==want;}
TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.right=new TreeNode(0);p=p.right;}assert !isBalanced(r);assert isBalanced(new TreeNode(0));

reference.title: Check If a Binary Tree Is Height-Balanced
reference.approach: Check every node, then avoid repeated height calculations with recursive or iterative postorder.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java approaches were checked. The final version follows the article’s explicit stack and height map, using ArrayDeque and identity keys. The repeated-height complexity is stated as an upper bound; the source’s claim of quadratic work on a chain overlooks its immediate root-level rejection.

better.explanation: Return a subtree height when it is balanced, or −1 when any imbalance has been found. This combines height calculation and validation in one recursive postorder traversal. It is concise and uses only the call stack, but very deep trees need the iterative version.
better.space: O(h) recursion stack.

290.problem: Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes in a binary tree.
290.assumptions: The path may lie entirely inside a subtree and need not include the root. A single node has diameter 0. The helper’s height counts nodes; the final diameter counts edges. The input has no cycles.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has children 2 and 6
example.explanation: A longest path is 2 → 4 → 8 → 9. It contains four nodes and three edges.

290.baseline: For every node, calculate its left and right subtree heights separately and use their sum as a candidate. Also check both subtrees. Repeated height calculations take O(nh) time and become O(n²) on a chain.
290.approach:
At a node, the longest path turning there can use the deepest left branch and the deepest right branch. If child heights count nodes, leftHeight + rightHeight already counts the edges from this node out along both branches.

A postorder helper computes each height once. After getting both child heights, update the best diameter with their sum. Return 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight) to the parent. The parent can extend only one branch; returning the whole two-sided diameter would describe a branching shape rather than a single path.

The best diameter is local to each public call, so a later call cannot inherit an answer from an earlier tree. For a very deep chain, the two-BFS alternative below avoids recursive stack limits.
steps: Return height 0 for null.
Compute left and right heights.
Update the best edge count with leftHeight + rightHeight.
Return one plus the larger child height.
Return the saved best value from the public method.
290.space: O(h) recursion space. Very deep trees may exceed Java’s call stack; use the iterative graph/BFS alternative for those inputs.
pitfalls: The helper returns a height, while the public method returns a diameter.
Check the candidate at every node, not only the root.
Do not add 1 to leftHeight + rightHeight when the answer counts edges.
Reset the best result for each call.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.left=new TreeNode(2);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert diameterOfBinaryTree(r)==3;assert diameterOfBinaryTree(new TreeNode(1))==0;assert diameterOfBinaryTree(null)==0;

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}int want=0;for(String a:paths.values())for(String b:paths.values()){int common=0;while(common<Math.min(a.length(),b.length())&&a.charAt(common)==b.charAt(common))common++;want=Math.max(want,a.length()+b.length()-2*common);}assert diameterOfBinaryTree(root)==want;assert diameterByRepeatedHeights(root)==want;assert diameterByBFS(root)==want;}

reference.title: Calculate the Diameter of a Binary Tree
reference.approach: Avoid repeated heights with postorder, or find the diameter with two BFS passes on an undirected tree.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked, including the full BFS method. The recursive formula is preserved with call-local answer state. The graph alternative builds its adjacency lists iteratively, unlike the source’s recursive graph builder, so it also handles deep trees without recursion.

better.explanation: Treat child links as undirected edges. A BFS from any node reaches an endpoint of some diameter; a second BFS from that endpoint finds the diameter length. This is linear too, but stores a graph. The graph builder here also uses a queue, making the entire alternative safe from recursive depth limits.
better.time: O(n) for building the graph and two BFS traversals.
better.space: O(n) for the graph, distances and queues.

291.problem: Find the largest sum of node values along any non-empty simple path in a binary tree. A path may start and end anywhere.
291.assumptions: The tree is non-empty. A path cannot repeat a node or split into three branches. Node values may be negative. The code uses long for sums; the linked judge’s smaller bounds permit int, but wider sums avoid overflow in extended examples.

example.input: root −8 has left child 4 and right child 6; 6 has children 5 and 7
example.explanation: The best path is 5 → 6 → 7. Adding the root −8 would reduce the sum, so the best path stays inside the right subtree.

291.baseline: For every node, recalculate the best downward path from each child, combine useful gains with the node, and compare with answers inside both subtrees. Recalculating gains can take O(n²) time on a chain.
291.approach:
For each child, ask for its best path starting at that child and continuing downward through at most one branch. Ignore a negative gain by replacing it with zero: a path is allowed to stop instead of taking that branch.

At the current node, leftGain + value + rightGain is a complete candidate path. It may turn through both children. Update the best answer with that sum. But return only value + max(leftGain, rightGain) to the parent; returning both branches would create a fork when the parent extends it.

Start the saved answer at Long.MIN_VALUE, not zero. Every candidate includes a real node, so an all-negative tree correctly returns its least negative node. Keep this state local to the call.
steps: Return zero gain for a null child.
Compute and clamp both child gains to at least zero.
Update the best complete path using both child gains.
Return a single downward branch to the parent.
Return the best saved sum.
291.space: O(h) recursive call-stack space. Use the iterative alternative for trees too deep for Java recursion.
pitfalls: The best path need not include the root or end at a leaf.
Clamping child gains to zero does not permit an empty final path: the current node is always included.
Return one branch upward; use both branches only for a complete candidate.
Initialize the best answer below every valid value and reset it per call.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(-8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(6);r.right.left=new TreeNode(5);r.right.right=new TreeNode(7);assert maxPathSum(r)==18;TreeNode a=new TreeNode(-5);a.left=new TreeNode(-2);a.right=new TreeNode(-9);assert maxPathSum(a)==-2;assert maxPathSum(new TreeNode(-7))==-7;

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(41)-20);Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(41)-20);boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}Map<String,TreeNode>at=new HashMap<>();for(Map.Entry<TreeNode,String>e:paths.entrySet())at.put(e.getValue(),e.getKey());long want=Long.MIN_VALUE;for(String a:at.keySet())for(String b:at.keySet()){int shared=0;while(shared<Math.min(a.length(),b.length())&&a.charAt(shared)==b.charAt(shared))shared++;long sum=at.get(a.substring(0,shared)).val;for(int length=a.length();length>shared;length--)sum+=at.get(a.substring(0,length)).val;for(int length=b.length();length>shared;length--)sum+=at.get(b.substring(0,length)).val;want=Math.max(want,sum);}assert maxPathSum(root)==want;assert maxPathSumRepeated(root)==want;assert maxPathSumIterative(root)==want;}
TreeNode r=new TreeNode(Integer.MAX_VALUE);r.left=new TreeNode(Integer.MAX_VALUE);r.right=new TreeNode(Integer.MAX_VALUE);assert maxPathSum(r)==6442450941L;assert maxPathSumIterative(r)==6442450941L;

reference.title: Find the Maximum Path Sum in a Binary Tree
reference.approach: Calculate each downward gain once, using both branches for the answer and one branch for the parent.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. This version widens sums to long, keeps answer state local and explicitly rejects an empty input. The article notes depth limits; the additional iterative method implements the same recurrence without recursion.

better.explanation: For a deep tree, calculate the same gains with explicit postorder frames. Store completed child gains by node identity, then combine them when the parent’s ready frame is popped. This is a practical stack-safe alternative, not a faster asymptotic algorithm; it uses O(n) map space instead of only the recursive path.
better.space: O(n) stored gains plus O(h) frames.

292.problem: Decide whether two binary trees have the same shape and the same value at every corresponding position.
292.assumptions: Two empty trees are equal. A left child in one tree must match a left child in the other; moving the same value to the right changes the tree. Separate objects can still represent identical trees.

example.input: tree A: root 8 with left child 4; tree B: root 8 with right child 4
example.explanation: The values are the same, but they occupy different child positions.

292.baseline: Recursively compare the roots, then corresponding left subtrees and corresponding right subtrees. This directly follows the definition and uses O(h) call-stack space.
292.approach:
Keep corresponding nodes paired in an explicit stack. Two missing nodes match. Exactly one missing node means the shapes differ. Two existing nodes must have equal values. Once those checks pass, schedule their corresponding children.

Push the right pair before the left pair to process the left side first, though either order is correct for equality. A pair object may contain null references; the stack itself receives a non-null pair. This matters because ArrayDeque does not accept a null element.
steps: Push the pair of roots.
Pop one pair and handle the two-null and one-null cases.
Reject different values.
Push matching child positions as pairs.
Return true if all pairs match.
292.time: O(n + m) as a general upper bound for trees with n and m nodes; equal n-node trees require O(n) comparisons. The method stops at the first mismatch.
292.space: O(h) stack space for the pending corresponding paths, with h bounded by the larger tree height.
pitfalls: Equal traversal values without null markers do not establish equal shape.
Compare values at matching positions, not object identity.
Do not pair left with right; that checks a different relationship.
Do not push a raw null into ArrayDeque.
tests: assert isSameTree(null,null);assert !isSameTree(new TreeNode(1),null);TreeNode a=new TreeNode(8),b=new TreeNode(8);a.left=new TreeNode(4);b.right=new TreeNode(4);assert !isSameTree(a,b);b.right=null;b.left=new TreeNode(4);assert isSameTree(a,b);b.left.val=5;assert !isSameTree(a,b);
