reference.title: Check If Two Binary Trees Are Identical
reference.approach: Compare corresponding nodes recursively or with a queue or stack of pairs.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java implementations were checked. This version uses two-element node arrays instead of a NodePair class; null children remain inside a non-null pair, preserving ArrayDeque compatibility.

better.explanation: A queue of corresponding pairs performs the same checks level by level. It also avoids recursion; its working memory depends on width rather than height. There is no time advantage over the stack version.
better.time: O(n + m) upper bound, with early termination on a mismatch.
better.space: O(w) queued pairs, where w is bounded by the larger level width.

293.problem: Return the nodes level by level, alternating the output direction: left to right at the root, right to left on the next level, then left to right again.
293.assumptions: Only the output direction alternates. The underlying child links do not change. The result contains a separate list for each level. A null root returns an empty list.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has children 2 and 6; 9 has left child 7
example.explanation: The second level reverses direction. The third level returns to normal left-to-right order.

293.baseline: Run ordinary level-order traversal and reverse every second level list. The total reversal work is O(n), so this is already linear overall.
293.approach:
Keep normal BFS discovery order: add each left child before its right child. For a level of size s, put the ith removed node at position i when going left to right, or at s − 1 − i when going right to left.

This changes where values are written without changing which nodes the queue processes next. Save the level size before adding children, and flip the direction only after the whole level is complete.
steps: Queue the root and start leftToRight as true.
Save the current level size and create that many output slots.
Poll each node and write it at i or size − 1 − i.
Always queue children left first, then right.
Append the level and flip direction.
293.space: O(w) queue and current-level space, plus O(n) returned output.
pitfalls: Flip direction once per level, not once per node.
Keep queue insertion order consistent even on reversed output levels.
ArrayList.set requires existing slots; capacity alone does not create elements.
Reversing completed alternate levels is also O(n), not an asymptotically slower solution.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.left=new TreeNode(2);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);r.right.left=new TreeNode(7);assert zigzagLevelOrder(r).equals(List.of(List.of(8),List.of(9,4),List.of(2,6,7)));assert zigzagLevelOrder(null).isEmpty();

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}List<TreeNode>ordered=new ArrayList<>(paths.keySet());ordered.sort(Comparator.<TreeNode>comparingInt(x->paths.get(x).length()).thenComparing(x->paths.get(x)));List<List<Integer>>want=new ArrayList<>();for(TreeNode node:ordered){int depth=paths.get(node).length();if(depth==want.size())want.add(new ArrayList<>());want.get(depth).add(node.val);}for(int i=1;i<want.size();i+=2)Collections.reverse(want.get(i));assert zigzagLevelOrder(root).equals(want);}

reference.title: Zig Zag or Spiral Traversal
reference.approach: Use BFS levels and alternate the position where each value is written.
reference.adaptation: The public statement, examples and alternate-level reversal hint were checked. No public Java editorial was available. This authored implementation follows the same BFS level structure described in the current level-order foundation article.

294.problem: Return the anti-clockwise boundary of a binary tree: root, left boundary, leaves from left to right, then right boundary from bottom to top.
294.assumptions: Include each node once. Side boundaries exclude leaves. The left boundary begins at root.left and prefers left children, falling back to right; the right boundary begins at root.right and prefers right, falling back to left. A missing root-side subtree has no side boundary. Repeated values in different nodes remain repeated in the output.

example.input: root 8 has children 4 and 9; 4 has children 2 and 6; 9 has left child 7
example.explanation: 4 is the non-leaf left boundary; 2,6,7 are leaves; 9 is added last as the reversed right boundary.

294.baseline: A single DFS can carry left-boundary and right-boundary flags. Record left-boundary nodes before their descendants and right-boundary nodes afterward; record leaves once. This also takes O(n). The explicit three-part method below makes each boundary rule easier to inspect.
294.approach:
Add the root unless it is a leaf. Walk the left side from root.left, preferring left and falling back to right, recording only non-leaves. Next, collect all leaves in left-to-right DFS order. Finally, walk the right side from root.right, preferring right and falling back to left; save non-leaves and append them in reverse.

Excluding leaves from both side walks prevents duplication. A single-node tree is handled by the leaf pass, so its root appears exactly once. For a tree with only a right branch, there is no left boundary: the leaf is listed before the reversed right-boundary ancestors.

The leaf walk here uses an explicit stack, so the three-part version also works on deep trees without recursive calls.
steps: Add a non-leaf root.
Walk and record the non-leaf left boundary.
Collect leaves with left-first DFS.
Collect the non-leaf right boundary and append it in reverse.
294.space: O(h) leaf-stack and right-boundary working space, plus O(n) possible output.
pitfalls: Boundary traversal is not the same as left view plus right view.
Do not deduplicate by value: distinct boundary nodes can have equal values.
Exclude leaves from side boundaries and handle a single root once.
Reverse the right boundary only; leaves stay left to right.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.left=new TreeNode(2);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);r.right.left=new TreeNode(7);assert boundaryTraversal(r).equals(List.of(8,4,2,6,7,9));assert boundaryTraversal(new TreeNode(5)).equals(List.of(5));assert boundaryTraversal(null).isEmpty();

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}Map<String,TreeNode>at=new HashMap<>();List<String>leafPaths=new ArrayList<>();for(Map.Entry<TreeNode,String>e:paths.entrySet()){at.put(e.getValue(),e.getKey());if(e.getKey().left==null&&e.getKey().right==null)leafPaths.add(e.getValue());}Collections.sort(leafPaths);List<Integer>want=new ArrayList<>();if(n==1)want.add(root.val);else{want.add(root.val);String left=null,right=null;for(String path:leafPaths){if(path.startsWith("L")&&left==null)left=path;if(path.startsWith("R"))right=path;}if(left!=null)for(int length=1;length<left.length();length++)want.add(at.get(left.substring(0,length)).val);for(String path:leafPaths)want.add(at.get(path).val);if(right!=null)for(int length=right.length()-1;length>=1;length--)want.add(at.get(right.substring(0,length)).val);}assert boundaryTraversal(root).equals(want);assert boundaryByFlags(root).equals(want);}

TreeNode r=new TreeNode(0),p=r;for(int i=1;i<100000;i++){p.right=new TreeNode(i);p=p.right;}List<Integer>a=boundaryTraversal(r);assert a.size()==100000&&a.get(0)==0;for(int i=1;i<a.size();i++)assert a.get(i)==100000-i;

reference.title: Boundary Traversal of a Binary Tree
reference.approach: Separate the left boundary, leaves and reversed right boundary, or propagate boundary roles in one DFS.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java approaches were checked, including root setup and flag propagation. The three-part version replaces only its recursive leaf collection with an explicit stack. Node identity is preserved through traversal; no value-based deduplication is used.

294.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(h) recursive stack space; deep chains can exhaust the Java call stack.

295.problem: Group the nodes of a binary tree into vertical columns, from left to right. Within a column, list shallower nodes first. If two nodes share both row and column, list their values in ascending order.
295.assumptions: The root is at row 0, column 0. A left child moves one row down and one column left; a right child moves one row down and one column right. Repeated values are kept. An empty tree returns an empty list.

example.explanation: The nodes 7 and 2 both sit at row 2, column 0. Their values must be sorted, even though a left-to-right BFS visits 7 first.

295.baseline: Record every node as (column, row, value), sort by those three fields, and start a new output list whenever the column changes. This is a useful direct solution and already takes O(n log n) time.
295.approach:
Give every node a row and column. An outer TreeMap keeps columns in order. Inside each column, a second TreeMap keeps rows in order. At each exact position, a min-heap keeps values in order.

Walk the tree with a queue and insert each value into its position’s heap. Then read the maps from left to right and top to bottom, removing the smallest value from each heap until it is empty. A heap can contain duplicate values, so no node disappears.

Both this method and sorting all records take O(n log n) time. The nested containers make the three ordering rules explicit; they do not improve the asymptotic bound.
steps: Queue the root at (row 0, column 0).
Insert each value into the heap for its column and row.
Queue the left child at (row + 1, column − 1) and the right child at (row + 1, column + 1).
Read ordered columns and rows; poll each heap into its column’s output list.
295.space: O(n) for queued positions, ordered containers, and output.
pitfalls: BFS order alone does not sort equal-position values.
A Set would lose duplicate node values. Use a PriorityQueue.
Iterating over a PriorityQueue does not give sorted order; repeatedly poll it.
Sort values only after column and row. A small deeper value must not move ahead of a shallower node.
tests: assert verticalTraversal(null).isEmpty();TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(7);r.right.left=new TreeNode(2);assert verticalTraversal(r).equals(List.of(List.of(4),List.of(8,2,7),List.of(9)));r.left.right.val=Integer.MAX_VALUE;r.right.left.val=Integer.MIN_VALUE;assert verticalTraversal(r).get(1).equals(List.of(8,Integer.MIN_VALUE,Integer.MAX_VALUE));r.left.right.val=2;r.right.left.val=2;assert verticalTraversal(r).get(1).equals(List.of(8,2,2));

reference.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
reference.approach: Record and sort positions, or use ordered column/row maps with min-heaps for equal-position values.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java solutions were checked. The primary code keeps the source’s TreeMap → TreeMap → PriorityQueue structure. The sorting version uses an explicit stack instead of recursive DFS to collect records.

296.problem: Return the top view of a binary tree: one visible value per vertical column, ordered from the leftmost column to the rightmost.
296.assumptions: The root has column 0. Left and right children have columns one lower and one higher. Keep the shallowest node in each column. For equal depth, keep the node encountered first in left-to-right level order. This tie rule follows the source Java.

example.explanation: Both 7 and 2 lie below 8 in column 0, so 8 hides them from above.

296.baseline: Collect every node with its column, depth, and BFS visit order. Sort by column, depth, then visit order. Take the first node in each column. This works but sorts more information than the answer needs.
296.approach:
Use BFS because it visits shallower nodes before deeper nodes. The first node seen in a column is therefore the one visible from above. Save it once and never replace it. Enqueue left before right so equal-depth ties follow the source’s left-to-right order.

A HashMap stores the chosen value for each column. Also remember the smallest and largest column reached. Read that whole integer range to produce the answer. There cannot be a gap: reaching column 3 from column 0 requires passing through columns 1 and 2.
steps: Queue the root at column 0.
For each node, save its value only if its column has no saved value.
Queue left before right, adjusting the column by −1 or +1.
Read saved values from the minimum column through the maximum column.
296.space: O(n) for the queue, map, and output.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite a saved column; that would move toward the bottom view.
DFS cannot safely keep the first node it visits. It may reach a deep node before a shallower one in another subtree.
Do not sort tied values as in vertical traversal. Top view uses visit order.
A column is a horizontal position, not a node’s depth.
tests: assert topView(null).isEmpty();TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(7);r.right.left=new TreeNode(2);assert topView(r).equals(List.of(4,8,9));

reference.title: Top View of Binary Tree
reference.approach: Sorting records, DFS with minimum depth, and BFS keeping the first node per column.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. The main version follows the source’s HashMap, BFS, and minimum/maximum column range; ArrayDeque replaces LinkedList. Equal-depth ties retain the first left-to-right node.

296.baselineTime: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

better.explanation: DFS can arrive at a deep node first, so remember the smallest depth seen for each column. Replace an entry only for a strictly smaller depth. Visit left before right to preserve the required tie rule. A TreeMap gives left-to-right output.
better.space: O(n), including O(h) recursive stack space. A very deep tree can overflow Java’s call stack.

297.problem: Return the bottom view of a binary tree: keep the deepest node in each vertical column, then list the chosen values from left to right.
297.assumptions: The root has column 0; left and right children move one column left and right. If two nodes have the same column and depth, the node visited later in left-to-right level order wins. An empty tree returns an empty list.

example.explanation: At column 0, both 7 and 2 are deeper than 8. They have equal depth, so 2 wins because level order visits it later.

297.baseline: Record each node’s column, depth, and BFS visit order. Sort by these three fields and take the last record in each column. This directly follows the definition but requires O(n log n) sorting.
297.approach:
BFS visits shallower levels before deeper levels. Each time a node arrives, replace the saved value for its column. A later value is either deeper, or at the same depth and later in level order. In either case, it is the required replacement.

Queue left children before right children so the tie rule is consistent. Keep the smallest and largest column reached, then read that range from a HashMap. The tree cannot skip a column on its way to a farther one.

This differs from top view in one key line: top view saves a column only once; bottom view overwrites it every time.
steps: Queue the root at column 0.
Overwrite the saved value at each node’s column.
Enqueue left before right with adjusted columns.
Read the final values from the smallest column through the largest.
297.space: O(n), including the queue, column map, and output.
pitfalls: Use the later level-order node for equal-depth ties, not the smaller value.
If using DFS, compare depths; a late DFS node may be shallower.
DFS must replace on equal depth as well, with left-first traversal.
Bottom view is not just the list of leaves. An internal node may remain visible in its column.
tests: assert bottomView(null).isEmpty();TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(7);r.right.left=new TreeNode(2);assert bottomView(r).equals(List.of(4,2,9));assert bottomBySorting(r).equals(bottomView(r));assert bottomByDfs(r).equals(bottomView(r));

reference.title: Bottom View of Binary Tree
reference.approach: Sort position records, track maximum depth with DFS, or overwrite each column during BFS.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked, including the equal-depth tie rule. The main version follows the source’s HashMap and BFS range approach, using ArrayDeque.

297.baselineTime: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

better.explanation: Track the deepest node seen at each column during left-first DFS. Replace when the new depth is greater than or equal to the saved depth. Equality lets a later node at the same level win. Read the TreeMap in column order.
better.space: O(n), including O(h) recursive stack space. Deep trees may exceed Java’s call-stack limit.

298.problem: Return the right-side view of a binary tree. Also learn the matching left-side view: choose one extreme node at each depth and list the values from top to bottom.
298.assumptions: The pinned practice link asks for the right-side view. Both variants are included because the sheet title covers both. A view can include a node from the opposite subtree if that subtree reaches farther down. Empty input gives an empty list.

example.explanation: At the first child level, 9 is rightmost. At deeper levels only 7 and then 6 exist, even though both belong to the root’s left subtree.

298.baseline: Process one level at a time with BFS. Its first node belongs to the left view and its last node belongs to the right view. This is already O(n); DFS is an alternative that trades queue width for path depth.
298.approach:
For the right view, visit a node, then its right subtree, then its left subtree. The first node reached at each depth is the rightmost node at that depth. Add it only when depth equals the number of values already in the answer.

Why does that check work? If the answer contains d values, depths 0 through d − 1 already have an entry. Reaching depth d means we have discovered a new level. Later nodes at that depth are skipped.

For the left view, reverse the child order. Both child subtrees must still be visited; following only right or only left edges misses visible nodes below a shorter subtree.
steps: Start at depth 0 with an empty result.
Return immediately for null.
Add the node if this is the first visit to its depth.
For right view, recurse right then left; for left view, recurse left then right.
298.space: O(h) recursion stack and O(h) output, where h is the number of levels. Use the BFS version if recursion may be too deep.
pitfalls: A right-view node does not have to be a right child.
Side views choose by depth; top and bottom views choose by column.
Do not change the BFS loop bound as children join the queue.
The first-visit DFS condition depends on exploring the required side first.
tests: assert rightSideView(null).isEmpty();assert leftSideView(null).isEmpty();TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(7);r.left.right.left=new TreeNode(6);assert rightSideView(r).equals(List.of(8,9,7,6));assert leftSideView(r).equals(List.of(8,4,7,6));

reference.title: Left and Right Views of a Binary Tree
reference.approach: BFS takes level extremes; ordered DFS records the first node at each depth.
reference.adaptation: The current public lesson was read in full. It contains detailed BFS/DFS algorithms but no Java code tab. These authored Java methods implement those algorithms; rightSideView matches the pinned LeetCode question, and leftSideView covers the other half of the sheet title.

298.baselineTime: O(n) time, O(w) queue space, and O(h) output space.

299.problem: Check whether a binary tree is a mirror image of itself, including both node values and missing-child positions.
299.assumptions: An empty tree and a single-node tree are symmetric. Equal values alone are not enough: each existing node must have a matching node at the reflected position.

example.explanation: The two 4s match, and their outside children both contain 6. If the second 6 were right.left instead, the tree would not be symmetric.

299.baseline: Compare the two child subtrees recursively. Match left.left with right.right, and left.right with right.left. Both missing means a match; exactly one missing means failure. This uses O(h) call-stack space.
299.approach:
Keep pairs of nodes that should be mirrors of each other. Start with the root’s left and right children. Pop one pair, compare existence and values, then push its outside and inside child pairs.

Crossing the child directions is the whole idea: reflection swaps left and right. Comparing left with left would test whether the subtrees are identical, which is a different question.

The stack version performs the same comparisons as recursion but avoids Java call-stack limits. Each stack item is a non-null array that can contain null nodes, because ArrayDeque itself cannot store null elements.
steps: An empty root is symmetric. Otherwise push its two children as a pair.
Skip a pair containing two nulls; reject a pair containing only one null.
Reject unequal values.
Push crossed child pairs and continue until no pairs remain.
299.space: O(h) explicit stack space, where h is tree height.
pitfalls: Include null positions. Palindromic lists of values can hide a structural mismatch.
Compare crossed child directions.
After two nulls match, continue checking other pairs rather than returning true immediately.
Keep state local so a second call cannot inherit a previous failure.
tests: assert isSymmetric(null);assert isSymmetric(new TreeNode(3));TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(4);r.left.left=new TreeNode(6);r.right.right=new TreeNode(6);assert isSymmetric(r);r.right.left=r.right.right;r.right.right=null;assert !isSymmetric(r);assert !symmetricRecursive(r);assert !symmetricQueue(r);

Random random=new Random(288);for(int test=0;test<600;test++){int n=1+random.nextInt(80);TreeNode root=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));Map<TreeNode,String>paths=new IdentityHashMap<>();paths.put(root,"");List<TreeNode>open=new ArrayList<>();open.add(root);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){TreeNode parent=open.get(random.nextInt(open.size())),child=new TreeNode(random.nextInt(10));boolean left=parent.left==null&&(parent.right!=null||random.nextBoolean());if(left)parent.left=child;else parent.right=child;paths.put(child,paths.get(parent)+(left?"L":"R"));if(parent.left!=null&&parent.right!=null)open.remove(parent);open.add(child);}Map<String,Integer> values=new HashMap<>();for(TreeNode x:paths.keySet())values.put(paths.get(x),x.val);boolean want=true;for(String path:values.keySet()){StringBuilder mirror=new StringBuilder();for(char ch:path.toCharArray())mirror.append(ch=='L'?'R':'L');if(!Objects.equals(values.get(path),values.get(mirror.toString())))want=false;}assert isSymmetric(root)==want;assert symmetricRecursive(root)==want;assert symmetricQueue(root)==want;TreeNode full=new TreeNode(0);full.left=root;Map<TreeNode,TreeNode> copies=new IdentityHashMap<>();for(TreeNode x:paths.keySet())copies.put(x,new TreeNode(x.val));for(TreeNode x:paths.keySet()){copies.get(x).left=copies.get(x.right);copies.get(x).right=copies.get(x.left);}full.right=copies.get(root);assert isSymmetric(full);assert symmetricRecursive(full);assert symmetricQueue(full);full.right.val++;assert !isSymmetric(full);}

reference.title: Check If a Binary Tree Is Symmetric
reference.approach: Compare mirrored pairs recursively, with a queue, or with an explicit stack.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. The code keeps crossed child comparisons, using ArrayDeque and two-element node arrays instead of the source’s NodePair class.

better.explanation: Use a queue of mirrored pairs to check the tree level by level. The comparisons are identical to the stack version; only the order of pending work changes. This avoids recursion but may store a wide level.
better.space: O(w), where w is the maximum level width.

300.problem: Find the path from the root to a chosen node. Also return all root-to-leaf paths for the current practice link attached to this sheet row.
300.assumptions: The pinned title says “Root to Node Path”, but its link now asks for all root-to-leaf paths. These are different tasks, so both methods are included. A leaf has no children. rootToNode accepts a node reference, so duplicate values are unambiguous; it returns an empty list when the target is absent.

example.input: root 8; children 4 and 9; 4.right = 7; target is node 4
example.explanation: A target path may stop at an internal node. A leaf path must continue until neither child exists.

300.baseline: For all leaf paths, pass a separate path copy to every child. Each branch can then change its list safely, but repeated partial-path copying wastes work. The backtracking version keeps one working path instead.
300.approach:
When entering a node, append it to the current path. For all leaf paths, save a copy only when a leaf is reached. Visit the children, then remove the current node before returning to its parent. This final removal lets the next branch reuse the same list.

For one target path, stop when the exact target node is found. Return true up the successful chain without removing those nodes. If both child searches fail, remove the current node and return false. The remaining list is either the requested path or empty.

Always copy a completed leaf path. Saving the working list itself would make every result point to the same changing object.
steps: Append the current node on entry.
For leaf paths, copy the list at a leaf; otherwise explore both children.
Remove the last item when leaving a completed branch.
For a target path, keep the successful branch and undo only failed branches.
300.time: O(n) for one target path; O(n + k) for all leaf paths, where k is the total number of values returned across all paths.
300.space: O(h) working path and recursive stack, plus O(k) output for all leaf paths. Deep trees can exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
pitfalls: A missing left child does not make a node a leaf if its right child exists.
Use new ArrayList<>(path) when storing a leaf path.
Remove by index path.size() − 1, not by node value.
Do not treat a different node with the same value as the requested target.
tests: assert rootToLeafPaths(null).isEmpty();assert rootToNode(null,new TreeNode(0)).isEmpty();TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.right=new TreeNode(7);assert rootToNode(r,r.left).equals(List.of(8,4));assert rootToLeafPaths(r).equals(List.of(List.of(8,4,7),List.of(8,9)));assert rootToNode(r,new TreeNode(4)).isEmpty();List<List<Integer>>a=rootToLeafPaths(r);a.get(0).set(0,-1);assert a.get(1).get(0)==8;

reference.title: Print root to leaf path in Binary Tree
reference.approach: Copy partial paths, then improve to one backtracked path; use early success for a single target.
reference.adaptation: Both public root-to-leaf Java methods were checked. The original sheet’s root-to-node title is retained and covered with the target-path method checked in Striver’s LCA article. The current link’s all-leaf variant has a separate method.

300.baselineTime: O(nh + k) time and O(h²) auxiliary space in the worst case, excluding O(k) output.

301.problem: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree: the deepest node that is an ancestor of both.
301.assumptions: This is an ordinary binary tree, not a binary search tree. Both target node references are present, as guaranteed by the linked problem. A node is its own ancestor. Comparisons use node identity, so the methods also work when values repeat.

example.explanation: Both targets lie below 4 in different child branches. For targets 4 and 6, the answer is also 4 because a node can be its own ancestor.

301.baseline: Find the root-to-node path for each target. Compare the paths from the root and keep the last identical node. This directly follows the definition and takes O(n) time with O(h) saved-path space.
301.approach:
Ask each subtree to return the useful node it finds: a target, their common ancestor, or null. If the current node is either target, return it. Otherwise search both children.

If both child results are non-null, the targets split across the two sides, so the current node is their meeting point. If only one result is non-null, pass that result upward. It may already be the LCA, or it may be a target whose other target lies below it.

The guarantee that both targets exist matters. Without it, this compact method can return the one target it found even when the other is absent. The parent-map version below explicitly detects missing targets.
steps: Return null for an empty subtree.
Return the current node if it is either target.
Search both child subtrees.
Return the current node for two non-null results; otherwise return the one non-null result.
301.space: O(h) recursive stack. Use the iterative parent-map version for a very deep tree.
pitfalls: Do not use BST value comparisons on an ordinary binary tree.
An ancestor target can itself be the answer.
Compare node references rather than values.
The compact recursive method relies on both targets being present.
tests: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(8);r.left=new TreeNode(4);r.right=new TreeNode(9);r.left.left=new TreeNode(2);r.left.right=new TreeNode(6);assert lowestCommonAncestor(r,r.left.left,r.left.right)==r.left;assert lowestCommonAncestor(r,r.left,r.left.right)==r.left;assert lowestCommonAncestor(r,r.left,r.right)==r;

reference.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in a Binary Tree
reference.approach: Compare root paths, walk parent links, or combine recursive subtree results.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. The main method follows the source’s recursive split test. The iterative version adds a queue-exhaustion guard and returns null when a target is absent; maps and sets explicitly use node identity.

better.explanation: Build parent links with BFS. Mark all ancestors of p, then walk upward from q until reaching a marked node. This uses O(n) storage but avoids recursive depth limits. The membership guard also handles a missing target.
better.space: O(n).

302.problem: Return the greatest width among the levels of a binary tree. Count empty positions between the leftmost and rightmost existing nodes on a level.
302.assumptions: This row links to LeetCode 662, which guarantees that the answer fits a signed 32-bit integer. Width includes internal gaps; it is not simply the number of nodes in the queue. Empty input returns 0 as a useful extension.

example.explanation: The last level has positions [2, empty, empty, 7]. Only two nodes exist there, but the width is four.

302.baseline: Lay out every possible position at each level, including gaps. The distance between the two outermost nodes gives the width. Materializing all those gaps can require exponential space, so keep position numbers instead.
302.approach:
Pretend the tree is stored in a complete-tree array: a node at index i has children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. Queue only real nodes, together with those indices. The width of a level is lastIndex − firstIndex + 1.

Raw indices grow rapidly even for a narrow deep tree. Before processing each level, subtract its first index from every index on that level. Subtracting the same number preserves all gaps. Generate child indices from these smaller numbers.

Use long for intermediate positions. Under the linked problem’s 32-bit width guarantee, normalized positions and their doubled children remain safely within long. Normalization does not make arbitrarily huge widths fit in an integer; the guarantee is still needed.
steps: Queue the root with position 0.
At each level, save its node count and first position.
Normalize each removed position by subtracting that first position.
Enqueue real children with complete-tree positions, then update the answer from the level’s first and last normalized positions.
302.space: O(w) queued real nodes, where w is the largest actual node count at a level. Gaps do not occupy queue entries.
pitfalls: Count internal missing positions, but not gaps outside the outermost nodes.
Use long before multiplying positions by two.
Normalize once per level using the same base for all its nodes.
A long chain can have huge raw indices while its width remains only one.

303.problem: Check that every non-leaf node equals the sum of its immediate children’s values.
303.assumptions: A missing child contributes 0. A leaf automatically passes, regardless of its value. Negative values are allowed by the current problem. This is a check: do not change the tree to make the property true. Empty input returns true.

example.input: root 12; left child 5 with children 2 and 3; right child 7
example.explanation: 12 = 5 + 7 and 5 = 2 + 3. The leaves 2, 3, and 7 need no further sum check.

303.baseline: Recursively check the current node’s child sum and then check both subtrees. This is already O(n). A queue performs the same checks without risking a deep recursive call stack.
303.approach:
Visit every node. Skip leaves because the problem explicitly exempts them. For any other node, add its existing children’s values, treating a missing child as zero. If that sum differs from the parent value, return false immediately.

Passing at the root is not enough. A node farther down can still break the rule, so continue until all nodes pass. Only immediate children contribute to a node’s check; adding the whole subtree would test a different property.
steps: An empty tree passes. Otherwise queue the root.
Skip the sum comparison for a leaf.
Add the immediate child values and compare with the parent.
Reject a mismatch; otherwise enqueue the children and continue.
303.space: O(w) queue space, where w is the maximum level width.
pitfalls: Do not require leaves to equal zero.
Check the sum of immediate children, not all descendants.
Do not mutate values: this question asks whether the existing tree satisfies the property.
Use long for the sum so two int values cannot overflow before comparison.

304.problem: Return the values of all nodes exactly k edges away from a target node in a binary tree.
304.assumptions: The target is a node reference in the tree and k is nonnegative. Answers may be returned in any order. The target itself is the answer for k = 0. As an extension, this implementation returns an empty list for a missing target, empty tree, or negative k.

example.input: root 8; children 4 and 9; 4.left = 2; 2.right = 6; target = node 4; k = 2
example.explanation: 6 is reached by 4 → 2 → 6. The other answer requires moving upward first: 4 → 8 → 9.

304.baseline: Treat each tree edge as an undirected graph edge, then run BFS from the target. This works in O(n), but it duplicates child links that are already stored in the tree. Keeping only the missing parent links is enough.
304.approach:
A node already knows its children, but it does not know its parent. First walk from the root and save each child’s parent in a map. Now every node has up to three neighbors: left child, right child, and parent.

Run BFS from the target. The initial queue is distance 0. After expanding one whole queue level, the new queue is distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. Stop expanding when the distance reaches k; the queue then contains exactly the required nodes.

Mark nodes when they enter the queue. Without that visited set, a node and its parent would keep sending the search back to each other.
steps: Build child-to-parent links from the root.
Queue and mark the target at distance 0.
Expand exactly one complete BFS level at a time through unvisited children and parent.
After k expansions, return the queued values. If the queue emptied sooner, return no values.
304.space: O(n) for parent links, visited nodes, queue, and output.
pitfalls: Search upward as well as downward.
Count edges: the target starts at distance 0.
Mark neighbors before enqueueing them.
Track node identities, not values, so repeated values do not merge distinct nodes.

reference.approach: Add parent links and expand BFS levels; alternatively propagate target distance through recursion.
reference.adaptation: The article’s graph explanation and the complete parent-map and recursive Java methods were checked. The primary implementation follows parent-map BFS, with explicit node-identity tracking and missing-target guards.

better.explanation: To avoid a parent map, return the distance to the target from each recursive call, or −1 if absent. At the target, collect descendants k edges down. At each ancestor, include that ancestor if its distance is k; otherwise search its opposite subtree with k − ancestorDistance − 1 edges remaining. This is O(n) overall because those opposite subtrees are disjoint, although a subtree may also have been examined while searching for the target.
better.space: O(h) recursive stack, plus output. A deep tree can exceed Java’s call-stack limit.

305.problem: Find how many seconds it takes for fire starting at one node to reach every node in a binary tree.
305.assumptions: Fire spreads simultaneously along every edge to unburned neighbors. The start node burns at time 0. The pinned practice problem gives a unique start value; all node values are unique and the start exists. The wrapper below resolves that value to a node. Empty input returns 0; an absent start in a nonempty tree is rejected.

example.explanation: The burning front is {2} at time 0, {4} at time 1, {8} at time 2, {9} at time 3, and {7} at time 4.

305.baseline: Build an undirected adjacency list for the tree, then expand BFS from the start. Every BFS layer is one second. This is already O(n); storing only parent links avoids duplicating existing child links.
305.approach:
Save each node’s parent, then start a BFS at the burning node. During one round, process exactly the nodes that are burning at the current time. Their unburned children and parents form the next round.

Increase the elapsed time only if at least one new node caught fire. Processing the last burning layer does not add another second: there is nowhere left for the fire to spread. This gives 0 for a single-node tree.

Equivalently, the answer is the largest edge distance from the start to any node. Fire travels along all paths at once, so times from different branches are not added together.
steps: Build parent links and find the unique node whose value equals start.
Put that node in the queue and burned set.
For one complete layer, add any unburned child or parent.
Increase time if the layer spread to a new node; finish when the queue is empty.
305.space: O(n) for parent links, burned nodes, and the BFS queue.
pitfalls: The start burns at time 0, so a single node takes zero seconds.
Do not add the times of separate branches; they burn simultaneously.
Keep a burned set to prevent moving back and forth across an edge.
The practice wrapper assumes unique values; the recursive helper instead accepts an exact node reference.

306.problem: Count the nodes in a complete binary tree without visiting every node.
306.assumptions: The input must be complete: every level except possibly the last is full, and the last level fills from left to right. Equal outer heights prove a subtree is perfect only under this assumption. The pinned LeetCode interface returns int; the count is assumed to fit int.

example.explanation: The root’s outer heights differ, so split the tree. Its left subtree is perfect with three nodes; its right subtree has two. Add the root: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

306.baseline: Visit each node and return 1 + leftCount + rightCount. This works on any binary tree but takes O(n), ignoring the complete-tree structure.
306.approach:
Count the nodes on the all-left path and on the all-right path from the current root. If those heights are equal, the subtree is perfect because the input is complete. A perfect tree with h levels contains 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^(h−1) = 2^h − 1 nodes. Return that count immediately.

If the heights differ, count both child subtrees and add one for the root. At most one child subtree needs further splitting; the other is perfect and can be counted from its height. Across O(log n) levels, height scans take O(log² n) time.
steps: Return 0 for null.
Measure the leftmost and rightmost heights in nodes.
For equal heights, return 2^height − 1.
Otherwise return 1 plus both child counts.
306.time: O(log² n) for a complete tree.
pitfalls: Do not apply the equal-height shortcut to an arbitrary tree with holes.
Heights count levels here: a leaf has height 1.
In Java, ^ means XOR, not exponentiation. Use a shift for powers of two.
The complete-tree assumption is what allows whole subtrees to be skipped.

307.problem: Decide whether two ordinary traversal types guarantee a unique arbitrary binary tree, assuming distinct node values and consistent traversal data.
307.assumptions: The practice question encodes preorder as 1, inorder as 2, and postorder as 3. It asks about the guarantee provided by the types, not whether one particular pair of arrays happens to have a unique answer. No extra full-tree, BST, or null-marker information is given.

example.explanation: Preorder identifies the root. Its location in inorder separates the left and right subtrees. Repeat the same reasoning inside each part.

307.baseline: List the nine ordered pairs of traversal types. Preorder + inorder and postorder + inorder work in either order. Two copies of the same type do not add information, and preorder + postorder cannot resolve a single child’s side.
307.approach:
One traversal must tell us which node is the root, and the other must separate its left and right subtrees. Preorder gives the root first; postorder gives it last. Inorder puts the root between its two subtrees.

So, among the three allowed types, the types must differ and one must be inorder. For preorder [8, 4] and postorder [4, 8], node 4 could be either the left or right child of 8. Both trees fit, so that pair does not guarantee uniqueness.

There are useful exceptions outside this question: preorder and postorder determine a full tree with distinct values, and preorder with a marker for every missing child describes an arbitrary tree. Duplicate values also remove the usual guarantee unless node identities or other structure are supplied.
steps: Reject two equal traversal types.
Check whether either type is inorder.
Return true only when both conditions hold.
pitfalls: This predicate does not validate actual traversal arrays. Their values and order must still be consistent.
Preorder + postorder can be unique for some particular trees, but does not guarantee uniqueness for every arbitrary tree.
Distinct values matter when using a value-to-inorder-index map.
Do not silently assume a full tree or a BST. Those are extra constraints.

308.problem: Reconstruct a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals.
308.assumptions: Values are distinct and the traversals describe the same tree. Preorder visits root, left, right; inorder visits left, root, right. The methods return newly allocated nodes and do not change the input arrays. Empty arrays produce null.

example.output: root 8; left subtree rooted at 4 with children 2 and 6; right child 9
example.explanation: 8 is first in preorder. In inorder, [2, 4, 6] lies left of 8 and [9] lies right. The next unused preorder value, 4, starts the left subtree.

308.baseline: Take the next preorder value as root and linearly search for it inside the current inorder range. Build the left and right ranges recursively. Repeating these searches can take O(n²) time on a skewed tree.
308.approach:
Build a map from each value to its inorder position. Keep a cursor pointing to the next unused preorder value. A recursive call receives the inorder range belonging to its subtree.

Read the next preorder value as the root. Its inorder position splits that range into a left part and a right part. Build the left subtree first, then the right, because that is the order in which the shared preorder cursor encounters their values.

An empty inorder range means a missing child. Every nonempty call consumes exactly one preorder value and creates exactly one node. The index map removes repeated scanning, giving O(n) expected time.

Start a local preorder cursor at 0.
For a nonempty inorder range, consume its root and look up the split position.
Build left first, then right; attach them and return the root.
308.space: O(n) index/validation storage and O(h) recursion, plus O(n) returned nodes. Deep skewed trees can exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
pitfalls: With one forward preorder cursor, construct the left subtree before the right.
Search only the current inorder range, not an unrelated subtree.
Do not reuse a cursor from a previous call.
A value-to-index map requires distinct values.

309.problem: Reconstruct a binary tree from its inorder and postorder traversals.
309.assumptions: Values are distinct and both traversals describe the same tree. Postorder visits left, right, root. The pinned interface takes inorder first and postorder second. Input arrays remain unchanged; empty arrays return null.

example.output: root 8; left subtree rooted at 4 with children 2 and 6; right child 9
example.explanation: The last postorder value is 8. Reading backward, 9 comes next, so build the right subtree before the left subtree rooted at 4.

309.baseline: Read postorder backward and search linearly for each root in its current inorder range. This reconstructs the tree but can spend O(n²) time repeating inorder scans.
309.approach:
The last unused postorder value is the root of the current subtree. Find its position in inorder to separate the left and right ranges.

A backward postorder cursor sees Root → Right → Left. Build the right subtree first so it consumes the correct values, then build the left subtree. This order is essential when sharing one cursor; it is the reverse of the preorder construction.

Store inorder positions in a HashMap to find each split in expected constant time. Empty ranges return null, and each nonempty range consumes one value and creates one node.
steps: Map inorder values to their positions.
Start the postorder cursor at the final index.
Consume a root and find its split in the current inorder range.
Build right before left, then return the connected root.
309.space: O(n) index/validation storage and O(h) recursion, plus O(n) output nodes. Deep skewed trees may exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
pitfalls: A backward shared cursor requires right-before-left construction.
Do not confuse this method’s inorder, postorder parameter order with the preorder question.
Use inclusive range boundaries consistently.

309.baselineTime: O(n²) worst-case time and O(h) recursive space, excluding the new tree. Assumes valid, distinct traversal arrays.

310.problem: Convert a binary tree to a string and reconstruct a new tree with exactly the same values and child positions.
310.assumptions: This guide’s primary codec uses level order, commas between tokens, and # for every missing child. There is no trailing comma; an empty tree is exactly #. Negative and duplicate values are allowed. The preorder alternative uses a different token order, so each serializer must be paired with its own decoder.

example.explanation: The first # says 4 has no left child. Without that marker, −2 would be attached on the wrong side.

310.baseline: Use preorder with a marker for every null child. Write root, left subtree, then right subtree; read tokens in the same recursive order to rebuild the tree. This is O(n), but a very deep tree can overflow the call stack.
310.approach:
A value-only traversal loses shape. For example, a root with one left child and a root with one right child can have the same preorder values. Null markers keep those two shapes distinct.

For level-order serialization, queue both child positions of each real node. Record # for an empty position and do not expand it further. For decoding, create the root, then take the next two tokens for each queued parent: left first, right second. Queue any children that were actually created.

A tree with n real nodes has n + 1 null child positions, so the complete format has 2n + 1 tokens. The decoder below rejects missing or extra tokens rather than silently returning a partial tree.
steps: Serialize each queued position as its value or #.
For a real node, queue both child positions, including nulls.
Decode the root, then consume two child tokens per real parent.
Finish only when all parents and all tokens are consumed.
310.time: O(n) for int-valued nodes; equivalently O(L) in serialized text length L.
310.space: O(w) traversal queue. The serializer builds O(L) output; the decoder also allocates O(L) split tokens and O(n) new nodes.
pitfalls: Preserve missing positions; do not serialize values alone.
ArrayDeque rejects null, so the serializer uses LinkedList for queued empty positions.
Do not decode preorder text with the level-order decoder.
Do not claim constant total memory: the text, split tokens, and reconstructed tree all occupy space.

311.problem: Produce preorder traversal (Root → Left → Right) using constant auxiliary space and restore the tree before finishing.
311.assumptions: The input is an ordinary mutable tree with no cycles. Duplicate values are allowed. Every temporary link must be removed before the method returns. The output list is separate from the O(1) traversal workspace. The pinned old-sheet practice link points to inorder, despite this row’s preorder title; this page teaches preorder, matching the current Striver preorder article. The next row covers inorder.

example.explanation: The root is recorded before entering the left subtree. The temporary return link from 6 to 8 is removed before completion.

311.baseline: A recursive traversal follows the required order directly, but uses O(h) call-stack space. An explicit stack has the same space bound. Morris traversal stores return links temporarily inside the tree instead.
311.approach:
When a node has a left subtree, find that subtree’s rightmost node, called the inorder predecessor. Its empty right reference can temporarily point back to the current node. This thread remembers where to return without a stack.

On the first encounter, create the thread and move left. On the second encounter, the predecessor already points to current: remove that thread and move right. Stop the predecessor search when it sees current, or it could follow the temporary cycle forever.

For preorder, record the current value on the first encounter, before moving left. Do not record it again when removing the thread. A node without a left child is recorded immediately.

Although predecessor searching is nested inside the loop, each relevant edge is followed only a constant number of times overall. Total work is O(n).
steps: If current has no left child, record it and move right.
Otherwise find its predecessor, stopping at null or a right reference back to current.
On first encounter, record current, create the thread and move left.
On second encounter, remove the thread, and move right.
311.space: O(1) auxiliary traversal space, plus O(n) for the returned values.
pitfalls: Compare node references when detecting a thread, not node values.
Restore predecessor.right to null on the second encounter.
Do not return early after creating threads; unfinished cleanup can leave cycles.
Use a stack-based traversal when temporary mutation or concurrent access is not acceptable.

reference.approach: Use predecessor threads and visit after returning from the left subtree.
reference.adaptation: The complete current public lesson and dry run were checked. It has no Java tab, so this is an authored Java implementation of its threading steps. Tests verify both traversal order and restoration of every original child reference.

312.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space, plus the output.

313.problem: Flatten a binary tree in place into a right-child chain following its original preorder. Reuse the existing nodes and set every left reference to null.
313.assumptions: The pinned LeetCode method returns void and modifies the supplied tree. The source article returns the same root; the pointer operations are identical. This operation permanently changes the tree, unlike Morris traversal’s temporary threads. Empty input needs no work.

example.output: 8 → 4 → 6 → 5 → 9 through right references; every left is null
example.explanation: The original left subtree comes before the original right subtree. Node 5 must remain before 9 even though the first splice point is node 6.

313.baseline: Save all node references in preorder, then reconnect consecutive references through right and clear every left reference. This is easy to check but needs O(n) storage for the saved list.
313.approach:
At the current node, preorder needs the whole left subtree before the original right subtree. If a left child exists, find the rightmost node along that left subtree’s right-child chain. Attach the original right subtree there, move the left subtree to current.right, and clear current.left. Then advance right.

The splice point is not necessarily the last node in final preorder: it may have a left subtree of its own. When traversal reaches it, the same rewiring rule moves that left subtree ahead of its saved right continuation. This is why no nodes are skipped or lost.

The method uses only two moving references and finishes with the original nodes connected in preorder.
steps: Start current at the root.
If a left subtree exists, find its rightmost node.
Attach current.right there before moving current.left to current.right.
Clear current.left and advance to current.right.
313.time: O(n): predecessor searches and forward traversal together follow each relevant link only a constant number of times.
313.space: O(1) auxiliary space. No new tree nodes are created.
pitfalls: Preserve the original right subtree before replacing current.right.
Clear every left reference.
The rightmost splice node can have a left subtree; it is not always the final preorder node.
For reverse-recursive flattening, reset previous for each call so separate trees do not become connected.

reference.adaptation: All three public Java methods were checked. The main code keeps the source’s constant-space rewiring, with void return for the pinned LeetCode interface. better.explanation: Build the chain backward. Process right, then left, then the current node. previous is the already-built continuation: point current.right to it, clear current.left, then move previous to current. This avoids the full reference list but still uses recursion.

314.problem: Understand the ordering rule of a binary search tree and why inorder traversal returns its values in sorted order.
314.assumptions: We use a strict BST: every value anywhere in a node’s left subtree is smaller, and every value anywhere in its right subtree is larger. Values are distinct. Other duplicate policies exist, but they must be stated separately. A BST is not automatically balanced.

example.input: root 8; left subtree has 4 with children 2 and 6; right subtree has 12 with children 10 and 14
example.explanation: All of 8’s left-subtree values are smaller than 8, and all right-subtree values are larger. This condition repeats at every node.

314.baseline: An ordinary binary tree only limits each node to two children; it does not order values. Finding a value may require visiting every node. A BST adds the ordering rule that lets a search choose one child direction.
314.approach:
The rule applies to entire subtrees, not only immediate children. For example, putting 10 under the right child of node 4 still breaks the rule if 4 belongs to the left subtree of 8. The value 10 is too large for that whole side of 8.

Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Since the three parts are ordered by value, the result is sorted. The Java example builds a small BST and reads it with an explicit stack.

Search, insertion, and deletion follow paths of length at most the tree height h. They take O(h), which is O(log n) when balanced and O(n) for a chain. Ordinary insertion does not balance the tree; inserting sorted values can produce that chain.
steps: Check the smaller-left, larger-right rule across every whole subtree.
Build nodes and connect them with left and right references.
Read inorder by finishing the left side, recording the node, then visiting the right side.
Keep tree height in mind when judging search performance.
314.time: O(n) for inorder traversal. Search/insert/delete depend on height: O(h).
314.space: O(h) traversal stack and O(n) output. The tree itself stores O(n) nodes.
pitfalls: Smaller immediate children do not prove that all descendants satisfy the rule.
A BST can be completely skewed. Do not promise logarithmic operations without a balancing condition.
Inorder is sorted only when the input actually satisfies the BST rule.
Assigning one node reference to another variable does not copy the tree.

reference.title: Binary Search Tree (BST): Introduction and Operations
reference.approach: Strict ordering across whole subtrees and sorted inorder traversal.
reference.adaptation: The public foundation lesson was read. It has no Java tab, so this is an authored construction and traversal example. Complexity is expressed as O(height); choosing one subtree does not guarantee halving the node count in an unbalanced BST.

315.problem: Find a target value in a binary search tree and return the existing node containing it, including its subtree. Return null if it is absent.
315.assumptions: The input is a valid strict BST with distinct values. Returning a node returns a reference to the existing subtree, not a copy and not just its value. The method does not modify any child references.

example.input: root 8; children 4 and 12; 4 has children 2 and 6; target = 4
example.output: the existing node 4, with children 2 and 6
example.explanation: 4 is smaller than 8, so move left once. The target node is found and returned with its existing children.

315.baseline: Recursively compare the target with the current value and search only the appropriate child. This uses the BST rule correctly, but keeps O(h) recursive calls on a path.
315.approach:
Compare the target with the current node. If equal, return that node. If smaller, continue left: the current node and everything to its right are too large. If larger, continue right for the symmetric reason.

Each comparison leaves only one possible child subtree. No backtracking is needed because the rejected side cannot contain the target. Reaching null means the target is absent.

Iteration keeps only the current reference, so it uses constant extra space. The number of comparisons still depends on height; a skewed BST may require visiting every node.
steps: Start at the root.
Return the current node on equality.
Move left for a smaller target or right for a larger target.
Return null if the path ends.
315.time: O(h): O(log n) when balanced, O(n) in the worst case.
pitfalls: Return the matching node reference, not a newly created node.
The one-branch rule is valid only for a BST.
A search must not detach or replace child references.

316.problem: Return the smallest and largest values in a binary search tree, as [minimum, maximum].
316.assumptions: The tree is a valid strict BST. The current Striver practice problem guarantees a nonempty tree and permits negative values. This implementation returns an empty array for an empty tree as an explicit extension, rather than using a value such as −1 that could be a real answer.

example.input: root 8; left child 4 with right child 6; right child 12 with left child 10
example.explanation: Keep moving left to reach 4 and right to reach 12. The minimum and maximum can have a child on the opposite side; they need not be leaves.

316.baseline: Traverse every node while tracking the smallest and largest values. That costs O(n) and works for any binary tree. A BST lets us ignore all but its two outer paths.
316.approach:
The smallest value cannot be to the right of the current node. If a left child exists, every value there is smaller, so move left. When no left child remains, the current value is the minimum.

Find the maximum in the same way by following right children. The two searches may share the root, but each takes at most h steps. No sorting, recursion, or full traversal is needed.
steps: For an empty tree, return an empty result.
Follow left children to find the minimum.
Starting again at the root, follow right children to find the maximum.
Return the two values in minimum-then-maximum order.
316.time: O(h), which is O(log n) for a balanced BST and O(n) for a chain.
pitfalls: The minimum can have a right child, and the maximum can have a left child.
Restart from the root before finding the opposite extreme.
Negative values are allowed, so −1 is not a safe missing-value marker.
This shortcut requires BST ordering, not merely a binary-tree shape.

317.problem: Find the smallest BST value greater than or equal to a key (its ceiling).

317.baseline: Collect the inorder traversal, which is sorted. Scan it, remembering the last value at most the key and stopping at the first value at least the key. This costs O(n) time and storage.
317.approach:
A value smaller than the key cannot be a ceiling, and neither can anything in its left subtree. Move right. A value larger than the key is a possible ceiling; remember it, then move left to look for a smaller value that still qualifies.

The linked problem asks for both floor and ceiling. One walk can track both: a smaller node updates floor and sends us right; a larger node updates ceil and sends us left. An exact match is both answers. When the path ends, the saved candidates are the closest qualifying values, or −1 if none was found.

On equality, return [key, key].
A smaller current value updates floor before moving right.
A larger current value updates ceil before moving left; return the final pair when the path ends.

pitfalls: Floor and ceil include equality; strict predecessor/successor are different questions.
The return order is [floor, ceil], even on this single-topic sheet row.
Keep the last valid candidate when moving to a null child.
A BST discards one subtree per comparison, not necessarily half its nodes.

319.problem: Insert a new value into a binary search tree and return the resulting root.
319.assumptions: The linked problem guarantees that the value is absent. We insert it as a new leaf and preserve all existing nodes. For an empty tree, the new node becomes the root. As a stated extension, inserting an existing value leaves this strict BST unchanged.

example.explanation: 10 is greater than 8, so move right. It is smaller than 12, whose left position is empty, so attach the new leaf there.

319.baseline: Recursively choose left or right, and assign the returned subtree back to that child reference. The null base case creates the new leaf. This takes O(h) time and O(h) call-stack space.
319.approach:
Follow the same comparisons used for search. Keep walking while the required child exists. At the first empty child position, attach a new node and stop.

Every comparison adds a restriction: moving right from 8 means the new value must exceed 8; moving left from 12 means it must be below 12. Following the whole path satisfies all ancestor restrictions automatically.

Use a separate current reference so the original root is still available to return. This basic insertion does not rebalance the tree, so insertion order affects its shape and future performance.
steps: If root is null, return a new node.
Compare the value with current and choose one child direction.
If that child is absent, create the new leaf there. Otherwise continue down that child.
Return the original root.
319.time: O(h), ranging from O(log n) when balanced to O(n) for a chain.
319.space: O(1) auxiliary space and one new node.
pitfalls: Assign root = insertIntoBST(root, value), because an empty tree needs a new root.
Recursive insertion must reconnect the returned child subtree.
Ordinary insertion does not keep a BST balanced.
Do not create a second copy of an existing value unless the problem defines a duplicate policy.

320.problem: Remove a key from a binary search tree and return the updated root while preserving the remaining values and BST ordering.
320.assumptions: The BST has distinct values. If the key is absent, return the same tree unchanged. This implementation removes the matching node object from the returned tree and reuses all other node objects, without copying successor values. The root can change.

example.input: root 8; left child 4; right child 12 with children 10 and 14; delete 8
example.output: new root 12; its left child is 10; 10.left is 4; 12.right is 14
example.explanation: Promote the original right subtree. Its smallest node, 10, has an empty left reference where the entire old left subtree can be attached.

320.baseline: Recursively search for the key and return a replacement subtree when found. A helper handles zero, one, or two children. The recursive caller reconnects that returned subtree to its parent.
320.approach:
First handle deletion of the root. Otherwise walk down the BST and look for a child whose value matches the key, so its parent reference can be updated directly.

For a node with no left child, its right child replaces it. With no right child, its left child replaces it. For two children, promote the right subtree and attach the old left subtree to the leftmost node of that right subtree.

Why is that attachment valid? Every old-left value is below the deleted key, and every old-right value is above it. The right subtree’s minimum has no left child, so that empty position can safely hold all the old-left values. No new tree nodes or value replacements are needed.
steps: Handle an empty tree or a matching root.
Follow comparisons until the matching child is found.
Replace that child using the zero/one/two-child helper.
Return the original root unless the root itself was deleted.
320.time: O(h), including the search and replacement path.
pitfalls: Always retain the returned root; deleting the root may promote another node.
Attach the old left subtree at the minimum of the promoted right subtree, not at an occupied child position.
An absent key must not change the tree.
Other valid solutions copy a successor’s value; this version instead reconnects whole subtrees.

321.problem: Find the kth smallest and kth largest values in a binary search tree. Ranks start at 1.
321.assumptions: The pinned LeetCode question asks only for kthSmallest; the sheet title and Striver article cover both ranks, so both methods are included. The tree has distinct values. Valid ranks satisfy 1 ≤ k ≤ n. This code rejects an invalid rank rather than returning a value that could be mistaken for an answer.

example.explanation: Counting from the small end gives 2, then 4. Counting from the large end gives 12, then 10.

321.baseline: Save the entire inorder traversal. The kth smallest value is at index k − 1; the kth largest is at index n − k. This takes O(n) time and O(n) stored values.
321.approach:
Inorder produces increasing values, so count visits until the kth value is reached. Reverse inorder—right, node, left—does the same from the largest end.

An explicit stack lets us pause each traversal. For the small end, push a left chain, pop its next smallest node, then continue from its right subtree. Reverse the directions for the large end. Return immediately on the kth pop.

Only the path and pending ancestors are stored. A single query takes O(h + k) time and O(h) space. These ordinary stack traversals do not modify the tree, so stopping early leaves no temporary links behind.
steps: Reject a nonpositive rank.
Push the outer chain: left for smallest, right for largest.
Pop one node and decrease the remaining rank; return its value at zero.
Continue from its opposite child, or reject k if traversal ends too soon.
321.time: O(h + k) per rank query; O(n) in the worst case. Asking for both ends keeps the same asymptotic bound.
pitfalls: Ranks are 1-based; list indices are 0-based.
Reset counters for every call if using recursion.
The smallest query goes left first; the largest goes right first.
Do not return early from a threaded Morris traversal without restoring every thread. This implementation uses an ordinary stack.

322.problem: Check whether a binary tree obeys strict BST ordering at every node.
322.assumptions: Every value in a node’s left subtree must be smaller, and every value in its right subtree must be larger. Equal values are invalid. Empty input is valid. Values can include Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE.

example.explanation: 10 is larger than its parent 4, but it still belongs to the left subtree of 8, where every value must be below 8.

322.baseline: Carry an allowed open interval down the tree. A left child inherits the lower bound and gets its parent as upper bound; a right child inherits the upper bound and gets its parent as lower bound. Use long bounds so all int values fit strictly inside the initial interval.
322.approach:
Inorder traversal of a strict BST must be strictly increasing. Visit the left subtree, compare the current value with the previously visited value, then continue right. Reject a value that is less than or equal to the previous one.

This catches distant ancestor violations too. In the example, inorder reads 4, 10, 8, 12, and the drop from 10 to 8 reveals the problem. Checking only direct parent-child pairs would miss it.

The explicit stack below performs inorder without recursive depth limits. previous is local to the call, so validating one tree cannot affect a later call. Both this method and the bounds method take O(n); neither is asymptotically faster.
steps: Push the current node’s left chain.
Pop the next inorder node.
Reject it if its value is not strictly greater than the previous value.
Remember it and continue from its right child.
pitfalls: The condition applies to entire subtrees, not only immediate children.
Strict ordering rejects duplicates.
Do not use Integer.MIN_VALUE as an exclusive initial lower bound: that would reject a valid node with that value.
Keep the previous node local or reset it between calls.

323.problem: Find the lowest common ancestor of two existing nodes in a binary search tree.
323.assumptions: The tree is a valid strict BST with distinct values, and both target nodes exist in it. A node counts as its own ancestor. The function returns an existing node reference and does not change the tree. The split rule alone does not verify that supplied targets exist.

example.input: root 8; children 4 and 12; 4 has children 2 and 6; targets 2 and 6
example.explanation: Both targets are below 8 on the left. At 4, one target is smaller and one is larger, so their paths split there.

323.baseline: Recursively descend left when both target values are smaller, or right when both are larger. The first node where neither condition holds is the answer. This needs O(h) recursive space.
323.approach:
If both targets are smaller than current, their lowest common ancestor must be in the left subtree. If both are larger, it must be in the right subtree. Continue in that one direction.

Otherwise, the two targets lie on different sides, or current is one of the targets. Return current. At a split, neither child subtree can contain both targets, so no lower common ancestor exists. If current is a target, it is already the lowest possible ancestor of itself and the other node.

BST ordering makes one path enough. For an ordinary binary tree, these value comparisons cannot tell us where a target lies.
steps: Start at the root.
Move left if both target values are smaller.
Move right if both target values are larger.
Otherwise return the current node.
323.time: O(h): O(log n) when balanced and O(n) for a chain.
pitfalls: Both targets must exist for the split-point conclusion to be valid.
The answer can equal one of the target nodes.
Do not use this shortcut on an ordinary unordered binary tree.
Use comparisons rather than multiplying signed differences, which can overflow.

324.problem: Construct a binary search tree from its preorder traversal.
324.assumptions: Values are distinct and the input is a valid BST preorder, as in the linked problem. The primary version additionally rejects duplicate or invalid preorder sequences. It returns newly allocated nodes and leaves the input unchanged. Empty input produces null.

example.output: root 8; left subtree 4 with children 2 and 6; right subtree 12 with left child 10
example.explanation: After building the subtree below 4, the next value 12 cannot fit below 8 on the left. Leave it unread until constructing 8’s right subtree.

324.baseline: Insert the values one by one into an empty BST. A valid preorder inserts each parent before its descendants and reproduces the original tree, but repeated searches can take O(n²) time.
324.approach:
Keep one cursor for the next unread preorder value and give each subtree an allowed open interval. If the next value is outside that interval, this subtree is empty: return null without advancing the cursor. The value may belong to a later subtree.

If the value fits, consume it as the root. Build the left subtree with a smaller upper bound, then the right subtree with a larger lower bound. The inherited opposite bounds preserve restrictions from all ancestors.

Every node is consumed once, so construction is linear. long bounds allow both int extremes. After the root is built, unread values mean the input was not a valid strict-BST preorder; reject it instead of returning only a prefix.
steps: Start a local cursor at 0 with long minimum and maximum bounds.
Return null without consuming a value if it is outside the current range.
Otherwise create the node and advance the cursor.
Build left then right with narrowed bounds; verify all input was consumed.
324.space: O(h) recursive stack plus O(n) returned nodes. A deeply skewed input can exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
pitfalls: Do not advance the cursor when a value fails the current subtree’s bounds.
Carry both ancestor bounds; comparing only with the direct parent can admit an invalid value.
Use strict inequalities for distinct-key BSTs.
The binary-search split alternative relies on valid preorder structure even though the array is not numerically sorted.

325.problem: Find the strict inorder predecessor and successor of a key in a binary search tree.
325.assumptions: The predecessor is the largest value strictly below the key; the successor is the smallest value strictly above it. Equality does not qualify. The key need not exist. Node-returning methods use null for absence, so negative values remain unambiguous. The TUF-style value wrapper returns [predecessor, successor], using −1 for missing values.

example.explanation: The key itself is excluded. Floor and ceiling would both be 6, but predecessor and successor use strict inequalities.

325.baseline: Save all node references in inorder. The last node below the key is the predecessor, and the first node above it is the successor. This costs O(n) time and storage.
325.approach:
For the predecessor, a smaller current value is a candidate. Remember it and move right to look for a larger value that is still below the key. If current is at least the key, move left.

For the successor, reverse those choices: a larger current value is a candidate, and moving left may find a smaller qualifying value. A value at most the key sends us right.

Run both searches from the root. They do not need to locate the key itself; they only maintain the closest qualifying candidates. Returning node references also gives access to the actual successor node when a node-based interface is required.
steps: Walk from the root for the predecessor, saving smaller candidates and trying right.
Restart from the root for the successor, saving larger candidates and trying left.
Keep equality out of both answers.
Return the candidate nodes, or null for a missing side.
pitfalls: A node is never its own strict predecessor or successor.
Do not stop at equality; its left/right subtrees may contain the answers.
The value wrapper’s −1 marker cannot distinguish absence from a real −1. Use the node methods when that distinction matters.
