326.problem: Implement a BST iterator that returns values in increasing order, then use two iterators to merge the values of two BSTs into one sorted list.
326.assumptions: The pinned row is titled “Merge 2 BST’s”, but its practice link is LeetCode’s BST Iterator. Both tasks are covered explicitly. mergeBsts returns sorted values; it does not construct or rebalance a new tree. Values shared by the two inputs are kept twice. Neither tree may be modified while its iterator is active.

example.input: first BST values {2, 6, 10}; second BST values {4, 6, 9}
example.explanation: Each iterator exposes its next smallest value. Choose the smaller one each time, keeping both copies of 6 because they came from different input nodes.

326.baseline: Precompute inorder values in a list. An iterator then advances a list index. For merging, build both sorted lists and merge them with two indices. This uses O(n + m) stored input values before producing the answer.
326.approach:
Pause inorder traversal with a stack. The constructor pushes the root’s left chain, placing the smallest node on top. next pops that node, then pushes the left chain of its right subtree. The stack top is again the next smallest pending node. hasNext only checks whether the stack is empty.

To merge, keep one current value from each iterator. Append the smaller value and advance only that iterator. If one ends, take the rest from the other. This is the same comparison used to merge two sorted arrays, but the values arrive as needed.

One next call can push a long chain, so its worst-case cost is O(h). Across a full traversal each node is pushed and popped once, giving amortized O(1) per next call.
steps: Initialize each iterator with its root’s left chain.
Pop the next node and prepare the left chain under its right child.
For merging, compare the two current values and advance the smaller side.
Drain whichever side remains after the other ends.
326.time: Iterator initialization O(h); next O(h) worst-case and O(1) amortized; hasNext O(1). Merging consumes O(n + m) total time.
326.space: O(h1 + h2) iterator stacks for merging, plus O(n + m) output. One iterator uses O(h).
pitfalls: hasNext must not consume a value.
After popping a node, prepare its right subtree’s left chain.
Keep equal values from different trees; merging is not deduplication.
Changing the tree during iteration invalidates the pending traversal.

reference.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
reference.approach: Pause inorder with a stack; merge two resulting sorted streams.
reference.adaptation: Both public iterator Java implementations were checked. The lazy version uses ArrayDeque and an explicit exhausted-iterator exception. The two-iterator merge is an authored extension to cover the preserved row title, while BSTIterator covers the actual linked exercise.

326.baselineTime: O(n) initialization and O(n) stored values for an eager iterator; O(n + m) time/storage for merging two saved lists.

327.problem: Decide whether two different nodes in a BST have values that add up to the target.
327.assumptions: The usual problem supplies a strict BST. A node cannot be used twice. The iterator implementation also accepts a BST whose inorder values are nondecreasing, so two distinct nodes with the same value may form a pair. Sums use long to avoid overflowing int.

example.explanation: 2 + 9 is 11. These values belong to different nodes. A single node with value 5 would not satisfy target 10.

327.baseline: Save inorder values in a sorted list, then use one index at each end. Move the lower index when the sum is too small and the upper index when it is too large. Stop when the indices meet.
327.approach:
Use two paused inorder traversals. One returns nodes from smallest to largest; the other returns them from largest to smallest. They act like the two indices in the sorted-list solution, without saving the full list.

If the sum is too small, keeping the smaller value cannot help: every remaining partner is no larger than the current largest value. Advance the ascending iterator. If the sum is too large, advance the descending iterator instead.

Stop when both iterators point to the same node. Comparing node identity prevents using a node twice, while still allowing two separate equal-valued nodes. Each iterator pushes and pops any node at most once.
steps: Prepare ascending and descending stacks.
Read one node from each end.
Compare their long sum with the target; advance only the necessary end.
Return false when the two node references meet.
327.space: O(h) for the two iterator stacks.
pitfalls: One node cannot form a pair with itself.
Cast before adding: (long) a + b. Casting an already overflowed int sum is too late.
The two-pointer argument requires sorted inorder values.
Do not modify the tree while the iterators are active.

reference.approach: Sorted inorder two pointers, then ascending and descending stack iterators.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. This adaptation returns nodes from the iterators and stops on node identity rather than comparing endpoint values. Sums use long; the source adds int values.

327.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(n) saved values, plus O(h) traversal stack.

328.problem: Repair a BST in which the values of exactly two nodes were swapped. Keep every node and child connection in place.
328.assumptions: Values were distinct before the swap. Only two values changed position; the shape is unchanged. Null and already valid trees are handled as no-ops. Inputs with more extensive corruption are outside this contract.

example.explanation: The drops 5 > 3 and 4 > 2 identify 5 and 2 as the swapped values. Exchange those two values without moving nodes.

328.baseline: Collect all values, sort them, then assign the sorted values during inorder traversal. This restores ordering but uses O(n) storage and O(n log n) sorting time. It does more work than needed when only two values are misplaced.
328.approach:
Inorder should be strictly increasing. Compare each visited node with the previous node. A decrease reveals an inversion. At the first inversion, remember the previous node as first and the current node as middle. At a second inversion, remember the current node as last.

If there are two inversions, exchange first and last. If there is only one, the swapped values were adjacent in inorder, so exchange first and middle.

The explicit traversal stack avoids recursive calls on a long chain. All tracking variables are local to the method, so repairing another tree cannot reuse stale nodes from an earlier call.
steps: Visit nodes in inorder with a stack.
Record first and middle at the first decrease.
Record last if another decrease appears.
Swap first with last, or with middle when there was only one decrease.
pitfalls: Adjacent swaps create one inversion; separated swaps create two.
Exchange values, not node references or child links.
Do not use a numeric sentinel for previous; Integer.MIN_VALUE can be a real value.
The article’s optimal prose describes this linear method, but its current optimal Java tab repeats the sorting solution. This implementation follows the prose.

reference.approach: Find one or two inorder inversions and swap the misplaced values.
reference.adaptation: The sorting Java and optimal prose were checked. The current optimal Java tab duplicates the sorting code, so the linear implementation here is authored from the stated inversion algorithm, with an explicit stack and local state.

329.problem: Find the number of nodes in the largest subtree that is a valid BST inside an arbitrary binary tree.
329.assumptions: A subtree includes its root and every descendant below that root. You cannot discard an inconvenient child. BST comparisons are strict, so duplicate values invalidate a containing subtree. An empty tree has answer 0.

example.input: root 10; left child 5 with children 1 and 8; right child 15 with right child 7
example.explanation: The subtree rooted at 5 is a BST of size 3. The subtree rooted at 15 is invalid because its right child is smaller. The whole tree is therefore invalid too.

329.baseline: Try each node as a subtree root. Check every descendant against inherited lower and upper bounds, then count the nodes of valid subtrees. Repeated checks can cost O(n²).
329.approach:
A parent needs only a small report from each child: the smallest value, the largest value, and a size. If both child subtrees are valid and left maximum < current value < right minimum, the whole subtree is a BST. Add the two sizes and one for the current node.

For an invalid subtree, return impossible bounds: minimum = Long.MIN_VALUE and maximum = Long.MAX_VALUE. These make an ancestor’s strict comparison fail. Its size field carries the best valid subtree found below it.

An empty child uses the opposite bounds: minimum = Long.MAX_VALUE and maximum = Long.MIN_VALUE. It imposes no restriction and contributes size zero. Long sentinels stay outside the full int value range, including its endpoints.
steps: Get reports for the left and right subtrees using postorder.
Check the strict ordering around the current value.
If valid, combine sizes and extend the minimum and maximum.
If invalid, return impossible bounds and the larger child answer.
329.space: O(h) live recursive stack and reports. A very deep tree may exceed Java’s call-stack limit.
pitfalls: A largest BST subtree is different from selecting an arbitrary subset of nodes.
Use strict comparisons; equality is not valid under this contract.
Empty and invalid reports use opposite sentinel bounds. Mixing them up accepts invalid trees.
The size field means whole-subtree size for a valid report and best descendant answer for an invalid report.

reference.approach: Postorder minimum/maximum/size reports with invalid sentinel bounds.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. The postorder report and long sentinels are retained; TreeNode.val replaces the article’s Node.data to match the other tree guides.

329.baselineTime: O(n²) worst-case upper bound; O(h) recursion space.

330.problem: Describe a graph using vertices and edges, and distinguish direction from edge weights.
330.assumptions: Vertices are numbered 0 through V−1. An undirected edge allows movement both ways; a directed edge allows only its stated direction. A weight is a separate property and can appear in either graph type. This example accepts valid vertex numbers.

example.output: directed: 0→1→2; undirected: both connections work both ways
example.explanation: The weights 7 and 4 might represent distances. They do not decide whether travel is one-way or two-way.

330.baseline: An edge list simply stores each connection as a pair, or a triple when a weight is present. To find every neighbor of one vertex, scanning the whole edge list takes O(E).
330.approach:
Think of vertices as places and edges as permitted moves. In a directed graph, storing 0 → 1 does not imply 1 → 0. In an undirected graph, store both directions so either endpoint can find the other.

An adjacency list keeps each vertex’s outgoing connections together. The Arc class stores the destination and weight. An isolated vertex still gets an empty list: it exists even though it has no edges.

A path follows a sequence of allowed edges. A cycle returns to its start. A connected undirected graph has a path between every pair; otherwise it has several components. Direction changes reachability, so undirected component logic should not be applied unchanged to directed graphs.
steps: Create one adjacency list for every vertex.
Store each directed edge at its starting vertex.
For an undirected graph, also store the reverse connection.
Keep the weight alongside the destination.
330.space: O(V + E); an undirected edge creates two stored arcs.
pitfalls: Direction and weight are independent choices.
An isolated vertex must not disappear from the representation.
For an undirected graph, the sum of degrees is 2E; a self-loop contributes two.
For a directed graph, list size is outdegree. Indegree counts arcs arriving from other lists.

reference.approach: Vertices, edges, direction, weights, adjacency, and degree.
reference.adaptation: The current public introduction was read. It has no Java solution. This is an authored Java example of its graph types; the pinned legacy introduction URL currently returns Page Not Found.

331.problem: Represent an undirected graph as an adjacency matrix and compare it with an adjacency list.
331.assumptions: The pinned row says C++, but this tracker guide uses Java as requested. Vertices are 0-based. The matrix records whether an edge exists; repeated edges do not create multiple true entries. Use edge counts instead if multiplicity matters.

example.explanation: Row 0 has true at column 2. Because the connection is undirected, row 2 also has true at column 0.

331.baseline: Keep the input edge list. Checking whether a particular pair is connected may require scanning all E edges. A matrix pays more storage to make this check immediate.
331.approach:
Allocate a V by V boolean array. matrix[u][v] tells us whether u and v share an edge. For each undirected edge, set both matrix[u][v] and matrix[v][u]. Java initializes every other entry to false.

This is convenient when the graph is dense or pair checks are frequent. It uses O(V²) storage even when there are few edges. Listing the neighbors of one vertex requires scanning its entire row.

An adjacency list instead stores only actual neighbors. It uses O(V + E) storage and visits only the existing edges during traversal. Neither representation is always best: choose based on the operations and graph size.
steps: Allocate a square boolean array.
Set both symmetric entries for each undirected edge.
Check an edge with matrix[u][v].
Use adjacency lists for sparse graphs when scanning neighbors is the main operation.
331.time: O(V² + E) to allocate and fill; O(1) per edge-existence check.
pitfalls: One-way edges need only matrix[u][v], not its symmetric entry.
A boolean matrix loses duplicate-edge counts and cannot store weights.
For weighted graphs, zero may be a real weight, so it is not always a safe no-edge marker.
Large sparse graphs can make a matrix prohibitively large.

reference.adaptation: The current graph introduction and public traversal contract were checked. Both legacy graph-representation article URLs currently return Page Not Found. This is an authored Java implementation, not a verified copy of their unavailable code.

332.problem: Build a Java adjacency list for an undirected graph and read the neighbors of each vertex.
332.assumptions: Vertices are 0-based and edge endpoints are valid. Each row of the returned list contains neighbors, not the vertex itself. Neighbor order follows edge insertion order. Repeated edges remain repeated entries; an undirected self-loop adds two entries.

example.explanation: Edge 0–2 adds 2 to list 0 and 0 to list 2. List 0 keeps 2 before 1 because those edges were inserted in that order.

332.baseline: A V by V boolean matrix also represents the graph. It gives constant-time pair checks, but uses O(V²) storage and scans V columns to list one vertex’s neighbors.
332.approach:
Create the outer list, then create a separate inner list for every vertex. Do this even for isolated vertices. For each input edge [u,v], append v to u’s list and u to v’s list.

The separate inner lists matter. Reusing the same ArrayList object for every vertex would make every vertex appear to share the same neighbors.

To traverse neighbors, use for (int next : graph.get(vertex)). This scans only that vertex’s stored connections. Over the whole undirected graph, the loops inspect 2E entries, so the total is O(E).
steps: Allocate V independent ArrayList objects.
Add each edge to both endpoint lists.
Keep insertion order unless a problem explicitly asks for sorted neighbors.
Read graph.get(v) to access v’s neighbors.
332.time: O(V + E) to build; O(degree(v)) to scan one vertex’s neighbors.
pitfalls: Creating only the outer list leaves no inner lists to append to.
Do not use one shared inner list for all vertices.
This guide uses 0-based vertices; a 1-based judge requires conversion or V + 1 lists.
If a judge wants each output row to start with the vertex label, prepend it only when formatting output.

reference.adaptation: The current graph introduction and public traversal contract were checked. Both legacy graph-representation article URLs currently return Page Not Found. This is an authored Java implementation, not a verified copy of their unavailable code.

333.problem: Count the connected components of an undirected graph, including isolated vertices.
333.assumptions: An edge list describes V vertices numbered 0 through V−1. Two vertices belong to the same component if a path connects them. The empty graph returns 0 as an extension. The method does not change the edges.

example.explanation: The groups are {0,1,2}, {3,4}, and {5}. The last vertex counts even though it has no edge.

333.baseline: For each unassigned vertex, repeatedly scan the whole edge list to discover more reachable vertices. This works, but repeated full scans waste time compared with storing neighbors once.
333.approach:
Start a traversal at the first unvisited vertex. It reaches exactly one connected component: every discovered vertex has a path from the start, and every vertex with such a path is eventually discovered. Mark all of them.

Continue scanning vertex labels. An already visited vertex belongs to a component we counted. An unvisited vertex starts a different component, so increment the count and traverse again.

The outer loop is essential. A traversal started only at 0 cannot count disconnected groups or isolated vertices elsewhere.
steps: Build both directions of every edge.
Scan all vertex labels.
For each unvisited label, add one to the count and mark its whole reachable group.
Return the number of traversal starts.
333.space: O(V + E) including adjacency lists; O(V) traversal state.
pitfalls: Count traversal starts, not individual visited vertices.
An isolated vertex is a component of size one.
Mark a vertex when adding it to the queue to avoid duplicate work.
This is undirected connectivity; strongly connected directed components are a different problem.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=0;i<n-1;i++)e[i]=new int[]{i,i+1};assert countComponents(n,e)==1;

reference.title: Connected Components
reference.approach: Start a traversal from every still-unvisited vertex.
reference.adaptation: The public edge-list statement was checked. Its solution is not public without sign-in; this Java follows the connected-component traversal also verified in the public province article.

334.problem: Return the breadth-first traversal of a graph, starting at vertex 0.
334.assumptions: The source guarantees a connected undirected graph. This method also handles disconnected inputs by returning only the component reachable from 0. It preserves edge insertion order within adjacency lists; other neighbor orders can produce different valid BFS sequences.

example.explanation: Visit 0, then its neighbors 2 and 1, then the next layer 3 and 4. A queue makes the earlier discoveries leave first.

334.baseline: With an adjacency matrix, the same queue traversal must scan all V possible neighbors for each processed vertex, costing O(V²). Adjacency lists avoid scanning missing edges.
334.approach:
BFS explores in layers. Put vertex 0 into a queue. Remove its front vertex, record it, and add any unvisited neighbors at the back. Mark a neighbor as visited immediately when it enters the queue.

All vertices one edge from 0 are discovered before vertices two edges away are processed. This is why BFS can find shortest paths by edge count in an unweighted graph. Within one layer, the exact order depends on the neighbor lists.

The visited array stops cycles from sending us around forever and prevents two parents from queuing the same vertex twice.
steps: Mark 0 and enqueue it.
Remove the front vertex and append it to the traversal.
Mark and enqueue each new neighbor.
Repeat until the queue is empty.
334.time: O(V + E), including building adjacency lists.
334.space: O(V + E) including the graph; O(V) queue, visited array, and output.
pitfalls: Using a stack changes the traversal to depth-first behavior.
Do not delay marking until removal from the queue.
BFS minimizes edge count, not arbitrary weighted cost.
Do not claim one unique traversal without specifying neighbor order.

reference.title: Traversal Techniques
reference.approach: BFS uses a queue; DFS finishes one branch before trying another.
reference.adaptation: The public problem and edge-list input were checked. No public Java editorial was available. Its first example uses a neighbor order different from the listed edge insertion order; these implementations consistently preserve insertion order and show matching examples.

335.problem: Return the depth-first traversal of a graph, starting at vertex 0.
335.assumptions: The source supplies a connected undirected graph. Neighbor order follows edge insertion order. On a disconnected input, the method visits only 0’s component. The explicit stack simulates recursive DFS without using Java’s call stack.

example.explanation: After reaching 2, finish its branch through 3 before returning to 0 and exploring 1 and 4.

335.baseline: Recursive DFS marks and records the current vertex, then recursively visits each unvisited neighbor. It is concise, but a long chain can exhaust Java’s call stack.
335.approach:
DFS pauses a vertex while it explores one of its neighbors. A stack frame therefore needs both the vertex and the index of the next neighbor to inspect.

Look at the top frame. If all its neighbors are finished, remove it and resume the parent. Otherwise advance its neighbor index. When that neighbor is unvisited, mark it, record it, and push a new frame.

This reproduces recursive DFS exactly for the same neighbor order. Simply pushing all neighbors and marking them immediately can choose a different DFS tree, so this version makes the paused work explicit.
steps: Mark and record 0; push its frame with next-neighbor index zero.
Inspect the next neighbor in the top frame.
Push an unvisited neighbor and explore it before resuming the parent.
Pop frames whose neighbor lists are exhausted.
335.space: O(V + E) including adjacency lists; O(V) explicit stack and other traversal state.
pitfalls: Mark a vertex before exploring its neighbors so cycles terminate.
DFS order depends on neighbor order.
A DFS path is not necessarily a shortest path.
An outer loop over unvisited starts is needed to visit every disconnected component.

reference.approach: BFS uses a queue; DFS finishes one branch before trying another.
reference.adaptation: The public problem and edge-list input were checked. No public Java editorial was available. Its first example uses a neighbor order different from the listed edge insertion order; these implementations consistently preserve insertion order and show matching examples.

335.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and graph storage; O(V) recursive stack in the worst case.

336.problem: Count provinces: groups of cities connected directly or through other cities.
336.assumptions: The input is a symmetric N by N adjacency matrix with ones on its diagonal. Matrix indices are cities, not spatial grid coordinates. A 1 at [u][v] means a road-like connection between city u and city v.

example.explanation: Cities 0 and 2 form one province. Cities 1 and 3 each form their own. Their positions in the matrix do not need to touch.

336.baseline: Recursive DFS from each unvisited city marks its province by scanning matrix rows. This already takes optimal O(N²) time for inspecting a general adjacency matrix, but may build a deep call stack.
336.approach:
Treat one city as a starting point. Scan its row to find directly connected cities, then scan those cities’ rows to find indirect connections. A queue keeps this search iterative.

When the queue empties, the whole province has been marked. Continue through the city labels. Each still-unvisited city begins another province.

There are N rows of N entries. Even if very few connections exist, every processed row is scanned, so time is O(N²), not O(N + E) for this representation. The input already stores the graph; no extra adjacency list is required.
steps: Keep one visited flag per city.
Start a BFS at each unvisited city and increment the province count.
Scan a city’s matrix row for unvisited connected cities.
Return the count after all city labels have been considered.
336.space: O(N) extra space; the input matrix is not copied.
pitfalls: Do not use four-direction grid movement; rows and columns are city labels.
A symmetric matrix represents undirected connections.
The diagonal ones should not cause repeat visits.
Count isolated cities as provinces.

reference.title: Number of Provinces: Count Connected Components
reference.approach: Scan adjacency-matrix rows with DFS or BFS; DSU is another option.
reference.adaptation: All three public Java approaches were checked. The main BFS and recursive alternative retain the article’s row-scan method. ArrayDeque and boolean visited flags replace LinkedList and integer flags.

336.baselineTime: O(N²) time and O(N) recursive/visited space.

337.problem: Count graph components when connections are given in a matrix, and convert the linked edge-list variant when needed.
337.assumptions: The pinned title says “Problem in Matrix”, but its link is an edge-list Connected Components task. Both interfaces are included. Here matrix[u][v] describes a connection between vertices u and v; this is not an island grid whose adjacent cells are connected.

example.input: 4 vertices; edges [[0,3], [1,2]]; or the equivalent symmetric adjacency matrix
example.explanation: The groups are {0,3} and {1,2}. A matrix cell’s physical neighbors have no role in this graph.

337.baseline: Convert the matrix into adjacency lists and run a component traversal. This works but adds storage; scanning the existing matrix directly is simpler when it is already the input.
337.approach:
The component-counting idea stays the same across representations: find an unvisited vertex, count one new group, then visit everything reachable from it. Only the way we find neighbors changes.

For the matrix form, scan the current vertex’s row. For the linked edge-list form, first build adjacency lists and scan only stored neighbors. The code includes findCircleNum for a symmetric matrix and countComponents for the linked edge-list contract.

Do not reinterpret this row as counting islands in a picture. An island grid uses cells as vertices and defines movement by directions; an adjacency matrix uses row and column numbers as vertex labels.
steps: Choose the interface that matches the actual input.
For a matrix, scan complete rows; for edges, build neighbor lists.
Start one traversal per unvisited vertex.
Include vertices with no outgoing connections.
337.time: O(V²) for a matrix; O(V + E) for an edge list.
337.space: O(V) extra for matrix BFS; O(V + E) including adjacency lists for edge input.
pitfalls: The pinned title and linked task use different input representations.
An adjacency matrix is not a four-direction land/water grid.
Do not forget isolated vertices when building from edges.
These methods assume undirected connections.

reference.title: Connected Components
reference.approach: Count traversal starts, using the neighbor representation supplied by the problem.
reference.adaptation: The linked public task takes an edge list despite the pinned matrix title. Both contracts are covered; the matrix method was checked against the public Number of Provinces Java article.

338.problem: Find how many minutes it takes for every fresh orange to become rotten, or return −1 if some can never be reached.
338.assumptions: 0 is empty, 1 is fresh, and 2 is rotten. Rot spreads up, down, left, and right. All initially rotten oranges start together. This implementation changes reachable fresh cells to 2 in the input grid. An empty grid returns 0.

example.explanation: At minute 1, rot reaches the second and fourth cells from opposite ends. At minute 2, it reaches the middle. Starting from only one end would give the wrong time.

338.baseline: Scan the whole grid once per minute. Mark newly affected cells with temporary value 3 so they cannot spread during the same minute, then turn all 3s into 2s. If a round changes nothing while fresh cells remain, return −1.
338.approach:
Put every initially rotten orange into one queue and count the fresh oranges. The initial queue is minute 0. Process exactly the queue’s current size for one minute; newly rotten cells are added behind that layer and spread in the next round.

Mark a fresh neighbor as rotten before adding it. Two nearby rotten cells may both reach it, but it should enter the queue and reduce the fresh count only once.

Stop as soon as the fresh count reaches zero. If the queue empties first, a fresh cell is separated from every source by empty cells, so the answer is −1.
steps: Collect all rotten sources and count fresh cells.
Process one fixed queue layer per minute.
Change fresh neighbors to rotten as they enter the queue.
Return elapsed minutes if none remain fresh; otherwise return −1.
338.space: O(R × C) queue space in the worst case.
pitfalls: Newly rotten oranges must wait until the next minute to spread.
Start from every rotten source simultaneously.
No fresh oranges means zero minutes, even if there are no rotten oranges either.
Empty cells block the spread; diagonal contact does not help.
tests: assert orangesRotting(new int[][]{{2,1,1,1,2}})==2;assert orangesRotting(new int[][]{{2,0,1}})==-1;assert orangesRotting(new int[][]{{0,2}})==0;assert orangesRotting(new int[0][])==0;

reference.title: Rotting Oranges: Minimum Time to Rot All Oranges
reference.approach: Minute-by-minute simulation, then multi-source BFS layers.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The same marking and layer logic is used with ArrayDeque and an explicit empty-grid guard.

338.baselineTime: O((R × C)²) worst-case time and O(1) extra space.

339.problem: Recolor the connected region containing a chosen starting pixel.
339.assumptions: The image is a nonempty rectangular matrix and the starting coordinate is valid. Only cells with the starting cell’s original color qualify, using four-direction movement. The returned matrix is the same input object, modified in place.

example.explanation: The lower-right 4 is disconnected from the start. Matching color alone is not enough; there must be a path through cells of that color.

339.baseline: Recursive DFS recolors the current cell, then calls itself on its four neighbors. It visits the same region as BFS, but can overflow Java’s call stack on a large region.
339.approach:
Save the starting color before changing any cell. If the new color is identical, return immediately: recoloring would not mark cells as visited.

Otherwise recolor the start and add it to a queue. For each removed cell, inspect its four neighbors. Recolor and enqueue any in-bounds neighbor that still has the old color.

Recoloring serves two purposes: it produces the answer and marks the cell as processed. We need no separate visited matrix, because an already recolored cell no longer matches the old color.
steps: Remember the old color and return early if it equals the new one.
Recolor the starting cell before enqueuing it.
Expand only through four-direction neighbors still holding the old color.
Return the same modified image.
339.time: O(K) for K cells in the starting region, at most O(R × C); O(1) if colors match.
pitfalls: Changing every matching color in the image would also change disconnected regions.
Check oldColor == newColor before traversal.
Diagonal cells do not connect in this problem.
Copy the image first if the caller needs to preserve the original.

reference.title: Flood Fill Algorithm
reference.approach: Recolor-before-expanding with recursive DFS or a BFS queue.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. The same old-color guard and four-direction logic are retained; ArrayDeque replaces LinkedList.

339.baselineTime: O(K) time and up to O(K) recursive stack, where K is the region size.

340.problem: Detect whether any component of an undirected graph contains a cycle, using BFS.
340.assumptions: The input is an undirected adjacency list: every edge appears at both endpoints. The practice statement excludes self-edges. The explanation assumes a simple graph. Empty graphs and isolated vertices have no cycle.

example.explanation: Vertices 0, 1, and 2 form a triangle. Vertex 3 is isolated, but that does not remove the cycle elsewhere.

340.baseline: DFS can detect the same condition by remembering the parent in each recursive call. It has the same O(V + E) time; BFS uses an explicit queue instead of a recursive stack.
340.approach:
Every undirected edge is stored twice. After moving from 0 to 1, seeing 0 in 1’s neighbor list is normal: it is the reverse of the edge we just used. This alone is not a cycle.

Store each queued vertex together with the parent that discovered it. An unvisited neighbor becomes a new queue entry. A visited neighbor different from the parent gives another route to an already reached vertex, so a cycle exists.

Restart BFS at each unvisited vertex. A cycle can sit in a component that vertex 0 cannot reach.
steps: Start a queue for each unvisited component.
Store pairs of vertex and discovery parent.
Mark new neighbors when they enter the queue.
Return true for a visited neighbor other than the parent; otherwise finish all components and return false.
340.space: O(V) extra beyond the input adjacency lists.
pitfalls: A visited parent is not evidence of a cycle.
Mark on insertion so multiple parents cannot queue the same vertex.
Checking only the component of 0 misses disconnected cycles.
This parent rule is for undirected graphs. Directed cycle detection needs an active-path or indegree rule.

reference.title: Detect a Cycle in an Undirected Graph
reference.approach: Track each traversal parent and detect an already visited non-parent neighbor.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches and the adjacency-list practice contract were checked. The same parent rule and outer component loop are retained with List interfaces and ArrayDeque.

340.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) recursive/visited space.

341.problem: Detect an undirected cycle using depth-first search and parent tracking.
341.assumptions: The adjacency list stores both directions of every edge. The graph may be disconnected. The practice excludes self-edges; the explanation uses a simple graph. Recursive depth can reach V on a chain.

example.explanation: DFS follows 0 → 1 → 2. At 2, neighbor 0 is already visited and is not its parent 1, revealing the cycle.

341.baseline: BFS carries a parent alongside each queued vertex and applies the same visited-non-parent check. It avoids recursive call depth and has the same time complexity.
341.approach:
Mark the current vertex before following any edge. For an unvisited neighbor, recursively explore it with the current vertex as its parent. If that recursive call finds a cycle, return true immediately.

For a visited neighbor, ignore the immediate parent. Any other visited neighbor completes an alternate path and confirms a cycle. The parent exception prevents counting a single undirected edge twice as a cycle.

Use one visited array across all starts. Start a new DFS only at an unvisited vertex so every component is checked once.
steps: Mark a vertex as soon as DFS enters it.
Recurse into unvisited neighbors while passing the current vertex as parent.
Reject only the normal reverse edge to the parent.
Propagate true immediately and repeat across components if no cycle was found.
341.space: O(V) visited array and recursive stack.
pitfalls: Forgetting to return a true result from a child loses detected cycles.
The root has no parent; use −1 with 0-based vertex labels.
Recursive DFS can overflow on a long chain; use the BFS alternative for such inputs.
A directed graph requires a different cycle test.

reference.title: Detect a Cycle in an Undirected Graph
reference.approach: Track each traversal parent and detect an already visited non-parent neighbor.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches and the adjacency-list practice contract were checked. The same parent rule and outer component loop are retained with List interfaces and ArrayDeque.

341.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) queue/visited space.

342.problem: For every cell in a binary matrix, find its four-direction distance to the nearest zero.
342.assumptions: This is the tracker’s linked LeetCode 01 Matrix contract, which guarantees at least one zero. Striver’s current article instead asks for the nearest one. The code includes both wrappers over the same BFS. All cells are traversable; zeros and ones are not obstacles. With no matching source, the extension returns −1 for every cell.

example.explanation: The zero at the upper right is distance 0. Each horizontal or vertical move adds one; diagonal moves are not allowed.

342.baseline: Collect the source cells. For each cell, compare its Manhattan distance with every source and keep the smallest. This works because the grid has no blocked cells, but can require O((R × C)²) comparisons.
342.approach:
Start from the answers we already know: every zero has distance 0. Put all of them into the queue together. Set other distances to −1, meaning unvisited.

When a cell with distance d is removed, give each unvisited neighbor distance d + 1 and enqueue it. BFS expands all distance-0 sources before distance-1 cells, then distance-2 cells, and so on. The first arrival at a cell is therefore its nearest-source distance.

For Striver’s nearest-one variant, change only which value is placed in the initial queue. The direction rules and BFS loop are identical.
steps: Initialize all distances to −1.
Set each target-valued cell to distance 0 and enqueue it.
Assign current distance + 1 to each unvisited orthogonal neighbor.
Use target 0 for updateMatrix and target 1 for nearestOne.
342.space: O(R × C) for the result and queue. The input is unchanged.
pitfalls: The pinned problem asks for zeros, while the current Striver article asks for ones.
Both cell values are traversable; neither acts as a wall.
Running a separate BFS from each cell repeats work.
Assign the distance before enqueuing to avoid repeated entries.
tests: assert Arrays.deepEquals(updateMatrix(new int[][]{{1,1,0},{1,1,1}}),new int[][]{{2,1,0},{3,2,1}});assert updateMatrix(new int[0][]).length==0;

reference.title: Distance of the Nearest Cell Having 1 in a Binary Matrix
reference.approach: Compare Manhattan distances, then expand a multi-source BFS.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The pinned LeetCode statement was also checked: it targets zero, unlike this article’s one. Two explicit wrappers preserve both contracts. The baseline returns −1 when no source exists, matching BFS instead of the source baseline’s rows + cols sentinel.

342.baselineTime: O(R × C × K) for K source cells, at most O((R × C)²); O(R × C) storage.

343.problem: Change every enclosed region of O cells into X, while preserving all regions connected to a board edge.
343.assumptions: The rectangular board contains only X and O. Connections use up, down, left, and right. A region is safe if any of its cells can reach a boundary O through other O cells. Modify the board in place.

example.explanation: The middle pair of O cells has no path to an edge and is captured. The O on the right edge stays O. Diagonal contact between them does not connect the regions.

343.baseline: Start recursive DFS from every boundary O, marking its whole region with #. Then capture unmarked O cells and restore # to O. This is already O(R × C), but its recursion may be deep.
343.approach:
It is easier to identify the cells that must survive. Every boundary O is safe. Every O connected to one of those cells is safe too. Start a queue from all boundary O cells and temporarily mark each safe cell with # before enqueuing it.

After this search, any O still on the board has no path to an edge. Change those cells to X. Restore the temporary # markers to O.

Marking before insertion also handles corners and one-row boards: the same cell may be encountered while scanning two borders, but it only enters the queue once.
steps: Mark and enqueue boundary O cells from all four borders.
Expand through orthogonally adjacent O cells, marking each with #.
Turn remaining O cells into X.
Restore every # to O.
pitfalls: An interior O can still be safe through a long path to the border.
Do not count diagonal contact as a connection.
Restore temporary markers before returning.
The source’s BFS section currently displays DFS Java; the queue implementation here follows its BFS prose.

reference.title: Surrounded Regions: Replace Enclosed O Cells with X
reference.approach: Mark boundary-connected cells, capture the rest, then restore safe cells.
reference.adaptation: The public DFS Java and BFS prose were checked. The BFS section’s Java currently repeats the DFS implementation. The main queue version is authored from the described BFS, while the recursive alternative follows the checked DFS code.

343.baselineTime: O(R × C) time and up to O(R × C) recursive stack.

344.problem: Count land cells that cannot reach the edge of the grid through other land cells.
344.assumptions: 1 is land and 0 is water. Movement is four-directional. Count individual trapped cells, not the number of islands. The implementation removes boundary-connected land by changing it to 0; enclosed land remains 1.

example.explanation: The three connected inner land cells cannot escape. The bottom-right land cell touches the border and is excluded. The answer counts three cells, although they form only one island.

344.baseline: Recursive DFS from boundary land removes all land that can escape. Count the remaining ones. This has the same time complexity as BFS but may need a deep recursive stack.
344.approach:
Walking from land to the boundary is equivalent to walking from boundary land back to it, because every permitted move works both ways. Start from every land cell on the four edges.

Change each discovered land cell to water before adding it to the queue. This marks it as processed and removes it from the eventual count. Continue through its land neighbors until no boundary-connected land remains.

Now every remaining 1 is trapped. Add those cells, not their connected groups, to get the answer.
steps: Enqueue all boundary land, changing it to 0 immediately.
Remove every land cell reachable from those sources.
Scan the grid after the queue empties.
Count the remaining ones.
pitfalls: The answer counts trapped cells, not trapped components.
A land cell need not itself touch the border to escape.
Corners can appear in two border scans; mark before enqueuing.
The input is changed. Copy it first if you need the original grid later.

reference.title: Number of Enclaves: Count Land Cells Trapped in a Grid
reference.approach: Remove boundary-connected land with DFS or multi-source BFS, then count remaining cells.
reference.adaptation: The public DFS and BFS Java methods were checked. The same destructive marking and border traversal are retained, with a shared enqueue helper and empty-grid handling.

344.baselineTime: O(R × C) time and up to O(R × C) recursive stack.

345.problem: Find the length of the shortest word sequence from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time.
345.assumptions: Words contain lowercase English letters and have equal length. Every word after beginWord must appear in the dictionary, including endWord. The answer counts words, not changes. The source uses distinct endpoints; this implementation returns 1 when they are equal as an explicit extension.

example.explanation: One shortest sequence is cat → cot → cog → dog. It makes three changes but contains four words.

345.baseline: Explicitly connect every pair of words that differs at one position, then run BFS. Pairwise comparisons cost O(N²L) before traversal. This is useful as a simple reference implementation, but we can generate neighbors without building all edges.
345.approach:
A word is a graph vertex. Changing one character to make another dictionary word is an edge of cost one. BFS therefore finds the fewest changes. Start the sequence length at 1 because beginWord is already one word.

For each removed word, try all letters a through z at each position. Look up each candidate in a set of unused dictionary words. Remove a candidate as soon as it is discovered and add it to the queue. Its first discovery already has the shortest distance, so later visits cannot improve the answer.

Restore the original character before moving to the next position. Otherwise later candidates could accidentally differ in two positions.
steps: Return 0 if the target is absent; handle equal endpoints separately.
Enqueue the beginning word at sequence length 1.
Generate one-letter candidates and remove discovered dictionary words immediately.
Return the current length when the target is removed from the queue.
345.time: O(26 × N × L²): each of N words tries 26L candidates, with O(L) string construction and hashing.
345.space: O(NL) stored word content, plus queue/set references.
pitfalls: The target must be in the dictionary, but the starting word need not be.
Count words: one direct change has answer 2.
Restore the changed character between positions.
Immediate removal works for shortest length; it needs adjustment when collecting every shortest sequence.

reference.title: Word Ladder I: Shortest Transformation Length
reference.approach: Generate one-character neighbors and run BFS with immediate dictionary removal.
reference.adaptation: The public Java solution was checked. This version uses fixed queue layers instead of parallel word/level queues, skips unchanged characters, and explicitly handles equal endpoints outside the source’s distinct-word contract. The pairwise-graph baseline is an authored comparison.

345.baselineTime: O(N²L) pair comparisons plus O(N + E) BFS; O(NL + E) space.

346.problem: Return every shortest valid word-transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord.
346.assumptions: Words have equal length and contain lowercase letters. Every word after the beginning must be in the dictionary, including the target. Return an empty list when unreachable. Sequence order is unrestricted. Equal endpoints return [[beginWord]] as an extension.

example.explanation: All three sequences have four words. The word dot can be reached through cot or dat at the same level; keeping only one parent would lose a valid answer.

346.baseline: Keep whole partial sequences in a BFS queue. Allow a word to be reached again at the same shortest depth, but reject longer revisits. This works, yet copies the same prefixes repeatedly and can consume much more memory than saving parent links.
346.approach:
First use BFS to find the shortest routes, saving parent links instead of full paths. Before expanding a level, remove all words in that level from the unused dictionary. Keep newly discovered next-level words available until the current level finishes. This lets two current words both become parents of the same child.

When the target is found, finish the entire current level. Stopping inside the loop would miss other equally short ways to reach it. Do not expand a further level.

Then backtrack from the target through its saved parents. Reaching the beginning completes one sequence; copy and reverse it before saving. Each parent link moves back one BFS level, so this reconstruction cannot cycle.
steps: Keep sets for the current and next BFS levels.
Remove current-level words together before generating neighbors.
Record every parent reaching a next-level word, including the target.
After the target’s first level is complete, backtrack through the parent map to build all answers.
346.time: O(26NL² + P) with Java string references in output, where P counts all word occurrences across returned paths. Writing the word characters takes O(PL).
346.space: O(NL + M + P), allowing stored strings, M parent references, and output references; generated string keys can add content storage. Output may be exponential.
pitfalls: Removing a newly found word immediately can lose other shortest parents.
Finish the current level after finding the target.
Copy each finished path before saving; the working path is reused during backtracking.
Returning all shortest paths can require exponential output even though BFS itself is efficient.

reference.title: Word Ladder II: Find All Shortest Transformation Sequences
reference.approach: BFS levels retain all shortest parents; reverse backtracking builds each sequence.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Java method was checked. Level-delayed removal and full-level completion are retained. The whole-path BFS is an authored comparison, and equal endpoints are handled explicitly.

346.baselineTime: For Q queued partial paths of length at most D, O(Q × (NL + ND)) upper-bound work and O(QD + NL) storage. Q can be exponential.

347.problem: Count different island shapes, treating shifted copies as the same shape.
347.assumptions: Land is 1, water is 0, and islands use four-direction connectivity. The current Striver problem permits translation only: rotations and reflections remain different. The pinned link points to the Premium “II” variant; a separate rotation/reflection method is included below. Both methods consume the grid by changing visited land to 0.

example.explanation: Shifting A cannot make it match B, but rotating it can. Choose the equality rule before choosing the signature.

347.baseline: Recursive DFS records each cell’s row and column offsets from the island’s first cell. A fixed neighbor order gives matching signatures to translated copies. This is O(R × C), but recursion can be deep.
347.approach:
An island’s absolute position does not describe its shape. Subtract the first cell’s coordinates from every visited cell. Two islands that differ only by a shift now have the same relative coordinates.

Use row-major scanning to choose the first cell, then BFS with a fixed neighbor order. Translated copies visit matching offsets in the same order. Join the coordinate pairs with separators and put that signature in a set. The set size is the number of different shapes.

If rotations and reflections should also match, one signature is not enough. Create all eight orientations, normalize and sort each one, and choose the smallest resulting signature as a common representative. That is a separate, more expensive equality rule, not a change to Striver’s translation-only answer.
steps: Scan for each unvisited land cell.
Collect its island with BFS in a fixed direction order.
Subtract the starting coordinates and serialize the ordered offset pairs.
Store signatures in a set and return its size.
347.time: O(R × C) expected time with fixed-width coordinates and hash sets.
347.space: O(R × C) for collected cells, queue, and signatures.
pitfalls: Same area does not mean same shape.
Use separators between coordinates to avoid ambiguous concatenation.
Traversal-order signatures require the same neighbor order and starting-cell rule.
Do not merge rotated shapes in the translation-only problem.
Copy the grid before comparing two methods, because each consumes its land.

reference.title: Number of Distinct Islands: Count Unique Island Shapes
reference.approach: Fixed-order relative-coordinate signatures for translation-only equality.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. The main method keeps the article’s translation-only BFS rule and delimiters. The pinned Premium II editorial was not accessible. The separately labelled eight-orientation extension is authored and tested, not claimed as source Java.

347.baselineTime: O(R × C) expected time and O(R × C) worst-case stack/signature space.

better.explanation: Different contract: also identify rotations and reflections. For every island, consider (±row, ±col) and (±col, ±row), giving eight orientations. Subtract each orientation’s minimum row and column, sort its coordinates, and encode it. Pick the lexicographically smallest encoding. Equivalent islands have the same set of normalized orientations, so they select the same key. This is an extension, not an optimization of translation-only counting.
better.time: O(RC + Σ k log k) over island sizes k; eight orientations are a constant factor.
better.space: O(R × C) including stored signatures and temporary coordinates.

348.problem: Decide whether every vertex can be assigned one of two colors so that the endpoints of every edge have different colors.
348.assumptions: The pinned LeetCode problem supplies an undirected adjacency array, graph[u] = neighbors of u. The current TUF practice instead takes an edge list; a wrapper handles that input too. Disconnected graphs must be checked component by component.

example.explanation: Color 0 and 2 blue, and 1 and 3 orange. Every edge crosses between colors. Adding edge 0–2 creates a triangle and makes such coloring impossible.

348.baseline: BFS can assign opposite colors when discovering neighbors. It has the same linear time as DFS and avoids recursive stack depth. Trying every one of 2^V color assignments is a much slower way to check the definition.
348.approach:
Start an uncolored component with color 0. Every neighbor must have color 1. From a color-1 vertex, every neighbor must have color 0, and so on.

If a neighbor is uncolored, give it the opposite color and continue DFS. If it already has the same color as the current vertex, the constraints conflict, so return false.

An odd cycle forces its final edge to join equal colors. An even cycle can alternate colors all the way around. The method does not need to find or count cycles explicitly; the color conflict detects the problem.
steps: Initialize colors to −1 for uncolored vertices.
Start DFS with color 0 at every uncolored component.
Assign each new neighbor the opposite color.
Return false for an edge joining equal colors.
348.space: O(V) traversal space; the edge-list wrapper also builds O(V + E) adjacency storage.
pitfalls: A disconnected odd cycle still makes the graph non-bipartite.
Do not require both color groups to be nonempty; isolated vertices are allowed.
An undirected cycle is not automatically a failure: even cycles are bipartite.
Recursive DFS may overflow on a long chain; the queue alternative avoids that.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]a=new int[n][];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=i==0?new int[]{1}:i==n-1?new int[]{n-2}:new int[]{i-1,i+1};assert bipartiteBfs(a);

reference.title: Bipartite graph
reference.approach: Two-color each component and reject equal-color edge endpoints.
reference.adaptation: The public TUF edge-list statement and the pinned LeetCode adjacency-array contract were checked. No public TUF Java editorial was available. These authored DFS and BFS implementations use the stated two-coloring rule, with an explicit input wrapper.

348.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) queue/color space.

349.problem: Detect a directed cycle by tracking which vertices are still on the active DFS path.
349.assumptions: Edges are directed, and the graph may be disconnected. Seeing a previously finished vertex is allowed. The pinned row links to Course Schedule II, which needs an order rather than a boolean; a findOrder wrapper is included for that linked task.

example.explanation: Vertex 2 can be reached from two places, but there is no route back. Adding 2→0 would create a cycle.

349.baseline: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes vertices of indegree zero. If it cannot process all vertices, a cycle exists. It has the same linear time and avoids recursion.
349.approach:
Keep two facts separate. visited means a vertex has been reached at some point. active means its DFS call has started but has not finished.

An edge to an active vertex closes a directed path back to an ancestor, so it proves a cycle. An edge to a finished vertex does not: that vertex’s outgoing paths were already checked without finding a cycle.

Clear active when leaving a vertex normally. Start DFS from every still-unvisited vertex. For the linked ordering task, record vertices on completion and reverse that list, returning no order if a cycle is found.
steps: Set both visited and active when entering a vertex.
Explore unvisited outgoing neighbors.
Report a cycle when an outgoing neighbor is active.
Clear active on completion; check all components.
349.space: O(V) extra for cycle detection; O(V + E) including course-graph construction.
pitfalls: Visited alone is insufficient: a DAG can have paths that merge.
Do not apply the undirected parent exception to directed edges.
A self-loop is a directed cycle.
The pinned course link returns an ordering; use findOrder rather than the boolean helper.

reference.title: Detect a Cycle in a Directed Graph
reference.approach: Separate visited and active-path state; Kahn’s processed count is an iterative alternative.
reference.adaptation: Both public cycle-detection Java methods were checked. The linked Course Schedule II Java was also checked to supply its prerequisite-direction and ordering wrapper. Boolean flags replace integer visited arrays.

349.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space; a returned order shorter than V means a cycle.

350.problem: Return any topological ordering: each directed edge u→v must place u before v.
350.assumptions: The linked practice guarantees a DAG and supplies adjacency lists. This implementation additionally returns an empty array for cyclic inputs. Several orders may be valid; the answer need not match an example exactly. Empty graphs return an empty valid order.

example.explanation: Both 0 and 1 must precede 2, and 2 must precede 3. There is no edge deciding whether 0 or 1 comes first.

350.baseline: Kahn’s algorithm chooses vertices with no remaining incoming edges. It also gives a valid order in O(V + E). The DFS method below instead records vertices after their outgoing work is finished.
350.approach:
In DFS, finish every outgoing neighbor before recording the current vertex. For an edge u→v, v will therefore be recorded before u. Reversing the finished list puts u before v, as required.

Use states 0 = unseen, 1 = active, and 2 = finished. Reaching state 1 reveals a cycle, so no ordering is possible. State 2 can be reused safely because that vertex’s outgoing paths are already finished.

Run DFS from every unseen vertex to include disconnected components and isolated vertices. Reverse the complete postorder only after all DFS calls succeed.
steps: Track unseen, active, and finished vertices.
Explore each outgoing neighbor before appending the current vertex.
Reject an edge to an active vertex.
Reverse the finished list after all components are explored.
350.space: O(V) state, recursive stack, and output.
pitfalls: Appending on entry gives DFS discovery order, which is not generally topological.
Reverse the finish order exactly once.
Do not return a partial order after detecting a cycle.
A long dependency chain can exhaust the recursive stack; use Kahn’s queue alternative.

reference.title: Topological sort or Kahn's algorithm
reference.approach: DFS reverse finishing order, with active-path detection for invalid cyclic input.
reference.adaptation: The public DAG practice contract was checked. Its Java editorial is not public. The reverse-postorder Java algorithm was checked in the public Course Schedule II article and adapted to a supplied adjacency list.

350.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) queue/indegree/output space.

351.problem: Build a topological order with Kahn’s algorithm by repeatedly choosing vertices with no remaining prerequisites.
351.assumptions: The input is a directed adjacency list. The source practice guarantees a DAG, but this code returns an empty array if a cycle prevents a complete order. Vertex labels are 0-based. A FIFO queue returns one valid order, not necessarily the smallest lexicographic order.

example.explanation: Initially 0 and 1 have indegree zero. Processing both removes the two incoming edges of 2; only then can 2 be taken, followed by 3.

351.baseline: DFS can append each vertex after its outgoing neighbors and reverse the result. It has the same O(V + E) time, but uses a recursive stack rather than a queue of currently available vertices.
351.approach:
Indegree counts how many incoming edges remain. A zero-indegree vertex can appear next because no unfinished vertex must come before it. Put all such vertices into the queue.

Remove one, append it to the order, and reduce the indegree of each outgoing neighbor. When a neighbor’s count becomes zero, all its incoming requirements have been removed, so enqueue it.

If the queue empties before every vertex is processed, a cycle remains: vertices on that cycle keep an incoming edge from one another. Return no order in that case, rather than returning only the removable prefix.
steps: Count every incoming edge.
Queue all initial zero-indegree vertices.
Append each removed vertex and subtract its outgoing contributions.
Accept the order only if it contains every vertex.
351.space: O(V) indegrees, queue, and output beyond the supplied graph.
pitfalls: Indegree belongs to the destination of u→v, not the source.
A vertex becomes ready only after its count reaches zero.
Disconnected and isolated vertices must appear too.
Nodes left unprocessed may include downstream nodes as well as actual cycle members.

reference.title: Topological sort or Kahn's algorithm
reference.approach: Repeatedly remove zero-indegree vertices and update their outgoing neighbors.
reference.adaptation: The public DAG practice statement was checked. Kahn’s Java loop was checked in the public directed-cycle and Course Schedule II articles and adapted to an existing adjacency list.

351.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) recursive/state/output space.

352.problem: Detect a directed cycle using the number of vertices Kahn’s algorithm can remove.
352.assumptions: The graph is directed and may be disconnected. The result is true when any directed cycle exists, including a self-loop. An empty graph has no cycle.

example.explanation: Only 0 starts with indegree zero. Removing it cannot release the cycle between 1 and 2. Vertex 3 also stays blocked, although it is not itself on the cycle.

352.baseline: DFS can detect an edge back to an active vertex. This uses O(V + E) time and O(V) recursive state. Kahn’s method replaces active-path reasoning with remaining incoming-edge counts.
352.approach:
A finite DAG always has a vertex with indegree zero. If every vertex had an incoming edge, following incoming edges repeatedly would eventually revisit a vertex and reveal a cycle.

Remove zero-indegree vertices one by one and reduce their neighbors’ counts. If the graph is acyclic, the same reasoning keeps finding a new source until all vertices are removed. If a cycle exists, its vertices never lose their last incoming cycle edge.

Count removals. Fewer than V means at least one cycle exists somewhere; it does not mean every unremoved vertex lies on a cycle.
steps: Count indegrees and queue all zeros.
Remove ready vertices while reducing outgoing neighbors’ indegrees.
Count each removed vertex once.
Return processed != V.
pitfalls: Return true for incomplete processing, not complete processing.
Do not confuse a blocked downstream vertex with a cycle member.
Count every duplicate edge consistently if the supplied representation contains duplicates.
Undirected adjacency lists contain reverse edges and cannot be passed here as a directed-cycle model.

reference.title: Detect a Cycle in a Directed Graph
reference.approach: A Kahn processed count below V proves a directed cycle.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java cycle methods were checked. This keeps the source’s indegree and processed-count method with ArrayDeque.

352.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) recursive/visited space.

353.problem: Decide whether every course can be completed while respecting its prerequisites.
353.assumptions: A pair [course, prerequisite] means the prerequisite must come first. Course labels range from 0 to numCourses−1. Courses with no listed relationships still exist and must be included. A zero-course input returns true as an extension.

example.explanation: Take 0, then 1 and 2 in either order, then 3. Requiring 0 after 3 as well would create a circular dependency.

353.baseline: DFS on prerequisite→course edges detects cycles using visited and active-path arrays. Any active-path edge makes completion impossible. This has the same linear time but uses recursion.
353.approach:
Convert each pair into an edge from the prerequisite to the course. A course’s indegree is the number of prerequisites still waiting to be completed.

Begin with every zero-indegree course. Completing one releases one requirement from each dependent course. Enqueue a dependent only after all of its requirements are gone.

If this process completes every course, return true. Otherwise a circular dependency prevents some courses from ever becoming available. No scheduling choice can break such a cycle without violating a requirement.
steps: Build prerequisite→course edges.
Count incoming requirements for each course.
Complete available courses and release their dependents.
Return whether the completed count equals the total.
353.time: O(V + E), where V is courses and E is prerequisite pairs.
353.space: O(V + E) including the dependency graph.
pitfalls: Pair order is [course, prerequisite], so the edge goes from the second entry to the first.
All prerequisites must be satisfied, not just one.
No prerequisites means every course is feasible.
A cycle in any disconnected component makes the overall answer false.
tests: assert canFinish(5,new int[0][]);assert !canFinish(4,new int[][]{{1,0},{3,2},{2,3}});assert !canFinish(1,new int[][]{{0,0}});assert canFinish(2,new int[][]{{1,0},{1,0}});
int n=100000;int[][]p=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)p[i-1]=new int[]{i,i-1};assert canFinish(n,p);

reference.title: Course Schedule I
reference.approach: Model prerequisites as directed edges and check whether Kahn’s algorithm completes every course.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java approaches were checked. The prerequisite direction, completed-count check, and all-course initialization are retained. The DFS alternative uses local boolean arrays through the checked directed-cycle helper.

353.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and graph storage, plus O(V) recursive/visited space.

354.problem: Return an order that completes all courses after their prerequisites, or an empty array if that is impossible.
354.assumptions: Each pair is [course, prerequisite], so create prerequisite→course. Any valid complete order is accepted. Courses without dependencies still appear once. An empty array means failure for positive course counts; for zero courses it is the valid empty order.

example.explanation: Courses 0 and 1 come before 2, and 2 comes before 3. Course 4 is independent and may appear anywhere.

354.baseline: DFS detects cycles using three states, appends each course after exploring its outgoing neighbors, then reverses the finish list. It returns an empty array when a cycle is encountered.
354.approach:
Use the same availability rule as Course Schedule I, but save each completed course. Initially queue every course with zero indegree. Remove a course, append it to the order, and reduce each dependent’s indegree.

A dependent enters the queue only when all prerequisites have been completed, so every appended course is safe to take at that point. Independent courses may be interleaved in several valid ways.

Check the final count before returning. A partial order is not a solution when a cycle blocks the remaining courses.
steps: Build the dependency graph and indegree counts.
Queue all courses with no outstanding prerequisites.
Append courses as they leave the queue, releasing dependents.
Return the complete order, or an empty array if fewer than all courses were processed.
354.space: O(V + E) including graph, queue, indegrees, and returned order.
pitfalls: Do not compare against one exact example order when several orders are valid.
Return every course exactly once, including isolated courses.
A cycle requires an empty result rather than a partial prefix.
A FIFO queue does not guarantee lexicographically smallest order; use a priority queue only if that extra requirement is stated.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(findOrder(3,new int[][]{{1,0},{2,1}}),new int[]{0,1,2});assert findOrder(3,new int[][]{{1,0},{2,1},{0,2}}).length==0;
int n=100000;int[][]p=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)p[i-1]=new int[]{i,i-1};int[]a=findOrder(n,p);assert a.length==n&&a[0]==0&&a[n-1]==n-1;

reference.title: Course Schedule II
reference.approach: Return the complete Kahn order, or reverse DFS finish order after cycle checks.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked. The graph builder and generic ordering helper separate the prerequisite input conversion from the same algorithm.

354.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and graph storage; O(V) recursion/state/output space.

355.problem: Return all vertices from which every possible directed path eventually reaches a terminal vertex.
355.assumptions: A terminal vertex has no outgoing edges. One route to a terminal is not enough: if another route can enter a cycle, the starting vertex is unsafe. Return safe labels in ascending order.

example.explanation: Vertex 2 is terminal and 3 leads only to 2. Vertex 1 loops forever. Vertex 0 is unsafe because it can choose the route to 1, even though it also has a route to 2.

355.baseline: DFS can classify vertices as unseen, active, safe, or unsafe. A vertex is safe only after every outgoing neighbor is proven safe. This uses O(V) extra space but can recurse deeply.
355.approach:
Begin with terminal vertices, whose safety is already certain. Reverse the edges so that a safe vertex can tell its predecessors that one of their outgoing choices is safe.

Keep a count of each vertex’s outgoing edges that have not yet been proved safe. Whenever a safe neighbor is removed from the queue, reduce the corresponding predecessor’s count. A predecessor becomes safe only when that count reaches zero.

Vertices in a cycle never lose all their cycle edges. Vertices that can reach those cycles stay blocked too. Finally scan labels in increasing order to produce sorted output without a separate sort.
steps: Build reverse edges and count original outgoing edges.
Queue all terminal vertices.
Remove proven-safe vertices and decrement their predecessors’ remaining counts.
Mark newly released predecessors safe and return safe labels in ascending order.
355.space: O(V + E) for reverse edges and traversal state.
pitfalls: Safety requires every path to terminate, not just one path.
Start from outdegree zero in the original graph, not indegree zero.
A vertex that merely reaches a cycle is unsafe too.
A self-loop makes its vertex unsafe.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]a=new int[n][];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=i+1<n?new int[]{i+1}:new int[0];assert eventualSafeNodes(a).size()==n;a[n-1]=new int[]{n-1};assert eventualSafeNodes(a).isEmpty();

reference.title: Find Eventual Safe States
reference.approach: Reverse Kahn propagation from terminals, or DFS classification of all outgoing paths.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. The BFS result uses a final ascending scan instead of the source Java’s sort, matching the article’s O(V + E) prose. The DFS alternative uses explicit unsafe state rather than leaving active flags set after failed calls.

355.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and O(V) state/recursive space. States: 0 unseen, 1 active, 2 safe, 3 unsafe.

356.problem: Infer one valid character order from words already sorted in an unknown alphabet.
356.assumptions: Return each character that appears in the words exactly once. Return an empty string if a longer word precedes its own prefix or if the ordering rules form a cycle. Several alphabets may be valid. This Java char implementation suits ordinary single-code-unit letters; it does not split Unicode supplementary characters correctly.

example.explanation: The comparisons require a before b and z before c. The a→b rule appears twice but is still only one graph edge. Other orders satisfying both rules are valid too.

356.baseline: DFS can detect active-path cycles and reverse the characters’ finish order. It uses the same precedence graph and has the same linear expected complexity with hash-set neighbors.
356.approach:
Compare adjacent words from left to right. Only the first differing position tells us a letter order. Once that position decides which word comes first, later positions provide no additional rule.

If one word is a full prefix of the other, the shorter word must come first in every alphabet. A longer-first pair is invalid even when no graph cycle exists. Include every observed character in the graph, including characters that receive no edge.

Deduplicate the edges, then apply Kahn’s algorithm. Start with letters of indegree zero and release their outgoing neighbors. If the result omits any observed character, the precedence rules contain a cycle.
steps: Register every observed character.
For each adjacent word pair, add only its first mismatch as an edge.
Reject a longer word before its own prefix.
Topologically order all characters and reject incomplete output.
356.time: O(C + U + E) expected time for C input characters, U distinct letters, and E distinct precedence edges.
356.space: O(U + E) for the graph and ordering state.
pitfalls: Use only the first mismatch, not every differing position.
Detect invalid prefixes separately from cycles.
Duplicate rules must not inflate indegrees when the adjacency set stores one edge.
Do not invent absent alphabet letters when the contract asks only for observed characters.
A valid output is not necessarily unique or lexicographically smallest.
tests: assert alienOrder(new String[]{"abc","ab"}).isEmpty();assert alienOrder(new String[]{"z","x","z"}).isEmpty();String s=alienOrder(new String[]{"za","zb","ca","cb"});assert s.length()==4&&s.indexOf('a')<s.indexOf('b')&&s.indexOf('z')<s.indexOf('c');assert alienOrder(new String[]{"a","a"}).equals("a");

reference.title: Alien Dictionary Using Topological Sort
reference.approach: Extract first-mismatch constraints, reject invalid prefixes, and topologically sort distinct characters.
reference.adaptation: Both public Java methods were checked. HashSet neighbors replace TreeSet, and indegrees are computed after deduplication. The prefix check uses one shared-prefix scan instead of allocating a substring. The pinned Premium editorial was not accessed.

356.baselineTime: O(C + U + E) expected time and O(U + E) storage, including O(U) recursion.

357.problem: Find the shortest number of edges from a source to every vertex in an undirected graph whose edges all cost one.
357.assumptions: Vertices are 0-based, the source is valid for a nonempty graph, and edges are undirected. Return −1 for unreachable vertices and 0 for the source. This returns distances, not the actual paths.

example.explanation: Both routes to 2 use two edges. Vertex 4 has no route from 0, so its distance stays −1.

357.baseline: Repeatedly scan every edge and improve distances in both directions. After at most V−1 rounds, all shortest simple paths are covered. This costs O(VE); BFS avoids rescanning edges across many rounds.
357.approach:
BFS visits vertices in increasing distance from the source. A queued vertex at distance d can discover neighbors at distance d + 1. By the time such a neighbor is first discovered, every shorter layer has already had a chance to reach it.

Use −1 as both the unvisited marker and the final unreachable answer. Set a neighbor’s distance before enqueuing it, so another route at the same or a later layer does not add duplicate work.

Build both directions of every input edge. A directed version would store only the stated direction, but the same unit-weight BFS rule would still apply.
steps: Build undirected adjacency lists.
Fill distances with −1 and set source distance to 0.
Enqueue each unvisited neighbor with current distance + 1.
Return the distance array after the queue empties.
357.space: O(V + E) including adjacency lists; O(V) distance and queue storage.
pitfalls: Source distance is 0 because no edge is needed to stay there.
The first-visit rule relies on equal edge costs.
Do not start at vertex 0 unless it is the requested source.
Leave disconnected vertices at −1.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(shortestPath(5,new int[][]{{0,1},{1,2},{0,3},{3,2}},0),new int[]{0,1,2,1,-1});assert shortestPath(0,new int[0][],0).length==0;
int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=0;i<n-1;i++)e[i]=new int[]{i,i+1};assert shortestPath(n,e,n-1)[0]==n-1;

reference.title: Shortest Path in an Unweighted Undirected Graph Using BFS
reference.approach: BFS assigns minimum edge counts on first discovery.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Java method was checked. Its two-way adjacency, −1 initialization, and first-visit distance rule are retained. The redundant edge-count parameter is omitted; the round-based baseline is an authored comparison.

357.baselineTime: O(VE) worst-case time and O(V) distance storage.

358.problem: Find shortest weighted distances from vertex 0 to every vertex in a directed acyclic graph.
358.assumptions: Each edge is [from, to, weight]. The linked practice uses positive weights whose path sums fit int. The long-distance helper also supports negative weights in a DAG and keeps Long.MAX_VALUE as its unreachable marker. The judge-style int wrapper converts unreachable to −1. Cyclic inputs are rejected.

example.explanation: Vertex 1 improves from 7 to 3 through 2. Processing 1 after its predecessors ensures that 3 receives 3 + 4 = 7, not the earlier longer value.

358.baseline: DFS can build the same topological order by finishing outgoing neighbors first, then reversing the finish list. Relax edges in that order. It has the same linear time as Kahn’s method, but recursion can be deep.
358.approach:
A DAG lets us process vertices in an order where every edge points forward. Before a vertex is processed, every possible predecessor has already passed its best distance to it. We can therefore relax each outgoing edge once.

Build a topological order with indegrees. Start all distances at infinity except distance[0] = 0. For each vertex in order, skip it if unreachable; otherwise try distance[vertex] + weight for each neighbor and keep the smaller value.

Negative edges do not break this argument because no edge can lead back to an already processed vertex. The DAG requirement matters more than the sign of the weights. Keep unreachable separate from numeric distances internally, since a valid negative distance could equal −1.
steps: Build weighted directed adjacency and a topological order.
Reject the graph if fewer than V vertices appear in that order.
Set source 0 to distance 0 and skip unreachable vertices.
Relax every outgoing edge once in topological order, then format unreachable results.
358.space: O(V + E) including weighted adjacency and topological-order storage.
pitfalls: Ordinary BFS order is not enough when edge weights differ.
