Never add a weight to the unreachable sentinel.
Do not process vertices by numeric label unless that label order is known to be topological.
Use the long helper when sums exceed int or when −1 must be distinguished from unreachable.
A DAG can have negative edges, but this method is not valid on arbitrary cyclic graphs.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(shortestPath(4,new int[][]{{0,1,7},{0,2,2},{2,1,1},{1,3,4}}),new int[]{0,3,2,7});assert Arrays.equals(dagDistances(4,new int[][]{{0,1,Integer.MAX_VALUE},{1,2,Integer.MAX_VALUE}}),new long[]{0,Integer.MAX_VALUE,2L*Integer.MAX_VALUE,Long.MAX_VALUE});assert dagDistances(0,new int[0][]).length==0;

boolean failed=false;try{dagDistances(2,new int[][]{{0,1,1},{1,0,1}});}catch(IllegalArgumentException e){failed=true;}assert failed;failed=false;try{dagByDfs(1,new int[][]{{0,0,1}});}catch(IllegalArgumentException e){failed=true;}assert failed;
int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][3];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)e[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i,10000};assert dagDistances(n,e)[n-1]==999990000L;

reference.title: Shortest Path in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
reference.approach: Construct a topological order with DFS or Kahn, then relax each reachable outgoing edge once.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods and the positive-weight practice limits were checked. This adaptation uses long distances, skips unreachable vertices, detects invalid cycles, and uses checked int conversion in the judge-style wrapper. The source DFS uses an int sentinel; its Kahn version uses long internally.

358.baselineTime: O(V + E) time and graph storage, with O(V) recursive stack.

359.problem: Find the shortest weighted distance from a source to every vertex in an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights.
359.assumptions: Edges are [u,v,weight] and work both ways. Zero weights are allowed. The pinned practice requires 10^9 for unreachable vertices and has bounds that keep valid shortest distances below that marker. The long helper supports larger sums and uses Long.MAX_VALUE for unreachable. The source must be valid for a nonempty graph.

example.explanation: The direct route to 1 costs 9, but 0→2→1 costs 2. The zero-weight edge keeps 3 at distance 2. Vertex 4 is unreachable.

359.baseline: Keep tentative distances and linearly scan all unsettled vertices to choose the smallest one. Settle it and relax its outgoing edges. This is Dijkstra’s same greedy rule, but minimum selection costs O(V²) overall.
359.approach:
A tentative distance is the best route found so far. Repeatedly take the smallest tentative distance. With nonnegative edges, reaching that vertex through any other unsettled vertex cannot make it cheaper, because the other route already costs at least as much and can only add more.

A min-heap makes this choice efficient. For each outgoing edge, try current cost + weight. If it improves the neighbor, update the distance and insert a new heap pair. Java’s PriorityQueue does not update old pairs automatically.

The old pair may still be removed later. If its cost no longer matches distance[vertex], skip it. Use strict improvement when inserting so zero-weight cycles do not create endless equal-cost entries.
steps: Build two-way weighted adjacency and initialize source distance to 0.
Remove the smallest distance–vertex pair.
Skip it if a better distance has already replaced it.
Relax outgoing edges and insert only strict improvements.
359.time: O(V + E log(E + 1)) with a lazy heap; commonly O((V + E) log V) for simple graphs.
359.space: O(V + E) including adjacency and up to O(E) heap entries.
pitfalls: Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights.
A vertex’s first discovery is not necessarily its shortest route.
Use long for sums and a comparator that does not subtract and overflow.
The pinned judge’s unreachable marker is 10^9, unlike the article’s −1.
Do not mutate the cost inside an object already stored in the heap.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][3];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)e[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i,1};assert dijkstraDistances(n,e,0)[n-1]==n-1;

reference.title: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
reference.approach: Select the smallest tentative distance using a min-heap, and skip stale entries.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods and the pinned practice statement were checked. The article returns −1 for unreachable vertices, while the practice requires 10^9. The int wrapper follows the practice; the long helper keeps Long.MAX_VALUE for unreachable. Negative weights are explicitly rejected, and checked conversion avoids silent int overflow.

359.baselineTime: O(V² + E) time and O(V + E) space including the graph.

360.problem: Understand why Dijkstra uses a min-priority queue, and why a normal FIFO queue with first-visit marking is insufficient for weighted shortest paths.
360.assumptions: The graph has nonnegative weights. This row shares the Dijkstra practice link, so the same working implementation is included. The heap stores [distance,vertex] pairs ordered by distance, not by vertex label. The int wrapper uses the pinned judge’s 10^9 unreachable marker.

example.explanation: The route through 2 improves vertex 1 before the old cost-9 entry is processed. FIFO discovery order would encounter 1 through its expensive direct edge first.

360.baseline: A heap is not required for correctness if we scan every unsettled vertex to find the smallest tentative distance. That selection costs O(V) per vertex and O(V²) overall. The heap speeds up this specific operation.
360.approach:
A FIFO queue answers “which item arrived first?” Dijkstra needs “which currently known route costs least?” Those are the same ordering only when every edge has equal cost, which is the special case handled by BFS.

The priority queue keeps the smallest cost available at the front. An improved route is inserted as a new pair because Java’s PriorityQueue has no efficient built-in decrease-key operation. Older pairs remain until removed, then fail the stale-cost check.

Use the distance array as the current record and heap entries as snapshots of earlier discoveries. Never change an entry’s sort key in place: the heap will not rearrange itself just because a field changed. Also avoid remove(Object) for each improvement; that search is linear in Java’s PriorityQueue.
steps: Order heap pairs by their stored distance.
Insert a fresh pair whenever a route strictly improves.
Compare popped cost with the current distance array to discard old snapshots.
Relax neighbors only from a current minimum entry.
360.time: O(V + E log(E + 1)) for this lazy min-heap implementation, compared with O(V² + E) for linear selection.
360.space: O(V + E); stale pairs can make the heap larger than V.
pitfalls: PriorityQueue iteration is not sorted order; repeatedly poll/remove the minimum.
Ordering by vertex number does not implement Dijkstra.
First-visit BFS marking is wrong for unequal weights.
A queue that repeatedly relaxes improved distances is a different algorithm; it does not inherit BFS’s linear bound.
The heap changes selection cost, not the nonnegative-weight requirement.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][3];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)e[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i,1};assert dijkstraDistances(n,e,0)[n-1]==n-1;

reference.title: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
reference.approach: Select the smallest tentative distance using a min-heap, and skip stale entries.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods and the pinned practice statement were checked. The article returns −1 for unreachable vertices, while the practice requires 10^9. The int wrapper follows the practice; the long helper keeps Long.MAX_VALUE for unreachable. Negative weights are explicitly rejected, and checked conversion avoids silent int overflow.

rows: Skip: 9 differs from the current distance 2

360.baselineTime: O(V² + E) time and O(V + E) storage. This is the same greedy selection rule without a heap.

361.problem: Find the shortest clear path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell of the linked binary-matrix problem.
361.assumptions: The pinned LeetCode problem uses 0 as open, permits eight directions including diagonals, and counts visited cells. Striver’s current maze article uses 1 as open, four directions, arbitrary endpoints, and counts moves. Both contracts are included explicitly; the primary method follows the pinned link and leaves the input unchanged.

example.explanation: The two open cells touch at a corner, so the linked problem allows one diagonal move. The path contains two cells. Under four-direction movement, that diagonal alone would not be a route.

361.baseline: Repeatedly scan reachable open cells and improve their neighbors’ distances until no distance changes. At most N²−1 rounds suffice for simple paths, but this can take O(N⁴). BFS processes cells in distance order and avoids those repeated scans.
361.approach:
Every allowed move costs one, so use BFS. Mark the starting distance as zero moves and enqueue it. For each removed cell, inspect its allowed neighbors, skipping blocked cells and cells already assigned a distance.

The first time the destination is reached gives the minimum number of moves. The pinned problem asks for cells in the path, so add one to that move count. This makes a single open cell return 1.

The shared helper makes the variant choices explicit. shortestPathBinaryMatrix uses open value 0 and eight directions. mazeDistance uses open value 1 and four directions, returning moves directly. Mixing any of these choices changes the problem.
steps: Reject blocked endpoints before starting.
Run BFS with the required open value and movement directions.
Assign each neighbor’s distance before enqueuing it.
For the pinned matrix task, convert moves to visited cells by adding one.
361.time: O(N²) for the square pinned matrix; O(R × C) for the rectangular maze variant.
361.space: O(R × C) for distances and the queue.
pitfalls: The article and pinned problem disagree on open value, directions, endpoints, and what the length counts.
A single open matrix cell returns 1; equal walkable maze endpoints return 0 moves.
Diagonal movement is allowed even when both neighboring side cells are blocked in the pinned problem.
Do not modify the input if it is needed for another query.
tests: assert shortestPathBinaryMatrix(new int[][]{{0,1},{1,0}})==2;assert shortestPathBinaryMatrix(new int[][]{{0}})==1;assert shortestPathBinaryMatrix(new int[][]{{1}})==-1;assert mazeDistance(new int[][]{{1}},new int[]{0,0},new int[]{0,0})==0;assert mazeDistance(new int[][]{{0}},new int[]{0,0},new int[]{0,0})==-1;

reference.title: Shortest Distance in a Binary Maze Using BFS
reference.approach: Use BFS for unit-cost grid movement, with explicit endpoint and movement rules.
reference.adaptation: The complete public maze Java and the pinned LeetCode 1091 statement were checked. The primary wrapper adapts the article’s BFS to zero-open, eight-direction, cell-count semantics. The separate maze wrapper retains one-open, four-direction, move-count semantics. The repeated-relaxation baseline is an authored comparison.

361.baselineTime: O(N⁴) worst-case time and O(N²) distance storage.

better.explanation: Different contract: the current Striver maze article takes arbitrary valid source and destination coordinates, treats 1 as walkable, allows only four directions, and counts moves. The shared BFS helper implements these choices directly. This is a variant wrapper, not an optimization of the eight-direction problem.
better.space: O(R × C).

362.problem: Find a top-left to bottom-right path whose largest single height change is as small as possible.
362.assumptions: Movement is up, down, left, or right. Every cell is traversable. Effort is the maximum adjacent height difference along the path, not the sum. The pinned constraints give a nonempty rectangular grid with heights from 1 to 10^6, so int differences are safe.

example.explanation: Going down then right has differences 3 and 3, so its effort is 3. Going right first creates a jump of 9. The answer is the largest step on the chosen route, not 3 + 3.

362.baseline: Try effort limits from 0 up to the height range. For each limit, run BFS using only edges whose height difference is at most that limit. The first reachable limit is optimal, but trying every integer can be slow.
362.approach:
Use a Dijkstra-style heap, but change what a route costs. Extending a route with current effort e across a jump of size d gives effort max(e,d), not e + d. Keep the smallest effort found for each cell.

Remove the smallest current effort from the heap and skip stale entries. Once the destination is removed with its current best effort, return it. Extending any other route cannot lower that route’s existing largest jump, so no unprocessed larger effort can produce a better answer.

The threshold view gives another useful method: if a limit works, every larger limit works too. Binary search finds the first feasible limit using the same BFS check as the simple solution.
steps: Set the source effort to 0 and other efforts to infinity.
Remove the smallest current heap effort and skip stale entries.
For each neighbor, try max(current effort, height difference).
Return when the destination is removed with its current best effort.
362.space: O(R × C) for efforts and heap states.
pitfalls: Using addition solves a different objective.
Return when the destination is popped with current effort, not when it is first discovered.
A single cell has effort 0 because there is no height change.
Do not apply first-visit BFS marking to weighted effort without fixing a threshold.
For arbitrary int heights, cast to long before subtraction; the stated judge bounds are what make int safe here.
tests: assert minimumEffortPath(new int[][]{{1,10},{4,7}})==3;assert minimumEffortPath(new int[][]{{99}})==0;assert effortBinarySearch(new int[][]{{99}})==0;assert effortByLimits(new int[][]{{99}})==0;

reference.title: Path with Minimum Effort
reference.approach: Threshold BFS, binary search on feasible effort, and minimax Dijkstra relaxation.
reference.adaptation: All three complete public Java methods and the pinned height bounds were checked. The same max-based relaxation and stale-state check are retained. An unreachable defensive fallback throws instead of silently returning zero; valid nonempty height grids always have a route.

362.baselineTime: O((H + 1)RC) time for height range H, and O(RC) space.

better.explanation: Binary search the effort limit. At a given limit, BFS answers whether the destination is reachable using only allowed jumps. If it works, lower the upper bound; otherwise raise the lower bound past that limit. The reachability check and height-range helper are in the simple solution above.
better.time: O(RC log(H + 1) + RC), including the height-range scan.
better.space: O(RC) for each BFS check.

363.problem: Find the cheapest directed flight route using at most k intermediate stops.
363.assumptions: At most k stops means at most k + 1 flights. Cities are 0-based, endpoints are valid, and prices are nonnegative. Return −1 if no allowed route exists. The long helper protects sums; the int wrapper matches the pinned judge’s bounded-price interface.

example.explanation: The cheap route to city 3 uses all three allowed flights, leaving no flight to reach 4. The valid route 0→3→4 costs 9. Keeping only the cheapest cost per city would lose it.

363.baseline: Enumerate every route with at most k + 1 flights and keep the cheapest arrival. The flight limit makes this finite even with cycles, but the number of routes can grow exponentially.
363.approach:
Let distance[v] mean the cheapest cost using at most the number of flights already allowed. Initially, only the source is reachable with zero flights. One round allows one more flight.

At the start of a round, clone the distance array. Read departure costs only from the old array and write improvements only to the clone. The clone already preserves cheaper routes using fewer flights. After every flight is checked, replace the old layer with the new one.

This separation is essential. Updating and reading the same array could chain several flights during one round, depending on input order. After k + 1 rounds, the destination entry is the cheapest allowed route. No priority queue is needed for this bounded Bellman–Ford method.
steps: Initialize source cost to 0 and all other costs to infinity.
Repeat k + 1 rounds, each starting with a copy of the previous layer.
Relax every flight using only previous-layer departure costs.
Read the destination after the allowed rounds; convert infinity to −1.
363.time: O((k + 1)(V + E)), including the O(V) array copy in each round.
363.space: O(V) for two consecutive distance layers.
pitfalls: Stops and flights differ by one.
Read the old layer and write the new layer; in-place relaxation can violate the stop limit.
A cheaper arrival using more flights does not always dominate a costlier arrival using fewer flights.
Flight edges are directed.
The source article’s O((k + 1)E) time statement omits array-copy work; this implementation includes it.

reference.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
reference.approach: Bounded Bellman–Ford with separate flight-count layers; alternatively use a heap keyed by cost and flights used.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked. The copied-layer method is primary because it is simpler and avoids heap overhead. Its complexity includes the array copies. A checked int wrapper matches the pinned judge, while core costs remain long.

363.baselineTime: Exponential route enumeration; each recursive call scans E flights. O(k + 1) recursive space.

better.explanation: Another source method: use a cost-ordered heap, but track best[flightsUsed][city] rather than one cost per city. Two arrivals with different flight counts have different remaining options. Stop expanding a state after k + 1 flights. With nonnegative prices, the first current destination state removed from the heap has minimum valid cost. This can finish early, but has more memory and heap overhead than the primary copied-layer method.
better.time: O((k + 2)V + (k + 1)E log((k + 1)E + 2)) as a lazy-heap upper bound.
better.space: O((k + 2)V + (k + 1)E) for the state table, graph, and heap.

364.problem: Send a signal from node k along directed weighted edges. Find when every node has received it, or return −1 if some node is unreachable.
364.assumptions: Nodes are numbered 1 through n. Travel times are nonnegative. The signal can spread along several edges at once. The long helper handles large sums; the int wrapper matches the pinned judge.

example.explanation: Node 3 receives the signal at time 2, node 2 at time 5 through node 3, and node 4 at time 6. The direct edge taking 9 is not the best route to node 2.

364.baseline: Use Bellman–Ford: scan every edge up to n − 1 times and improve arrival times. A round with no changes lets you stop early. Finally take the maximum arrival time, unless a node is unreachable.
364.approach:
Think about each node separately first: when can it receive the signal earliest? That is its shortest-path distance from k. All nodes have received the signal only when the last of those earliest arrivals happens, so the answer is the maximum distance, not their sum.

Use Dijkstra because travel times cannot be negative. The heap gives the smallest known arrival time. If that entry is older than the current distance, skip it. Otherwise, try sending the signal along each outgoing edge and save any earlier arrival. Keep processing until the heap is empty, then inspect every node.
steps: Store each edge only from its source to its destination.
Start k at time 0 and put it in a min-heap.
Remove the earliest entry, skip stale entries, and improve outgoing arrivals.
Return −1 if any node is unreachable; otherwise return the largest distance.
364.time: O(V + E log(E + 2)) with a lazy heap; O((V + E) log V) for the simple graph in the judge.
364.space: O(V + E) for adjacency, distances, and heap entries.
pitfalls: Use the maximum distance, not the sum: the signal spreads concurrently.
Edges are directed; adding a reverse edge changes reachability.
Do not stop after the first newly reached node or mark a node final when first inserted.
Zero-weight edges are allowed here.
The source method returns long; the checked int wrapper fits the judge’s bounded result.
tests: assert networkDelay(new int[][]{{1,2,Integer.MAX_VALUE},{2,3,Integer.MAX_VALUE}},3,1)==2L*Integer.MAX_VALUE;assert networkDelayTime(new int[0][],1,1)==0;assert networkDelayTime(new int[][]{{1,2,0},{2,3,0}},3,1)==0;

reference.title: Network Delay Time Using Dijkstra’s Algorithm
reference.approach: Bellman–Ford baseline and Dijkstra with a min-heap; take the maximum shortest distance.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked. The explanation uses a new example and makes simultaneous signal spread explicit. Core distances stay long; a checked int wrapper matches the pinned judge.

364.baselineTime: O(VE + V) time and O(V) extra space. Uses lastArrival from the primary snippet.

365.problem: Count the routes from intersection 0 to n − 1 whose total travel time is as small as possible. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.
365.assumptions: Roads are undirected, with at most one road per pair and strictly positive travel times, as required by the linked LeetCode problem. Its network is connected; this code also returns 0 for an unreachable destination. There is one empty route when n = 1.

example.explanation: The minimum time is 4. The routes are 0→1→3, 0→2→1→3, and 0→2→3. A route with a longer time contributes nothing to the count.

365.baseline: For a small graph, enumerate simple routes. Record their total times, keep only the smallest time, and count the ties. Positive weights mean a shortest route never needs to revisit a node. The number of simple routes can still grow factorially.
365.approach:
Keep two answers for each intersection: distance tells us its shortest time, and ways tells us how many routes achieve that time. Start with distance[0] = 0 and ways[0] = 1.

Run Dijkstra. When a candidate route is shorter, the old routes are no longer useful: replace the distance and copy the current node’s route count. When the candidate ties the best time, add the current node’s count. A longer candidate changes nothing.

Strictly positive road times matter. Every predecessor on a shortest route has a smaller distance, so Dijkstra finishes its count before that count is passed onward. Equal-distance updates need no new heap entry. Use long for distances, and apply modulo only to counts.
steps: Build adjacency in both directions.
Initialize source distance to 0 and source count to 1.
On a shorter route, replace the distance and count and push a heap entry.
On an equal route, add the count modulo 1,000,000,007.
Return the destination count.
365.time: O((V + E) log V) for this simple graph.
365.space: O(V + E) for adjacency, the heap, distances, and counts.
pitfalls: A shorter route replaces the count; it does not add to it.
An equal route adds the count without adding another heap entry.
Use long for total time: 200 edges near one billion overflow int.
Do not reduce distances modulo anything; that would change their order.
This counting method assumes positive weights. Zero-weight cycles require a different definition of what counts as a route.
tests: int[][]e={{0,1,2},{0,2,1},{2,1,1},{1,3,2},{2,3,3}};assert countPaths(4,e)==3;assert countPathsByEnumeration(4,e)==3;assert countPaths(1,new int[0][])==1;assert countPaths(3,new int[][]{{0,1,1}})==0;

reference.title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination: Count Shortest Paths
reference.approach: Dijkstra with a distance array and a shortest-route count array.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Java method was checked. The linked LeetCode constraints confirm strictly positive road times; this is stated and enforced explicitly. The small-graph route-enumeration baseline is an authored teaching comparison.

365.baselineTime: Factorially many route prefixes in a dense graph; O(V + E) space for adjacency, visited flags, and the recursion stack.

366.problem: Starting from start, repeatedly multiply by any number in arr and take the remainder modulo 100000. Find the fewest operations needed to reach end.
366.assumptions: Each multiplier is a positive int. start and end lie from 0 through 99999. Multipliers may be reused. Return −1 if end cannot be reached.

example.explanation: One shortest sequence is 2→6→24. The first multiplication uses 3 and the second uses 4.

366.baseline: Trying every multiplication sequence repeats the same values many times and can run forever around a cycle. You could first build every edge between all 100000 possible values, but that stores transitions we can calculate when needed.
366.approach:
The numbers are the graph. Each possible remainder is a node, and multiplying once is an edge. Every edge costs one operation, so use BFS.

Mark a value when it first enters the queue. That first discovery already uses the fewest operations. This also prevents loops such as multiplying by 1 over and over. There are only 100000 possible remainders, so the search eventually finishes even if the target is unreachable.

The multiplication can overflow int before the remainder is taken. Cast current to long before multiplying, then convert the small remainder back to int.
steps: Return 0 immediately when start equals end.
Set every distance to −1, then set the start distance to 0 and enqueue it.
For each removed value, try every multiplier and compute the next remainder using long.
Visit each new remainder once; return its distance as soon as it equals end.
If the queue empties, return −1.
366.time: O(M + NM), where M = 100000 and N is the number of multipliers. Each reachable remainder tries N multipliers; initializing distances costs O(M).
366.space: O(M) for distances and the queue. No explicit edges are stored.
pitfalls: Apply modulo after each multiplication, not only at the end of a sequence.
Use (long) current * multiplier; casting the already overflowed product is too late.
The values do not have to increase, so sorting or a greedy choice of the biggest multiplier is unsuitable.
Check start == end before BFS.
Mark on discovery so cycles do not create endless queue entries.
tests: assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{3,4},2,24)==2;assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{1,1},8,9)==-1;assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{2,3},0,1)==-1;assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{3},7,7)==0;assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{100000},17,0)==1;assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{Integer.MAX_VALUE},99999,(int)(99999L*Integer.MAX_VALUE%100000))==1;

int current=7;Map<Integer,Integer>first=new HashMap<>();while(!first.containsKey(current)){first.put(current,first.size());current=(int)(current*99999L%100000);}for(var e:first.entrySet())assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{99999},7,e.getKey())==e.getValue();assert minimumMultiplications(new int[]{99999},7,8)==-1;

reference.title: Minimum Multiplications to Reach End
reference.approach: BFS over modulo-100000 residues, discovering each value once.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Java method was checked, including its early zero-step return and cast before multiplication. The guide explains the implicit graph without introducing a heap.

367.problem: Find shortest distances from one source in a directed graph that may contain negative edges. Return [-1] if a negative cycle can be reached from that source.
367.assumptions: Vertices are 0-based. The core method uses Long.MAX_VALUE for unreachable nodes and long distances. The judge wrapper returns 100000000 for unreachable nodes and checked int distances. A negative cycle in a disconnected region does not invalidate this source’s result.

example.explanation: The negative edge improves the route to 2 from 7 to 2. Vertex 3 is then reached at cost 5. No route reaches vertex 4.

367.baseline: For nonnegative edges, Dijkstra is faster. With negative edges, finalizing the currently nearest vertex can be wrong. Repeated edge scans let later improvements flow through the graph instead.
367.approach:
To relax an edge u→v means to ask: would going to u and then taking this edge improve the current answer for v? If yes, save that smaller distance. Ignore edges whose starting vertex is unreachable.

Repeat a full edge scan up to V − 1 times. A shortest path without a negative cycle can be chosen without repeating vertices, so it has at most V − 1 edges. Each full scan propagates at least one more edge of every such path; input order may propagate more.

Then scan once more. If a reachable edge can still improve a distance, some reachable negative cycle lets us keep lowering costs. Return [-1]. Otherwise the distances are final. A scan that changes nothing allows an early stop.
steps: Initialize source distance to 0 and other distances to infinity.
Make up to V − 1 full passes, relaxing reachable edges.
Stop early if a pass changes nothing.
Make one extra scan: a remaining improvement means a reachable negative cycle.
Convert unreachable values only when formatting the judge result.
367.time: O(VE + V) time, including initialization and the extra cycle scan.
367.space: O(V) for distances and the returned result.
pitfalls: Only a negative cycle reachable from the source causes [-1].
Never add a weight to the infinity sentinel.
A negative edge is not automatically a negative cycle.
The source prose requests 100000000 for unreachable nodes, but its Java returns its long infinity sentinel directly. The wrapper here explicitly performs the required conversion.
In-place scans are valid here. The copied layers needed by a flight-count limit solve a different requirement.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(bellmanFord(5,new int[][]{{0,1,4},{0,2,7},{1,2,-2},{2,3,3}},0),new int[]{0,4,2,5,100000000});assert Arrays.equals(bellmanFord(3,new int[][]{{0,1,1},{1,2,-3},{2,1,1}},0),new int[]{-1});assert Arrays.equals(bellmanFord(3,new int[][]{{1,2,-3},{2,1,1}},0),new int[]{0,100000000,100000000});assert Arrays.equals(bellmanFord(1,new int[][]{{0,0,-1}},0),new int[]{-1});

reference.title: Bellman–Ford Algorithm: Shortest Paths with Negative Edges
reference.approach: Repeated relaxation followed by one extra scan for a reachable negative cycle.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Java method was checked. Its long infinity return differs from the article’s stated 100000000 contract, so this guide separates the long core from a judge-format wrapper and documents that difference.

368.problem: Find the shortest distance from every vertex to every other vertex in a directed graph supplied as an adjacency matrix.
368.assumptions: In the pinned practice problem, −1 means no edge and all actual weights are nonnegative. A vertex has distance 0 to itself. shortestDistance updates the int matrix in place; the long helper leaves the input untouched and uses −1 for unreachable pairs.

example.explanation: Going from 0 through 1 to 2 costs 7, improving the direct cost 10. There is still no route back from 2 to either earlier vertex.

368.baseline: Run a single-source shortest-path algorithm once for each starting vertex. That is useful for a sparse graph. With a small matrix, Floyd–Warshall handles all pairs using three simple loops.
368.approach:
Initially, a distance is either a direct edge, zero for staying at the same vertex, or infinity. Now allow vertex 0 as a possible intermediate stop. For every pair, ask whether going through 0 is cheaper. Then allow vertex 1, then vertex 2, and so on.

At the start of iteration middle, the matrix already contains the best routes whose intermediate vertices come before middle. A best route with middle available either avoids it or splits into from→middle and middle→to. Take the cheaper of those options.

The intermediate-vertex loop must be outermost. Also check that both halves exist before adding them. Finally turn infinity back into −1 for the problem’s output format.
steps: Copy direct weights into a long distance matrix, using infinity for absent edges and 0 on the diagonal.
For each middle vertex, try every ordered pair from, to.
If both halves exist, compare the direct answer with distance[from][middle] + distance[middle][to].
Convert infinity to −1; the judge wrapper writes the result back into the original matrix.
368.space: O(V²) extra space in this long-matrix implementation.
pitfalls: Keep middle as the outer loop. A single from-to-middle pass is not the same dynamic program.
Treat −1 as missing, not as a negative edge. The pinned problem has no actual negative weights.
Do not add infinity to a finite number.
Directed distances need not be symmetric.
A general version can handle negative edges, but negative cycles need separate reporting. That is outside this pinned nonnegative contract.

reference.title: Floyd–Warshall Algorithm
reference.approach: All-pairs shortest paths with the intermediate vertex as the outer loop.
reference.adaptation: The public practice statement and constraints were checked; its solution requires sign-in. The complete Floyd–Warshall Java in Striver’s public “Find the City” article was checked and adapted to this directed matrix input, in-place judge interface, and −1 output convention.

369.problem: Return the city that can reach the fewest other cities within distanceThreshold. If several cities tie, return the greatest index.
369.assumptions: Roads are undirected and have positive weights. A city does not count itself. Distance equal to the threshold qualifies. The implementation keeps the cheaper of duplicate roads as a harmless extension to the judge’s unique-road input.

example.explanation: Cities 0 and 3 each reach one other city; cities 1 and 2 each reach two. The tie between 0 and 3 goes to 3.

369.baseline: You could solve a shortest-path problem separately from every city. The source gives repeated Dijkstra as an alternative; it often saves work on sparse graphs, especially when few cities lie within the threshold.
369.approach:
First compute every pair’s shortest distance with Floyd–Warshall. For each city, count how many other cities have distance at most the threshold. Keep the city with the smallest count.

Visit city indices in increasing order and replace the answer when count <= bestCount. The equality is deliberate: a later city has a larger index, so it wins a tie.

A road longer than the threshold might be irrelevant, but a series of short roads can also exceed it. Count by total shortest-path distance, not by the number or weight of direct edges alone.
steps: Initialize the distance matrix with 0 on the diagonal and infinity elsewhere.
Store each road in both directions, keeping the smaller weight for duplicates.
Run Floyd–Warshall with the intermediate vertex outermost.
Count qualifying other cities for each source.
Replace the answer on a smaller or equal count.
pitfalls: Use <= threshold, not < threshold.
Exclude the source city itself.
Tie-breaking chooses the greatest index, so equality must replace the earlier answer.
Unreachable cities do not count, even with a very large threshold.
The Dijkstra alternative prunes only because weights are positive.
tests: int[][]e={{0,1,2},{1,2,2},{2,3,2}};assert findTheCity(4,e,2)==3;assert findTheCityByHeap(4,e,2)==3;assert findTheCity(4,new int[0][],100)==3;assert findTheCity(3,new int[][]{{0,1,3},{1,2,3}},6)==2;

reference.title: Find the City with the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
reference.approach: Floyd–Warshall and repeated threshold-pruned Dijkstra, with greatest-index tie-breaking.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked. The guide retains both source approaches, uses long distances, and makes the equality checks and exclusion of the source explicit.

better.explanation: For a sparse graph, run Dijkstra from each city instead of storing an all-pairs matrix. Only enqueue candidate distances within the threshold: a positive road can never bring an over-budget route back under it. Count each current heap removal except the source. The same <= bestCount comparison resolves ties.
better.time: O(V(V + E) log V) for a simple graph; threshold pruning can reduce actual work.
better.space: O(V + E) for adjacency and one source’s heap and distances.

370.problem: Connect every vertex of an undirected weighted graph using a tree with the smallest possible total edge weight.
370.assumptions: The pinned graph is connected, has positive weights, and uses 0-based vertices. A spanning tree contains every vertex and exactly V − 1 edges. The code also handles zero or negative weights, and explicitly rejects disconnected input as an extension.

example.explanation: Keep 0–1 and 1–2, costing 5 + 2. All vertices remain connected. Keeping all three edges would create a cycle and cost more.

370.baseline: Choose every possible subset of V − 1 edges, test whether it connects all vertices, and take the smallest total. Connectivity plus V − 1 edges guarantees a tree. This direct definition is useful for tiny examples but has exponentially many subsets.
370.approach:
A spanning tree is a set of connections, not a route from a source. It must reach every vertex, contain no cycle, and have V − 1 edges. An MST is the cheapest such set; more than one set may have the same minimum cost.

Prim starts with any vertex and grows one tree. Split the vertices into those already included and those outside. Choose the cheapest edge crossing that split. This choice is safe: if an MST did not use it, adding it creates a cycle; another crossing edge on that cycle can be removed without increasing the cost.

The heap stores candidate connection costs. When a vertex is accepted, add just the edge that brought it into the tree. Do not add its entire distance from the starting vertex; that would solve a different problem.
steps: Start vertex 0 with a dummy connection of cost 0.
Remove the cheapest candidate edge; ignore it if its destination is already in the tree.
Accept the new vertex and add that edge’s weight to the total.
Offer its edges to vertices still outside the tree.
Finish after accepting all vertices.
370.time: O(V + E log(E + 2)) with the lazy edge heap; O(E log V) for a connected simple graph.
370.space: O(V + E) for adjacency, the heap, and inclusion flags.
pitfalls: An MST minimizes total chosen edge weight, not all source-to-vertex distances.
Accept a vertex when its cheapest valid entry is removed, not when first inserted.
The starting vertex can change which tied MST is chosen, but not its weight.
A disconnected graph has a spanning forest, not one spanning tree.
The initial zero-cost heap entry is not a real tree edge.
tests: assert mstWeight(3,new int[][]{{0,1,Integer.MAX_VALUE},{1,2,Integer.MAX_VALUE}})==2L*Integer.MAX_VALUE;assert mstWeight(1,new int[0][])==0;boolean rejected=false;try{mstWeight(3,new int[][]{{0,1,1}});}catch(IllegalArgumentException e){rejected=true;}assert rejected;assert mstWeight(3,new int[][]{{0,0,-99},{0,1,8},{0,1,2},{1,2,3}})==5;

reference.title: Find the MST Weight
reference.approach: Prim grows one tree using the cheapest crossing edge; Kruskal joins components in sorted edge order.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked, along with the practice page’s Java signature. The article uses an edge list; the judge uses List<List<List<Integer>>> adjacency, so both entry points are included. Totals use long internally, and disconnected input is rejected rather than returning a partial tree.

370.baselineTime: O(2^E × VE) with the straightforward subset connectivity scan; O(V) extra space. Restricted to at most 22 edges for this teaching baseline.

371.problem: Use Prim’s algorithm to compute the minimum spanning-tree weight of a connected undirected graph.
371.assumptions: The pinned graph is connected, has positive weights, and uses 0-based vertices. A spanning tree contains every vertex and exactly V − 1 edges. The code also handles zero or negative weights, and explicitly rejects disconnected input as an extension.

example.explanation: Keep 0–1 and 1–2, costing 5 + 2. All vertices remain connected. Keeping all three edges would create a cycle and cost more.

371.baseline: Choose every possible subset of V − 1 edges, test whether it connects all vertices, and take the smallest total. Connectivity plus V − 1 edges guarantees a tree. This direct definition is useful for tiny examples but has exponentially many subsets.
371.approach:
Keep a growing tree and a heap of edges that could attach another vertex. Heap entries store an edge’s weight, not a cumulative path distance.

Remove the cheapest entry. If its destination is already included, it is an obsolete candidate; skip it. Otherwise accept the vertex, add that edge weight, and offer all its edges to vertices still outside. Every accepted edge crosses from the current tree to a new vertex, so it cannot form a cycle.

The heap can contain several entries for one vertex. This is expected. The included array ensures that only the first valid removal pays for that vertex. Prim’s greedy choice is justified by the cut property: a cheapest edge across the current included/outside split belongs to some MST.
steps: Start vertex 0 with a dummy connection of cost 0.
Remove the cheapest candidate edge; ignore it if its destination is already in the tree.
Accept the new vertex and add that edge’s weight to the total.
Offer its edges to vertices still outside the tree.
Finish after accepting all vertices.
371.time: O(V + E log(E + 2)) with the lazy edge heap; O(E log V) for a connected simple graph.
371.space: O(V + E) for adjacency, the heap, and inclusion flags.
pitfalls: An MST minimizes total chosen edge weight, not all source-to-vertex distances.
Accept a vertex when its cheapest valid entry is removed, not when first inserted.
The starting vertex can change which tied MST is chosen, but not its weight.
A disconnected graph has a spanning forest, not one spanning tree.
The initial zero-cost heap entry is not a real tree edge.

reference.approach: Prim grows one tree using the cheapest crossing edge; Kruskal joins components in sorted edge order.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked, along with the practice page’s Java signature. The article uses an edge list; the judge uses List<List<List<Integer>>> adjacency, so both entry points are included. Totals use long internally, and disconnected input is rejected rather than returning a partial tree.

rows: Only vertex 0 is included after removing the dummy entry. Candidate connections are 0–1 at cost 5 and 0–2 at cost 6.
Take the edge of weight 5. Vertex 1 offers a cheaper connection to vertex 2 with weight 2.
Take weight 2, so the total is 7. The old weight-6 entry is unnecessary. The heap key is 2 here, not the path distance 5 + 2.

372.problem: Maintain disjoint groups of nodes. Merge two groups and quickly tell whether two nodes belong to the same group.
372.assumptions: Nodes are 1 through n, matching Striver’s foundation lesson. Index 0 is unused. Groups only merge; this structure does not remove connections. The boolean union result is an addition: true means two previously separate groups were joined. The linked practice judge differs: it uses 0-based nodes and calls both union methods on one object. Use the combined DisjointSet class in “Another approach” for that judge.

example.input: n = 6; merge(1,2), merge(3,4), merge(2,4); then ask connected(1,3), connected(1,6)
example.explanation: Nodes 1, 2, 3, and 4 are now one group. Nodes 5 and 6 remain separate. The exact representative chosen for the four-node group does not affect these answers.

372.baseline: Give every node a group label. To merge two groups, scan all nodes and replace one label with the other. Connectivity checks take O(1), but a merge takes O(n). The baseline below shows this simple method.
372.approach:
Represent each group as a parent tree. A root points to itself and stands for the whole group. findParent follows parent links to that root, then makes every visited node point directly to it. That shortcut is path compression.

To merge, find both roots first. If they match, nothing changes. Otherwise attach the lower-rank root below the higher-rank root. If their ranks tie, choose one root and increase its rank by one.

Rank is an upper bound used to keep trees shallow, not the number of nodes. After path compression, it need not equal the tree’s actual height. Do not decrease it or increment it after every merge.
steps: Initialize each node as its own parent. Start ranks at 0.
Find roots with path compression.
Do nothing if the roots already match.
Attach the lower-rank root to the higher-rank root; increment only on a tie.
Answer connectivity by comparing representatives.
372.time: O(n) initialization; O(α(n)) amortized per union or find with path compression and balancing. α grows so slowly that this is effectively constant for practical inputs.
372.space: O(n) for the two arrays, with at most O(log n) recursion depth before compression.
pitfalls: Compare roots, not immediate parents.
Repeatedly merging the same group must do nothing.
Rank is not component size and is not recomputed after compression.
This 1-based class is separate from the 0-based DSU used in graph solutions.
The article’s separate examples are 1-based. The practice judge is 0-based and can mix policies; its combined implementation below maintains both metadata arrays after every merge.
tests: RankDSU d=new RankDSU(6);assert d.unionByRank(1,2);assert d.unionByRank(3,4);assert d.unionByRank(2,4);assert d.find(1,3);assert !d.find(1,6);assert !d.unionByRank(1,4);assert !d.unionByRank(5,5);
RankDSU d=new RankDSU(100000);for(int i=2;i<=100000;i++)assert d.unionByRank(i-1,i);for(int i=1;i<=100000;i++)assert d.find(1,i);

373.problem: Maintain disjoint groups of nodes. Merge two groups and quickly tell whether two nodes belong to the same group. Also report a group’s size.
373.assumptions: Nodes are 1 through n, matching Striver’s foundation lesson. Index 0 is unused. Groups only merge; this structure does not remove connections. The boolean union result is an addition: true means two previously separate groups were joined. The linked practice judge differs: it uses 0-based nodes and calls both union methods on one object. Use the combined DisjointSet class in “Another approach” for that judge.

example.input: n = 6; merge(1,2), merge(3,4), merge(2,4); then ask connected(1,3), connected(1,6)
example.explanation: Nodes 1, 2, 3, and 4 are now one group. Nodes 5 and 6 remain separate. The exact representative chosen for the four-node group does not affect these answers.

373.baseline: Give every node a group label. To merge two groups, scan all nodes and replace one label with the other. Connectivity checks take O(1), but a merge takes O(n). The baseline below shows this simple method.
373.approach:
Keep a parent tree for each group, with the node count stored at its root. findParent compresses the path to the root so later lookups are shorter.

To merge, compare the sizes of the two roots. Attach the smaller group’s root below the larger group’s root, then add their sizes at the surviving root. If both nodes already share a root, return without adding anything.

A size entry on a non-root may be out of date. Always ask size[findParent(node)], not size[node]. Union by size and union by rank are alternative policies; this class uses size throughout.
steps: Initialize each node as its own parent. Start sizes at 1.
Find roots with path compression.
Do nothing if the roots already match.
Attach the smaller group to the larger group and add the sizes.
Answer connectivity by comparing representatives.
373.time: O(n) initialization; O(α(n)) amortized per union or find with path compression and balancing. α grows so slowly that this is effectively constant for practical inputs.
373.space: O(n) for the two arrays, with at most O(log n) recursion depth before compression.
pitfalls: Compare roots, not immediate parents.
Repeatedly merging the same group must do nothing.
Only the root’s size is authoritative; query through findParent.
This 1-based class is separate from the 0-based DSU used in graph solutions.
The article’s separate examples are 1-based. The practice judge is 0-based and can mix policies; its combined implementation below maintains both metadata arrays after every merge.

374.problem: Use Kruskal’s algorithm to find the minimum total weight needed to connect every vertex without cycles.
374.assumptions: The pinned graph is connected, undirected, and 0-based. Its adjacency list stores each edge at both endpoints. The edge-list helper uses long totals and also handles negative weights; disconnected input is rejected explicitly.

example.explanation: Accept weights 1 and 2. Skip weight 3 because its endpoints are already connected. Accept weight 4 to attach vertex 3. The tree costs 1 + 2 + 4.

374.baseline: Enumerate subsets of V − 1 edges and test connectivity, as in the MST introduction. That works only for tiny graphs. The complete baseline below is useful for checking small examples.
374.approach:
Sort the edges from cheapest to most expensive. Start with each vertex in its own component. For each edge, ask the DSU whether its endpoints are already connected. If yes, adding it would create a cycle, so skip it. Otherwise join the components and add its weight.

Unlike Prim, Kruskal may build several small trees before joining them. Every accepted edge joins two components, reducing their number by one. Starting from V components, exactly V − 1 successful joins produce one spanning tree.

The cheap-edge choice is safe by the cut property: for the current components, a cheapest edge that connects two different components can belong to some MST. Equal weights may lead to different trees with the same total.
steps: Copy and sort the edge list by weight.
Create a DSU with one component per vertex.
Skip edges whose endpoint roots already match.
Union different components and add that edge’s weight.
Stop after V − 1 accepted edges.
374.time: O(V + E log E + Eα(V)) time; sorting dominates for a connected graph.
374.space: O(V + E) for DSU arrays and the copied edge references.
pitfalls: Do not simply take the first V − 1 sorted edges: some may form a cycle.
An undirected adjacency list stores each edge twice; the wrapper keeps u < v once.
Use Integer.compare or comparingInt, not weight subtraction that may overflow.
The source sorts its edge array in place. This adaptation sorts a shallow copy and never changes the edge rows.
A disconnected graph cannot reach V − 1 successful joins.
tests: assert kruskalWeight(3,new int[][]{{0,1,Integer.MAX_VALUE},{1,2,Integer.MAX_VALUE}})==2L*Integer.MAX_VALUE;assert kruskalWeight(1,new int[0][])==0;assert kruskalWeight(3,new int[][]{{0,0,-99},{0,1,8},{0,1,2},{1,2,3}})==5;boolean rejected=false;try{kruskalWeight(3,new int[][]{{0,1,1}});}catch(IllegalArgumentException e){rejected=true;}assert rejected;

reference.title: Find the MST Weight — Kruskal’s Algorithm
reference.approach: Sort edges and join different DSU components using path compression and union by size.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Kruskal Java was checked, and the practice Java template was inspected. The adaptation preserves caller edge order, uses long totals, rejects disconnected input, and includes the practice adjacency-list wrapper.

374.baselineTime: O(2^E × VE) time and O(V) extra space, restricted to at most 22 edges.

375.problem: Move existing network cables so all n computers become connected, using as few cable moves as possible. Return −1 if there are not enough cables.
375.assumptions: Computers are 0-based. Each undirected connection is a cable that can be removed and reattached between any two computers. One move relocates one cable; it does not create a new cable. The LeetCode entry point is makeConnected.

example.explanation: Computers 0–3 form one component and computer 4 is isolated. The triangle has a spare cable; move it to connect computer 4.

375.baseline: Build adjacency and count components by BFS or DFS. If there are at least n − 1 cables, the answer is components − 1. This traversal approach is already linear and is often the simplest for a fixed graph.
375.approach:
If there are C components, joining all of them needs at least C − 1 new connections between components. DSU counts C while reading the cables: begin with n components, and subtract one for each successful union.

Why is the total cable count enough to decide whether moves are possible? Keeping a spanning tree inside each component uses n − C cables. The remaining m − (n − C) cables are spare. We need at least C − 1 spares, which simplifies to m >= n − 1.

So first reject too few cables. Then count successful unions and return components − 1. This is the same spare-edge reasoning used in Striver’s public hint, with the algebra simplified.
steps: Return −1 if fewer than n − 1 cables exist.
Start with n separate DSU components.
Union each cable’s endpoints; decrement the component count only when a union succeeds.
Return components − 1.
375.time: O(n + mα(n)) time, including DSU initialization.
pitfalls: Count isolated computers as components.
A failed union identifies a spare cable; it must not decrement the component count.
You need components − 1 moves, not one move per isolated computer.
The early cable-count test is necessary; DSU alone cannot manufacture missing cables.
tests: assert makeConnected(5,new int[][]{{0,1},{1,2},{2,0},{2,3}})==1;assert makeConnectedByTraversal(5,new int[][]{{0,1},{1,2},{2,0},{2,3}})==1;assert makeConnected(4,new int[][]{{0,1}})==-1;assert makeConnected(1,new int[0][])==0;
int n=100000;int[][]edges=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)edges[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i};assert makeConnected(n,edges)==0;assert makeConnectedByTraversal(n,edges)==0;

reference.title: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected
reference.approach: Count DSU components and compare available spare edges with components − 1.
reference.adaptation: The public statement and Union-Find hint were checked. The solution tab requires sign-in, so no claim is made about its Java. This Java uses the fully checked DSU pattern from Striver’s public DSU/MST lessons and simplifies the spare-edge inequality to m >= n − 1.

375.baselineTime: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) space. The DSU alternative saves adjacency storage; it is not an asymptotic speed improvement here.

376.problem: Remove as many stones as possible. A stone may be removed only if another remaining stone shares its row or its column.
376.assumptions: Coordinates are distinct and nonnegative, bounded as in the pinned problem. Connections may pass through chains of shared rows and columns; diagonal proximity alone does not connect stones.

example.explanation: The first three stones form a chain. Remove [0,0], then [0,2], leaving [3,2]. The isolated stone [8,8] must stay.

376.baseline: Treat each stone as a graph vertex. To find its neighbors, scan all other stones for a matching row or column. A stack traversal counts components in O(N²) time; the answer is N minus that count.
376.approach:
One stone must remain in each connected component: its final stone has no partner to justify removal. You can remove all the others. To see why, take any spanning tree of the component and repeatedly remove a leaf; its parent still remains. Thus a component with k stones permits k − 1 removals.

To count components efficiently, make rows and columns the DSU nodes. A stone joins its row node to its column node. Row 2 and column 2 are different things, so shift every column ID by maxRow + 1. Chains of stones now join the corresponding coordinate nodes.

Count components only among coordinates that actually occur. Unused rows or columns represent no stones and must not be subtracted from the answer.
steps: Find the row and column ranges; place column IDs after all row IDs.
Union each stone’s row ID with its shifted column ID.
Record all used coordinate IDs.
Count distinct roots among those used IDs.
Return number of stones minus the root count.
376.time: O(R + C + Nα(R + C)), where R = maxRow + 1 and C = maxCol + 1.
376.space: O(R + C + N) for DSU arrays and used/root sets; the sets contain at most R + C distinct IDs.
pitfalls: Keep row and column ID ranges separate.
Do not count unused coordinate nodes as stone components.
The DSU component size counts coordinate nodes, not stones; it cannot directly give the answer.
Connected does not mean every pair directly shares a row or column.
For huge sparse coordinates, compress coordinate IDs rather than allocate through the largest coordinate. This source-aligned version uses the pinned coordinate bounds.
tests: int[][]s={{0,0},{0,2},{3,2},{8,8}};assert removeStones(s)==2;assert removeStonesByTraversal(s)==2;assert removeStones(new int[][]{{0,1},{1,0}})==0;assert removeStones(new int[0][])==0;
assert removeStones(new int[][]{{10000,10000},{10000,0},{0,0}})==2;int[][]stones=new int[1000][2];for(int i=0;i<1000;i++)stones[i]=new int[]{5000,i};assert removeStones(stones)==999;

reference.title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column Using DSU
reference.approach: Count stone components by traversal or by joining separate row and column DSU nodes.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked. The guide keeps the source’s coordinate-offset method, explains why exactly one stone remains per component, and uses distinct roots among used coordinates. Its tests also enumerate legal removal orders.

377.problem: Merge account records that share an email address, including connections through other records. Return each merged name followed by its unique emails in sorted order.
377.assumptions: Every account has a name and at least one email. Records belonging to one person have the same name, but different people may share a name. The order of merged accounts does not matter. Email matching is exact; do not lowercase or otherwise rewrite addresses.

example.explanation: The first and third records share b@x. The second record stays separate even though its name is also Riya.

377.baseline: Compare every pair of accounts for a shared email, then traverse the resulting components. This is easy to understand but repeatedly checks many pairs that share nothing.
377.approach:
An email identifies a connection; a name does not. Map each email to the first account index where it appears. When the same email appears in another account, union those two account indices. A chain of shared emails is then handled automatically by DSU.

Do all unions before collecting the result. For each unique email in the map, find the final root of its recorded account and put the email in that root’s bucket. Sort each bucket and prepend the root account’s name.

The email map has one entry per distinct email, so repeated email strings do not create duplicates in the result. Choosing a different account as the root does not change the merged emails.
steps: Create a DSU over account indices and an email-to-account map.
For each email, remember its first account or union with the account already recorded.
After every union is complete, group unique emails by final account root.
Sort each group’s emails and prepend the corresponding name.
377.time: O(A + Tα(A) + U log U) expected time with bounded-length strings: A accounts, T email occurrences, U unique emails. Sorting across all groups is at most O(U log U).
377.space: O(A + U) extra storage, plus the output.
pitfalls: Equal names alone never justify a merge.
Merge transitively: A sharing with B and B with C puts all three together.
Collect buckets after the unions; representatives can change during merging.
Return each email once, and sort emails within every account.
Do not merge by names or normalize email text beyond the problem’s exact-match rule.

reference.title: Accounts Merge
reference.approach: Join account components through shared email addresses, then sort unique emails by final root.
reference.adaptation: The public statement and grouping hint were checked. The solution tab requires sign-in, so its Java was not inspectable. This implementation applies the checked public DSU pattern to the specified account/email contract; the traversal baseline is an authored comparison.

377.baselineTime: O(A²L + T log U) expected time for at most L emails per account and bounded string length; O(A + T) space.

378.problem: Start with an all-water grid. After each operation turns one cell into land, report the number of four-directional islands.
378.assumptions: rows and cols may differ. Every operation is within the grid. Repeating an already-land cell changes nothing, but still produces an answer. The code uses the pinned LeetCode method name numIslands2.

example.explanation: The first two cells are separate islands. Adding the middle cell joins them. Repeating it leaves the count at one, and the final cell attaches to that island.

378.baseline: After each update, scan the whole grid and count islands with BFS. This correctly handles every case, but repeats O(rows × cols) work for each operation.
378.approach:
Make a DSU node for every grid position, but keep a separate land array: water nodes are not islands yet. Map (row, col) to row × cols + col.

When a new land cell appears, first count it as one new island. Check its four neighbors. Each successful union with a land neighbor joins two previously separate islands, so subtract one. A failed union means the neighbor already belongs to the same island; subtracting again would be wrong.

If the cell was already land, append the existing count immediately. Do not increase it or repeat the unions. Only additions are supported; removing land could split a component and requires a different approach.
steps: Allocate DSU and land flags for rows × cols cells.
For an already-land update, append the unchanged count.
Otherwise activate the cell and increment the island count.
Union it with each valid land neighbor; decrement only for a successful union.
Append the current count after every operation.
378.time: O(RC + Kα(RC)) time, including initialization; each of K updates checks at most four neighbors.
378.space: O(RC) for DSU and land flags, plus O(K) output.
pitfalls: Use row × cols + col, not row × rows + col on a rectangular grid.
Water has a DSU slot but is not an active island.
Repeated land additions must leave the count unchanged.
Subtract once per successful component merge, not once per adjacent land cell.
A new cell may touch the same island from several sides.

reference.title: Number of Islands II
reference.approach: Activate land cells and use DSU to merge only distinct adjacent land components.
reference.adaptation: The public statement, repeated-cell example, constraints, and neighbor-union hint were checked. The older public tutorial URL now returns Page Not Found; the practice solution is not claimed as inspected. This Java applies the checked DSU pattern and uses the linked LeetCode entry point.

378.baselineTime: O(KRC) time and O(RC + K) space including the answer.

379.problem: Find the largest four-directional island you can obtain by changing at most one water cell into land.
379.assumptions: The grid is a nonempty n × n binary matrix. Diagonals do not connect. An all-land grid returns n²; an all-water grid returns 1. The primary DSU method leaves the grid unchanged.

example.explanation: The top-left island has area 3. Flipping a cell beside it gives area 4. Flipping the middle cell touches that same island from two sides, but its area must be added only once.

379.baseline: Try every zero: temporarily change it to one, count island areas, then restore it. Also consider the unchanged grid. This costs O(n⁴), but provides a direct way to check tiny grids.
379.approach:
First group the existing land into islands with DSU. The size at each land root is that island’s area. Water nodes are left unused.

Now examine each zero independently. If we flip it, its new island contains that cell plus the distinct islands touching its four sides. Put those neighboring roots in a set, then add each root’s size once. Without the set, a U-shaped island touching several sides would be counted repeatedly.

Do not actually union the zero during these trials. Each trial assumes this is the only flipped cell. Keep the largest candidate. If there is no zero, return n².
steps: Union adjacent land cells using id = row × n + col.
For each zero, collect the distinct roots of adjacent land cells.
Its candidate area is 1 plus those components’ sizes.
Take the maximum candidate, or n² when the grid is already all land.
379.space: O(n²) for DSU; each temporary root set contains at most four entries.
pitfalls: Deduplicate neighboring roots before adding areas.
Count only land neighbors; water DSU slots also start with size 1 but are not islands.
Do not permanently merge a trial zero: later trials must be independent.
Handle all-land and all-water grids.
The labeling alternative below changes grid values into island IDs; pass a copy if you need the binary grid afterward.
tests: int[][]a={{1,1,0},{1,0,0},{0,0,1}};assert largestIsland(a)==4;assert largestIslandByTrials(a)==4;assert largestIslandByLabels(copyGrid(a))==4;assert largestIsland(new int[][]{{1,1,1},{1,0,1},{1,1,1}})==9;assert largestIsland(new int[][]{{0}})==1;assert largestIsland(new int[][]{{1}})==1;

reference.title: Making a Large Island
reference.approach: Try each flip directly, label existing islands, or join land cells with DSU and combine distinct neighboring components.
reference.adaptation: All three complete public Java methods were checked. DSU is primary to match this sheet section. The source’s recursive flood fills are adapted to queues so a large connected grid does not exhaust Java’s call stack. The labeling method retains its documented input mutation.

379.baselineTime: O(n⁴) time and O(n²) extra space.

better.explanation: Label each existing island with an ID starting at 2 and store its area. A queue flood fill replaces the source’s recursive traversal. For each zero, collect distinct neighboring IDs and add their areas plus one. This is O(n²), and it changes the grid to hold IDs. It answers the same one-flip question without DSU.
better.space: O(n²) for the queue and area map; the grid itself stores labels.

380.problem: Find the earliest water level at which you can move from the top-left to the bottom-right cell through four-directional neighbors.
380.assumptions: The pinned n × n grid contains every distinct elevation from 0 through n² − 1. At time t, only cells of elevation at most t can be used. Movement takes no time; the answer is the largest elevation needed along the best route.

example.explanation: At water level 1, the start and destination are both available but disconnected. Level 2 opens the top-right cell, giving the route 0→2→1.

380.baseline: Try water levels 0, 1, 2, … and run BFS using only cells at or below that level. The first successful level is the answer. This is a direct simulation but repeatedly scans the grid.
380.approach:
Imagine the water rising one level at a time. When a cell becomes available, it forms a new flooded component. Join it to every already-available neighbor. As soon as the start and destination belong to the same component, there is a usable route between them.

Because the elevations are distinct and cover 0 through n² − 1, an array can tell us which cell opens at each time. No sorting is needed. Keep an active flag because a DSU slot for a cell exists even before the water reaches it.

This solves a minimum-maximum path problem: we minimize the highest cell on the route. We do not add elevations or count steps.
steps: Build positionAtHeight so each water level identifies the newly available cell.
Activate that cell and union it with its active four-directional neighbors.
Check that both endpoints are active and share a root.
Return the first level for which they are connected.
380.time: O(n²α(n²)) time under the pinned distinct 0…n²−1 elevation constraint.
380.space: O(n²) for positions, active flags, and DSU arrays.
pitfalls: Include the start cell’s elevation in the required water level.
Having both endpoints underwater is not enough; they must be connected.
The route cost is its maximum elevation, not a sum or a difference between adjacent heights.
Only active cells may be unioned.
The direct position array relies on the pinned elevation permutation. For arbitrary elevations, sort cells by height or use the heap alternative.
tests: assert swimInWater(new int[][]{{0,2},{3,1}})==2;assert swimByHeap(new int[][]{{0,2},{3,1}})==2;assert swimByLevels(new int[][]{{0,2},{3,1}})==2;assert swimInWater(new int[][]{{3,0},{2,1}})==3;assert swimInWater(new int[][]{{0}})==0;
assert swimByHeap(new int[][]{{0,Integer.MAX_VALUE},{Integer.MAX_VALUE,0}})==Integer.MAX_VALUE;assert swimByHeap(new int[][]{{7}})==7;assert swimByHeap(new int[][]{{3,3},{3,3}})==3;

reference.title: Swim in Rising Water
reference.approach: Activate cells in elevation order and detect endpoint connectivity; alternatively minimize the largest elevation along a path.
reference.adaptation: The public problem statement and its distinct-elevation constraints were checked. The solution requires sign-in and the older tutorial URL returns Page Not Found. These are authored, tested implementations using the checked public DSU and minimax-path patterns, not a claim that unavailable source Java was inspected.

380.baselineTime: O(n⁴) time and O(n²) space. Binary search over levels reduces the repeated-search time to O(n² log(n²)).

better.explanation: A heap can also track the least water level needed to reach each cell. Moving to a neighbor changes the route cost to max(current level, neighbor height). Start with grid[0][0], and return when the destination’s current entry is removed. This works for arbitrary nonnegative elevations too; it does not need the permutation constraint used by the DSU position array.
better.space: O(n²) for best levels and the heap.

381.problem: Find every undirected edge whose removal increases the number of connected components.
381.assumptions: Vertices are 0-based. The linked LeetCode problem starts connected, but these methods also handle disconnected graphs. Parallel edge occurrences have separate IDs. Results use smaller endpoint first and are sorted for easy comparison.

example.explanation: The first three edges form a cycle, so each has an alternate route. Edge 2–3 is the only connection to vertex 3.

381.baseline: Remove one exact edge occurrence, count the components, and compare with the original count. If the count increases, that edge is a bridge. This is a direct check but repeats a traversal for every edge.
381.approach:
DFS gives each vertex a discovery number. low[u] records the earliest discovery number reachable from u’s DFS subtree by tree edges followed by at most one non-parent back edge. Think of it as the earliest place that subtree can get back to without using its parent edge.

After finishing a child v of u, check low[v] > discovery[u]. If true, the child subtree cannot get back to u or anything earlier, so u–v is its only connection: a bridge. Equality means there is an alternate way back to u, so the edge is not a bridge.

The code uses explicit DFS frames. A frame remembers which neighbor to process next; when it finishes, it passes low information back to its parent. Each undirected edge has an ID so only the actual incoming edge is skipped, not a parallel edge.
steps: Build adjacency entries containing both neighbor and edge ID.
Assign discovery and low values on first entering a vertex.
For a visited non-parent neighbor, lower low[u] using that neighbor’s discovery time.
After a child finishes, use its low value to update the parent and test the bridge condition.
Start another DFS for any unvisited component, then normalize and sort the result.
381.time: O(V + E + B log B), where B is the number of returned bridges. The DFS is linear; sorting the output adds B log B.
381.space: O(V + E) for adjacency, arrays, explicit DFS frames, and results.
pitfalls: Use > for bridges; >= would incorrectly reject an alternate path back to the parent.
For an already discovered neighbor, use its discovery time, not its low value.
Skip the exact parent edge ID so parallel edges remain visible.
Update the parent only after the child frame finishes.
The source’s O(V + E) statement describes traversal; its sorted result also incurs sorting work.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)e[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i};List<List<Integer>>b=findBridges(n,e);assert b.size()==n-1;assert b.get(0).equals(List.of(0,1));assert b.get(n-2).equals(List.of(n-2,n-1));

reference.title: Bridges in a Graph Using Tarjan’s Algorithm
reference.approach: Edge-removal baseline and iterative low-link DFS with parent edge IDs.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods were checked, including the iterative DFS return handling. The guide retains edge IDs and normalized sorting, accounts for sorting cost, adds the LeetCode entry point, and extends the baseline to compare component counts on disconnected graphs.

381.baselineTime: O((E + 1)(V + E) + B log B) time and O(V + E) space.

382.problem: Find vertices whose deletion, together with their incident edges, increases the number of connected components. Return their indices in ascending order, or [-1] if none exist.
382.assumptions: The undirected graph may already be disconnected and may contain self-loops or parallel edges. Vertices are 0-based. The primary helper accepts the article’s edge list; the overloaded ArrayList adjacency entry point matches the pinned Java template.

example.explanation: Removing 2 separates the triangle from the chain. Removing 3 isolates vertex 4. Removing 4 itself does not split any remaining vertices.

382.baseline: Count the original components. Then exclude each candidate vertex and count again. A larger count means it is an articulation point. Comparing with the original count is necessary when the graph starts disconnected.
382.approach:
Use DFS discovery times and low values, as in bridge detection. For a non-root vertex u, inspect each DFS child v after its subtree finishes. If low[v] >= discovery[u], that subtree cannot reach an ancestor of u without using u. Deleting u separates it, so u is an articulation point.

The equality case counts here. A back edge reaching u saves a parent edge from being a bridge, but it cannot save the graph when u itself is deleted.

A DFS root has no parent side, so it needs a separate rule: it is an articulation point only when it has more than one DFS child. Count DFS children, not all neighbors. Two neighbors inside the same DFS subtree do not make the root an articulation point.
steps: Build neighbor/edge-ID adjacency and start DFS in every component.
On discovering a child, increment the frame’s DFS-child count.
On returning from a child, propagate its low value.
Mark a non-root parent when child low >= parent discovery.
Mark a root only when it has at least two DFS children.
Collect marked vertices in ascending index order.
382.time: O(V + E) time. Scanning the marker array gives sorted output without sorting.
382.space: O(V + E) for adjacency, explicit DFS frames, arrays, and output.
pitfalls: For a non-root articulation point use >=; bridge detection uses >.
The root rule counts DFS children, not degree.
An isolated vertex is not an articulation point: removing it decreases the component count.
Start DFS in every component and reset the child count for every root.
Skip only the incoming edge ID; a parallel edge is a separate back connection.
tests: int n=100000;int[][]e=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)e[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i};List<Integer>a=articulationPoints(n,e);assert a.size()==n-2;assert a.get(0)==1;assert a.get(a.size()-1)==n-2;

reference.title: Articulation Points in a Graph Using Tarjan’s Algorithm
reference.approach: Vertex-removal baseline and iterative low-link DFS with a separate root-child rule.
reference.adaptation: Both complete public Java methods and the practice Java signature were checked. Named frame fields replace the source’s numeric frame slots for readability. The adjacency wrapper matches the pinned ArrayList interface and ignores self-loops, which cannot affect articulation status.

382.baselineTime: O(V(V + E)) time and O(V + E) space.

383.problem: Count the strongly connected components of a directed graph: maximal groups in which every vertex can reach every other vertex.
383.assumptions: Vertices are 0-based. Follow edge directions. A single isolated vertex is an SCC. The practice Java entry point accepts ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adjacency; an edge-list overload matches the public article.

example.explanation: The groups are {0,1}, {2,3}, and {4}. A route from the first group into the second does not merge them because there is no route back.

383.baseline: Run a reachability search from every vertex. Two vertices belong to the same SCC exactly when each can reach the other. Group by that relation. This is straightforward but stores O(V²) reachability and repeats many searches.
383.approach:
Kosaraju uses two passes. First, run DFS on the original graph and record a vertex only after all its outgoing DFS work finishes. This is finish order, not discovery order.

Think of each SCC as one box. Edges between boxes cannot form a cycle, or those boxes would be one SCC. Reverse finish order starts with a source box among the remaining boxes. Now reverse all edges. That box has no outgoing edge to another unvisited box, so a traversal from it stays inside exactly one SCC.

Process vertices in reverse finish order on this reversed graph. Each new traversal counts one component. Reset visited between passes. The first pass needs true DFS finishing behavior; the second pass only needs to mark reachable vertices.
steps: Build the graph and its transpose by reversing every directed edge.
Run DFS across all components and append each vertex when its frame finishes.
Clear visited.
Scan finish order backward; traverse the transpose from each unvisited vertex.
Count one SCC per new second-pass traversal.
383.time: O(V + E) time for graph construction and both passes.
383.space: O(V + E) for the transpose, traversal stacks, visited array, and finish order.
pitfalls: One-way reachability is not strong connectivity.
Append a vertex when DFS finishes it, not when it is first pushed.
Use reverse finish order for the second pass.
Reset visited and traverse the transpose in the second pass.
BFS does not supply the first pass’s DFS finishing order. It can replace the second pass’s marking traversal.
tests: int[][]e={{0,1},{1,0},{1,2},{2,3},{3,2},{3,4}};assert kosaraju(5,e)==3;assert sccByReachability(5,e)==3;assert kosaraju(4,new int[0][])==4;assert kosaraju(3,new int[][]{{0,1},{1,2}})==3;assert kosaraju(1,new int[][]{{0,0}})==1;

int n=100000;int[][]chain=new int[n-1][2];for(int i=1;i<n;i++)chain[i-1]=new int[]{i-1,i};assert kosaraju(n,chain)==n;int[][]cycle=Arrays.copyOf(chain,n);cycle[n-1]=new int[]{n-1,0};assert kosaraju(n,cycle)==1;

reference.title: Kosaraju’s Algorithm for Strongly Connected Components
reference.approach: Iterative DFS finish order followed by traversal of the transpose in reverse finish order.
reference.adaptation: The complete public Java method and the practice Java adjacency signature were checked. Named frames make finish-time behavior explicit. Both the article’s edge-list interface and the pinned adjacency interface are included; the repeated-reachability baseline is an authored comparison.
